A recent tissue culture was positive for Stenotrophomonas maltophilia, Mucor, and Candida parapsilosis, and her antibiotic regimen consists of 100 mg minocycline twice daily, 1 g imipenem/cilastin intravenous every 8 h, 5 mg/kg IV amphotericin B every 24 h as tolerated, and oral 125 mg vancomycin four times daily.
Her prognosis remained guarded, with differential diagnoses including idiopathic subcutaneous thrombotic vasculopathy, non-uremic calciphylaxis sin calcifications, or an autoimmune response to her COVID vaccination. She reported depression, and high levels of pain despite a rigorous pain control regimen. She chose not to see the lesions on her bilateral lowerextremities since November as she believed it would worsen her mental health. Although it was difficult at times to havehope, she and her family continued to search for answers and have aggressive treatment goals. She wanted to share her story with the medical field in hope other providers would be able to provide insight to help her, and future patients with similar afflictions. In early February, the patient was transitioned to comfort care and passed away surrounded by her family.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 32-year-old female presented with tender erythematous lower extremity nodules appearing 4 weeks after her second Moderna COVID-19 vaccination that progressed to extensive, intractably painful necrotic leg and bilateral flank ulcers.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Four weeks after her second mRNA-1273 (Moderna) COVID-19 vaccine, the patient developed tender erythematous lower limb nodules and retiform purpura initially treated with oral prednisone (50 mg/day) and colchicine (0.6 mg BID) for presumed cutaneous polyarteritis nodosa. Her lesions rapidly progressed into deep adipose-eroding necrotic ulcers across both legs and flanks requiring repeated surgical debridements, ICU sedation for severe pain, and multiple antimicrobial, anticoagulant, and immunomodulatory regimens.
subjective.past_medical_history: Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, psoriasis, 3 possible first-trimester pregnancy losses, and chronic diarrhea; no family history of similar vascular/ulcerative disease.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for severe intractable leg/flank ulcer pain, 'gravel-like' subcutaneous sensation, depression, and antibiotic-associated C. difficile diarrhea.

objective.physical_examination: Initial tender erythematous subcutaneous nodules and ulcerating retiform purpura on bilateral lower extremities that progressed to deep, extensive, full-thickness necrotic ulcers eroding into subcutaneous adipose tissue across both legs and bilateral flanks.
objective.routine_investigations: Heterozygous prothrombin G20210A mutation; negative SS-A, SS-B, Jo-1, RF, anti-CCP, ANA, DNase B, anti-TG2, PR3/MPO-ANCA, SPEP/immunofixation, C3c/C4c, tuberculosis testing, HBV, HCV, HIV, Lyme serology, cold agglutinins, JAK2, PNH flow cytometry, antithrombin III, Factor V Leiden, PF4 antibodies, antiphospholipid panel, and protein C/S levels. Wound cultures sequentially isolated ESBL-producing E. coli, Klebsiella, Stenotrophomonas maltophilia, Mucor, and Candida parapsilosis; stool testing confirmed Clostridioides difficile infection.
objective.advanced_workup: Colonoscopy was negative for inflammatory bowel disease; chest/abdomen/pelvis MR angiography was negative for medium/large-vessel vasculitis; lower extremity vascular studies were normal. Re-review of the initial punch biopsy, repeat leg punch biopsy, and deep flank incisional biopsy all demonstrated subcuticular fat necrosis and diffuse small-vessel fibrin thrombosis with rare microvascular calcification and negative direct immunofluorescence (no IgG, IgA, IgM, or C3 deposits), diagnostic of subcutaneous thrombotic vasculopathy / non-uremic calciphylaxis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Cutaneous tuberculosis, systemic vasculitis, and antiphospholipid syndrome were excluded, and serial deep skin biopsies confirmed severe refractory subcutaneous thrombotic vasculopathy / non-uremic calciphylaxis temporally following COVID-19 vaccination in a patient with a prothrombin G20210A mutation. Despite multiple surgical debridements, anticoagulation (warfarin, apixaban, heparin, high-dose enoxaparin complicated by spontaneous retroperitoneal hemorrhage, and argatroban), antiplatelet/rheologic agents (aspirin, dipyridamole, pentoxifylline), corticosteroids, IVIG, 7 sessions of plasmapheresis, intravenous sodium thiosulfate (25 g 5×/week), and targeted antimicrobials (ertapenem, ampicillin-sulbactam, imipenem, minocycline, oral vancomycin, fluconazole, micafungin, amphotericin B), her necrotic wounds progressed and she transitioned to comfort care and died in early February 2022.

raw_case_text: The patient was a 67-year-old man who had been on HD for 39 years due to chronic renal failure. About 3 months earlier, he had noticed discomfort in the tongue and was referred by a dialysis doctor for examination. His medical history other than chronic renal failure (at 27 years old) included right nephrectomy for renal cell carcinoma (at 47 years old), left nephrectomy for renal cell carcinoma (at 50 years old), parathyroidectomy (at 51 years old), surgery for lumbar spinal stenosis (at 56 years old), surgery for destructive spondyloarthropathy (at 59 years old), right-side colon resection for ileus due to intestinal tuberculosis (at 63 years old), surgical decompression of carpal tunnel syndrome (at 66 years old), and ileal biopsy suggestive of amyloidosis (at 67 years old). Histopathological examination of the specimen from ileal biopsy showed amorphous eosinophilic deposits on the vessel wall (Figures 1(a) and 1(b)). Immumohistochemically, deposits were positive for beta2m (Figure 1(c)). Current medications included alfacalcidol, ursodeoxycholic acid, sevelamer hydrochloride, and lanthanum carbonate hydrate, and the serum beta2m level was 20.7 mg/L. In addition, the renal cell carcinomas and surgical decompression of carpal tunnel syndrome were not treated at the referring hospital and detailed data were not available. On oral examination, a collection of painless, relatively hard, rugged whitish-yellow papules was found on the ventral surface of the tongue tip (Figure 2). No movement disorder of the tongue was apparent. The patient showed no difficulty in eating or dysphagia. No abnormal findings were found in other sites of the oral cavity or regional lymph nodes. Biopsy was performed under local anesthesia. Histopathologically, the specimen showed amorphous eosinophilic extracellular deposits in the subepithelial region (Figure 3(a)). Extracellular deposits showed positive results from DFS staining, and also from potassium permanganate- (KMnO4-) DFS staining and beta2m staining (Figures 3(b)-3(d)). The pathological diagnosis was amyloidosis, strongly suggestive of DRA. At the 6-month follow-up, no significant change in systemic DRA was seen, including tongue symptoms.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 67-year-old man on maintenance hemodialysis for 39 years presented with a 3-month history of tongue tip discomfort and painless hard whitish-yellow sublingual papules.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Three months prior to dental/oral surgery referral by his dialysis physician, the patient noticed lingual discomfort and nodular papules on the ventral surface of his tongue tip without dysphagia or impaired tongue mobility.
subjective.past_medical_history: End-stage renal failure on maintenance hemodialysis for 39 years (since age 27); bilateral nephrectomies for renal cell carcinoma (right at age 47, left at age 50); parathyroidectomy (age 51); lumbar spinal stenosis surgery (age 56); destructive spondyloarthropathy surgery (age 59); right hemicolectomy for ileus secondary to intestinal tuberculosis (age 63); carpal tunnel decompression (age 66); and ileal biopsy confirming beta2-microglobulin amyloidosis (age 67).
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for mild tongue discomfort; negative for dysphagia, mastication difficulty, or lingual dysmotility. Home medications: alfacalcidol, ursodeoxycholic acid, sevelamer hydrochloride, and lanthanum carbonate hydrate.

objective.physical_examination: A cluster of painless, firm, rugged whitish-yellow papules on the ventral surface of the tongue tip with intact tongue motility and no regional cervical lymphadenopathy.
objective.routine_investigations: Elevated serum beta2-microglobulin (beta2m) level at 20.7 mg/L.
objective.advanced_workup: Prior ileal biopsy had shown vascular wall amorphous eosinophilic deposits positive for beta2-microglobulin. Excisional/incisional biopsy of the ventral tongue papules under local anesthesia demonstrated subepithelial extracellular amorphous eosinophilic deposits that stained positively with direct fast scarlet (DFS), potassium permanganate-pretreated DFS (KMnO4-DFS), and anti-beta2-microglobulin immunohistochemistry.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Lingual biopsy histopathology with DFS, KMnO4-DFS, and anti-beta2-microglobulin immunohistochemistry confirmed oral/lingual dialysis-related beta2-microglobulin amyloidosis (DRA) in a 39-year hemodialysis patient with prior resected intestinal tuberculosis. At 6-month follow-up, his lingual and systemic DRA remained clinically stable.

raw_case_text:
A 62-year-old woman was admitted to the neurology department of Tianjin Huanhu Hospital. The patient complained of paroxysmal falls accompanied by impaired consciousness for the last nine days and paroxysmal limb twitch accompanied by gibberish speech for four days. Initially, the patient experienced tonic-clonic seizures, accompanied by impaired consciousness. Later, the patient experienced tonic seizures with head turning to the right and retained consciousness similar to faciobrachial dystonic seizures (FBDS) (Supplementary Materials S1). These incidences occurred more than ten times in a day. The patient was first seen in another hospital, and a brain MRI was done. The MRI showed no abnormalities. The patient was started on sodium valproate, diazepam, and levetiracetam (drug doses unknown). Due to no clinical improvement, the patient was referred for further management. The patient had no previous history of hypertension, coronary heart disease, diabetes, cerebrovascular disease, mental illness, hepatitis, tuberculosis, and no family history of any hereditary disease.
On admission, the patient had a body temperature of 36.3 C, a heart rate of 91 beats/min, a respiratory rate of 20 breaths/min, and a blood pressure of 162/85 mmHg. The neurological assessment revealed that the patient had cognitive dysfunction (poor memory and poor calculation ability). However, other categories of the neurological examination, including cranial nerves, motor system, reflexes, sensation, coordination, movement, gait, and signs of meningeal irritation, were normal.
The serum testing of routine blood tests, coagulation profile, liver function and kidney function tests, blood sugars, lipid profile, and serological testing for hepatitis B, syphilis, and HIV were negative. In addition, the results of anti-nuclear antibodies, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, rheumatoid factors, thyroid-stimulating hormone receptor antibodies, anti-thyroglobulin antibodies, and serum tumor markers, including carcinoembryonic antigen, squamous cell carcinoma antigen, cytokeratin-19 fragment, carbohydrate antigen 199, carbohydrate antigen 125, and neuron-specific enolase were normal. The patient had abnormal serum chloride levels of 95mmol/L. Further, the serum AE-related antibodies determined with both tissue-based and cell-based indirect immunofluorescence (IIF) assay in V-Medical Laboratory (Guangzhou, China), including anti-N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor (NMDAR), anti-leucine-rich glioma-inactivated 1 (LGI1), anti-contactin-associated protein-like 2 (CASPR2), anti-gamma-aminobutyric-acid B receptor (GABABR), anti-dipeptidyl-peptidase-like protein-6 (DPPX), and anti-glutamic acid decarboxylase 65 (GAD65) and paraneoplastic neurological syndrome (PNS)-related antibodies including anti-Hu, anti-Ri, anti-Yo, anti-Ma2, anti-CV2, and anti-amphiphysin, was remarkable only for positive anti-LGI1 antibody with a titer of 1:16 (normal <1:10). The CSF showed slight leukocytosis of 10 x 106 / L with lymphocytic predominance. However, the pressure, color, turbidity, glucose levels, chloride levels, Gram staining, acid-fast staining, ink staining, metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS), AE-related antibodies which were also determined with both tissue-based and cell-based IIF assay in V-Medical Laboratory (Guangzhou, China), and PNS-related antibodies of the CSF were normal. The patient had a positive RPR with a serum titer of 1:16 and a positive TPPA. Subsequently, TPPA and RPR in CSF were tested, and both results were positive.
The electroencephalography (EEG)showed irregular slow waves with medium to high amplitudes in the right temporal lobe, which spread to the other lobes and showed sharp waves (Figure 1). The brain MRI showed increased signals on T2-weighted and FLAIR imaging in the medial temporal lobe (Figure 2A). The gadolinium-enhanced MRI of the brain showed mild to moderate cord enhancement in the right temporal lobe (Figure 2B). Syphilis can cause multiple system damage. Therefore, magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) was carried out to investigate vascular stenosis or vasculitis-like changes. However, the results revealed no abnormalities (Figure 2C). Moreover, CT of the chest, echocardiography, abdominal ultrasound, urinary tract ultrasound, electromyography, and nerve conduction velocities of the limbs were normal.
Therefore, uncertainty arose as to whether the patient had both anti-LGI1 encephalitis and NS or whether the LGI1 antibody and LE manifestations were due to the NS. The patient received intravenous penicillin sodium 3.5 million units every 4 h for 14 days to treat the NS. Furthermore, the patient was initiated on intravenous sodium valproate 400 mg two times daily and oral levetiracetam 500 mg two times daily. The drugs were then changed to oral sodium valproate 500 mg two times daily and oral levetiracetam 750 mg two times daily. Improvement was noted with no convulsions and normal cognitive function. Two months later, the serum TPPA was still positive. In addition, the serum RPR was still positive with a titer of 1:8, while the serum LGI1 antibody was positive with a titer of 1:10. Furthermore, a revaluation of the CSF showed that the CSF TPPA and RPR were positive. However, the other CSF tests remained negative. In addition, a repeat of the EEG showed no epileptiform wave emission (Figure 3). Moreover, a repeat of the brain MRI showed no abnormality (Figure 2D). A second course of intravenous penicillin G sodium 3.2 million units every 4 h for 14 days was started. After another four months, the serum TPPA was still positive, the serum RPR test was positive with a titer of 1:8, while the serum LGI1 antibody was negative. Changes in TPPA, RPR, and LGI1 antibodies during the syphilitic treatment are shown in Figure 4. A repeat of the EEG and brain MRI showed normal findings. The third course of intravenous penicillin G sodium 3.2 million units every four hours, was given for 14 days. In addition, oral doses of sodium valproate 500 mg two times daily and levetiracetam 750 mg two times daily were continued. The patient was then followed up for additional three months. The patient reported no further convulsive episodes. In addition, the memory and calculation ability were noted to be normal.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 62-year-old woman presented with a 9-day history of paroxysmal falls with impaired consciousness and a 4-day history of frequent (>10/day) faciobrachial dystonic-like limb twitches, head-turning, and gibberish speech.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Nine days prior to neurology admission, the patient developed generalized tonic-clonic seizures with loss of consciousness, followed 4 days prior by >10 daily episodes of right head version, limb twitching with preserved consciousness resembling faciobrachial dystonic seizures (FBDS), and incoherent speech refractory to outside valproate, diazepam, and levetiracetam.
subjective.past_medical_history: No history of hypertension, coronary artery disease, diabetes, stroke, psychiatric illness, hepatitis, tuberculosis, or hereditary diseases.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for frequent seizures, falls, gibberish speech, and memory/calculation decline.

objective.physical_examination: Temperature 36.3 °C, HR 91 bpm, RR 20 breaths/min, BP 162/85 mmHg. Neurological exam revealed cognitive dysfunction (impaired memory and calculation) and frequent (>10/day) tonic/faciobrachial dystonic-like seizures with rightward head version; cranial nerves, motor strength, reflexes, sensation, coordination, gait, and meningeal signs were otherwise normal.
objective.routine_investigations: Hypochloremia (serum chloride 95 mmol/L); normal CBC, coagulation, hepatorenal panel, glucose, lipids, ANA, ANCA, RF, thyroid antibodies, and tumor markers (CEA, SCCA, CYFRA 21-1, CA19-9, CA125, NSE); negative HBV and HIV serologies. Serum syphilis serology was positive (RPR 1:16, TPPA positive), and serum autoimmune encephalitis panel (tissue- and cell-based IIF) was positive for anti-LGI1 antibodies at a titer of 1:16 (normal <1:10; negative for NMDAR, CASPR2, GABABR, DPPX, GAD65, and paraneoplastic antibodies). EEG showed right temporal medium-to-high amplitude irregular slow waves and sharp waves; chest CT, TTE, abdominal/renal ultrasound, and limb EMG/NCV were normal.
objective.advanced_workup: Brain MRI demonstrated T2/FLAIR hyperintensity in the medial temporal lobe with mild-to-moderate right temporal cord-like gadolinium enhancement and normal MR angiography. Lumbar puncture CSF showed mild lymphocytic pleocytosis (WBC 10 × 10^6/L) with normal pressure, glucose, and chloride, negative Gram, acid-fast, and India ink stains, negative CSF mNGS, and negative CSF autoimmune/paraneoplastic antibodies, whereas both CSF TPPA and CSF RPR returned positive.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Tuberculous and viral/fungal meningoencephalitis were excluded by negative CSF acid-fast staining and mNGS, and positive serum and CSF TPPA/RPR alongside a 1:16 serum anti-LGI1 antibody titer and mesial temporal lobe MRI hyperintensity confirmed neurosyphilis presenting as anti-LGI1-antibody-positive limbic encephalitis with faciobrachial dystonic-like seizures. Without administering corticosteroids or immunotherapy, three 14-day courses of high-dose intravenous penicillin G sodium (3.5 then 3.2 million units q4h) plus oral sodium valproate (500 mg BID) and levetiracetam (750 mg BID) achieved complete seizure cessation, cognitive normalization, seronegative conversion of anti-LGI1 antibodies, and complete resolution of EEG and brain MRI abnormalities.

raw_case_text: A 37-year-old HIV-1 positive, antiretroviral therapy naive woman was admitted to the ICU with a history of a generalized maculopapular rash, joint pains, pyrexia, fatigue and delirium. She had been diagnosed with HIV-1 infection in 2006 and as per local guidelines at the time was never initiated on antiretroviral therapy as her CD4+ lymphocyte count had always been >500 cells/mul at regular clinic follow up. On examination, she appeared ill with a pyrexia of 39.1 C and a generalized maculopapular rash (Fig. 1). Her knee, elbow and ankle joints were markedly swollen. She was also found to have axillary and inguinal lymphadenopathy, a 4 cm splenomegaly but no hepatomegaly. Except for features in keeping with delirium, no other abnormal neurological signs were noted. On this admission she had a CD4+ cell count of 616 cells/mul, a HIV viral load of 102 000 copies/mL and her HTLV-1 serology also tested strongly positive. Except for a markedly raised serum calcium level of 4.48 mmol/L, the rest of her laboratory work-up including full blood count, electrolytes, renal and liver function test, blood and urine culture, autoimmune screen, serum protein electrophoresis, serum angiotensin converting enzyme (S-ACE), parathyroid hormone (PTH) assay, beta-2 microglobulin, urinary Bence-Jones protein, joint fluid analysis and a nasopharangeal swab for the detection of respiratory viruses were unremarkable. A full body CAT scan showed extensive lymphadenopathy in the axillary, inguinal, pelvic and para-aortic regions. Radio-isotopic bone scanning showed increased uptake in the juxta-articular areas of the elbow and knee joints. Histology of a skin lesion biopsy showed a vasculitic infiltration of abnormal looking T cells, whilst lymph node biopsy and bone marrow aspiration and trephine specimens confirmed the diagnosis of acute ATLL. Her hypercalcaemia initially proved refractory to stepwise conventional calcium lowering therapy that included large volume saline diuresis (normal saline at 200 mL/h x 24 h, then 120 mL/h x 48h), loop diuretics (80 mg of furosemide 12h x 3 days), corticosteroids (100 mg of hydrocortisone 8h x 3 days) and intravenous bisphosphonate therapy (4 mg of zolendronic acid over 15 min x 1 dose). On the fifth day, due to a lack of improvement in the degree of hypercalcaemia and her persistent delirium, she was initiated on a modified SLED (slow low efficiency haemodialysis) regimen with a low calcium (1 mmol/L) containing dialysate. After receiving 4 h of SLED on Day 5 and the same on Day 6, her serum calcium level had corrected to within normal limits and her delirious state had dramatically improved. Upon stabilization of her condition in the ICU, she was transferred to the oncology department where chemotherapy and combination antiretroviral therapy (zidovudine/lamivudine/efavirenz) were initiated. Unfortunately she demised a month later from chemotherapy associated neutropenia and septic shock.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 37-year-old antiretroviral-naive HIV-1-positive woman was admitted to the intensive care unit with a generalized maculopapular rash, polyarthralgia/joint swelling, high fever, fatigue, and acute delirium.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Diagnosed with HIV-1 in 2006 and never started on ART per prior local guidelines because her CD4+ counts consistently remained >500 cells/µL, the patient developed acute fever, fatigue, generalized skin rash, painful swelling of the knees, elbows, and ankles, and delirium.
subjective.past_medical_history: HIV-1 infection diagnosed in 2006 (ART-naive with preserved CD4+ counts >500 cells/µL).
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for generalized maculopapular rash, knee/elbow/ankle joint pain and swelling, high fever, fatigue, and delirium.

objective.physical_examination: Acutely ill and delirious (without focal neurological deficits) with high fever (39.1 °C), a generalized maculopapular skin rash, marked symmetric swelling of the bilateral knee, elbow, and ankle joints, axillary and inguinal lymphadenopathy, and 4 cm splenomegaly without hepatomegaly.
objective.routine_investigations: Laboratory workup revealed severe life-threatening hypercalcemia (serum calcium 4.48 mmol/L) and strongly positive HTLV-1 serology, while CBC, renal and liver function tests, blood and urine cultures, autoimmune screen, serum protein electrophoresis, urinary Bence-Jones protein, serum ACE, intact PTH, beta-2 microglobulin, synovial fluid analysis, and respiratory viral PCR were unremarkable.
objective.advanced_workup: Admission CD4+ T-lymphocyte count was 616 cells/µL. Whole-body CT demonstrated extensive axillary, inguinal, pelvic, and para-aortic lymphadenopathy; radioisotope bone scan showed increased juxta-articular uptake at the elbows and knees. Skin biopsy showed vasculitic infiltration by atypical T-lymphocytes, and excisional lymph node biopsy along with bone marrow aspirate and trephine biopsy confirmed acute adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma (ATLL).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: HTLV-1-associated acute adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma (ATLL) presenting with severe paraneoplastic hypercalcemic crisis (4.48 mmol/L) and delirium in a 37-year-old woman with untreated HIV-1 co-infection (plasma HIV viral load 102,000 copies/mL, CD4+ count 616 cells/µL; confirmed by strongly positive HTLV-1 serology and skin, lymph node, and bone marrow biopsies). Because her hypercalcemia and delirium were refractory to 4 days of high-volume normal saline diuresis, intravenous furosemide (80 mg q12h), intravenous hydrocortisone (100 mg q8h), and zoledronic acid (4 mg IV), she underwent two 4-hour sessions of low-calcium (1 mmol/L) sustained low-efficiency dialysis (SLED) on days 5 and 6, achieving normocalcemia and complete resolution of delirium. She was transferred to oncology and initiated on systemic chemotherapy and cART (zidovudine/lamivudine/efavirenz), but died 1 month later from chemotherapy-induced febrile neutropenia and septic shock.

raw_case_text: In February 2016, a 19-year-old woman coming from Ivory Coast was admitted to a peripheral hospital of our city for persistent fever. After she resulted positive for a screening HIV-Ab test, she was referred to the Infectious and Tropical Diseases Department. At admission she had deep asthenia, chills, fever (max 38.8 C), and tachycardia (110 bpm); examination revealed mono-lateral tonsillar hypertrophy and submandibular lymphadenopathy. Laboratory investigations showed pancytopenia (haemoglobin 8.7 g/dL - normal value 12.0-16.0 g/dL, white blood cells 3,050/muL -n.v. 4.00-10.80x103/muL, platelets 80,000/muL - n.v. 130-400x103/muL), increased lactate dehydrogenase (5,201 U/L - n.v. 136-234 U/L ), increased levels of C Reactive Protein (63.3 mg/L - n.v. < 5.0 mg/L ), and high ferritin and triglycerides serum levels (> 40,000 ng/mL and 440 mg/dL - n.v. 20-120 ng/mL and <150 mg/dL respectively). Baseline lymphocytes CD4+ T-cell count was 19 cell/muL and HIV-RNA was 1,787,000 cp/mL. In addition, the patient resulted positive for EBV-DNA (1,297 cp/mL), CMV-DNA (266 cp/mL), and HBV-DNA (> 700,000,000 UI/mL), and for blood stool test. Suspecting a lymphoproliferative disorder evolving in haemophagocytic syndrome, a bone marrow biopsy was performed and steroid treatment was started. Consequently, we performed biopsies of the gut, lateral-cervical lymph node, and tonsil. Microscopical evaluation of hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) sections of the bone marrow showed a prominent lymphohistiocytic infiltrate with budding yeast cells inside macrophages, suggestive of histoplasmosis, which was confirmed by Grocott Methenamine Silver stain (GMS) and periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) stain. Antifungal treatment with liposomal Amphotericin B was started while steroid therapy was gradually reduced. She rapidly became afebrile and, in the following weeks, we observed a slow regression of symptoms. Histological examination of submandibular lymph node, tonsil and colic mucosa also confirmed the diagnosis (Figures 1, 2 and 3). Histoplasma spp serology was negative, while culture of bone marrow aspirate showed H. capsulatum growth. After three weeks of induction therapy, she continued on maintenance therapy with itraconazole, and cART with tenofovir/emtricitabine + dolutegravir was prescribed. The patient was referred to the Outpatient Clinic. She attended at the first follow-up visit ten days after the hospital discharge with improved clinical conditions and blood exams. However in April 2016 she returned to Ivory Coast and was re-linked to care in October 2016. At the time of the visit lymphocytes CD4+ T count was 29 cell/muL, HIV-RNA was 153,300 cp/mL and HBV DNA was 212,600,000 UI/mL. During her stay in Ivory Coast, she interrupted both antiretroviral therapy and histoplasmosis maintenance therapy; moreover, at the moment of the new visit she was pregnant and after proper counseling, she decided to carry on the pregnancy. Only antiretroviral therapy with tenofovir/emtricitabine + atazanavir/ritonavir was re-started and a close follow-up was scheduled. After three weeks she was admitted to the Intensive Care Unit (ICU) for internal abortion, complicated by septic shock. She was treated with wide spectrum antibiotic therapy (meropenem and vancomycin) without any microbiological isolation and she went through several transfusions and mechanical ventilation. Once stabilized, she was transferred to our Department, she was febrile, pancytopenic and with a skin lesions on her chest, suggestive of histoplasmosis reactivation so that antifungal treatment with liposomal Amphotericin B was reintroduced. Bone marrow biopsy confirmed the suspect. The same day antiretroviral therapy with tenofovir/emtricitabine + dolutegravir was reintroduced. In the following weeks, a slow progressive improvement of the conditions was observed, therefore she was transferred to a facility with proper social support and health assistance. At the time of the last visit in December 2017, the patient was asymptomatic and fully adherent with cART and histoplasmosis prophylaxis. Last CD4+ T-cell count was 150 cell/muL and a low-level viral load was detected for HIV and HBV (33 copies/mL and 95 UI/mL respectively).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 19-year-old woman from Ivory Coast presented in February 2016 with persistent high fever (up to 38.8 °C), chills, profound asthenia, and unilateral sore throat/tonsillar enlargement.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Admitted initially to a peripheral hospital for persistent fever and found to be HIV-antibody positive, she was transferred to the Infectious and Tropical Diseases Department with high fever, chills, severe fatigue, and unilateral tonsillar hypertrophy. After initial successful treatment for disseminated histoplasmosis and HIV/HBV co-infection, she returned to Ivory Coast from April to October 2016, discontinued all medications, conceived, and suffered an intrauterine fetal demise/septic abortion 3 weeks after re-linkage to care, followed by cutaneous and bone marrow relapse of disseminated histoplasmosis.
subjective.past_medical_history: Native of Ivory Coast; newly diagnosed advanced HIV-1 and high-viremia chronic HBV co-infection in February 2016; subsequent pregnancy complicated by septic internal abortion in October–November 2016.
subjective.review_of_systems: Initial presentation: persistent fever (38.8 °C), chills, profound asthenia. Relapse (November 2016): fever and anterior chest skin lesions.

objective.physical_examination: Initial admission (February 2016): temperature 38.8 °C, tachycardia (110 beats/min), unilateral tonsillar hypertrophy, and submandibular lymphadenopathy. Post-ICU relapse (November 2016): febrile with papulonodular skin lesions over the anterior chest.
objective.routine_investigations: February 2016 admission labs showed pancytopenia (hemoglobin 8.7 g/dL [normal 12.0–16.0], WBC 3,050/µL [normal 4,000–10,800], platelets 80,000/µL [normal 130,000–400,000]), markedly elevated LDH (5,201 U/L [normal 136–234]), elevated CRP (63.3 mg/L [normal <5.0]), hyperferritinemia (>40,000 ng/mL [normal 20–120]), hypertriglyceridemia (440 mg/dL [normal <150]), positive fecal occult blood, positive EBV-DNA (1,297 copies/mL), positive CMV-DNA (266 copies/mL), and massively elevated HBV-DNA (>700,000,000 IU/mL). Histoplasma serology was negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Baseline CD4+ T-cell count was 19 cells/µL in February 2016, 29 cells/µL in October 2016, and 150 cells/µL in December 2017. Bone marrow biopsy, submandibular lymph node biopsy, tonsillar biopsy, and colonic mucosal biopsy (H&E, GMS, and PAS stains) all demonstrated prominent lymphohistiocytic infiltrates with abundant intracellular budding yeast cells of Histoplasma capsulatum inside macrophages, and bone marrow aspirate culture grew H. capsulatum (repeated bone marrow biopsy in November 2016 confirmed relapse).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Newly diagnosed advanced HIV-1 infection (baseline HIV-RNA 1,787,000 copies/mL, CD4+ count 19 cells/µL) and chronic HBV co-infection (HBV-DNA >700,000,000 IU/mL) complicated by disseminated Histoplasma capsulatum infection (involving bone marrow, tonsil, lymph nodes, colon, and skin) and secondary hemophagocytic syndrome-like hyperferritinemia (>40,000 ng/mL). Initial 3-week induction with intravenous liposomal amphotericin B followed by oral itraconazole maintenance and tenofovir/emtricitabine + dolutegravir achieved clinical remission. Following a 6-month treatment interruption in Ivory Coast and an ICU admission for septic miscarriage (treated with meropenem and vancomycin), her relapsed disseminated histoplasmosis was re-induced with liposomal amphotericin B alongside tenofovir/emtricitabine + dolutegravir and social-support placement; by December 2017, she was asymptomatic and fully adherent with a CD4+ count of 150 cells/µL, HIV-RNA of 33 copies/mL, and HBV-DNA of 95 IU/mL.

raw_case_text:
A 55-year-old woman, with HIV/HCV (genotype 3a) coinfection diagnosed in 1991, and previous intravenous drug user, has been followed by our outpatient department since 1998. The patient had been treated with antiretrovirals since 1991, with a good immunovirologic response. In 2005, she received anti-HCV therapy with pegIFN and ribavirin for 24 weeks, but the HCV infection relapsed after treatment discontinuation. Hereafter, she regularly followed her antiretroviral therapy and had an HIV-RNA load persistently < 50 copies/mL and stable clinical condition. Despite this, in summer 2007, she developed two consecutive episodes of acute kidney injury (AKI) associated with cholestatic acute hepatitis. At the time of her first hospital admission, her antiretroviral therapy (ART) with tenofovir disoproxil fumarate 245 mg q.d., lamivudine 300 mg q.d., and fosamprenavir 700 mg b.i.d. was stopped, in the suspicion of possible renal damage. Blood tests revealed acute kidney failure, with a serum creatinine level of 6.3 mg/dL associated with blood urea nitrogen 67 mg/dL and uric acid 10.6 mg/dL. Other notable results were hyperbilirubinemia (19.8 mg/dL, normal range 0.20 - 1.20 mg/dL), hepatic failure, with a coagulative deficit (prothrombin time 25), and metabolic acidosis. Anti-smooth-muscle-antibodies (ASMA) were positive (160 : 1), while antinuclear antibodies (ANA), antibodies directed against proteins that bind to nucleic acids (ENA), antibodies directed against phospholipids and antineutrophil cytoplasmic (ANCA), adrenal cortex antibodies (ACA), antimitochondrial antibodies (AMA), and anti-liver-kidney microsomal (ALKM) antibody were negative. Urinalysis showed proteinuria, hematuria, and pyuria. Abdomen ultrasound showed a liver enlargement without focal lesions, a modest ascites, and enlarged kidneys with an increment of arterials resistances. The patient's management required hemodialysis, albumin, vitamin K, and human plasma. At the same time, the patient started methylprednisolone therapy (250 mg daily, then reduced to 40 mg daily). After clinical and chemistry improvement, the patient was discharged with oral steroid treatment (prednisone 25 mg daily), which was subsequently tapered. Three months later, after steroid discontinuation and ART still discontinued, a new onset of AKI (serum creatinine levels 6.0 mg/dL) required hospital admission. A kidney biopsy was performed showing tubule-interstitial nephritis and focal glomerulosclerosis (Figure 1). Blood tests confirmed the presence of ASMA antibodies as well as negativity for ANA, ENA, p-ANA, c-ANCA, LKM (liver-kidney microsomal), ACA, and AMA. Then, methylprednisolone 40 mg daily was restarted with success (Serial serum creatinine levels are reported in Figure 2). At discharge, oral prednisone (37.5 mg daily) was prescribed, and it was tapered over a period of 4 weeks. In January 2008, considering the progressive improvement of renal function (creatinine 1.0 mg/dL), the consultant nephrologist suggested stopping steroid treatment and starting maintaining treatment with mycophenolate mofetil (MMF), 1,000 mg b.i.d. Following the starting of MMF, the patient exhibited negative ASMA antibodies. 
She also restarted ART with abacavir 300 mg b.i.d., lamivudine 150 mg b.i.d., and lopinavir/ritonavir 400/100 b.i.d.. MMF was continued with good adherence and tolerance until November 2009, when, after 2 years of good clinical condition, it was discontinued. Four weeks after the suspension of MMF, the patient experienced a new deterioration of liver and renal function that required the reintroduction of MMF, at a dosage of 500 mg b.i.d., and new hospital admission (Figure 1). In the following years, she continued ART, switching to darunavir/ritonavir (800/100 mg), etravirine 200 mg x 2, and maraviroc 150 mg x 2 and continued MMF. In June 2012, a new episode of cholestatic hepatitis developed, without renal involvement. A liver biopsy was obtained showing coexisting chronic HCV-related hepatitis and autoimmune hepatitis. Immunosuppressive therapy was enhanced with steroidal therapy (1 mg/kg), but she refused to continue. Thus, she was put on an increased dosage of MMF, of 1,000 mg b.i.d.. This therapy was continued in the following years with improvement of renal and hepatic parameters. In September 2015, the patient received anti-HCV treatment with sofosbuvir 400 mg q.d. plus daclatasvir 60 mg q.d. for 12 weeks without ribavirin. Before the starting of HCV treatment, maraviroc was stopped to avoid expected drug-drug interaction. Sustained virological response (SVR) was achieved, and, 3 months later, in agreement with the nephrologists, the patient halved the MMF dosage, and stopped it after other 12 weeks. Subsequent blood tests showed a permanent negativity of HCV-RNA load, with creatinine and hepatic enzymes persistently within the normal range (creatinine persistently < 0.95 mg/dL, and bilirubin < 1.20 mg/dL) and negative ASMA antibodies 12 months after MMF suspension. Since the patient no longer needed to keep an NRTI-sparing regimen, a single-tablet-regimen with rilpivirine/emtricitabine/tenofovir disoproxil fumarate was reintroduced.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 55-year-old woman with long-term treated HIV-1 and relapsed genotype 3a chronic hepatitis C virus (HCV) co-infection presented in summer 2007 with recurrent episodes of severe acute kidney injury and acute icteric cholestatic hepatitis.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Diagnosed with HIV and genotype 3a HCV in 1991 (with HCV relapse after 24 weeks of pegylated interferon and ribavirin in 2005) and virologically suppressed for HIV (<50 copies/mL) on tenofovir disoproxil fumarate, lamivudine, and fosamprenavir, the patient presented in summer 2007 with severe acute kidney injury (creatinine 6.3 mg/dL) and cholestatic acute hepatitis (bilirubin 19.8 mg/dL). Although stopping ART and giving high-dose corticosteroids induced remission, she suffered severe renal flares (creatinine 6.0 mg/dL) upon steroid discontinuation (while still off ART) and again in November 2009 4 weeks after stopping maintenance mycophenolate mofetil (MMF), followed by an isolated cholestatic hepatitis flare in June 2012.
subjective.past_medical_history: HIV-1 and HCV (genotype 3a) co-infection diagnosed in 1991; former intravenous drug user; prior 24-week course of pegIFN and ribavirin in 2005 with HCV relapse.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for jaundice/cholestasis and acute oliguric/non-oliguric renal failure during flares. Home medications at initial 2007 flare: tenofovir disoproxil fumarate 245 mg QD, lamivudine 300 mg QD, and fosamprenavir 700 mg BID.

objective.physical_examination: Jaundiced with modest ascites during the acute summer 2007 hepatorenal flare.
objective.routine_investigations: Initial 2007 admission labs showed serum creatinine 6.3 mg/dL (relapsing to 6.0 mg/dL off steroids), BUN 67 mg/dL, uric acid 10.6 mg/dL, severe hyperbilirubinemia (19.8 mg/dL; normal 0.20–1.20 mg/dL), coagulopathy (prothrombin time 25%), metabolic acidosis, and urinalysis with proteinuria, hematuria, and pyuria. Autoimmune panel was positive for anti-smooth muscle antibodies (ASMA titer 1:160) and negative for ANA, ENA, antiphospholipid, ANCA, ACA, AMA, and anti-LKM antibodies. Abdominal ultrasound showed hepatomegaly without focal lesions, mild ascites, and enlarged kidneys with increased arterial resistive indices.
objective.advanced_workup: Renal biopsy during the second 2007 AKI flare demonstrated tubulointerstitial nephritis and focal segmental glomerulosclerosis. Liver biopsy during the June 2012 cholestatic flare demonstrated coexisting chronic HCV hepatitis and autoimmune hepatitis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: HCV-triggered autoimmune hepatitis (ASMA 1:160 positive) coexisting with immune-mediated tubulointerstitial nephritis and focal glomerulosclerosis in a 55-year-old woman with virologically suppressed HIV-1 infection (plasma HIV-RNA persistently <50 copies/mL). Acute 2007 flares were managed with temporary hemodialysis, albumin, vitamin K, plasma, and intravenous methylprednisolone (250 mg tapered to oral prednisone), followed in January 2008 by steroid-sparing maintenance with mycophenolate mofetil (MMF 500–1,000 mg twice daily, which seroreverted ASMA and normalized creatinine to 1.0 mg/dL) alongside NRTI-sparing/adjusted ART (abacavir/lamivudine/lopinavir/ritonavir, later darunavir/ritonavir + etravirine + maraviroc). In September 2015, eradication of genotype 3a HCV with a 12-week ribavirin-free regimen of sofosbuvir (400 mg QD) plus daclatasvir (60 mg QD) achieved sustained virological response (SVR) and permitted permanent discontinuation of MMF 6 months later, with persistently normal renal/hepatic function (creatinine <0.95 mg/dL, bilirubin <1.20 mg/dL), negative ASMA at 12 months off MMF, and transition to single-tablet rilpivirine/emtricitabine/tenofovir disoproxil fumarate.

raw_case_text:
A 56-year-old man with AIDS for four years, non-compliant with his antiretroviral therapy (ART) presented with altered mental status and somnolence for four days. His family reported progressive weakness affecting his ambulation over a period of three weeks. There was no history of sick contacts, recent travel, animal exposure, or illicit drug use. An unintentional weight loss of about twenty pounds over the past four months was also reported. Patient had been started on ART four weeks prior to his hospital admission. Patient's home medications were elvitegravir/cobicistat/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide (fixed dose combination), azithromycin and dapsone.
On physical examination, he was cachectic and somnolent, temperature was 97.5 F, blood pressure 112/74 mm Hg, heart rate 95 bpm, respiratory rate 16 with oxygen saturation 98% on room air. EKG showed sinus rhythm with premature atrial complexes and shortened QT interval (corrected 376ms).
Laboratory investigations were significant for normocytic anemia with a hemoglobin of 9.8 g/dL, leukopenia 3.3 x 103/microL, thrombocytopenia 120 x 103/microL, BUN 43 mg/dL (RI 8-20mg/dL), creatinine 2.09 mg/dL (RI 0.4-1.3 mg/dl), corrected calcium 16.49 mg/dL (RI 8.9-10.3 mg/dL), ionized calcium 7.8 mg/dL (RI 4.5-5.6 mg/dL), phosphorus 4.4 mg/dL (RI 2.4-4.7 mg/dL), and albumin 2.6 g/dL (RI 3.5-4.8 g/dL). Other notable initial laboratory findings included 25-hydroxyvitamin D level 56 ng/ml (RI 30-100 ng/ml), 1,25 dihydroxyvitamin D level 44.1 pg/ml (RI 19.9-79.3 pg/ml), parathyroid hormone (PTH) 4 pg/mL (RI 15-65 pg/mL) with PTH-related peptide levels undetectable. Of note, CD4 count was 36/mm3 and viral load was 617,000 before initiation of antiretroviral therapy.
He received intravenous fluids and pamidronate with calcitonin. His serum calcium declined to 9.8 mg/dL (RI 8.9-10.3 mg/dL), kidney function improved with BUN 39mg/dL (RI 8-20mg/dL) and creatinine 1.26 mg/dL (RI 0.4-1.3 mg/dl) by hospital day three. There was improvement in patient's mental status within one day of treatment initiation.
Serum protein electrophoresis revealed monoclonal gammopathy with Free Kappa/Lambda ratio of 1.31 (0.26-1.65) and serum Monoclonal Immunoglobulin (Ig) G was also elevated at 2359. Lactate dehydrogenase level (LDH) was 281 IU/L (RI 98-192 IU/L) and beta-2- microglobulin was 12 mg/L (RI 0.6-2.4mg/L). Whole body skeletal survey revealed no focal uptake. There was no evidence of parenchymal lung disease or mediastinal lymphadenopathy on Computerized Tomography (CT) scan of Chest (Figure 1). CT scan of Abdomen and Pelvis revealed hepatosplenomegaly with large retroperitoneal, retrocrural, and mesenteric lymphadenopathy (Figure 2(a,b)) which had an intense focal uptake on Gallium scan with no abnormal lung uptake (Figure 3). The presence of Monoclonal IgG along with hepatosplenomegaly and retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy, elevated LDH were all strongly suggestive of initial presumptive diagnosis of a lymphoproliferative disease. Lymphoma was strongly suspected and he underwent a bone marrow biopsy and lymph node biopsies twice. Bone marrow biopsy revealed mild plasmacytosis (5%), normocellular marrow (50%) with mature trilineage, no evidence of myelodysplasia, acute leukemia or lymphoma. A subsequent biopsy of the lymph nodes showed fragments of fibrous tissue with lymphohistiocytic infiltrate (Figure 4) and many acid-fast bacilli on special stain (Figure 5). Results of bone marrow biopsy and lymph node biopsy were not consistent with lymphoma which promoted investigation for other causes of hypercalcemia and lymphadenopathy. Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Mycobacterium avium complex Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) were also negative. Three sputum samples for acid fast bacilli (AFB) smear were negative.
Patient was initially started on Vancomycin and meropenem for presumed sepsis. As lymph node biopsy smear was positive for AFB; rifabutin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol were commenced as well as azithromycin for tuberculous and nontuberculous mycobacterium pending further identification. Calcium level remained within normal range and his medical condition improved. He was then discharged with medical follow up and continues to show sustained clinical improvement. However, pre-antibiotic blood cultures drawn in a sodium heparin tube subsequently grew Mycobacterium identified by genomic analysis as M. abscessus subspecies abscessus at four weeks. Bone marrow culture remained without any growth.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 56-year-old man with AIDS presented with a 4-day history of altered mental status and somnolence and a 3-week history of progressive generalized weakness impairing ambulation, 4 weeks after restarting antiretroviral therapy.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Diagnosed with AIDS 4 years earlier with prior ART non-compliance, the patient had restarted elvitegravir/cobicistat/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide 4 weeks prior to admission (at baseline CD4 count 36 cells/mm3 and HIV viral load 617,000 copies/mL). Over the preceding 4 months he lost ~20 lbs, over the preceding 3 weeks he developed progressive lower limb/generalized weakness affecting walking, and 4 days before admission he became increasingly somnolent and confused.
subjective.past_medical_history: History of AIDS for 4 years with prior medication non-adherence; restarted ART 4 weeks prior. Denied sick contacts, recent travel, animal exposure, or illicit drug use.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for 4-day somnolence/confusion, 3-week progressive weakness, and 20-lb weight loss over 4 months. Home medications: elvitegravir/cobicistat/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide, azithromycin, and dapsone.

objective.physical_examination: Cachectic and somnolent on admission; temperature 97.5 °F, blood pressure 112/74 mmHg, heart rate 95 beats/min, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, and SpO2 98% on room air.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission labs revealed severe PTH-independent hypercalcemia (corrected calcium 16.49 mg/dL [RI 8.9–10.3], ionized calcium 7.8 mg/dL [RI 4.5–5.6], phosphorus 4.4 mg/dL, suppressed intact PTH 4 pg/mL [RI 15–65], undetectable PTHrP, normal 25-OH vitamin D 56 ng/mL, and normal/inappropriately unsuppressed 1,25-(OH)2 vitamin D 44.1 pg/mL), acute kidney injury (BUN 43 mg/dL, creatinine 2.09 mg/dL), hypoalbuminemia (2.6 g/dL), normocytic anemia (hemoglobin 9.8 g/dL), leukopenia (WBC 3.3 x 10^3/µL), and thrombocytopenia (platelets 120 x 10^3/µL). SPEP showed an IgG monoclonal gammopathy (IgG 2,359 mg/dL, normal kappa/lambda ratio 1.31), elevated LDH (281 IU/L), and elevated beta-2 microglobulin (12 mg/L). Three sputum AFB smears were negative. ECG showed sinus rhythm with PACs and a shortened QTc interval (376 ms); skeletal survey was negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Pre-ART CD4+ T-cell count (4 weeks prior) was 36 cells/mm3. Chest CT was normal; abdomen and pelvis CT and Gallium-67 scintigraphy demonstrated hepatosplenomegaly and intensely gallium-avid retroperitoneal, retrocrural, and mesenteric lymphadenopathy without pulmonary uptake. Bone marrow biopsy (normocellular 50%, 5% polyclonal/mild plasmacytosis, negative culture) and two retroperitoneal lymph node biopsies excluded lymphoma; the second lymph node biopsy demonstrated a fibrous lymphohistiocytic infiltrate containing numerous acid-fast bacilli (negative M. tuberculosis and MAC PCRs).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Disseminated Mycobacterium abscessus subsp. abscessus infection (bacteremia and retroperitoneal/mesenteric lymphadenitis) presenting as unmasking immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) and severe calcitriol/granuloma-mediated hypercalcemic crisis (corrected calcium 16.49 mg/dL) 4 weeks after initiating elvitegravir/cobicistat/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide in a 56-year-old man with advanced AIDS (baseline CD4+ count 36 cells/mm3, HIV viral load 617,000 copies/mL). Definitive pathogen identification of Mycobacterium abscessus subsp. abscessus was established at 4 weeks by genomic sequencing of mycobacterial growth from pre-antibiotic sodium-heparin blood cultures alongside AFB-positive retroperitoneal lymph node histopathology. Acute hypercalcemia and encephalopathy resolved within 1–3 days (calcium 9.8 mg/dL, creatinine 1.26 mg/dL) with IV hydration, pamidronate, and calcitonin, and the patient achieved sustained clinical improvement on antimycobacterial therapy (rifabutin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol, and azithromycin) and continued ART.

raw_case_text:
A 44-year-old woman admitted via the emergency department with a 3-month history of multiple ulcers and a 3-day history of rapidly progressive swelling and loss of vision in the right eye with associated fever. She had been diagnosed with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV)-infection 5 years previously, was placed on antiretroviral medications, but defaulted 3 months before presentation.
Before her contact with our team, she had been admitted on account of multiple expanding ulcers with purulent discharge and managed as a case of pyomyositis. After a 3-week stay in the hospital, she requested discharge as some ulcers had healed, while others were improving. Her CD4 +count was 67 cells/mm3.
She returned after 2 weeks on noticing the expansion of previously healing ulcers and the development of rapidly evolving new lesions. Concurrently, there was right ocular pain, swelling, and discharge, with progressively worsening visual loss.
Skin lesions were located on thighs, upper limbs, buttocks, perineum, and right eyelid, often beginning as discrete painful papules or pustules, with rapid progression (within 5-7 days) to pus formation, discharge, and eventual ulceration [Figures 1 and 2].
Examination revealed multiple ulcers on the aforementioned locations in various stages of evolution. The largest on the left thigh measured 6 cm x 10 cm, had an irregular undermined edge, with slough and islands of necrotic eschar on the ulcer floor. Ophthalmologic assessment of the right eye revealed upper lid edema with mild erythema and an overlying crusted and necrotic lesion on the nasal aspect. The conjunctiva, cornea, and sclera were all necrotic. A clinical diagnosis of ecthyma gangrenosum (EG) was entertained by the dermatologists, while panophthalmitis of the right eye was the presumptive diagnosis made by the ophthalmologists. She was commenced on intravenous levofloxacin, and her right eye was eviscerated and sent for histology. Intraoperative findings were extensive scleral necrosis, melted cornea, but relatively clear vitreous.
The white cell count was 4.5 x 109/L with 46% neutrophils (normal 4-11 x 109/L), while hematocrit was 20% (normal 36%-45%). Blood culture was negative; wound biopsy revealed an ulcerated epithelium with vascular congestion and areas of dermal hemorrhage and necrosis. There were also chronic inflammatory cells with features of hemorrhagic vasculitis. Culture of the specimen yielded growth of Pseudomonas aeruginosa sensitive only to cefepime, with intermediate sensitivity to ceftazidime, but resistant to levofloxacin, ciprofloxacin, and gentamicin. A concurrent definitive diagnosis of EG was eventually entertained by both dermatologists and ophthalmologists. Levofloxacin was discontinued and cefepime prescribed. The patient was, however, unable to procure the requisite medications, with a progressive deterioration in her clinical status, and eventual demise after 71 days of admission.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 44-year-old HIV-positive woman presented to the emergency department with a 3-month history of multiple recurrent purulent skin ulcers across her thighs, upper limbs, buttocks, and perineum, and a 3-day history of rapidly progressive right eye pain, swelling, purulent discharge, vision loss, and fever.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Having defaulted on her antiretroviral therapy 3 months earlier, the patient was initially hospitalized for 3 weeks for multiple expanding purulent skin ulcers managed as pyomyositis before requesting early discharge with partial healing. Two weeks after discharge, her previously healing ulcers expanded and new painful papules/pustules rapidly evolved within 5–7 days into necrotic ulcers over her extremities, buttocks, perineum, and right upper eyelid, accompanied for 3 days by right ocular pain, swelling, discharge, visual loss, and fever.
subjective.past_medical_history: Diagnosed with HIV infection 5 years prior; defaulted from antiretroviral therapy 3 months prior to presentation.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for multiple painful necrotic skin ulcers, fever, and acute right eye pain, swelling, discharge, and blindness. Off antiretroviral therapy for 3 months.

objective.physical_examination: Cutaneous examination revealed multiple ulcers in varying evolutionary stages across the thighs, upper extremities, buttocks, perineum, and right eyelid; the largest ulcer on the left thigh measured 6 x 10 cm with irregular undermined edges, slough, and central necrotic eschar. Ophthalmic examination of the right eye revealed upper eyelid edema, erythema, a nasal crusted necrotic lesion, and extensive full-thickness necrosis and melting of the conjunctiva, cornea, and sclera consistent with severe panophthalmitis.
objective.routine_investigations: CBC showed WBC 4.5 x 10^9/L (46% neutrophils; normal 4–11 x 10^9/L) and severe anemia with hematocrit 20% (normal 36–45%). Blood culture was negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Baseline CD4+ T-cell count was 67 cells/mm3. Right eye evisceration confirmed extensive scleral necrosis and corneal melting. Cutaneous ulcer biopsy histopathology demonstrated epidermal ulceration, vascular congestion, dermal hemorrhage and necrosis, and hemorrhagic vasculitis; wound tissue culture isolated multidrug-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa (sensitive only to cefepime, intermediate to ceftazidime, and resistant to levofloxacin, ciprofloxacin, and gentamicin).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Multifocal cutaneous ecthyma gangrenosum and destructive right-eye Pseudomonas aeruginosa panophthalmitis in a 44-year-old woman with advanced uncontrolled HIV/AIDS following a 3-month ART interruption (CD4+ count 67 cells/mm3; confirmed by hemorrhagic vasculitis on skin biopsy and culture isolation of multidrug-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa). She underwent right eye evisceration and was initially started on empirical IV levofloxacin; although therapy was switched to targeted cefepime upon susceptibility reporting, the patient was financially unable to procure cefepime, progressively deteriorated, and died on hospital day 71.

raw_case_text:
A 27-year-old albino woman of sub-Saharan African ancestry was referred from a regional hospital for assessment and treatment of a nodular lesion of the scalp which had emerged 8 months earlier and enlarged rapidly. Her medical history was notable for HIV infection, a BCC of the neck removed elsewhere, and significant sun exposure. Her family medical history was noncontributory. Physical examination revealed a large, purplish, protruding tumor (6.5/3.5 cm in size) on the left temporoparietal aspect of the head. The tumor was tender, ulcerative and showed signs of secondary bacterial infection (Fig. 1a). She presented marked solar damage illustrated by solar elastosis, multiple actinic keratoses, a patch of Bowen's disease on the neck, and several erosive and hyperkeratotic skin lesions on sun-exposed areas, which were clinically suggestive of non-melanoma skin cancers. Apart from these findings, a review of the systems was unremarkable. We considered in differential diagnosis: cutaneous lymphoma, malignant melanoma, MCC, and SCC. The baseline blood investigations revealed mild anemia (Hb 9.1 g/dL; RBC 3.32 x 1012), hypoalbuminemia (29 g/dL), and a deranged lymphocytic subset analysis (low CD4+ cell count of 109 cells/muL and high CD8+cell count of 1,849 cells/muL). Viral studies confirmed HIV seropositivity (viral load of 640 RNA copies/mL), past exposure to EBV, reactivation of CMV (both IgM and IgG positive), hepatitis B immunity as a result of past exposure, and HTLV-1 antibody screen positivity. The culture of the pus swab demonstrated Enterobacter cloacae and Enterococcus faecalis growth. Several skin biopsies were obtained from the scalp tumor and from suspected SCCs/BCCs of the neck, eyebrow, upper lip, and ears.
Histological examination of the scalp tumor showed an exophytic, ulcerated nodule consisting of extensively invaded dermis by a poorly differentiated tumor (Fig. 2a). The neoplastic cells were arranged in vague nests and sheets showing high mitotic activity and a degree of molding. The tumor was widely infiltrating up to subcutaneous tissue and focally in the skeletal muscles with evidence of both perineural and lymphovascular invasion. Furthermore, a multicentric, moderately differentiated, keratinized SCC was seen adjacent to the tumor (Fig. 2b). Immunoperoxidase stains revealed paranuclear dot-like positivity for cytokeratin CK20 (Fig. 2c), extensive positivity for neuroendocrine markers: synaptophysin and neuron-specific enolase, and for CD56 (Fig. 2d, e, f). More focal positivity was demonstrated for chromogranin A stain. The electron microscopy illustrated neurosecretory granules within the cytoplasm (Fig. 2g) confirming the diagnosis of MCC. All other specimens labeled left eyebrow, upper lip, right ear, and left ear showed infiltrating moderately differentiated SCCs on a background of marked solar elastosis. Further investigations were performed to evaluate the spread of the tumor. The patient had no evidence of local bone destruction (Fig. 3a), draining node involvement or occult systemic metastases at the time MCC was diagnosed as demonstrated by CT scan (head/neck, lungs), ultrasound of the thyroid and abdomen, PET-CT scan of the lymph nodes, MRI of the brain, biopsy of the lymph node from the regional nodal basin, and the ophthalmological examination. Consequently, MCC was interpreted as stage II B (T2 N0M0) according to the most recent edition of the AJCC staging system. Biospecimens obtained from the patient were sent overseas for MCPyV copy number detection by PCR and immunohistochemistry which did not reveal any evidence of transcripts related to MCPyV or expression of MCPyV-derived large T-antigen. Based on the HIV infection, the viral load, and the deranged CD4 lymphocyte count, the patient started HAART on a twice-daily regimen (Stavudin, Rifanovir). A radical surgical excision was performed, and a facial plastic surgeon reconstructed the surgical defect with a full-thickness skin graft. The patient was treated subsequently with adjuvant radiotherapy to the tumor bed with a planned total dose of 50 Gy divided in 25 fractions. She received only 3 sessions due to noncompliance. The patient declined further treatment as she became pregnant and elected not to have termination of pregnancy. Her general condition deteriorated drastically during the pregnancy and she had a recurrence of the tumor 5 months later with extensive lymph node involvement as demonstrated by PET-CT scanning (Fig. 1b, Fig. 3b). She delivered a premature infant who died soon at the age of 2 months of HIV-related comorbidities. The Department of Medical Oncology was consulted regarding the use of palliative chemotherapy, but the patient declined the treatment and died several months later of liver and lung metastases.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 27-year-old albino woman of sub-Saharan African ancestry with HIV infection was referred with an 8-month history of a rapidly enlarging, tender, ulcerated left temporoparietal scalp tumor.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Eight months prior to referral, a nodular lesion emerged on the left temporoparietal scalp and grew rapidly into a large, painful, ulcerated, secondarily infected tumor alongside multiple hyperkeratotic and erosive lesions across sun-exposed skin.
subjective.past_medical_history: Oculocutaneous albinism with severe chronic actinic skin damage; HIV infection; prior excision of a neck basal cell carcinoma (BCC). Family history was noncontributory.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for a painful, bleeding, ulcerated scalp mass and multiple sun-exposed skin tumors; systemic review otherwise unremarkable.

objective.physical_examination: Cutaneous examination revealed a large (6.5 x 3.5 cm), protruding, purplish, tender, ulcerated tumor on the left temporoparietal scalp with purulent secondary infection, accompanied by severe solar elastosis, multiple actinic keratoses, a neck plaque of Bowen disease, and multiple erosive/hyperkeratotic tumors on the left eyebrow, upper lip, and bilateral ears.
objective.routine_investigations: Baseline labs showed mild anemia (hemoglobin 9.1 g/dL, RBC 3.32 x 10^12/L) and hypoalbuminemia (29 g/L). Viral serologies confirmed HIV positivity, past EBV exposure, active CMV reactivation (CMV IgM and IgG positive), resolved HBV immunity, and positive HTLV-1 antibody screening. Scalp wound pus swab culture grew Enterobacter cloacae and Enterococcus faecalis.
objective.advanced_workup: Lymphocyte subset analysis showed severe CD4+ T-cell depletion (109 cells/µL) and elevated CD8+ T-cells (1,849 cells/µL). Biopsies and radical excision histopathology of the scalp mass demonstrated a poorly differentiated dermal/subcutaneous/muscular neuroendocrine carcinoma with nuclear molding, brisk mitoses, perineural and lymphovascular invasion, and an adjacent collision/multicentric moderately differentiated squamous cell carcinoma (SCC), plus synchronous SCCs on the left eyebrow, upper lip, and both ears. Immunohistochemistry of the scalp tumor showed paranuclear dot-like CK20 positivity and diffuse positivity for synaptophysin, NSE, CD56, and focal chromogranin A; electron microscopy confirmed cytoplasmic neurosecretory granules, while Merkel cell polyomavirus (MCPyV) PCR and large T-antigen IHC were negative. Head/neck/chest CT, brain MRI, thyroid/abdominal ultrasound, regional lymph node biopsy, and FDG PET-CT confirmed initial Stage IIB (T2N0M0) disease.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Stage IIB (T2N0M0) UV-driven, Merkel cell polyomavirus (MCPyV)-negative scalp Merkel cell carcinoma (MCC) colliding with squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) and multiple synchronous facial/auricular SCCs in a 27-year-old albino African woman with advanced HIV-1 (plasma HIV-1 RNA 640 copies/mL, CD4+ count 109 cells/µL, CD8+ count 1,849 cells/µL) and HTLV-1 co-infection. She was initiated on twice-daily HAART (stavudine-based regimen) and underwent radical scalp excision with full-thickness skin graft reconstruction, but defaulted after only 3 of 25 planned adjuvant radiotherapy fractions (50 Gy) upon becoming pregnant. Five months later, she suffered massive locoregional nodal recurrence on PET-CT, delivered a premature infant who died at 2 months of age from HIV-related complications, declined palliative chemotherapy, and died several months later from hepatic and pulmonary metastases.

raw_case_text:
A 57-year-old Indian male with HIV-positive status was admitted to our hospital with chief complaints of large-volume watery stools without blood or mucus, 3-4 times a day for 4 months with recent exacerbation for 1 week. This was also associated with nausea, loss of appetite, significant weight loss, generalized weakness, and dysphagia to solids. He denied personal or family history of allergies. He was diagnosed with HIV infection 17 years ago and was on treatment with antiretroviral drugs, namely raltegravir, lamivudine, and efavirenz. He was also diagnosed with pulmonary tuberculosis 5 months back for which he was on treatment with isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol. He unintentionally lost 20 kg of weight over the past 4 months. He further denied the use of laxatives or any complementary or alternative medications. He had stable vital signs, was cachectic, and had a normal systemic examination. His workup for chronic diarrhea included a normal thyroid function test and no opportunistic infections or helminthic infestation. Stool analysis including culture was negative for Clostridium difficile toxin, Cryptosporidium, Vibrio cholerae, acid-fast bacteria, or any other parasites. Serum IgE concentration was also within the normal range. Other investigations revealed hemoglobin 11.4 g/dL (13-18 g/dL), platelets 244,000/uL (140,000-440,000/uL), and total leukocyte count 4880/mm3 (4000-10000/mm3) with neutrophils 78.5% (40%-75%), lymphocytes 16.2% (20%-45%), and eosinophils 0.8% (1%-6%). His total protein was 5.4 g/dL (6.60-8.70 g/dL), albumin 1.8 g/dL (3.97-4.94 g/dL), absolute CD4 count 89.91/mm3 of blood (400-1600/mm3 of blood), absolute CD8 count 427.68/mm3 of blood (280-1400/mm3 of blood), CD4 (helper T-cells)% 11.1% (28-58%), CD8 (suppressor T-cells)% 52.8% (19-49%), CD4/CD8 0.21 (1.2-3.3), and HIV-1 viral load by TaqMan plasma (quantitative) 12,59,309 copies/mL.
On further investigations, esophagogastro duodenoscopy revealed white mucosal plaques in the esophagus consistent with esophageal candidiasis. The mucosa of the duodenum showed focal erosions with blunting of the villi as seen in Figure 1. Urease test was negative for Helicobacter pylori. Mucosal biopsies from the stomach and duodenum were taken. Histopathology study shown in Figure 2 revealed active inflammation in the gastric and duodenal mucosa with excess eosinophils (20 eosinophils/high-power field) and no microorganisms. This was consistent with EGE. He also had a colonoscopy which was normal. Rifampicin was stopped during this admission for a period of 2 weeks. However, the persistence of diarrhea ruled out drug-induced EGE. He was then started on oral prednisolone 40 mg once daily. The frequency of stools decreased and consistency improved. Prednisolone was gradually tapered over a period of 2 months. This was associated with an increase in the frequency of watery stools like before resulting in a readmission with dehydration and weight loss.
The patient was restarted on oral prednisolone 60 mg once daily. Along with cessation of diarrhea, his appetite and weight improved during follow-up after 30 days. On 6-month follow-up, he has regained 18 kg and has normal stools. He is currently on oral prednisolone 40 mg once daily.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 57-year-old HIV-positive Indian male on anti-tuberculosis and antiretroviral therapy presented with a 4-month history of large-volume non-bloody watery diarrhea (3–4 episodes/day, worsening over the past week), a 20 kg weight loss, anorexia, nausea, generalized weakness, and solid-food dysphagia.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Over the 4 months preceding admission—shortly after starting quadruple anti-tuberculosis therapy 5 months earlier for pulmonary tuberculosis—the patient experienced persistent large-volume watery diarrhea without blood or mucus (3–4 stools daily, acutely worsening 1 week prior to admission), accompanied by nausea, anorexia, a 20 kg unintentional weight loss, profound weakness, and dysphagia to solids.
subjective.past_medical_history: 17-year history of HIV-1 infection on antiretroviral therapy; pulmonary tuberculosis diagnosed 5 months prior and treated with first-line anti-tubercular therapy. Denied personal or family history of atopic/allergic disorders or laxative/herbal use.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for chronic watery diarrhea, 20 kg weight loss over 4 months, anorexia, nausea, weakness, and solid-food dysphagia; negative for hematochezia or melena. Home medications: raltegravir, lamivudine, efavirenz, isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol.

objective.physical_examination: Cachectic appearance with stable vital signs and an otherwise unremarkable systemic physical examination.
objective.routine_investigations: Labs showed mild anemia (hemoglobin 11.4 g/dL [normal 13–18]), platelets 244,000/µL, WBC 4,880/mm3 (78.5% neutrophils, 16.2% lymphocytes, 0.8% eosinophils), hypoproteinemia (total protein 5.4 g/dL [normal 6.60–8.70]), severe hypoalbuminemia (albumin 1.8 g/dL [normal 3.97–4.94]), and normal thyroid function and serum IgE levels. Stool cultures, Clostridium difficile toxin, Cryptosporidium, Vibrio cholerae, AFB stains, and ova/parasite exams were all negative.
objective.advanced_workup: T-lymphocyte subset analysis revealed severe immunosuppression: absolute CD4+ count 89.91 cells/mm3 (11.1%; normal 400–1,600), absolute CD8+ count 427.68 cells/mm3 (52.8%), and CD4/CD8 ratio 0.21. Colonoscopy was normal. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) revealed white esophageal plaques consistent with esophageal candidiasis and focal duodenal mucosal erosions with villous blunting (rapid urease test negative for Helicobacter pylori). Gastric and duodenal mucosal biopsies demonstrated active gastroduodenitis with dense mucosal eosinophilic infiltration (20 eosinophils/HPF) and no opportunistic microorganisms, diagnostic of eosinophilic gastroenteritis (EGE).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Primary mucosal eosinophilic gastroenteritis (EGE, confirmed by gastroduodenal biopsies showing >=20 eosinophils/HPF without peripheral eosinophilia or elevated IgE after comprehensive exclusion of enteric opportunistic parasites/bacteria and a 2-week rifampicin dechallenge) and concurrent esophageal candidiasis in a 57-year-old male with advanced virologically failing HIV-1 infection (plasma HIV-1 RNA 1,259,309 copies/mL by TaqMan PCR, CD4+ count 89.91 cells/mm3, CD4/CD8 ratio 0.21) and pulmonary tuberculosis. Oral prednisolone (40 mg daily) rapidly controlled his diarrhea, and after a diarrheal relapse during a 2-month steroid taper, re-initiation of oral prednisolone (60 mg daily tapered to 40 mg daily maintenance) achieved complete remission of diarrhea and an 18 kg weight gain at 6-month follow-up.

raw_case_text:
A 56-year-old man with no significant medical history presented to hospital with right hemiparesis which had developed gradually over 2-3 days. He had recently immigrated to Israel from Russia, spoke very little Hebrew and worked as a janitor. After initial workup, as the symptoms had lasted for over 24 hours, the patient was admitted to the internal medicine department with suspected stroke since there were no vacant beds in the neurology department. Vital signs were normal at admission. The patient's general appearance was unkempt; substance abuse, promiscuous sexual activity and exotic travel were denied. His physical examination revealed normal heart sounds without murmurs and bilateral vesicular breathing sounds on both lungs. The abdomen was soft and non-tender without any evidence of organomegaly. There was no evidence of pedal oedema. Skin examination revealed tinea unguium on all digits of the left hand. The patient had prominent facial seborrheic dermatitis. Neurological examination revealed mild seventh cranial nerve palsy on the left with right hemiparesis (strength of 3/5 in the right lower and upper limbs). Further investigation revealed abnormal liver function tests with elevated AST (139 IU/l), ALT (85 IU/l) and GGT (282 IU/l). CT of the brain (without contrast material) was normal. An electrocardiogram showed normal sinus rhythm. A posterior-anterior chest x-ray was normal.
Routine workup and management of stroke in a middle-aged adult were initiated upon admission. The patient's comparatively young age, low socioeconomic status and the fact that he was an immigrant, along with the dermatological findings, suggested CNS infection should be ruled out. Serological testing using the HIV combo test and immunoblot assay, HBV-hepatitis B core antigen (S/CO) and hepatitis B anti-surface (HbsAg) antibody (mlU/ml) including hepatitis Be antigen, HCV-hepatitis C antibody (S/CO) and syphilis-RPR, were all positive (Table 1). The CD4 count was 230 cells/mm3. The opening pressure of a lumbar puncture was 160 cm H2O. The CSF cell count was 66 cells/mm3 (PMN cells and mononuclear cells), the protein level was elevated (64 mg/dl), and glucose and lactate levels were within the normal range. CSF real-time PCR was positive for JC virus but negative for cryptococcal antigen, Toxoplasma gondii, Toxoplasma gondii IGM and syphilis VDRL. Culture for mycobacteria was negative.
The initial CT scan of the brain mentioned above was normal. However, MRI of the brain showed subacute stroke in the medulla together with general subcortical microangiopathic changes. Several characteristic findings associated with neurosyphilis were also seen. These included general atrophy, mesial temporal atrophy (Fig. 1) as well as an infarct in the midline medulla and left pyramid (Figs. 2 and 3). Further CT angiographic studies ruled out large-vessel vasculitis and other significant vascular anomalies. Trans-thoracic echocardiography showed no evidence of endocarditis.
After a working diagnosis of neurosyphilis was established, the patient was treated with intra-muscular benzathine penicillin G (for syphilis) and intravenous penicillin G sodium (for neurosyphilis) for 10 days. There was no Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction. Anti-retroviral treatment with a combination of dolutegravir, tenofovir and emtricitabine for HIV was also initiated. The patient received daily physiotherapy. Neurological improvement was noted and after 30 days of hospitalization, the patient was discharged and referred for continued rehabilitation.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 56-year-old male recent Russian immigrant to Israel presented with a 2-to-3-day history of gradually progressive right-sided hemiparesis.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Over the 2–3 days prior to hospital admission, the patient experienced gradually progressive weakness of his right upper and lower extremities lasting >24 hours before presentation.
subjective.past_medical_history: No previously known medical history; recently immigrated from Russia to Israel, working as a janitor. Denied substance abuse, high-risk sexual activity, or exotic travel.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for progressive right upper and lower limb weakness.

objective.physical_examination: Unkempt general appearance with normal vital signs, normal heart and lung auscultation, and a soft non-tender abdomen without organomegaly or pedal edema. Cutaneous examination revealed prominent facial seborrheic dermatitis and left-hand tinea unguium (onychomycosis) involving all five digits. Neurological examination demonstrated a mild left cranial nerve VII palsy and right hemiparesis (MRC muscle strength 3/5 in the right upper and lower extremities) consistent with a left medullary/pyramidal syndrome.
objective.routine_investigations: Liver function tests were elevated: AST 139 IU/L, ALT 85 IU/L, and GGT 282 IU/L. Serological workup was positive for fourth-generation HIV Ag/Ab combo and confirmatory HIV immunoblot, positive for HBV (anti-HBc, HBsAg/anti-HBs, HBeAg), positive for anti-HCV antibody, and positive for serum RPR. ECG and chest X-ray were normal.
objective.advanced_workup: Admission CD4+ T-cell count was 230 cells/mm3. Initial non-contrast head CT, CT angiography (excluding large-vessel vasculitis), and transthoracic echocardiography were normal. Brain MRI demonstrated an acute/subacute infarction in the midline medulla and left medullary pyramid alongside generalized cerebral and mesial temporal atrophy and subcortical microangiopathy. Lumbar puncture revealed opening pressure of 160 mmH2O, CSF pleocytosis (66 cells/mm3, mixed PMNs and mononuclear cells), elevated CSF protein (64 mg/dL), normal CSF glucose and lactate, positive CSF real-time PCR for JC virus, and negative CSF VDRL, cryptococcal antigen, Toxoplasma PCR/IgM, and mycobacterial culture.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Meningovascular neurosyphilis presenting with an acute left medullary pyramidal ischemic stroke (contralateral right hemiparesis and ipsilateral left facial nerve palsy) and concurrent CSF JC virus detection in a 56-year-old man with newly diagnosed HIV-1 (positive HIV combo and immunoblot, CD4+ count 230 cells/mm3), HBV, and HCV co-infections. Treated with intravenous aqueous penicillin G sodium for 10 days plus intramuscular benzathine penicillin G (without Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction), initiation of antiretroviral therapy with dolutegravir, tenofovir, and emtricitabine, and inpatient physical therapy, achieving neurological improvement and discharge to rehabilitation after 30 days.

raw_case_text:
A 27-year-old Thai male with AIDS from Saraburi Province presented with acute abdominal pain that had lasted for 4 days. He originated from Mukdahan Province, in Northeastern Thailand, but had moved to Saraburi Province which is situated in the southern part of Northeastern Thailand, 200 km from Bangkok. He denied other travel histories outside these areas during the past year. He was diagnosed with AIDS 2 months before at another hospital, which recorded an initial CD4 count of 91 cells/mm3 (unknown percentage and HIV viral load) and no complete immune status evaluation was performed. At the time, he presented with respiratory distress which was later identified as pneumocystis pneumonia and presumptive smear-negative pulmonary tuberculosis. He was given a 3-week course of trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole, and anti-tuberculosis treatment consisting of isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol during hospitalization. Anti-retroviral therapy (ART) comprising tenofovir disoproxil fumarate, emtricitabine, and efavirenz was introduced 2 weeks later when he was an outpatient.
