The anti-tuberculosis regimen was adjusted to isoniazid, rifampicin, ethambutol, and levofloxacin after 4 days, and a chest radiograph demonstrated complete resolution of prior pulmonary opacities after 50 days of treatment. He reported 100% adherence to both anti-tuberculosis treatment and ART and no other new medications had been added to the regimen. The CD4 count 8 weeks before this admission was 91 cells/mm3 (unknown percentage).
At this admission, he presented with abdominal pain mainly in the left upper quadrant that he described as a dull ache, without radiation. The pain was not related to eating food, physical activity, or position. He reported no other associated gastrointestinal complaints such as diarrhea or nausea. Two days later, he developed a high-grade fever without chills, with the highest temperature of 38.9  C. Abdominal pain persisted and partially responded to acetaminophen. In response to this, he attended the emergency department where a physical examination revealed a blood pressure of 120/75 mmHg, a heart rate of 110 beats/min, a temperature of 38.7  C, and a respiration rate of 20 breaths/min. His abdomen was soft, normal bowel sounds were heard, but tenderness on palpation in the left upper quadrant was evident. The spleen could not be palpated. The remaining physical examination was unremarkable including a negative complete skin examination, with no cutaneous lesions on his face, trunk, or extremities, and a neurological examination within normal limits.
Initial laboratory investigations revealed hemoglobin levels of 9.8 g/dL, a white blood cell count of 14,000 cells/mm3, and a platelet count of 225,000 cells/mm3 on a complete blood count. Serum galactomannan (GM) levels by Platelia enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) (BioRad)  were 6.84. The CD4 count on admission was 272 cells/mm3 (19%). A fungal blood culture obtained on hospital day 1 grew white to tan-colored, velvety and flat colonies with red soluble pigment (Figure 1) on day 9. Direct microscopic examination of the colonies with lactophenol cotton blue staining demonstrated septate hyphae and smooth conidia aloft phialides directly borne on metulae (Figure 2). A bone marrow culture grew similar colonies to the blood specimen (Figure 3) on day 12 after the procedure. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the abdomen revealed a small hypodense lesion with a thin enhancing rim at the spleen and extensive intra-abdominal lymphadenopathy (Figure 4). At the time, the patient was not able to provide sputum sample for culture and due to the high-risk procedure, intra-abdominal lymph node biopsy for culture and histologic analysis was not performed.
Because of a concern of disseminated fungal infection on admission, empirical intravenous amphotericin B deoxycholate was given at a dose of 1.5 mg/kg/day for 7 days. This was switched to liposomal amphotericin B at 3.2 mg/kg/day in response to acute kidney injury for a total of 21 days. Before discharge, a loading dose of itraconazole was initiated at 600 mg/day for 3 days, then 400 mg/day for the maintenance phase. Of note, plasma itraconazole levels drawn on day 4 were 0.13 mcg/mL, with the highest value throughout the treatment course of 0.21 mcg/mL. The patient continued to improve clinically and was discharged from the hospital after 29 days. Repeat imaging was initially planned at 6 months but was deferred at the patient's request. Serum GM levels 9 months after therapy had declined to 0.11, and he remained asymptomatic at the 12-month follow-up.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 27-year-old Thai male with recently diagnosed AIDS presented with a 4-day history of dull left upper quadrant abdominal pain and a 2-day history of high-grade fever up to 38.9 °C, 6 weeks after initiating antiretroviral therapy.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Diagnosed with AIDS 2 months earlier (baseline CD4+ count 91 cells/mm3) after presenting with Pneumocystis pneumonia and smear-negative pulmonary tuberculosis, the patient was treated with 3 weeks of TMP-SMX, anti-tuberculosis therapy (isoniazid, rifampicin, ethambutol, and levofloxacin), and ART initiated 6 weeks prior to current admission (tenofovir disoproxil fumarate, emtricitabine, and efavirenz) with 100% adherence and complete chest X-ray resolution at day 50. Four days prior to admission, he developed constant dull left upper quadrant abdominal pain unrelated to meals or posture, followed 2 days later by high fever (38.9 °C).
subjective.past_medical_history: AIDS diagnosed 2 months prior (baseline CD4+ count 91 cells/mm3); recent Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia and smear-negative pulmonary tuberculosis 2 months prior. Originated from Mukdahan Province and resided in Saraburi Province, Northeastern Thailand (non-endemic for talaromycosis).
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for dull left upper quadrant pain and high-grade fever (38.9 °C); negative for chills, nausea, diarrhea, or skin lesions. Home medications: tenofovir disoproxil fumarate, emtricitabine, efavirenz, isoniazid, rifampicin, ethambutol, and levofloxacin (100% adherent).

objective.physical_examination: Admission vital signs: temperature 38.7 °C, heart rate 110 beats/min, blood pressure 120/75 mmHg, and respiratory rate 20 breaths/min. Abdominal examination revealed left upper quadrant tenderness without palpable splenomegaly or peritonitis; complete skin and neurological examinations were normal.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission CBC showed hemoglobin 9.8 g/dL, leukocytosis (WBC 14,000 cells/mm3), and platelets 225,000 cells/mm3. Serum Platelia Aspergillus galactomannan (GM) ELISA index was markedly elevated at 6.84 (declining to 0.11 at 9 months).
objective.advanced_workup: Admission CD4+ T-cell count had risen to 272 cells/mm3 (19%; up from 91 cells/mm3 8 weeks earlier). Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT demonstrated a small rim-enhancing hypodense splenic lesion and extensive intra-abdominal lymphadenopathy. Both hospital day 1 fungal blood culture (after 9 days) and bone marrow aspirate culture (after 12 days) grew flat velvety colonies producing characteristic diffusible red pigment at 25 °C with lactophenol cotton blue microscopy showing septate hyphae and smooth conidia on phialides borne on metulae, confirming Talaromyces marneffei.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Unmasking disseminated Talaromyces marneffei infection (fungemia, bone marrow involvement, splenic lesion, and extensive intra-abdominal lymphadenitis without cutaneous lesions) presenting as immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) 6 weeks after ART initiation in a 27-year-old Thai male with AIDS (CD4+ count rising from 91 to 272 cells/mm3 [19%]; confirmed by blood and bone marrow cultures and cross-reactive serum galactomannan index of 6.84). Treated with intravenous amphotericin B deoxycholate (1.5 mg/kg/day for 7 days, switched due to acute kidney injury to liposomal amphotericin B 3.2 mg/kg/day to complete 21 days) followed by oral itraconazole (600 mg/day loading for 3 days, then 400 mg/day maintenance; plasma itraconazole level 0.13–0.21 µg/mL due to rifampicin/efavirenz induction). He was discharged on hospital day 29 and remained asymptomatic at 12-month follow-up with serum galactomannan index reduced to 0.11.

raw_case_text:
An 18 year old was diagnosed with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) by routine testing at his pediatrician's office and was referred to adolescent HIV clinic. His initial concern at diagnosis was some diarrhea that resolved without intervention. He remained worried about the weight loss from the diarrhea because he had always been what he considered to be "too thin". His weight returned to baseline by his second visit to our clinic. He reported prior diagnoses of schizophrenia and bipolar disorder in childhood, and was taking olanzapine and aripiprazole. He denied use of tobacco, alcohol or any recreational drugs. He delayed starting antiretroviral therapy for 2 years due to fear of side effects. He had read about atazanavir on the internet, and knew that discoloration of the eyes was a side effect. We discussed other options but he remained very fearful. He was aware of his viral load (26,400 copies/ml) and his CD4+ T cell count (660 cells/ul), and deferred antiretroviral therapy (ART).
At the age of 20 years, after some therapy sessions related to anxiety, he agreed to begin ART, initiating with emtricitabine-tenofovir, darunavir and ritonavir. His CD4+ T cell count at that time was 432 cells/ul (16%) and his HIV viral load count was 14,022 copies/ml. Four months later his CD4+ T cell count was 884 cells/ul and his HIV viral load was undetectable.
At the age of 23 the patient began requesting an appetite stimulant, stating that he was still "too thin". His height was 172 cm, weight 59Kg and body mass index (BMI) was 19 (normal 18.5-24). This data was discussed with him and we did not prescribe an appetite stimulant, but gave dietary recommendations for increasing weight and referred to a dietician. Two months later he began reporting knee and ankle pain from "exercise". He began to develop various joint complains including heel, knee and right hip pain. The right hip pain persisted for several months. He subsequently began to appear cushinoid and his BMI increased to 23. He had developed moon facies and striae on his abdomen.
At this time he reported obtaining a prescription 4 months earlier for 40 mg a day of megestrol from his primary care doctor to "improve my appetite because I have HIV". He further reported that he had increased the dose to 400 mg a day to make it work faster because he was fearful that people would see him looking thin and think he had acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS).
An x-ray of his hips with arthroscopy confirmed bilateral femoral head osteonecrosis with increased degeneration on the right side (Fig. 1). Surgery was recommended but he was fearful of surgery and would not consider it at that time.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 23-year-old HIV-positive man on suppressive antiretroviral therapy presented with bilateral knee, ankle, heel, and persistent right hip pain accompanied by rapid weight gain, moon facies, and abdominal striae after self-escalating oral megestrol acetate.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Diagnosed with HIV at age 18 (baseline CD4+ count 660 cells/µL, viral load 26,400 copies/mL) with body image anxiety about looking 'too thin', he initiated emtricitabine-tenofovir, darunavir, and ritonavir at age 20 (at CD4+ count 432 cells/µL [16%], viral load 14,022 copies/mL), achieving viral suppression and CD4+ recovery to 884 cells/µL within 4 months. At age 23 (with a normal BMI of 19 kg/m2), after the HIV clinic declined to prescribe an appetite stimulant, he obtained a prescription for megestrol acetate 40 mg/day from his primary care physician and self-escalated the dose to 400 mg/day over 4 months to avoid appearing thin, subsequently developing Cushingoid features and persistent right hip, knee, ankle, and heel pain.
subjective.past_medical_history: HIV infection diagnosed at age 18; childhood diagnoses of schizophrenia and bipolar disorder. Denied tobacco, alcohol, or recreational drug use.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for persistent right hip pain, knee/ankle/heel arthralgias, rapid weight gain, facial rounding, and abdominal striae. Home medications: emtricitabine-tenofovir, darunavir, ritonavir, olanzapine, aripiprazole, and self-escalated megestrol acetate 400 mg daily.

objective.physical_examination: Prior to megestrol use at age 23: height 172 cm, weight 59 kg, BMI 19 kg/m2 (normal 18.5–24). Four months after starting high-dose megestrol combined with ritonavir: overtly Cushingoid appearance with moon facies, abdominal violaceous/cutaneous striae, and BMI increased to 23 kg/m2.
objective.routine_investigations: Hip radiographs (combined with hip arthroscopy) demonstrated bilateral femoral head osteonecrosis (avascular necrosis) with more advanced degenerative collapse on the right side.
objective.advanced_workup: CD4+ T-cell count was 660 cells/µL at age 18, 432 cells/µL (16%) at ART initiation at age 20, and 884 cells/µL at 4 months on ART. Hip arthroscopy confirmed bilateral femoral head osteonecrosis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Iatrogenic Cushing syndrome and bilateral femoral head osteonecrosis (avascular necrosis, right worse than left) induced by high-dose megestrol acetate (self-escalated from 40 to 400 mg/day) potentiated by CYP3A4 inhibition from ritonavir in a 23-year-old man with virologically suppressed HIV infection (undetectable HIV viral load, CD4+ count 884 cells/µL on emtricitabine-tenofovir and darunavir/ritonavir). Orthopedic surgery was recommended for bilateral femoral head osteonecrosis, which the patient deferred due to fear of surgery.

raw_case_text:
A 28-year-old male patient with a history of HIV/AIDS complicated by numerous prior opportunistic infections, presented with progressive dyspnea on exertion and chronic, nonproductive cough. He also endorsed night sweats, chills, and nonbloody diarrhea, as well as weight loss over a period of a few months. He had been off antiretroviral therapy (ART) for the past 2 years. He had a history of intravenous drug use and resided at a rehabilitation facility.
On presentation, he was afebrile with unremarkable vital signs and normal oxygen saturation on room air. Physical examination was only notable for oral thrush, shotty right anterior cervical and submandibular lymphadenopathy, and faint inspiratory crackles on chest auscultation. No abnormal lesions were noted on a thorough skin examination.
Laboratory analysis was notable for a white blood count of 3 x 103/mm3and hemoglobin of 9.6 g/dL. CD4 count was 3 cells/mm3and viral load was 2,990,000 copies/mL. Renal, hepatic, and thyroid function, as well as electrolytes, were all within normal limits.
Initial chest radiograph was unremarkable. Computerized tomography (CT) of the chest showed multiple bilateral, right greater than left-sided, ill-defined peribronchovascular ground-glass nodules [Figure 1]. CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis with contrast showed periportal, celiac, mesenteric, and retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy, as well as several low-density lesions in the liver.
An extensive infectious investigation, including blood, sputum, and fungal cultures, and viral and fungal serologies, was negative. Initial bronchoscopy was remarkable for the absence of oral, laryngeal or endobronchial lesions, and bronchoalveolar lavage was negative. Bone marrow biopsy showed myeloid maturation arrest consistent with AIDS with no evidence of lymphoma or KS.
Sequential thallium 201 and gallium 67 scintigraphy was notable for abnormal delayed thallium uptake in and the absence of gallium uptake, raising concern for pulmonary KS over lymphoproliferative disorders or opportunistic infections [Figure 2]. Based on these findings, the patient underwent an ultrasound-guided core biopsy of a sub-centimeter submandibular lymph node which revealed central sarcomatoid proliferation with positive immunohistochemical staining for CD31, CD34, and HHV-8, confirming the diagnosis of KS [Figure 3].
Treatment with doxorubicin was initiated, and ART was resumed. On completion of two cycles of chemotherapy, the patient developed worsening pancytopenia and neutropenic fever. Repeat thoracic imaging was notable for significant progression of the ill-defined peribronchovascular infiltrates, interlobular septal thickening, and mediastinal and hilar lymphadenopathy [Figure 4]. The patient's course was complicated by bland alveolar hemorrhage due to progressive pulmonary KS and severe thrombocytopenia. Repeat bronchoscopy revealed characteristic red to slightly violaceous macular lesions in the endobronchial tree, not seen on examination 2 months prior [Figure 5]. The patient was deemed too ill to tolerate further chemotherapy or radiation for treatment of KS. His symptoms worsened, and he expired shortly thereafter.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 28-year-old male with advanced untreated HIV/AIDS presented with a several-month history of progressive exertional dyspnea, chronic nonproductive cough, night sweats, chills, non-bloody diarrhea, and weight loss.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Having discontinued antiretroviral therapy 2 years earlier, the patient experienced progressively worsening shortness of breath on exertion and a chronic dry cough over several months, accompanied by drenching night sweats, chills, watery non-bloody diarrhea, and unintentional weight loss.
subjective.past_medical_history: History of HIV/AIDS complicated by multiple prior opportunistic infections; off antiretroviral therapy for the past 2 years; history of intravenous drug use, currently residing at an inpatient rehabilitation facility.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for progressive exertional dyspnea, dry cough, night sweats, chills, non-bloody diarrhea, weight loss, and oral thrush; negative for cutaneous lesions.

objective.physical_examination: On admission, afebrile with normal vital signs and normal room-air oxygen saturation. Physical examination revealed oropharyngeal candidiasis (thrush), shotty right anterior cervical and submandibular lymphadenopathy, faint bilateral inspiratory pulmonary crackles, and a completely normal skin examination without mucocutaneous Kaposi sarcoma lesions.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission labs showed leukopenia (WBC 3.0 x 10^3/mm3) and anemia (hemoglobin 9.6 g/dL), with normal renal, hepatic, and thyroid function and normal electrolytes. Blood, sputum, and fungal cultures as well as viral and fungal serologies were negative. Initial chest radiograph was unremarkable.
objective.advanced_workup: Admission CD4+ T-cell count was 3 cells/mm3. Chest CT demonstrated bilateral (right greater than left) ill-defined peribronchovascular ground-glass nodules; contrast-enhanced abdomen/pelvis CT showed periportal, celiac, mesenteric, and retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy and multiple hypodense hepatic lesions. Initial bronchoscopy and BAL were negative for endobronchial lesions or pathogens, and bone marrow biopsy showed AIDS-related myeloid maturation arrest without lymphoma or KS. Sequential Thallium-201 and Gallium-67 scintigraphy revealed delayed thallium-avid, gallium-negative pulmonary uptake characteristic of Kaposi sarcoma, and ultrasound-guided core biopsy of a sub-centimeter submandibular lymph node confirmed Kaposi sarcoma (central sarcomatoid spindle-cell proliferation positive for CD31, CD34, and HHV-8). Repeat chest CT and bronchoscopy 2 months later (after 2 cycles of doxorubicin and ART resumption) demonstrated marked progression of peribronchovascular infiltrates, interlobular septal thickening, hilar/mediastinal lymphadenopathy, bland alveolar hemorrhage, and new red-to-violaceous endobronchial macular KS lesions.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Visceral/nodal and bronchopulmonary Kaposi sarcoma presenting without cutaneous involvement in a 28-year-old male with advanced AIDS (CD4+ count 3 cells/mm3, plasma HIV viral load 2,990,000 copies/mL), confirmed by thallium-positive/gallium-negative lung scintigraphy, CD31+/CD34+/HHV-8+ submandibular lymph node core biopsy, and subsequent endobronchial violaceous macules on repeat bronchoscopy. Despite resumption of ART and two cycles of systemic doxorubicin chemotherapy, the patient developed worsening pancytopenia, neutropenic fever, severe thrombocytopenia, progressive pulmonary KS (possibly exacerbated by KS-IRIS), and diffuse alveolar hemorrhage, and died shortly thereafter.

raw_case_text:
The patient is a chronically ill 8-year-old boy from Limpopo province in South Africa, living with his adoptive parents. He was born prematurely at 7 months' gestation, weighing 1.9 kg. There was a history of recent travel to the Kruger National Park, and to India 6 months prior to admission. All his vaccinations were up to date on history, but this was never confirmed. He was markedly underweight for his age (with weight-for-age and height-for-age z scores of -2 and -1, respectively, and body mass index of 13) with a 2-year history of abdominal distension, diarrhoea, failure to thrive and drenching night sweats. There was no history of chronic cough. His treatment up to the time of admission included nutritional and iron supplements and repeated courses of antibiotics. No clinical improvement was achieved with this management.
The patient was referred to a paediatric gastroenterologist in October 2016. He was acutely ill, severely wasted (17 kg) and pyrexial (39  C). He was clinically pale with a tachycardia and mild oedema of his lower limbs. Hepatosplenomegaly was detected, although there was no peripheral lymphadenopathy. His abdomen was severely distended, and he had recurrent diarrhoea and vomiting with marked intolerance of all foods.
Abdominal computed tomography (CT) scan and ultrasound revealed massively enlarged intra-abdominal lymph nodes (see Figure 1) with a moth-eaten appearance of the spleen. Prominent collateral circulation was seen, which was suggestive of portal hypertension.
Laboratory investigations confirmed that the patient was HIV-infected with a CD4 count of 59 cells/muL (7%) and HIV viral load of 453 780 copies/mL (log10 5.66). Further testing revealed mildly elevated liver enzymes. Moderate proteinuria was present and the faecal alpha-1 antitrypsin result was in keeping with a protein-losing enteropathy. His blood count showed microcytic hypochromic anaemia, with the iron function studies reflecting a pattern of reticuloendothelial iron blockade (see Table 1).
The differential diagnosis included tuberculosis or lymphoma. Over a period of 7 months, endoscopically and surgically obtained biopsy material was submitted for histology (see Table 2). Histological images of the duodenum and a lymph node are shown in Figure 2. The findings were consistent with non-tuberculous mycobacterial infection.
Further testing of the biopsy specimens included mycobacterial cultures, all of which showed no growth. Acid-fast bacilli (AFB) were noted during the processing of the tissue samples obtained from the intra-abdominal lymph nodes on 12 October 2016, and again in biopsy material obtained on 08 March 2017. Microscopy performed on a stool sample on 26 March 2017 also showed acid-fast organisms with a coccoid appearance. The polymerase chain reaction (PCR) assay for Mycobacterium avium complex was negative (artus  Mycobac. diff. LC PCR from Qiagen, Germany). Numerous PCR assays for Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex were negative, which include Nanogen (Nanogen Inc., San Diego, CA, USA), BD MAX (BD Diagnostics, Sparks, MD) and the Xpert  MTB/RIF assay (Cepheid Inc., CA, USA). The urinary lipoarabinomannan test conducted on 22 March 2017 was positive.
A cytomegalovirus (CMV) viraemia of 3974 copies/mL (log10 3.60) was measured in March 2017 together with a colon biopsy that was PCR positive for CMV. The Epstein Barr viral load at the time was 9318 copies/mL (log10 3.97).
Anti-mycobacterial treatment was started (rifampicin, isoniazid, ethambutol, pyrazinamide and clarithromycin) followed 4 weeks later with antiretroviral therapy (abacavir, lamivudine and efavirenz). The patient's HIV viral load was undetectable at 3 months, and his CD4 count at that stage was 101 cells/muL (6%). Clinically and radiologically, however, there was no improvement in his abdominal signs and symptoms. Malabsorption and refeeding syndrome was considered, and all treatment, including ganciclovir, was given intravenously. His antiretroviral medication was temporarily suspended until oral feeding could be tolerated. Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) was considered, and methylprednisone was initiated (1 mg/kg/dose) for 4 weeks, after which the dosage was tapered and stopped. The patient was given a period of bowel rest and free drainage, after which he was placed on an elemental diet. There was no clinical improvement and liver dysfunction worsened (see Table 1), and hence a decision was made to stop rifampicin, isoniazid and pyrazinamide.
In May 2017, a diagnosis of Mycobacterium genavense was made, based on sequencing of a mycobacterial 16S rRNA PCR product. This identity was subsequently confirmed using the HAIN Lifescience GenoType (Nehren, Germany) Mycobacterium AS assay that was performed directly on a histology specimen from May 2017. As a result of this finding, and in consultation with an infectious disease specialist and microbiologist, treatment was changed to include moxifloxacin, azithromycin and rifabutin for 2 years, with amikacin for the first 3 months. Methylprednisone was also restarted. Antiretroviral therapy, together with cotrimoxazole prophylaxis, was continued.
The patient's response to the new regimen was slow, and initially he was unable to tolerate food. Insertion of a nasogastric tube was required for continuous feeds together with total parenteral nutrition. At the time of writing this article (17 months of treatment completed), his clinical response had improved. He was able to tolerate small regular meals with no nausea, vomiting or diarrhoea. His weight gain had been slow (now up to 20 kg) despite nutritional supplementation. The hepatosplenomegaly and abdominal distension had improved markedly, and his HIV remains virologically suppressed.
Dr R. de Gama obtained consent from the patient's parents to publish this case report.

subjective.chief_complaint: An 8-year-old boy from Limpopo Province, South Africa, was referred in October 2016 with a 2-year history of progressive abdominal distension, chronic diarrhea, vomiting, severe failure to thrive, and drenching night sweats.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Over the 2 years preceding paediatric gastroenterology referral, the child suffered from severe abdominal distension, chronic diarrhea, emesis, marked food intolerance, failure to thrive, and drenching night sweats that failed to improve with iron/nutritional supplementation and repeated antibiotic courses.
subjective.past_medical_history: Born prematurely at 7 months' gestation (birth weight 1.9 kg), living with adoptive parents in Limpopo Province; travel history to Kruger National Park and to India 6 months prior to admission.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for 2-year abdominal distension, chronic diarrhea, vomiting, food intolerance, failure to thrive, fever, and drenching night sweats; negative for chronic cough.

objective.physical_examination: Acutely ill, severely wasted (weight 17 kg; weight-for-age z-score -2, height-for-age z-score -1, BMI 13 kg/m2), febrile (39.0 °C), pale, and tachycardic with mild bilateral lower limb pitting edema, severe abdominal distension, and hepatosplenomegaly without peripheral lymphadenopathy.
objective.routine_investigations: Labs showed microcytic hypochromic anemia with reticuloendothelial iron blockade, mildly elevated hepatic transaminases, moderate proteinuria, and elevated fecal alpha-1 antitrypsin diagnostic of protein-losing enteropathy. Urinary lipoarabinomannan (LAM) assay (March 2017) was positive, stool AFB microscopy (March 2017) showed coccoid acid-fast organisms, plasma CMV viral load was 3,974 copies/mL (log10 3.60), and plasma EBV viral load was 9,318 copies/mL (log10 3.97). Abdominal ultrasound showed massive intra-abdominal lymphadenopathy and splenic lesions.
objective.advanced_workup: Baseline CD4+ T-cell count was 59 cells/µL (7%; rising to 101 cells/µL [6%] at 3 months on ART). Abdominal CT demonstrated massive mesenteric/retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy, a 'moth-eaten' spleen, and portal collateral circulation consistent with portal hypertension. Endoscopic duodenal, colonic (CMV PCR positive), and surgical intra-abdominal lymph node biopsies (October 2016 and March 2017) showed sheets of foamy histiocytes loaded with acid-fast bacilli, while liquid/solid mycobacterial cultures failed to grow and PCRs for M. tuberculosis complex (Xpert MTB/RIF, BD MAX, Nanogen) and M. avium complex were negative. In May 2017, direct 16S rRNA PCR sequencing and Hain GenoType Mycobacterium AS line-probe assay on tissue confirmed Mycobacterium genavense.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Disseminated intestinal, nodal, and hepatosplenic Mycobacterium genavense infection causing severe protein-losing enteropathy and portal hypertension, complicated by CMV colitis/viremia and paradoxical/persistent abdominal IRIS, in an 8-year-old boy with newly diagnosed advanced HIV infection (baseline plasma HIV viral load 453,780 copies/mL [log10 5.66], CD4+ count 59 cells/µL [7%]). After failing initial empiric anti-TB/MAC therapy (rifampicin, isoniazid, ethambutol, pyrazinamide, and clarithromycin; stopped for hepatotoxicity and lack of response), definitive molecular identification of fastidious M. genavense in May 2017 prompted a 2-year targeted regimen of moxifloxacin, azithromycin, and rifabutin plus intravenous amikacin for the first 3 months, alongside IV ganciclovir for CMV, methylprednisolone (1 mg/kg) for IRIS, TPN/nasogastric elemental nutrition, cotrimoxazole prophylaxis, and abacavir/lamivudine/efavirenz. At 17 months of targeted therapy, his HIV viral load remained undetectable, hepatosplenomegaly and diarrhea resolved, and his weight increased to 20 kg.

raw_case_text:
A 52-year-old male of Asian-origin was referred for the diagnosis of multiple lesions in the oral cavity. The patient reported to be HIV-seropositive for 12 years, during which he did not follow the antiretroviral treatment adequately as he took medications on an intermittent basis. When the oral lesions first appeared, T CD4+ was 70 cells/mm3, and the patient changed his behaviour and adhered to the proposed treatment (Lamivudine, Tenofovir and Atazanavir). Four months after cART was initiated, the patient had significant improvement in the immune system and an increase in T CD4+ to 486 cells/mm3 together with undetectable viral load. Concomitantly, the patient observed an marked increase in the amount and size of the oral lesions, which began to be aesthetically and functionally inconvenient, even for daily routine activities, such as mastication. After four years living with the increase in the amount of oral mucosa lesions, the patient sought treatment.
The intraoral clinical examination detected extensive nodular lesions on the entire oral mucosa (i.e. palate, tongue, mouth floor, and alveolar, jugal and labial mucosa), extending to the oropharyngeal region. The lesions were asymptomatic, whitish and erythematous. The majority of the lesions, like those seen in the palate and tongue, were sessile and had a smooth surface, whereas the others were pedunculated and had papillary projections (Figures 1, 2 and 3).
Incisional biopsy was performed and the material obtained was sent for histopathological examination. The sections were stained with hematoxylin and eosin, revealing a mucosal fragment covered with parakeratinised stratified squamous epithelium and acanthosis areas forming either blunt or sharp projections, giving a papillomatous aspect to the epithelium. At higher magnification, one could observe the formation of micro-abscesses, clusters of neutrophils and diffuse presence of koilocyte-like cells (Figure 4). In addition, a tissue sample was submitted to DNA extraction and analyzed by INNO-Lipa HPV genotyping extra II test (INNO-Lipa Innogenetics N.V., Ghent, Belgium), as well as PCR sequencing with generic primers, revealing the presence of HPV-32.
Based on the clinical aspect of the lesions, histopathological findings and detection of HPV-32, it was possible to diagnose the presence of epithelial proliferation due to HPV infection. The unusual clinical presentation raised discussion on the lesions, suggesting that it might be a case of either focal epithelial hyperplasia (FEH), a lesion strongly associated with HPV-32,or condyloma acuminata aggravated by the syndrome of immune reconstitution (SIR).
Due to the extension of lesions in the patient and, consequently, the great number of surgical procedures that would be necessary, as well as the high viral infectivity rate (leading to the possibility of re-contamination of the mucosa during manipulation), treatment based on surgical removal was discarded. The treatment was initiated with topical application of podophyllin and trichloroacetic acid. Nevertheless, the long-term treatment unfortunately made adhesion difficult for the patient, who did not attend the appointments after some sessions.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 52-year-old Asian male with a 12-year history of HIV infection was referred for extensive, functionally and aesthetically debilitating warty and nodular lesions covering his entire oral cavity that had dramatically proliferated 4 months after starting combination antiretroviral therapy 4 years earlier.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Diagnosed with HIV 12 years prior with years of intermittent ART adherence, the patient first noticed oral mucosal lesions when his CD4+ count fell to 70 cells/mm3, prompting strict adherence to lamivudine, tenofovir, and atazanavir. Within 4 months of regular cART—as his CD4+ count surged to 486 cells/mm3 and his HIV viral load became undetectable—the oral lesions underwent explosive proliferation in number and size across the entire oral cavity, interfering with mastication and aesthetics for 4 years before referral.
subjective.past_medical_history: 12-year history of HIV infection; previously poorly adherent to ART, followed for the past 4 years by strict adherence to lamivudine, tenofovir, and atazanavir.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for extensive painless intraoral nodules impairing mastication. Home medications: lamivudine, tenofovir, and atazanavir.

objective.physical_examination: Intraoral examination revealed innumerable asymptomatic whitish-to-erythematous nodular and papillomatous lesions carpeting the entire oral mucosa—including the hard and soft palate, tongue, floor of the mouth, alveolar ridges, buccal mucosa, and labial mucosa—and extending into the oropharynx. Palatal and lingual lesions were predominantly sessile and smooth-surfaced, whereas labial and buccal lesions were pedunculated with papillary projections.
objective.advanced_workup: CD4+ T-cell count had increased from 70 cells/mm3 prior to regular cART to 486 cells/mm3 within 4 months of cART. Incisional oral mucosal biopsy histopathology demonstrated parakeratinized stratified squamous epithelium with marked papillomatous acanthosis forming blunt and sharp projections, epithelial microabscesses with neutrophilic clusters, and diffuse koilocytic changes. Tissue DNA extraction with INNO-LiPA HPV Genotyping Extra II and generic-primer PCR sequencing identified human papillomavirus genotype 32 (HPV-32).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Florid oral HPV-32-associated focal epithelial hyperplasia (Heck disease) / oral condylomata acuminata exacerbated by immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) following rapid CD4+ T-cell recovery (from 70 to 486 cells/mm3 with undetectable HIV viral load on lamivudine, tenofovir, and atazanavir) in a 52-year-old HIV-positive male. Due to pan-mucosal involvement and high risk of intraoperative viral autoinoculation precluding surgical excision, conservative chemical cauterization with serial topical applications of podophyllin and trichloroacetic acid was initiated; however, the patient defaulted from long-term follow-up after several sessions.

raw_case_text:
Patient is a 26-year-old female with a past medical history of HIV. She was infected at age 15 and showed poor adherence to antiretroviral medication. She reported the combined use of Tenofovir, Emtricitabine, and Efavirenz intermittently, mostly because she did not seek adequate healthcare due to feelings of shame about being associated with the disease. She also missed most of her follow-ups in the last year, and had no CD4 counts or viral load tests performed in over 6 months. She also suffered from intermittent episodes of coughing, bloody stools, and weight loss during this time; however, she didn't seek any medical attention.
She presented to our emergency room with a 10-day history of intermittent lower abdominal pain, nausea, biliary vomits and asthenia. Approximately 24 h prior to admittance, the pain became worse. On clinical examination, a dehydrated, hypotensive and tachycardic patient was encountered. Her abdomen was diffusely tender, and the pain became more intense on touch. Laboratory exams revealed mild leukocytosis and neutrophilia. An arterial gasometry revealed metabolic acidosis with hyperlactatemia.
In view of these findings, surgical consultation was requested and a diagnosis of diffuse peritonitis was reached. Aggressive fluid resuscitation with crystalloids was started and an emergency laparotomy was decided. At surgery, the peritoneal cavity was filled with 500 ml of pus and 2 bowel perforations were identified: a 1 x 1 cm perforation in the terminal ileum, 50 cm proximal to the ileocecal valve, and a 3 x 2 cm perforation in the cecum (Fig. 1A-C).
A right colectomy was decided, however, the surgical team had doubts about restoring bowel continuity. Nonetheless, since the patient became stable after reanimation and surgery, restoration was considered feasible. Given the context of an HIV patient with poor controls who would be unlikely able to handle an ileostomy, a primary anastomosis with close surveillance was decided. Resection began 10 cm proximal to the ileal perforation and ended near the hepatic flexure of the colon. Then, a side-to-side ileotransverse anastomosis was performed with 75 mm staples (ETHICON Linear Cutter NTLC75, Johnson & Johnson). Extensive washing of the peritoneal cavity was completed and the remainder of the procedure was performed without complications. Based on the historical, clinical, and laboratory data obtained, we initially considered intestinal perforation due to cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection as the probable etiology of peritonitis, and the differentials included, mycobacterial infections, fungal infections, neoplastic disease or Kaposi sarcoma. However, definitive pathology tests for the cause of the perforation were delayed due to the unavailability of an in-house pathologist. Furthermore, other essential tests including CD4 counts and HIV viral loads and antibodies (both IgM and IgG) were not available at our institution.
This situation was further complicated by the lack of resources from the patient and our hospital; nonetheless, we managed to send a blood sample to a nearby hospital for testing. Even under these harsh conditions, the patient had a good recovery. She was placed under broad-spectrum antibiotics (Piperacillin/Tazobactam) and was given a 3-day cycle of Ganciclovir. Antiretroviral Therapy (ART) was initiated as well. Meanwhile, sips of liquids were initiated on the second postoperative day without complications. She didn't have any episodes of fever, nausea, vomiting or signs of anastomosis leak.
At the 7th postoperative day, the patient requested to leave against medical advice (AMA), she signed the hospital consents and left our facility.
Two days after the patient went AMA, CD4 and HIV viral load results arrived along with the pathology report, revealing chronic inflammation of the resected bowel, and multiple ulcers affecting the mucosa of the ileum and the cecum. Also, multiple granulomas surrounded by inflammatory tissue were recognized, as well as some granulomas within the lymph nodes. Bowel perforation due to tuberculosis was confirmed as the final diagnosis, CD4 cell counts were estimated at 94 cells/mm3, and the viral load was estimated at over 106 genome copies (Fig. 2A-C).
Since tuberculosis in Ecuador is a mandatory declaration disease, we searched for the patient and found her in the coastal region of the country. Fortunately, she was stable and without complications. She was taken by the national healthcare system and admitted to a tertiary hospital for HIV and tuberculosis treatment.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 26-year-old HIV-positive female presented to the emergency room with a 10-day history of intermittent lower abdominal pain, nausea, bilious vomiting, and asthenia that acutely worsened 24 hours prior to admission.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Infected with HIV at age 15 with chronic non-adherence to tenofovir/emtricitabine/efavirenz due to stigma and no clinic follow-up for >6 months, the patient had experienced uninvestigated intermittent cough, hematochezia, and weight loss over the preceding year. Ten days prior to presentation, she developed lower abdominal pain, nausea, bilious emesis, and asthenia, with acute severe exacerbation of abdominal pain 24 hours before arrival.
subjective.past_medical_history: HIV infection diagnosed at age 15 (11-year history) with poor adherence to tenofovir, emtricitabine, and efavirenz.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for 10-day lower abdominal pain (acutely severe for 24 hours), nausea, bilious vomiting, asthenia, and preceding chronic cough, bloody stools, and weight loss. Irregular home use of tenofovir/emtricitabine/efavirenz.

objective.physical_examination: On admission, dehydrated, hypotensive, and tachycardic with diffuse severe abdominal tenderness and peritoneal signs consistent with generalized peritonitis.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission labs demonstrated mild leukocytosis with neutrophilia, and arterial blood gas showed metabolic acidosis with hyperlactatemia.
objective.advanced_workup: Send-out immunological testing reported a CD4+ T-cell count of 94 cells/mm3. Emergency exploratory laparotomy revealed 500 mL of purulent peritoneal fluid and two free intestinal perforations: a 1 x 1 cm perforation in the terminal ileum (50 cm proximal to the ileocecal valve) and a 3 x 2 cm perforation in the cecum. She underwent right hemicolectomy and distal ileal resection with primary stapled side-to-side ileotransverse anastomosis; histopathology of the resected ileocecal specimen and mesenteric lymph nodes demonstrated multiple mucosal ulcers and caseating/granulomatous inflammation diagnostic of intestinal tuberculosis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Simultaneous ileal and cecal tuberculous perforations causing generalized purulent peritonitis in a 26-year-old female with advanced uncontrolled HIV/AIDS (CD4+ count 94 cells/mm3, plasma HIV viral load >10^6 copies/mL; confirmed by resected ileocecal and nodal granulomatous histopathology). Managed with emergent right hemicolectomy and primary ileotransverse anastomosis, peritoneal lavage, broad-spectrum intravenous piperacillin/tazobactam, a 3-day empiric course of ganciclovir (for initially suspected CMV enterocolitis), and re-initiation of antiretroviral therapy. After leaving against medical advice on postoperative day 7 before pathology results returned, she was located by public health authorities in stable condition and admitted to a tertiary hospital for formal anti-tuberculosis and HIV therapy.

raw_case_text:
A 31-year-old man presented to the emergency department in December 2016 with new-onset tonic-clonic seizures, on a background of 19 kg weight loss, progressive lethargy and cognitive decline over the preceding 18 months. He had travelled extensively across the African subcontinent whilst working aboard a ship and during this time had engaged in unprotected intercourse with female sex workers.
Salient examination findings included nystagmus on right-lateral gaze, past-pointing in the left upper limb, brisk reflexes and an unsteady gait, suggestive of underlying cerebellar pathology. Following biochemical and serological investigations, the patient was diagnosed with HIV-1, with a viral load of 1 243 938 copies/mL and a CD4 lymphocyte count of 12 cells/microL. Initial computed tomography (CT) imaging revealed multiple lesions in the brainstem, cerebellum, basal ganglia and both cerebral hemispheres, with significant local mass effect and effacement of the left lateral ventricle. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain was also undertaken at this time, which demonstrated multiple ring-enhancing lesions (Figure 1). Mediastinal and hilar lymph node enlargement identified on CT imaging of the chest, abdomen and pelvis was felt to be in keeping with persistent generalised lymphadenopathy (PGL) because of advanced HIV as there was no palpable cervical, axillary or inguinal lymphadenopathy (Figure 2).
The patient was commenced on treatment for presumptive toxoplasmosis, with sulfadiazine/pyramethamine/folinic acid and adjunctive high-dose dexamethasone, levetiracetam. He also simultaneously commenced antiretroviral therapy (ART) comprising of tenofovir/emtricitabine and dolutegravir, along with prophylactic antibiotics and antifungals against opportunistic infections. Blood cultures were negative as was toxoplasma serum Immunoglobulin G (IgG). Tuberculosis with CNS involvement and cryptococcoma were considered as differential diagnoses; however, cryptococcal antigen was negative as subsequently were mycobacterial blood and induced sputum cultures. Cerebrospinal fluid examination was not attempted in light of the cerebellar lesions.
Following 2 weeks of toxoplasmosis treatment, there was no improvement in the appearances of the intra-cranial lesions on repeat MR brain imaging, with two new lesions being identified (Figure 3). At this point, alternative diagnoses such as systemic lymphoma with intra-cranial metastases and PCNSL were pursued over toxoplasmosis. A fluodeoxyglucose positron-emission tomography (FDG-PET-CT) and brain biopsy were, thus, arranged with the aim of obtaining a more definitive diagnosis.
FDG-PET-CT was undertaken 3 weeks following initial presentation and demonstrated high avidity activity only in the brain including the right parietal, right parieto-occipital and left frontal regions as well as the cerebellum and basal ganglia (standardised uptake value [SUV] max 7.3 compared with normal brain cortex). No FDG-avid mediastinal lymph nodes were identified and these appearances pointed towards the diagnosis of PCNSL, rather than systemic lymphoma with cerebral metastases.
The right parietal lobe brain biopsy demonstrated a suspicious lymphoid infiltrate. Mycobacterial and fungal stains were negative as was immunostaining for herpes simplex virus (HSV1), HSV2, cytomegalovirus (CMV) and John Cunningham virus (JCV). Epstein-Barr encoding region (EBER) in situ hybridisation staining was also negative; however, this was a likely false negative result, in the context of necrosis and ribonucleic acid (RNA) degradation. Within the necrotic areas, the cellular outlines and remains were strongly positive for CD20, CD79a and BCL2. They were negative for CD19, CD3, CD5, CD10, BCL6 and PAX5. Final histopathology results were in keeping with a high-grade B-cell lymphoma that was necrotic.
The patient was commenced on MATRix chemotherapy (rituximab, methotrexate, cytarabine, with omission of thioTEPA for the first two cycles) for HIV-associated primary cerebral lymphoma. Within 8 weeks of commencement of highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART), there was a 3log10 fold decrease in HIV-1 viral load. There has also been a marked improvement in cognitive function and gait following four cycles of MATRix chemotherapy (Figure 4).
Repeat MRI imaging 6 months following initial presentation also demonstrates a reduction in volume of the supra and infra-tentorial parenchymal and sub-ependymal lesions, with improvement in the degree of peri-lesional vasogenic oedema, in keeping with a positive disease response (Figure 5). The patient continues to make good progress and is currently being worked up for consolidative therapy with an autologous stem cell transplantation.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 31-year-old man presented to the emergency department in December 2016 with new-onset generalized tonic-clonic seizures superimposed on an 18-month history of 19 kg weight loss, progressive lethargy, and cognitive decline.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Over the 18 months preceding presentation, the patient experienced an unintentional 19 kg weight loss, progressive lethargy, and cognitive deterioration, culminating in acute generalized tonic-clonic seizures in December 2016.
subjective.past_medical_history: Previously healthy merchant seaman; epidemiological history notable for extensive travel across the African subcontinent while working aboard a ship and unprotected sexual intercourse with female commercial sex workers.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for new-onset tonic-clonic seizures, 19 kg weight loss, lethargy, cognitive decline, and gait unsteadiness.

objective.physical_examination: Neurological examination revealed right-lateral gaze-evoked nystagmus, left upper limb dysmetria (past-pointing), generalized hyperreflexia, cognitive impairment, and an ataxic gait, without palpable cervical, axillary, or inguinal lymphadenopathy.
objective.routine_investigations: Blood cultures, mycobacterial blood and induced sputum cultures, serum Toxoplasma IgG, and serum cryptococcal antigen were all negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Admission CD4+ T-lymphocyte count was 12 cells/µL. Head CT and contrast-enhanced brain MRI demonstrated multiple ring-enhancing lesions across the brainstem, cerebellum, basal ganglia, and bilateral cerebral hemispheres with local mass effect and left lateral ventricular effacement (growing with 2 new lesions after 2 weeks of empiric anti-toxoplasmosis therapy). Chest/abdomen/pelvis CT showed mild mediastinal and hilar lymphadenopathy consistent with HIV persistent generalized lymphadenopathy. Whole-body FDG-PET/CT at week 3 showed intense hypermetabolic uptake confined exclusively to the brain lesions (right parietal, right parieto-occipital, left frontal, cerebellum, and basal ganglia; SUVmax 7.3) with no FDG-avid systemic lymphadenopathy. Right parietal lobe brain biopsy confirmed necrotic high-grade B-cell primary CNS lymphoma (tumor cells strongly positive for CD20, CD79a, and BCL2; negative for CD3, CD5, CD10, BCL6, HSV-1/2, CMV, JCV, and fungal/mycobacterial stains).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Multifocal supra- and infratentorial HIV-associated primary central nervous system high-grade B-cell lymphoma (PCNSL: CD20+, CD79a+, BCL2+) unmasking newly diagnosed advanced HIV-1 infection (baseline plasma HIV-1 viral load 1,243,938 copies/mL, CD4+ count 12 cells/µL). After failing 2 weeks of empiric sulfadiazine/pyrimethamine/folinic acid and high-dose dexamethasone for initially suspected cerebral toxoplasmosis (with negative Toxo IgG), FDG-PET/CT and right parietal brain biopsy established PCNSL. Treatment with 4 cycles of MATRix immunochemotherapy (rituximab, high-dose methotrexate, and cytarabine, omitting thiotepa in cycles 1–2) alongside concurrent HAART (tenofovir/emtricitabine and dolutegravir) and levetiracetam achieved a 3-log10 reduction in HIV-1 viral load within 8 weeks, marked recovery of cognition and gait, and substantial supra-/infratentorial tumor regression on 6-month brain MRI prior to planned consolidative autologous stem cell transplantation.

raw_case_text:
A 63-year-old man presented with persistent, gradually aggravating headaches over a period of two months. They were continuous holocranial headaches evolving in a context of impaired general performance status. Subsequently, the patient presented again three weeks later with morning vomiting and complaining of blurred vision. The patient reported having been febrile for the preceding two months. His past medical history was unremarkable and he was not currently on medication. He was then admitted to the hospital of Tunis in September 2018 for an exploration of chronic febrile illness and headaches. The physical examination recorded a temperature of 38.5 C. The neurological exam showed a conscious patient well oriented in space and time who had neither meningeal nor vestibular syndrome. A bilateral paralysis of the sixth cranial nerve was found associated with bilateral hypo-acousia. However, he had no sensori- motor deficit and no neurological localizing signs. An eye fundus revealed a bilateral stage I papilledema. All others clinical examinations were normal. A basic metabolic panel revealed several abnormalities: an elevated C-reactive protein, lymphopenia, hyper-fibrinogenemia, and anemia (Table 1). A cerebral computed tomography scan and magnetic resonance imaging showed normal findings. However, an audiogram showed bilateral perceptive deafness. A lumbar puncture revealed an opening cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) pressure of 350mm of water, protein 0.69 g/L, glucose 0.3mmol/L, and WBC of 60x106/L (80% lymphocytes). An India ink stain was positive for Cryptococcus. CSF and serum cryptococcal antigen tests also returned positive (with titers of 1:10000 and 1:1000 respectively). Blood and CSF culture were positive and revealed the presence of Cryptococcus neoformans. The antifungal sensitivity test was also performed (Table 1). Therefore, a diagnosis of Cryptococcus meningoencephalitis was established.
The search for a cause of immunodeficiency that would explain this opportunistic infection, in a seemingly immuno-competent patient, was initiated. The serological testing for hepatitis B virus (HBV), hepatitis C virus (HCV), and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) were negative (CD4/CD8 ratio was 1.5). Serum protein electrophoresis revealed hypo-albuminemia 23.7 g/l (normal range: 37.7-45.6 g/l) with hypogammaglobulinemia 4.5g/l (normal range: 6.4-12.7g/l). Immunofixation electrophoresis detected monoclonal IgA-lambda (IgA-lambda) paraproteinemia at 0.6 g/l. The urine immunofixation revealed the presence of Bence Jones proteinuria type light chain lambda at 0.4 g/l. The serum level of IgA, IgG, and IgM concentrations were measured at 4.04 g/l (normal range: 0.80-3.1), 5.4 (normal range 6.5-15), and 0.45 g/l (normal range: 0.55-3.0) respectively. Quantitative evaluation of the free light chains showed excessively high lambda (lambda) chains at 183.14 mg/L (normal range: 5.71-26.3 mg/L) and kappa (kappa) chains at 9.47 mg/L (normal range: 3.3-19.4 mg/L) with a kappa/lambda free light chain ratio of <0.1 (normal range: 0.26-1.65). May-Grunwald-Giemsa stained bone marrow aspirate smears revealed an infiltration of 12% malignant plasma cells with atypically formed and partly bi- or multi-nucleated cells (Figure 1). The beta2-microglobulin was elevated at 3.82 mg/L (normal range: 0.8-3 mg/L). Based on these findings, consistent with the International Myeloma Working Group diagnostic criteria, a diagnosis of IgA-lambda multiple myeloma was determined. The patient was treated for the Cryptococcal infection with amphotericin B at 0.7 mg/kg/day concurrently with flucytosine at 100 mg/kg/day. Repeated CSF drainage was established to reduce CSF pressure. The induction treatment lasted 21 days, after which the CSF fungi culture became negative and the cryptococcal antigen test in serum and CSF both showed a decrease in antigen titers to 1: 10. He was then transitioned to oral fluconazole at 800 mg/day for 12 weeks. Upon the second week of consolidation treatment for the infection, the patient s treatment for IgA lambda type multiple myeloma was initiated with a chemotherapy regimen based on thalidomide, melphalan, and prednisone. The evolution was good without complication. No clinical or imaging examination evidence of neurologic complications was found during nine months after this episode.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 63-year-old man presented in September 2018 with a 2-month history of progressive continuous holocranial headaches, persistent fever, and declining performance status, complicated 3 weeks prior to admission by morning vomiting and blurred vision.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Over the 2 months preceding hospital admission in Tunis, the previously healthy patient experienced continuous, progressively worsening holocranial headaches and persistent fevers, followed 3 weeks prior to admission by intracranial hypertension symptoms including morning emesis, blurred vision, diplopia, and bilateral hearing loss.
subjective.past_medical_history: Unremarkable past medical history; taking no chronic medications.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for 2-month continuous headache, fever, general functional decline, morning vomiting, blurred vision, diplopia, and bilateral hearing loss.

objective.physical_examination: On admission, febrile (38.5 °C), conscious, and oriented to time and place without meningeal signs, vestibular syndrome, or sensorimotor deficits. Cranial nerve and ophthalmic examination revealed bilateral sixth cranial nerve (abducens) palsies, bilateral sensorineural hypoacusis (confirmed as bilateral perceptive deafness on pure-tone audiometry), and bilateral Stage I papilledema on fundoscopy.
objective.routine_investigations: Routine blood tests showed anemia, lymphopenia, elevated CRP, and hyperfibrinogenemia. Serologies for HIV, HBV, and HCV were negative. Serum protein electrophoresis, immunofixation, and free light chain assays revealed hypoalbuminemia (23.7 g/L; normal 37.7–45.6), hypogammaglobulinemia (4.5 g/L; normal 6.4–12.7), a monoclonal IgA-lambda paraprotein (0.6 g/L; total serum IgA 4.04 g/L, reduced IgG 5.4 g/L and IgM 0.45 g/L), urinary lambda Bence-Jones proteinuria (0.4 g/L), markedly elevated serum free lambda light chains (183.14 mg/L; normal 5.71–26.3) with free kappa 9.47 mg/L and kappa/lambda ratio <0.1, and elevated beta-2 microglobulin (3.82 mg/L; normal 0.8–3.0). Serum cryptococcal antigen was positive (titer 1:1,000) and blood cultures grew Cryptococcus neoformans.
objective.advanced_workup: CD4/CD8 T-cell ratio was normal at 1.5. Brain CT and MRI were normal. Lumbar puncture revealed severely elevated CSF opening pressure (350 mmH2O), CSF lymphocytic pleocytosis (WBC 60 x 10^6/L; 80% lymphocytes), elevated CSF protein (0.69 g/L), profound hypoglycorrhachia (glucose 0.3 mmol/L), positive CSF India ink stain, positive CSF cryptococcal antigen (titer 1:10,000), and positive CSF culture for Cryptococcus neoformans. Bone marrow aspirate smears (May-Grünwald-Giemsa) demonstrated 12% malignant, partly binucleated/multinucleated plasma cells.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Disseminated Cryptococcus neoformans meningoencephalitis and fungemia (confirmed by positive blood and CSF cultures, India ink, serum CrAg 1:1,000, and CSF CrAg 1:10,000 with intracranial hypertension causing bilateral CN VI palsy, papilledema, and sensorineural deafness) unmasking previously undiagnosed IgA-lambda multiple myeloma (12% marrow malignant plasma cells, IgA-lambda paraprotein, free lambda 183.14 mg/L, kappa/lambda <0.1) in an HIV-negative 63-year-old man. Treated with 21 days of induction intravenous amphotericin B (0.7 mg/kg/day) plus oral flucytosine (100 mg/kg/day) and serial therapeutic lumbar punctures (achieving negative CSF fungal cultures and reducing serum/CSF CrAg titers to 1:10), followed by 12 weeks of oral fluconazole consolidation (800 mg/day) and initiation of melphalan, prednisone, and thalidomide (MPT) chemotherapy during week 2 of consolidation, with complete neurological and clinical recovery sustained at 9-month follow-up.

raw_case_text:
A 23-year-old Hispanic female at 19 weeks of gestation, with medical history significant for preeclampsia and mild intermittent asthma, presented to the Emergency Room complaining of fever, dry cough, and shortness of breath for a week. The patient also reported painful swelling in her hands and feet associated with morning stiffness. She had tried acetaminophen at home which did not relieve her symptoms. Initial examination was remarkable for tachycardia (103 beats/min), tachypnea (20 breaths/min), and fever (101.8 F). Her lung examination was clear with equal air entry bilaterally. Joint exam showed swelling, tenderness, and warmth of bilateral ankles, knees, proximal interphalangeal joints, and metacarpal phalangeal joints. Laboratory studies were significant for lymphopenia (white blood cell count of 2.6 x 10/microL) and anemia (hemoglobin of 10.5 g/dL). Chest X-ray on admission did not show abnormalities.
Bilateral lower-extremity venous duplex studies did not show evidence of deep vein thromboses. Additionally, left knee arthrocentesis ruled out septic arthritis.
She was started empirically on ceftriaxone and azithromycin for possible community-acquired pneumonia. Her symptoms did not improve. C-reactive protein (CRP) and erythrocyte sedimentation rate were elevated (13 mg/L and 59 mm/h, respectively). Low complement levels were noted (C3 of 36 mg/dL and C4 of <8 mg/dL). The ANA test was positive. On day 5 of admission, she became tachypneic and hypoxic, saturating 84% on room air despite noninvasive ventilation. She was upgraded to the Intensive Care Unit where she required a high-flow nasal cannula.
Repeat chest X-ray showed new multifocal bilateral airspace opacities but no pleural effusions or pneumothorax (Figure 1).
Extensive infectious workup for viral, bacterial, and parasitic causes was negative. Notably, sputum cultures, blood cultures, and cultures for SARS-CoV-2, HIV, CMV, EBV, parvovirus B-19, hepatitis, and West Nile virus were negative. Legionella and Streptococcus urine antigens, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, QuantiFERON for tuberculosis, Lyme, Ehrlichia, Anaplasma, PCR for influenza A (subtypes H1 and H3), adenovirus, parainfluenza, and rhinovirus were also negative.
The patient was started empirically on IV methylprednisolone 60 mg daily for probable pneumonitis. This led to significant improvement of symptoms as her fever, tachypnea, hypoxia, cough, and arthralgias had resolved within 24 hours.
On further investigation, she was found to have positive anti-dsDNA (1 : 160 titers) and anti-SSA antibodies. CT chest was not pursued, given the risk of radiation exposure in pregnancy.
She never developed hemoptysis or significant drop in hemoglobin to favor of alveolar hemorrhage. The patient was diagnosed with new-onset SLE as per the EULAR/ACR 2019 criteria as she presented with fever, leukopenia, arthritis, pneumonitis, low complements, and positive serological lupus studies (ANA and anti-dsDNA). She was started on hydroxychloroquine 200 mg twice daily, and intravenous corticosteroids were switched to oral prednisone on the fourth day of IV methylprednisolone. This achieved adequate clinical and serological response as her CRP, hypocomplementemia, and pancytopenia significantly improved within 5 days.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 23-year-old Hispanic female at 19 weeks' gestation presented to the emergency room with a 1-week history of fever, dry cough, shortness of breath, and painful symmetric hand and foot joint swelling with morning stiffness.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Over the week preceding presentation, the pregnant patient developed persistent fevers, nonproductive cough, dyspnea, and symmetric polyarthritis involving her hands, wrists, knees, and ankles that failed to improve with home acetaminophen. After admission, she failed empiric ceftriaxone and azithromycin and progressed on hospital day 5 to severe hypoxemic respiratory failure (SpO2 84% on room air) requiring ICU transfer and high-flow nasal cannula oxygen.
subjective.past_medical_history: Gravida at 19 weeks' gestation; history of prior preeclampsia and mild intermittent asthma.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for 1-week fever, dry cough, progressive dyspnea, and symmetric hand/knee/ankle joint pain, swelling, and morning stiffness; negative for hemoptysis. Used acetaminophen prior to admission.

objective.physical_examination: Initial vital signs: temperature 101.8 °F, heart rate 103 beats/min, and respiratory rate 20 breaths/min (deteriorating on day 5 to severe tachypnea and SpO2 84% on room air). Initial lung auscultation was clear; rheumatologic examination demonstrated warmth, tenderness, and effusions/swelling of the bilateral ankles, knees, proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joints, and metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission labs showed leukopenia/lymphopenia (WBC 2.6 x 10^3/µL), anemia (hemoglobin 10.5 g/dL), elevated CRP (13 mg/L), elevated ESR (59 mm/h), hypocomplementemia (C3 36 mg/dL, C4 <8 mg/dL), positive ANA, positive anti-dsDNA (titer 1:160), and positive anti-SSA antibodies. Extensive infectious workup—including blood and sputum cultures, SARS-CoV-2, HIV, CMV, EBV, parvovirus B19, viral hepatitis, West Nile virus, urinary Legionella and Streptococcus pneumoniae antigens, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, QuantiFERON-TB, Lyme, Ehrlichia, Anaplasma, and respiratory viral PCR panel—was completely negative. Bilateral lower extremity venous duplex excluded DVT, and left knee arthrocentesis excluded septic arthritis. Initial chest X-ray was normal, whereas day 5 chest X-ray showed new multifocal bilateral airspace opacities without pleural effusion.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: New-onset systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) flare in the second trimester of pregnancy (19 weeks' gestation; HIV-negative) complicated by acute lupus pneumonitis, symmetric polyarthritis, leukopenia, hypocomplementemia (C3 36 mg/dL, C4 <8 mg/dL), and positive ANA, anti-dsDNA (1:160), and anti-SSA antibodies (fulfilling 2019 EULAR/ACR classification criteria). Administration of intravenous methylprednisolone (60 mg daily for 4 days, then transitioned to oral prednisone) plus oral hydroxychloroquine (200 mg twice daily) produced dramatic resolution of fever, hypoxemia, tachypnea, cough, and arthritis within 24 hours and normalization of cytopenias, CRP, and complement levels within 5 days.

raw_case_text:
A 54-year-old male presented to us with a history of headache for the past 3 months, which had gradually increased in severity over this period. It was associated with giddiness and blurring of vision. At the time of onset of the symptoms, he had visited his general practitioner, who had then done a full blood count, which had shown a low white cell count of 3.0/mm3(normal range being 4-11/mm3) with a low lymphocyte count of 0.6/mm3(normal range being 1-4/mm3). No further testing was done. This was diagnosed as a viral prodrome, and he was prescribed symptomatic therapy, but the symptoms still persisted for the next 2 and a half months. Fifteen days before presentation to our center, he was admitted to another hospital with severe headache, which lasted for 1 hour, which he described as an "unbearable headache." Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) brain was done at that hospital, which was normal. Unable to find a cause at that hospital, and with no improvement in his symptoms, he was transferred to our hospital for further evaluation.
He did not have a history of fever, vomiting, weight loss, rash, or a loss of appetite. There was no episode of loss of consciousness, seizure activity, motor weakness, or bowel or bladder involvement. He did not reveal any history of trauma or of any high-risk sexual behavior, drug abuse, or blood transfusion. He gave a history of pulmonary tuberculosis 25 years back, for which received treatment for 9 months. He was a known hypertensive for 3 years, which was well controlled with medications. His pulse rate, blood pressure, and temperature were normal. Neurological examination did not reveal any focal deficit. The rest of the systemic examination was unremarkable. MRI brain showed meningeal enhancement in bilateral cerebellar regions [Figure 1] with leptomeningeal enhancement in the right temporal [Figure 2] and right temporo-occipital [Figure 3] regions. Full blood count revealed a low white cell count of 2.5/mm3(normal range being 4-11/mm3) with a low lymphocyte count of 0.5/mm3(normal range being 1-4/mm3). Lumbar puncture was done, and the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis revealed 980 cells (normally < 5 cells/mm3), with a predominance of lymphocytes (60%), glucose was 32 mg/dL (normal is 25-35 mg/dL), and protein was 27 mg/dL (normal is 18-45 mg/dL). CSF polymerase chain reaction (PCR) for tuberculosis was negative. CSF examination for cyptococcal antigen was positive. CSF for viral PCR (herpes simplex virus, varicella-zoster virus [VZV], cytomegalovirus [CMV], and John Cunningham [JC] virus was negative. Lymphocyte flow cytometry was done, and the subset estimation showed low levels of CD4 T-cells, which were at 16% (normal range is above 25%), absolute CD4 count was 200/mm3(normally between 500 and 1500/mm3), whereas CD8 cell count was normal (29%). We further investigated to look for any cause for his immunocompromised state. ELISA for HIV-1 and HIV-2 and PCR for HIV-1 and HIV-2 were negative. Serum PCR for CMV, Epstein-Barr virus, VZV, and parvovirus B19 were negative. Serum PCR for human T-cell lymphotropic virus 1 and 2 was negative. Immunoglobulin levels were normal. Autoimmune workup including antinuclear antibody, anti-dsDNA, extractable nuclear antigens, and antiphospholipid antibodies was negative. Complement levels were normal. The bone marrow examination was normal. There was no evidence of aplasia or myelodysplasia. Once the diagnosis of cryptococcal meningitis was made, the first and foremost differential was HIV infection, but that was ruled out. Severe combined immunodeficiency was another possibility. However, in this condition, immunodeficiency-related infections often start manifesting in childhood and early adulthood. In our patient, cryptococcal meningitis occurred at the age of 54 years. The detailed workup ruled out any autoimmune conditions that could have caused such a clinical picture. He was treated with liposomal amphotericin-B. Flucytosine could not be given in view of its unavailability. He had an episode of generalized tonic-clonic seizures during his hospitalization with the compromise of his airways, and hence he was put on mechanical ventilatory support. His neurological condition progressively deteriorated during the course of his hospitalization, along with hemodynamic instability. He was thus put on inotropic support. Unfortunately, there was no improvement, and he passed away with worsening shock.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 54-year-old male presented with a 3-month history of progressively worsening headache accompanied by dizziness and blurred vision.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Three months prior to referral, the patient developed a gradually intensifying headache with giddiness and blurred vision; a full blood count at that time showed leukopenia (3.0 x 10^3/mm3) and lymphopenia (0.6 x 10^3/mm3) and was managed symptomatically as a viral prodrome. Fifteen days prior to transfer, he was hospitalized elsewhere for a 1-hour 'unbearable' headache with a normal brain MRI, and was subsequently referred due to persistent severe symptoms.
subjective.past_medical_history: Pulmonary tuberculosis 25 years prior, treated for 9 months; well-controlled hypertension for 3 years. Denied trauma, high-risk sexual behavior, illicit drug use, or blood transfusions.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for 3-month severe headache, giddiness, and blurred vision; negative at presentation for fever, vomiting, weight loss, rash, anorexia, seizures, focal weakness, or sphincter dysfunction (subsequently developed generalized tonic-clonic seizures during hospitalization).

objective.physical_examination: On admission, vital signs (pulse, blood pressure, and temperature), neurological examination, and systemic examination were all normal without focal neurological deficits. During hospitalization, he suffered a generalized tonic-clonic seizure with airway compromise and progressive hemodynamic shock.
objective.routine_investigations: Full blood count confirmed persistent leukopenia (WBC 2.5 x 10^3/mm3; normal 4–11 x 10^3/mm3) and lymphopenia (0.5 x 10^3/mm3; normal 1–4 x 10^3/mm3). HIV-1 and HIV-2 ELISA and PCR, HTLV-1/2 PCR, and serum PCRs for CMV, EBV, VZV, and parvovirus B19 were all negative. Quantitative immunoglobulins, C3/C4 complement levels, ANA, anti-dsDNA, ENA, and antiphospholipid antibodies were normal or negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Lymphocyte subset flow cytometry revealed idiopathic CD4+ T-lymphocytopenia: CD4+ T-cells 16% (normal >25%) and absolute CD4+ count 200 cells/mm3 (normal 500–1,500 cells/mm3) with normal CD8+ percentage (29%). Bone marrow examination was normal without aplasia or myelodysplasia. Repeat brain MRI demonstrated bilateral cerebellar meningeal enhancement and right temporal and temporo-occipital leptomeningeal enhancement. Lumbar puncture CSF analysis revealed marked pleocytosis (980 cells/mm3; 60% lymphocytes), glucose 32 mg/dL, protein 27 mg/dL, positive CSF cryptococcal antigen, and negative CSF tuberculosis PCR and viral PCRs (HSV, VZV, CMV, JCV).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Cryptococcal meningitis complicating idiopathic CD4+ T-lymphocytopenia (ICL; persistent leukopenia/lymphopenia with absolute CD4+ count 200 cells/mm3 [16%] and negative HIV-1/2 ELISA and PCR, negative HTLV-1/2 PCR, negative autoimmune panel, and normal bone marrow) in a 54-year-old male. Initiated on intravenous liposomal amphotericin B monotherapy (flucytosine was unavailable); however, the patient suffered a generalized tonic-clonic seizure requiring mechanical ventilation, progressed to refractory septic/neurogenic shock on vasopressors, and died.

raw_case_text: A 63-year-old HIV-negative man, with a history of well controlled diabetes mellitus, hypothyroidism, and Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD), presented to the ED complaining of acute-on-chronic lumbar pain. His home medications included insulin, atorvastatin, and levothyroxine. Upon arrival, patient was afebrile, with a blood pressure (BP) of 86/52 mmHg with orthostatic changes, rest of vital signs within normal limits. Patient was found somnolent, with tenderness on the left upper quadrant, without rebound. Rest of physical exam was within normal limits. Laboratory results showed a hemoglobin 9.4 g/dL (14 - 18 g/dL), leukocytes 17 x 103 leukocytes/microL (4 - 11 x 103/microL), serum bicarbonate 15 mmol/L (22 - 29 mmol/L), serum lactate 5.0 mmol/L (0.5 - 1.8 mmol/L) with anion gap (AG) LA of 28 (6 - 12), arterial blood gases pH 7.26 (7.38 - 7.44), paO2 83.4 mmHg (75 - 100 mmHg), paCO2 24.5 mmHg (38 - 42 mmHg), HCO3 10.8 mmol/L (23 - 26 mmol/L). Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) was 1,041 U/L (80 - 225 U/L). The rest of chemistry and infectious workup was within normal limits. Of note, 2 months prior to presentation, patient was incidentally found to have a left perinephric hematoma after he had an abdominal computer tomography (CT) for NAFLD workup. Upon admission, a repeat abdominal CT scan showed interval increase of the perinephric hematoma as well as gastric wall thickening (Figure 1). Urology recommended no surgical intervention. He was resuscitated with isotonic intravenous fluids, and was admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU), where he continued supportive care. Two days after admission, despite bicarbonate therapy and fluid resuscitation with complete resolution of shock, the patient remained with persistent AG metabolic acidosis and increasing lactic acid up to 14.5 mmol/L. A subsequent abdominal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed multiple rounded hypoenhancing lesions noted throughout the renal parenchyma bilaterally (Figure 2). A kidney biopsy was planned but aborted since the patient became acutely anemic (hemoglobin 5.6 g/dL) after an episode of melena. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy with biopsy showed a high-grade Burkitt's lymphoma (Figure 3). Further staging showed bone marrow involvement and extensive abdominal adenopathy. After two cycles of inpatient chemotherapy with dose-adjusted EPOCH-R (etoposide, prednisone, vincristine, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, and rituximab), the patient developed multifocal pneumonia complicated by respiratory failure. Following a prolonged ICU stay, after discussion with the family members, a decision of withdrawal of life-sustaining therapy was reached.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 63-year-old HIV-negative man presented to the emergency department with acute-on-chronic lumbar pain, hypotension, and somnolence.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Two months prior to admission, an outpatient abdominal CT performed for non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) had incidentally identified a left perinephric hematoma. He presented to the emergency department with acute exacerbation of lumbar back pain, orthostatic hypotension, somnolence, and severe lactic acidosis, and subsequently developed acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding (melena) on hospital day 2.
subjective.past_medical_history: Well-controlled diabetes mellitus, hypothyroidism, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD), and a left perinephric hematoma noted 2 months prior.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for acute-on-chronic lumbar pain, dizziness/orthostasis, somnolence, and subsequent melena. Home medications: insulin, levothyroxine, and atorvastatin.

objective.physical_examination: On arrival, afebrile, hypotensive (BP 86/52 mmHg with orthostatic changes), and somnolent, with left upper quadrant abdominal tenderness without rebound or guarding.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission labs showed anemia (hemoglobin 9.4 g/dL [normal 14–18], dropping acutely to 5.6 g/dL after melena), leukocytosis (WBC 17 x 10^3/µL [normal 4–11]), high-anion-gap lactic acidosis (serum bicarbonate 15 mmol/L, anion gap 28, serum lactate 5.0 mmol/L [normal 0.5–1.8] rising to 14.5 mmol/L on day 2 despite shock resolution; ABG pH 7.26, PaCO2 24.5 mmHg, PaO2 83.4 mmHg, HCO3- 10.8 mmol/L), and markedly elevated LDH (1,041 U/L [normal 80–225]). HIV and infectious workup were negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Admission abdominal CT demonstrated interval enlargement of the left perinephric hematoma and gastric wall thickening; subsequent abdominal MRI revealed multiple bilateral rounded hypoenhancing renal parenchymal masses. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy (performed after melena) with gastric biopsy, staging CT, and bone marrow biopsy confirmed disseminated Stage IV high-grade Burkitt lymphoma involving the stomach, bilateral kidneys, extensive abdominal lymph nodes, and bone marrow.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Stage IV sporadic (HIV-negative) Burkitt lymphoma involving the stomach, bilateral kidneys (initially masquerading as a spontaneous left perinephric hematoma), intra-abdominal lymph nodes, and bone marrow, complicated by severe Type B lactic acidosis (Warburg effect, lactate peaking at 14.5 mmol/L) and upper GI hemorrhage. Treated in the ICU with resuscitation and two cycles of inpatient dose-adjusted EPOCH-R immunochemotherapy (etoposide, prednisone, vincristine, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, and rituximab); however, his course was complicated by multifocal pneumonia and hypoxemic respiratory failure, and he died following family-directed withdrawal of life-sustaining support.

raw_case_text: A 63-year-old male with a history of previously treated hepatitis C presented to the clinic with a complaint of left testicular swelling for 3 months. On physical examination the left testicle was significantly enlarged. No clinically palpable lymphadenopathy could be appreciated. Ultrasound scan of the left testicle showed an enlarged testicle.
