He did not have any anogenital lesions. Multiple swabs were sent from the lesions for herpes simplex virus (HSV), varicella zoster virus (VZV), MPXV, and blood testing for syphilis. The serum rapid plasma reagin (RPR) titer was very high at 1:16384, confirming the diagnosis of secondary syphilis. The patient was treated with 2.4 million units of intramuscular benzathine penicillin. Interestingly, a lesion swabbed from his right armpit at the same time (2 days after completion of tecovirimat and 30 days after the first MPX lesion had appeared) remained positive for MPXV by PCR, albeit with a high cycle threshold of 37. After treatment with benzathine penicillin, the diffuse rash resolved in a few days, and the patient remained symptom-free. His serum RPR titer responded very well with drop to 1:256 over a period of 2 months. Multiple HIV 4th generation testing prior to and after this presentation remained negative.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 54-year-old HIV-negative male on emtricitabine/tenofovir PrEP presented initially with fever, headache, myalgias, and painful perianal, left thigh, and right forearm monkeypox lesions, followed 6 days into oral tecovirimat therapy by a new diffuse, painless, palmoplantar-involving maculopapular rash.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Three days after unprotected anal intercourse with an anonymous male partner, the patient developed fever, headache, myalgias, and 5-6 painful perianal, left thigh, and right forearm ulcers/lesions confirmed on day 14 as Monkeypox virus (MPXV) by PCR. Oral tecovirimat was initiated on day 19 with rapid resolution of the painful perianal/limb mpox lesions, but on day 6 of tecovirimat (day 25 of illness) he developed a new diffuse, painless maculopapular eruption covering his trunk, arms, legs, palms, and soles, prompting emergency department evaluation 2 days after completing his 14-day tecovirimat course.
subjective.past_medical_history: Otherwise healthy HIV-negative MSM taking daily HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis (emtricitabine/tenofovir disoproxil fumarate); unprotected sexual contact with an anonymous male partner 3 days before initial symptom onset.
subjective.review_of_systems: Initial: fever, headache, myalgias, and severe painful perianal/limb lesions. Day 25-35: diffuse painless maculopapular rash involving trunk, extremities, palms, and soles. Home medications: emtricitabine/tenofovir disoproxil PrEP and recent 14-day course of oral tecovirimat.

objective.physical_examination: Initial exam at day 14-19 showed 5-6 painful perianal, left thigh, and right forearm lesions. At day 35 (2 days post-tecovirimat), physical examination revealed complete resolution of the perianal lesions and a new diffuse erythematous maculopapular rash across the trunk, upper and lower extremities, palms, and soles.
objective.routine_investigations: Serial 4th-generation HIV antigen/antibody tests prior to and after presentation were negative, and lesion swabs for HSV and VZV were negative.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Confirmed monkeypox (mpox) and secondary syphilis co-infection in an HIV-negative PrEP user, established via initial positive perianal lesion MPXV PCR (with a right axillary swab at day 35 remaining weakly MPXV-PCR positive at Ct 37) and an extremely high serum RPR titer of 1:16,384. Following completion of 14 days of oral tecovirimat, he was treated with a single intramuscular dose of benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units, resulting in clearance of the diffuse secondary syphilis rash within a few days and a 64-fold decline in serum RPR titer from 1:16,384 to 1:256 at 2-month follow-up.

raw_case_text:
A 24-year-old heterosexual sexually active male, presented with asymptomatic erythematous lesions over the trunk and extensors for 5 days. There was no history of fever, and other constitutional symptoms before the development of the rash or similar complaints in his partner.
The patient was diagnosed with primary chancre over the shaft of the penis by his dermatologist which was confirmed with Treponema pallidum hemagglutination and venereal disease research laboratory (VDRL) reactivity a month ago (the titers of which were not available). He was treated with a tablet azithromycin 250 mg twice daily for 5 days. The chancre subsequently healed for 10-14 days.
On cutaneous examination, multiple well-defined erythematous macules and few papules were present over the chest, trunk, and palms [Figures 1-3]. There was complete sparing of the face, soles, and mucosa. No lymphadenopathy was noted. A healed atrophic scar was present over the shaft of the penis [Figure 4].
With a clinical diagnosis of secondary syphilis, we advised a repeat VDRL test which turned out to be reactive with a titer of 1:16. The patient was administered deep intramuscular injection of benzathine penicillin after a test dose, after which he was sent home.
Around 8 h after the injection, at his home, the patient complained of pruritis over existing lesions along with rapid spread of erythematous lesions covering the entire chest, back, and abdomen. No complaints of fever, myalgia, or shortness of breath. On examination, multiple well-defined widespread erythematous macules and papules were present over the chest, back, and abdomen [Figures 5 and 6]. There was no facial swelling or breathlessness. There was no mucosal involvement. A diagnosis of JHR was made. Tablet levocetirizine 10 mg and topical calamine lotion and clobetasol 0.05% ointment were prescribed. The lesions resolved overnight and the patient was symptomatically better by the next morning.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 24-year-old male presented with a 5-day history of asymptomatic erythematous lesions over his trunk, chest, palms, and extensor surfaces.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed asymptomatic erythematous macules and papules on his trunk and extensor surfaces 5 days prior to presentation without preceding fever or constitutional symptoms. One month earlier, he had been diagnosed by a dermatologist with a primary penile shaft chancre (reactive VDRL and TPHA, titers unavailable) and treated with oral azithromycin 250 mg twice daily for 5 days, with the penile ulcer healing over 10-14 days.
subjective.past_medical_history: Sexually active heterosexual male; history of primary penile chancre 1 month prior treated suboptimally with oral azithromycin. Female partner had no similar symptoms.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for asymptomatic trunk and palmar rash; negative for fever, myalgia, or constitutional symptoms prior to injection. Recent medication: oral azithromycin 250 mg BID for 5 days 1 month prior.

objective.physical_examination: Baseline cutaneous examination revealed multiple well-defined erythematous macules and scattered papules over the chest, trunk, extensor surfaces, and palms, with complete sparing of the face, soles, and oral/genital mucosa, and no lymphadenopathy. Genital exam showed a healed atrophic scar on the penile shaft. Eight hours after benzathine penicillin G injection, repeat exam showed an acute flare of widespread well-defined erythematous macules and papules covering the entire chest, back, and abdomen without facial angioedema, dyspnea, fever, or mucosal involvement.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Confirmed secondary syphilis (following inadequately treated primary syphilis) complicated by an isolated cutaneous Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction (JHR), established via positive serum VDRL (titer 1:16) and prior TPHA positivity. Administered a single deep intramuscular injection of benzathine penicillin G after a negative test dose. Eight hours post-injection, he developed pruritus and rapid generalization of the maculopapular rash without systemic symptoms or anaphylaxis, diagnosed as JHR and treated symptomatically with oral levocetirizine 10 mg, topical calamine lotion, and clobetasol 0.05% ointment, resulting in overnight resolution.

raw_case_text:
A 21-year-old female patient was admitted to the ophthalmology eye emergency room at Hospital Aleman with complaints of floaters ("red spots") in her left eye, which began the previous day. She denied any other associated visual symptoms.
At ocular examination, best corrected visual acuity was 20/20 and 20/40 in her right (OD) and left (OS) eyes, respectively. Slit lamp examination of the anterior segment was unremarkable in both eyes (OU). The intraocular pressure was 13 mm Hg in OU.
Fundus examination revealed disc swelling, dilated retinal veins, multiple peripheral venular saccular dilations, scattered cotton wool spots, retinal and disc neovascularization in OU. In OD, the vitreous was clear, while a vitreous hemorrhage was observed in OS (Fig. 1). Fluorescein angiography revealed in both eyes intense hyperfluorescence at the level of the disc, multifocal venous wall staining, multifocal paravenous leakage, multiple peripheral saccular venular dilations, diffuse retinal and macular edema, and retinal and disc neovascularization. In addition, posterior pole venular and arteriolar saccular dilations were also present in OD (Fig. 2). There was no evidence of retinal ischemia in OU.
Considering a presumptive diagnosis of retinal vasculitis, a complete blood count, liver function test, blood urea nitrogen, creatinine, fasting blood glucose level, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C reactive protein, venereal disease research laboratory (VDRL), fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption test (FTA ABS), PPD, HIV, brain magnetic resonance imaging with and without gadolinium, and spinal tap with measurement of the opening pressure were ordered. Laboratory results revealed a positive FTA ABS and a VDRL titer of 1:512. VDRL was negative in the cerebrospinal fluid. She was treated with 4 million units of intravenous penicillin G every 4 h for 2 weeks. Meprednisone was also added, at an initial dose of 1 mg/kg/day for 3 weeks, with a gradual tapering until its discontinuation 2 months later. Two weeks after the end of the antibiotic treatment course, BCVA in OD was 20/20, and in OS, it improved to 20/20. Fundus examination revealed persistence of the retinal and disc neovascularization. Therefore, monthly dose of 1.25 mg/0.05 mL of intravitreal bevacizumab was administered for 3 months. Fluorescein angiography after the third dose revealed a dramatic reduction of retinal and disc neovascularization, with disappearance of retinal vasculitis, although a mild retinal edema and papillitis persisted in both eyes (Fig. 3). At 1 year of follow-up, bilateral BCVA remained in 20/20. Fundus examination did not reveal abnormalities.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 21-year-old female presented to the ophthalmic emergency room with a 1-day history of floaters ('red spots') in her left eye.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient noticed acute-onset floaters described as 'red spots' in her left eye beginning the day prior to presentation.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for left-eye floaters; denied ocular pain, photophobia, or other systemic symptoms.

objective.physical_examination: Best-corrected visual acuity was 20/20 in the right eye (OD) and 20/40 in the left eye (OS). Slit-lamp examination of the anterior segment was unremarkable bilaterally (OU), and intraocular pressure was 13 mmHg OU. Fundus examination OU revealed optic disc swelling, dilated retinal veins, multiple peripheral venular saccular dilations, scattered cotton-wool spots, and retinal and optic disc neovascularization, with a clear vitreous OD and vitreous hemorrhage OS.
objective.routine_investigations: CBC, liver function tests, BUN, creatinine, fasting blood glucose, ESR, CRP, PPD tuberculin skin test, and HIV serology were ordered and unremarkable/negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Fluorescein angiography OU demonstrated intense optic disc hyperfluorescence, multifocal venous wall staining and paravenous leakage, multiple peripheral saccular venular dilations (plus posterior pole arteriolar and venular saccular dilations OD), diffuse retinal and macular edema, and retinal and optic disc neovascularization without retinal capillary nonperfusion/ischemia. Brain MRI with and without gadolinium and lumbar puncture with opening pressure measurement were normal, with a negative CSF VDRL.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Confirmed bilateral syphilitic occlusive-like retinal vasculitis with optic disc and retinal neovascularization and left vitreous hemorrhage, established via high-titer serum VDRL (1:512) and positive serum FTA-ABS (with negative CSF VDRL). Treated with intravenous aqueous penicillin G 4 million units every 4 hours for 14 days plus oral meprednisone 1 mg/kg/day for 3 weeks tapered over 2 months. Visual acuity improved to 20/20 OU 2 weeks post-antibiotics, and persistent retinal/disc neovascularization was treated with 3 monthly intravitreal bevacizumab (1.25 mg/0.05 mL) injections, achieving complete resolution of neovascularization and maintenance of 20/20 bilateral vision at 1-year follow-up.

raw_case_text:
An 18-year-old male was referred to our sexually transmitted infection service for a penile lesion that evolved over the last 6 weeks. Previous sexually transmitted and bloodborne infections (STBBI) screening that did not include a syphilis serology revealed anal chlamydia and gonorrhoea, treated with azithromycin, cefixime and doxycycline with no symptom improvement at the time of consultation. The patient, who had been circumcised in the past, identified as a man who has sex with men (MSM) and reported inconsistent barrier method use and four sexual partners in the last 3 months. Clinical evaluation revealed a crusty hyperkeratotic cap covering the whole glans with reduced meatal opening, synechias (Figure 1) and bilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy. Systemic symptoms and urethral discharge were absent.
Enzyme immunoassay (EAI) and rapid plasma reagin (RPR) tests confirmed a diagnosis of syphilitic balanitis of Follman (SBF). Treatment with 2.4 M units of Penicillin G Benzathine was initiated, resulting in rapid lesion improvement and complete resolution at 1-month follow-up (Figure 2).
Syphilis chancre is the hallmark of primary syphilis, and when present appears in the first 90 days after Treponema pallidum inoculation.   Classic presentation has been described as a single, unifocal, painless, indurated and moist erosion of several millimetres in the genital area or elsewhere. Many atypical syphilis chancre subtypes have been described.   SBF is a rare presentation of primary syphilis described as erosive balanitis associated with bilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy.   Differential diagnoses can include candidal, herpetic, atopic and psoriasic balanitis, or glans synechiae associated with lichen planus or lichen sclerosus. SBF diagnosis requires a high index of suspicion which can be facilitated by careful inquiry of STBBI risk factors and the finding of bilateral lymphadenopathy. Management includes penicillin G benzathine treatment with primary syphilis dosage, as well as STBBI screening and counselling.   In our patient, SBF clinical presentation, which is usually described as oozing and erosive, was further modified by the drying effect of his circumcised glans leading to a puzzling hyperkeratotic cap with hardened synechiae.
This case underscores the importance of comprehensive sexually transmitted illness (STI) testing and consideration of syphilis in sexually active MSM with atypical genital lesions, particularly when accompanied by lymphadenopathy. It also reinforces the idea that syphilis is indeed 'the great masquerader.'

subjective.chief_complaint: An 18-year-old male presented with a 6-week history of an evolving crusted hyperkeratotic penile glans lesion.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient was referred to the STI service for a penile glans lesion that had evolved over the preceding 6 weeks. Prior STBBI screening (which omitted syphilis serology) had detected anal Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae infections, but treatment with azithromycin, cefixime, and doxycycline produced no improvement in the penile lesion.
subjective.past_medical_history: History of prior circumcision and recent anal chlamydia and gonorrhea. Identifies as a man who has sex with men (MSM), reporting inconsistent barrier protection and 4 sexual partners over the preceding 3 months.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for crusted penile glans lesion and inguinal swelling; negative for systemic symptoms or urethral discharge. Recent medications: azithromycin, cefixime, and doxycycline.

objective.physical_examination: Genital examination revealed a crusty, hyperkeratotic cap covering the entire circumcised glans penis with narrowing of the urethral meatal opening, glans synechiae, and bilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Confirmed primary syphilitic balanitis of Follmann (SBF) modified by prior circumcision, established via reactive syphilis enzyme immunoassay (EIA) and reactive serum RPR. Treated with intramuscular benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units, resulting in rapid improvement and complete resolution of the glans lesion at 1-month follow-up.

raw_case_text: A 16-year-old girl was admitted to the hospital because of abnormal mental behaviour for more than seven months, which had been aggravated for nine days. Seven months previously, the girl developed mental and behavioural abnormalities after a heartbreak, which manifested as alternating low mood and emotional irritability, a lack of interest in social relations, and memory loss. Her parents, brother, and sister were in good health and the parents were nonconsanguineous. There was no family history of genetic diseases. Her parents took her to the local hospital for consultation, but the general physical examination and laboratory test results were normal, and no treatment was administered. A few months later, the patient's symptoms worsened; she refused to eat, drink, sleep, or communicate, exhibited slowness in movement, and was finally transferred to our hospital. The physical examination showed the following results: clear consciousness; able to answer simple questions; and no redness, ulcers or vegetation in the perianal skin. The bilateral Babinski sign and the right Oppenheim sign were positive. No obvious abnormalities were observed on cardiopulmonary or abdominal physical examinations. Tests for hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and human immunodeficiency virus were negative. The treponemal serological test result was positive and the toluidine red unheated serum test (TRUST) titre was 1:128. The results of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) testing results are as follows: White blood cells: 5.0 x106/L, Red blood cells: 2.5x106/L, Glucose:3.41 mmol/L, Cl-:128.3 mmol/L, Total protein:970.0 mg/L, Treponema pallidum particle agglutination test (TPPA): positive. Brain computed tomography (CT) showed a bilateral cerebral hemisphere gray matter junction area, scattered calcification in the bilateral lenticular nucleus and thalamus, bilateral semioval centre, lateral ventricle brain white matter region, a slightly widened and deepened sulcus, and a slightly narrowed frontal parietal gyrus (Figure 1). After admission, the possibility of neurosyphilis infection was considered. The patient was administered an intravenous penicillin G solution, oral olanzapine, and depakin for 12 days. After treatment, the patient's clinical symptoms improved, and she was discharged with her parents. We informed the patient to continue penicillin G treatment at a hospital near their home.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 16-year-old girl presented with a >7-month history of progressive behavioral and psychiatric abnormalities that worsened acutely over the preceding 9 days.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Seven months prior to admission, following a romantic breakup, the patient developed alternating low mood, emotional irritability, social withdrawal, and memory loss. Initial evaluation at a local hospital showed normal general physical and basic laboratory findings, and no treatment was given. Over the subsequent months, her condition worsened until 9 days prior to admission when she refused to eat, drink, sleep, or communicate and exhibited marked psychomotor retardation.
subjective.past_medical_history: No prior medical illnesses. Parents were healthy and non-consanguineous, siblings were healthy, and there was no family history of genetic or psychiatric disorders.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for mood lability, irritability, social withdrawal, memory decline, psychomotor slowing, and refusal to eat, drink, sleep, or speak.

objective.physical_examination: On admission, the patient had clear consciousness and could answer simple questions. Cardiopulmonary, abdominal, and perianal skin examinations were normal without ulcers or vegetations. Neurological examination revealed psychomotor slowing, bilateral positive Babinski signs, and a positive right Oppenheim sign.
objective.routine_investigations: Serological screening tests for hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and HIV were negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Non-contrast brain CT demonstrated hypoattenuation at the bilateral cerebral gray-white matter junctions and semioval centers, scattered calcifications in the bilateral lenticular nuclei and thalami, mildly widened and deepened cerebral sulci, and mild frontoparietal gyral atrophy. Lumbar puncture CSF analysis revealed WBC 5.0 x 10^6/L, RBC 2.5 x 10^6/L, glucose 3.41 mmol/L, chloride 128.3 mmol/L, and markedly elevated total protein of 970.0 mg/L.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Confirmed parenchymatous neurosyphilis presenting with psychiatric and cognitive manifestations in an adolescent, established via positive serum treponemal serology, high-titer serum TRUST (1:128), and positive CSF TPPA alongside elevated CSF protein (970.0 mg/L). Treated with intravenous penicillin G, oral olanzapine, and oral valproate (Depakine) for 12 days with clinical improvement, and discharged to complete her intravenous penicillin G course at a local hospital.

raw_case_text: A 2-day-old newborn baby born out of a nonconsanguineous parentage was admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit with respiratory distress. The birth weight was 2.78 kg. There was a history of thick meconium aspiration with a delayed cry. The baby cried after 2 min following the bag and mask ventilation. There was hepatosplenomegaly, with the liver being 7 cm and the spleen 4 cm, respectively. Investigations revealed total bilirubin 6.7 mg/dL (direct bilirubin 3.9 and indirect bilirubin 2.9), serum glutamic-oxaloacetic transaminase - 707 U/L, serum glutamic-pyruvic transaminase - 1574 U/L, alkaline phosphatase - 440 U/L, platelet - 80,000/cmm, total leukocyte count - 21,350/cmm, and C-reactive protein - 111.7. Urine and blood cultures were sterile. Chest X-ray was normal. Because of the presence of hepatosplenomegaly, the baby was thoroughly investigated for toxoplasmosis, hepatitis B, rubella, cytomegalovirus, herpes simplex infection and tuberculosis, which came out to be negative. On the 6th day, the baby developed peeling of the skin from the acral parts and trunk, for which dermatology consultation was sought. The mother gave a history of erythematous rash over the trunk and extremities on the 2nd day of birth. On dermatological examination, there was peeling of the skin from the palms and soles [Figure 1a and b]. Based on skin peeling from the acral areas, physiological desquamation of neonatal skin, continual peeling skin syndrome, and CS were kept as differentials. The patient was subsequently investigated. Venereal disease research laboratory (VDRL) titer of the mother and the baby came out as 1:4 and child 1:16, respectively. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis showed glucose 37 mmol/L, protein 191.92 mg/dL, cell count 15 cells/mm3, and lymphocytes 100% and CSF VDRL came out to be negative. The patient was finally diagnosed with CS based on clinical findings and laboratory reports and was started with aqueous crystalline penicillin G 50,000 IU/kg/day intravenously (IV) 12 hourly in the first 7 days of life, followed by 50,000 IU/kg per dose IV every 8 hourly for the next 3 days to complete a total 10 days of treatment.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 2-day-old male neonate presented to the NICU with acute respiratory distress at birth, followed on day 6 of life by acral and truncal skin desquamation.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Born with thick meconium aspiration and a delayed cry requiring 2 minutes of bag-and-mask ventilation, the newborn was admitted to the NICU at day 2 of life for respiratory distress and found to have hepatosplenomegaly. On day 6 of life, he developed prominent peeling of the skin over his palms, soles, and trunk.
subjective.past_medical_history: Born to non-consanguineous parents with a birth weight of 2.78 kg. Maternal history revealed an erythematous rash over the mother's trunk and extremities on the 2nd day postpartum.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for neonatal respiratory distress and acral/truncal skin peeling.

objective.physical_examination: Birth weight was 2.78 kg. Initial physical examination revealed hepatosplenomegaly with the liver palpable 7 cm and spleen 4 cm below the costal margin. Dermatological examination on day 6 of life showed prominent desquamation and peeling of the skin over the palms, soles, and trunk.
objective.routine_investigations: Blood investigations revealed conjugated hyperbilirubinemia with total bilirubin 6.7 mg/dL (direct 3.9 mg/dL, indirect 2.9 mg/dL), markedly elevated transaminases (AST/SGOT 707 U/L, ALT/SGPT 1,574 U/L), alkaline phosphatase 440 U/L, thrombocytopenia (platelets 80,000/mm3), leukocytosis (WBC 21,350/mm3), and elevated CRP (111.7 mg/L). Blood and urine cultures were sterile; chest X-ray was normal; TORCH and tuberculosis workup (Toxoplasma, HBV, rubella, CMV, HSV, and TB) was negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Lumbar puncture CSF analysis showed 15 cells/mm3 (100% lymphocytes), elevated protein 191.92 mg/dL, glucose 37 mmol/L [mg/dL], and a negative CSF VDRL.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Confirmed early congenital syphilis presenting with neonatal cholestatic hepatitis, hepatosplenomegaly, thrombocytopenia, and acral palmoplantar desquamation, established via a neonatal serum VDRL titer of 1:16 (fourfold higher than the maternal VDRL titer of 1:4). Treated with intravenous aqueous crystalline penicillin G 50,000 IU/kg/day divided every 12 hours during the first 7 days of life, then 50,000 IU/kg/dose IV every 8 hours for the next 3 days to complete a 10-day course.

raw_case_text: A 31-year-old woman presented with fatigue, weight gain, and lower extremity edema. One month prior, she had a fever of up to 38 C, which subsided naturally. One week prior, she developed headaches, nausea, and anorexia. Subsequently, she developed general malaise, edema of the face and bilateral lower legs, and a rapid weight gain of 8 kg. As her symptoms did not improve, she sought medical attention. During a review of systems, she admitted experiencing dizziness and sore throat but denied the occurrence of any other symptoms. She had a medical history of chlamydial urethritis that had been treated with azithromycin two years prior and no known drug allergies or medications; she did not use any illicit drugs. Her sexual history included multiple partners and unprotected sexual intercourse one to two times per week. Her body weight was 62 kg, an increase from the baseline value of 54 kg. Vital signs were stable, and physical examination revealed edema of the bilateral eyelids and lower extremities and bilateral cervical lymphadenopathies. Additionally, rash was observed on the bilateral forearms. The laboratory investigations revealed white blood cell counts 6300/microl, hemoglobin 18.3 g/dl, platelets 298,000/microl, serum creatinine level 1.89 mg/dl, total protein 4.8 g dl, albumin 1.3 g/dl. The urine creatinine/protein ratio was 10.9 g/g Cre. Because TPHA and RPR were positive and the reactive plasma reagin (RPR) titer was as high as 1:32, we performed a lumbar puncture to rule out neurosyphilis; however, no evidence of meningitis was observed. HIV antigen/antibody was negative. Therefore, we initiated 100 mg of doxycycline, orally every 12 h for 14 days, to treat secondary syphilis along with nephrotic syndrome. Initially, a renal biopsy was planned, but after her edema and proteinuria improved dramatically with only doxycycline, we decided not to perform a biopsy.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 31-year-old woman presented with fatigue, facial and bilateral lower-extremity edema, and a rapid 8-kg weight gain over 1 week.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: One month prior to presentation, the patient experienced a transient fever up to 38 C that resolved spontaneously. One week prior to presentation, she developed headaches, nausea, and anorexia, rapidly followed by generalized malaise, facial and bilateral leg edema, and an 8-kg weight gain (from 54 kg to 62 kg).
subjective.past_medical_history: History of chlamydial urethritis 2 years prior treated with azithromycin. Sexual history was notable for multiple partners and unprotected sexual intercourse 1-2 times per week. Denied illicit drug use.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fatigue, transient fever, headache, nausea, anorexia, dizziness, sore throat, facial/leg edema, 8-kg weight gain, and forearm rash; no known drug allergies and taking no home medications.

objective.physical_examination: Body weight was 62 kg (baseline 54 kg) with stable vital signs. Physical examination revealed bilateral eyelid edema, bilateral lower-extremity pitting edema, bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy, and an erythematous rash on both forearms.
objective.routine_investigations: Laboratory tests showed WBC 6,300/uL, hemoglobin 18.3 g/dL, platelets 298,000/uL, elevated serum creatinine 1.89 mg/dL, hypoproteinemia (total protein 4.8 g/dL), severe hypoalbuminemia (albumin 1.3 g/dL), and nephrotic-range proteinuria with a urine protein-to-creatinine ratio of 10.9 g/gCr. Serum HIV antigen/antibody screening was negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Lumbar puncture CSF analysis was normal with no evidence of meningitis/neurosyphilis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Confirmed secondary syphilis complicated by acute syphilitic nephrotic syndrome and acute kidney injury, established via positive serum TPHA and reactive serum RPR (titer 1:32) with negative CSF neurosyphilis workup. Treated with oral doxycycline 100 mg every 12 hours for 14 days, which resulted in dramatic resolution of her generalized edema and nephrotic-range proteinuria, obviating the need for a planned renal biopsy.

raw_case_text:
A 38-year-old Caucasian man presented a rash for 1 month that involved the face, trunk, and upper limbs. He was compliant with arthralgias, myalgias, asthenia, new onset stypsis, and mild anorectal pain. He reported his last sexual intercourse about 18 months ago, and he had self-healing genital and palmoplantar lesions more than 1 year ago. He denied any sexual relationship during the last 18 months, including oral sex and protected sexual intercourse, and he had never used illicit drugs. Physical examination showed two ulcerative lesions on the lips, painless bilateral cervical lymph nodes, and hyperkeratosis papules on the face, behind the left ear, on the neck, palms, soles, and scrotum (Fig. 1). A macular rash was in the trunk; erosive lesions were on the glans. Papular lesions were mild itching, and some of them were treated previously with cryotherapy for suspicion of common warts. He was afebrile, and his vital parameters were normal. Exams were all unremarkable but ALT (61, reference < 50 U/L). Treponemal test, rapid plasma reagin (RPR) for syphilis and serology for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) were ordered. Testing for HIV returned positive with a CD4 count of 385 (16.96 %, CD4/ CD8 = 0.3), HIV viral load of 43,400, and negative HIV p24 antigen. Syphilis serology was positive, with an elevated RPR titer of 1:128. A diagnosis of mucocutaneous relapse during untreated late latent syphilis with HIV coinfection was made. Molecular panel for sexually transmitted infection (Trichomonas vaginalis, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Mycoplasma genitalium, Chlamydophila trachomatis) on first-void urine and rectal swab was negative. Screening for opportunistic infections, including tuberculosis (Quantiferon Tb Gold), cryptococcosis (serum antigen), toxoplasmosis (serology), and leishmaniasis (serology and polymerase chain reaction) was unremarkable all but positive Toxoplasma gondii IgG serology.
The patient was treated with three doses of 2.4 million units of benzathine penicillin administered 1 per week. Antiretroviral therapy with a bictegravir-based regimen was started concurrently with the first administration. Macular rash of the trunk, glans erosions, anorectal pain, and stypsis disappeared after the first dose of penicillin. The other lesions had a progressive improvement in the next three weeks.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 38-year-old Caucasian man presented with a 1-month history of a mildly pruritic papular and macular rash over his face, trunk, palms, soles, and genitalia, accompanied by arthralgias, myalgias, asthenia, constipation, and mild anorectal pain.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: One month prior to presentation, the patient developed hyperkeratotic papules on his face, retroauricular area, neck, palms, soles, and scrotum (some previously treated with cryotherapy as suspected common warts), along with a truncal macular rash, lip ulcers, glans erosions, arthralgias, myalgias, fatigue, new-onset constipation (stypsis), and mild anorectal pain.
subjective.past_medical_history: Reported his last sexual intercourse approximately 18 months prior to presentation, followed >1 year ago by self-healing genital and palmoplantar lesions. Denied any sexual contact over the past 18 months and denied illicit drug use.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for mildly pruritic mucocutaneous rash, lip ulcers, arthralgias, myalgias, asthenia, constipation, and mild anorectal pain; negative for fever.

objective.physical_examination: Vital signs were normal and the patient was afebrile. Cutaneous and mucosal examination revealed two ulcerative lesions on the lips, painless bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy, hyperkeratotic papules on the face, left retroauricular region, neck, palms, soles, and scrotum, a macular rash over the trunk, and erosive lesions on the glans penis.
objective.routine_investigations: Routine blood tests were unremarkable except for mildly elevated ALT at 61 U/L (reference <50 U/L). HIV serology was positive with an HIV-1 viral load of 43,400 copies/mL and negative HIV p24 antigen. First-void urine and rectal swab multiplex PCR for Trichomonas vaginalis, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Mycoplasma genitalium, and Chlamydia trachomatis was negative. Opportunistic infection screening (QuantiFERON-TB Gold, serum cryptococcal antigen, Leishmania serology/PCR) was negative except for positive Toxoplasma gondii IgG.
objective.advanced_workup: CD4 T-lymphocyte count was 385 cells/mm3 (16.96%, CD4/CD8 ratio 0.3).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Confirmed mucocutaneous relapse of untreated late latent syphilis (secondary relapse) with newly diagnosed HIV-1 co-infection, established via positive treponemal test and high-titer serum RPR (1:128). Treated with intramuscular benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units once weekly for 3 consecutive weeks alongside concurrent initiation of bictegravir-based antiretroviral therapy. The truncal macular rash, glans erosions, anorectal pain, and constipation resolved after the first penicillin dose, and the remaining hyperkeratotic papules progressively cleared over the subsequent 3 weeks.

raw_case_text:
As shown in figure 1, 4 years after his first symptoms with extensive but unsuccessful diagnostics and treatments, including several MRIs, broad genetic analysis and multiple eye surgeries, he was referred to our neurological department for further evaluation. On referral, the patient suffered from severe gait ataxia due to diminished proprioception and absent deep tendon reflexes. Furthermore, diminished pupillary reflex to light with preserved constriction during convergence, described as an Argyll-Robertson pupil as well as an almost complete loss of vision were found. Syphilis screening test was positive, which was confirmed by serological confirmation tests and positive CSF studies (see 'Investigations'). On further interrogation, the patient disclosed a previous syphilis infection 30 years ago, which was likely treated insufficiently with an unknown oral antibiotic. Exact route or place of infection were not recallable. Due to the patient's history and clinical findings along with the laboratory results confirming serological and CSF syphilis activity, we were able to establish the diagnosis of tabes dorsalis.
A laboratory screening was conducted and revealed positive titres for a syphilis screening test. The diagnosis of syphilis was further confirmed by positive T. pallidum haemagglutination assay and serological activity with a rapid plasma reagin (RPR) of 1:8. A CSF study revealed pleocytosis with 93 cells/microL, predominantly mononuclear, elevated protein, albumin and lactate as well as an intrathecal synthesis of IgG-directed against T. pallidum (table 1).

subjective.chief_complaint: An adult male presented with a 4-year history of progressive severe gait ataxia and near-complete bilateral vision loss.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Over the preceding 4 years, the patient underwent extensive unsuccessful diagnostic workups (including multiple MRIs, broad genetic panels, and multiple eye surgeries) for progressive visual loss and gait instability before being referred to the neurology department.
subjective.past_medical_history: Upon targeted questioning after positive syphilis screening, the patient disclosed a prior syphilis infection 30 years earlier that had been insufficiently treated with an unknown oral antibiotic.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for severe gait unsteadiness and near-complete blindness.

objective.physical_examination: Neurological and ophthalmic examination revealed severe sensory gait ataxia secondary to impaired proprioception, absent lower-extremity deep tendon reflexes (areflexia), bilateral Argyll Robertson pupils (diminished pupillary light reflex with preserved convergence constriction), and near-complete bilateral loss of vision.
objective.advanced_workup: Lumbar puncture CSF analysis demonstrated mononuclear-predominant pleocytosis (93 cells/uL), elevated total protein, elevated CSF albumin and lactate, and positive intrathecal anti-Treponema pallidum IgG synthesis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Confirmed tertiary parenchymatous neurosyphilis (tabes dorsalis with optic atrophy and Argyll Robertson pupils) occurring 30 years after inadequately treated primary/early syphilis, established via positive syphilis screening, positive TPHA, reactive serum RPR (titer 1:8), CSF mononuclear pleocytosis (93 cells/uL), and intrathecal anti-Treponema pallidum IgG synthesis.

raw_case_text:
A 2-month-old infant (the weight 5kg) was presented to our department with a 2-week history of a diffuse pruritic rash, which started on his hands and arms before spreading rapidly over his entire body, presented as white, flat or minimally raised, moist plaques. A hernia body with a size of 2x2x1cm could be found at the navel of the infant and the surface is smooth and can be recovered. There is no hepatosplenomegaly during physical examination. Protruding hernia can be seen on the left scrotal wall, which can be retrieved (Figure 1). The infant felt painful of lower extremity and result in refusal to move it. Radiographic findings showed the multiple bony lesions characteristicare were periostitis and epiphysis with lower extremity (Figure 2). Extensive long-strip hyperplasia was seen in both femurs, tibia and fibula, the early calcification zone was widened and the density was increased, and bone destruction was seen in both tibia and proximal medial side (Wimberger sign). Differential diagnosis at that time included secondary syphilis, psoriasis, and acrodermatitis enteropathica.  
Further investigations, including routine blood test, hypersensitive c-reactive protein, human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), syphilis, hepatitis B, and C, were conducted. The results confirmed the diagnosis of secondary syphilis, indicating that the infection had been transmitted from the mother during pregnancy. TPPA assay was positive, and the rapid plasma reagin titre was 1:64. The result of TPPA was positive for his mother, and the rapid plasma reagin titre was 1:16, but his father was negative. Based on the above findings, a diagnosis of secondary syphilis was made.
After admission, and penicillin 5WU was given to the buttock muscle on the first and the second day and no adverse reactions occurred. On the third day, penicillin 50WU was given intravenously for 1/8 hour. The symptoms of the infant gradually became normal after one week.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 2-month-old male infant presented with a 2-week history of a diffuse pruritic rash and painful pseudoparalysis of the lower extremities.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Two weeks prior to presentation, the infant developed white, flat-to-minimally-raised moist plaques on his hands and arms that rapidly generalized over his entire body, accompanied by lower-extremity pain and refusal to move his legs (Parrot pseudoparalysis).
subjective.past_medical_history: Maternal testing revealed positive maternal TPPA and RPR (titer 1:16), whereas the father tested negative for syphilis.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for generalized rash, umbilical and left scrotal reducible bulges, and lower limb pain/refusal to move.

objective.physical_examination: Weight was 5 kg. Cutaneous examination showed generalized white, flat-to-minimally-elevated moist plaques across the body, hands, and arms. Abdominal and genital examination revealed a reducible 2 x 2 x 1 cm umbilical hernia, a reducible left indirect inguinoscrotal hernia, and no hepatosplenomegaly. Musculoskeletal examination showed lower-extremity tenderness with refusal to move the legs.
objective.routine_investigations: Routine blood tests, hs-CRP, and serologies for HIV, hepatitis B, and hepatitis C were negative or unremarkable. Lower-extremity radiographs demonstrated bilateral symmetric diaphyseal periostitis and metaphyseal osteochondritis/epiphyseal changes involving the femora, tibiae, and fibulae, with widened dense provisional calcification zones and bilateral proximal medial tibial metaphyseal bone destruction (Wimberger sign).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Confirmed early congenital syphilis (reported as congenital/secondary syphilis with Parrot pseudoparalysis and radiographic Wimberger sign; psoriasis and acrodermatitis enteropathica ruled out), established via positive infant TPPA and serum RPR titer of 1:64 (fourfold higher than the maternal RPR titer of 1:16). Treated with intramuscular penicillin (50,000 U) on hospital days 1 and 2 followed by intravenous penicillin (500,000 U every 8 hours) starting on day 3 without adverse reactions, achieving clinical resolution of symptoms within 1 week.

raw_case_text:
A 43-year-old man with migraine as medical history for which he did not take any active pharmacological treatment begins two hours before his arrival in the emergency room with diplopia, speech alteration, and decreased level of consciousness with frequent fluctuations. He denied the consumption of any associated toxics.
The physical examination revealed predominantly femoral right hemiparesis, binocular strabismus with limited convergence and vertical eye movements, nonreactive miotic pupils, and fluctuations in the level of consciousness with a score on the Glasgow Scale that varied between 8 and 10.
Among the complementary tests that were requested, the analyses showed no alterations (including toxic and drug profiles) and the baseline computerized axial tomography (TC) showed no haemorrhage or incipient signs of ischemia (Figure 1).
During his stay, the fluctuation in the level of consciousness persists and a right hemiparesis de novo is observed. Suspecting a posterior circulation stroke and in the absence of contraindications, intravenous thrombolysis was performed. The study was completed with the performance of computerized angiography that revealed a bilateral thalamic hypodensity predominantly in the posterior left thalamus (bitalamic infarction, probably Percheron) which was confirmed with the performance of magnetic resonance imaging (Figures 2 and 3), where a bilateral acute thalamic infarction compatible with Percheron syndrome is finally observed, appreciating hemorrhagic transformation in the left thalamus.
Due to the persistence of the alteration in the level of consciousness, the patient was admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU) for neurological control. During his stay in the ICU, the patient fully recovered his level of consciousness, persisting only at discharge a binocular diplopia of less intensity.
The study was completed with a study of autoimmunity, vitamin B12 and folic acid, serologies for brucellosis, human immunodeficiency virus, and syphilis that did not show any alterations and the performance of a regulated echocardiogram which revealed a patent foramen ovale, without intracardiac thrombosis.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 43-year-old man presented with a 2-hour history of acute binocular diplopia, speech alteration, right hemiparesis, and fluctuating decreased level of consciousness.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Two hours prior to emergency department arrival, the patient acutely developed double vision, slurred/altered speech, right lower-limb-predominant hemiparesis, and fluctuating stupor/somnolence.
subjective.past_medical_history: History of migraine headaches (not on prophylactic pharmacotherapy); denied illicit drug or toxin use.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for acute diplopia, speech disturbance, right hemiparesis, and fluctuating consciousness.

objective.physical_examination: Neurological examination revealed a fluctuating level of consciousness (Glasgow Coma Scale score varying between 8 and 10), nonreactive miotic pupils, binocular strabismus with vertical gaze palsy and impaired convergence, and right crural-predominant hemiparesis.
objective.routine_investigations: Routine blood chemistry, toxicology/drug screens, autoimmune panel, vitamin B12, folate, and infectious serologies for brucellosis, HIV, and syphilis were all normal or negative. Regulated echocardiography revealed a patent foramen ovale (PFO) without intracardiac thrombus.
objective.advanced_workup: Initial non-contrast head CT was normal, whereas subsequent CT angiography and brain MRI demonstrated acute bilateral paramedian thalamic infarctions (predominantly involving the posterior left thalamus with mild hemorrhagic transformation) diagnostic of an Artery of Percheron occlusion.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Confirmed acute bilateral paramedian thalamic ischemic stroke due to Artery of Percheron occlusion associated with a patent foramen ovale (meningovascular syphilis, HIV, brucellosis, and autoimmune vasculitis excluded). Treated acutely with intravenous thrombolysis and ICU neurocritical care monitoring, achieving full recovery of consciousness and discharge with only mild residual binocular diplopia.

raw_case_text:
A 47-year-old woman presented to the dermatology department with rashes on her left cheek and chest. Initially, a rash developed on the left cheek three months prior, with no obvious inducing factor and the patient gradually developed a similar rash on her left chest, and the area gradually increased. The rash did not cause any symptoms such as itching, irritation, or pain. Little improvement was noted after one month of external treatment with tacrolimus and halometasone creams, but the patient developed occasional tenderness.
The patient was in good health and denied any history of chronic disease, drug allergies, or genetic diseases. Physical examination revealed no obvious abnormalities in the heart, lung, or abdomen, and no swelling of any superficial lymph nodes in the body.
Clustered yellow papules (diameter 5 mm) with clear boundaries were found on the left cheek, covering an area of approximately 3 cm x 3 cm. The surface was smooth and had a waxy luster (Figure 1A). A similar rash was seen on the left chest, covering an area of approximately 6 cm x 3.5 cm with a clear boundary, smooth surface, waxy luster, mild infiltration and hypertrophy, normal skin temperature, and no tenderness (Figure 1B). Some of the papules were fused and varied in color (red, brown, deep red).
Blood test revealed that the total immunoglobulin E (IgE) level was 389.0 kU/L; the level of ferritin, a tumor biomarker, was below average at 9.70 microg/L. Blood analysis demonstrated negative results for hepatitis B, hepatitis C, syphilis and AIDS. Blood glucose levels were normal. High-resolution chest CT showed mild chronic inflammation in the left lung, multiple small lymph nodes in the mediastinum, and flocculent shadows in the anterior mediastinum in the region of the thymus. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a hepatic cyst. Histopathological examination of the left chest skin lesion showed a roughly normal epidermis with cell masses in the dermis. The phagocytic histiocytes had deep irregular nuclei with pale and frothy cytoplasm. Lymphocytes, plasma cells, a small number of neutrophils and eosinophils were observed in the mass upon hematoxylin and eosin (HE) staining (Figure 2). Emperipolesis phenomenon was also observed (Figure 3). IHC staining showed S100 (+) (Figure 4A), CD68 (+) (Figure 4B), and CD1a (-) (Figure 4C).
After relevant auxiliary examinations and whole-body physical and hematological examinations, it was confirmed that the patient had no lymph node enlargement or visceral involvement. Thus, the diagnosis of primary papulonodular-type CRDD was made.
No treatment was initiated and the skin lesions partially disappeared three months after diagnosis (Figure 5A and B). The patient is still being monitored via follow-up examinations (Figure 6).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 47-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of asymptomatic clustered waxy yellow-to-reddish-brown papules and plaques on her left cheek and left anterior chest.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Three months prior to presentation, the patient developed a painless, non-pruritic papular plaque on her left cheek without an identifiable trigger, followed by a larger similar plaque on her left chest. One month of topical tacrolimus and halometasone creams yielded minimal improvement with occasional mild tenderness.
subjective.past_medical_history: Previously healthy with no chronic systemic diseases, genetic disorders, or drug allergies.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for left cheek and left chest papulonodular plaques with occasional mild tenderness; negative for pruritus, fever, or systemic symptoms. Recent medications: topical tacrolimus and halometasone creams.

objective.physical_examination: Cardiopulmonary, abdominal, and superficial lymph node examinations were normal. Dermatological examination revealed a 3 x 3 cm cluster of well-demarcated 5-mm smooth, waxy yellow papules on the left cheek, and a 6 x 3.5 cm well-demarcated, mildly infiltrated plaque of coalescent red, brown, and yellow waxy papules on the left chest.
objective.routine_investigations: Blood tests showed elevated total serum IgE (389.0 kU/L), low serum ferritin (9.70 ug/L), normal blood glucose, and negative serologies for syphilis, HIV, hepatitis B, and hepatitis C. High-resolution chest CT showed mild chronic left lung inflammation, small mediastinal nodes, and anterior mediastinal thymic remnants; abdominal ultrasound showed a benign hepatic cyst.
objective.advanced_workup: Left chest skin biopsy histopathology demonstrated a normal epidermis overlying dermal sheets of large phagocytic histiocytes with pale, foamy cytoplasm and irregular nuclei exhibiting prominent emperipolesis (intact lymphocytes engulfed within histiocyte cytoplasm), admixed with lymphocytes, plasma cells, neutrophils, and eosinophils. Immunohistochemistry was positive for S100 and CD68 and negative for CD1a.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Confirmed primary papulonodular cutaneous Rosai-Dorfman disease (CRDD; secondary/nodular syphilis, Langerhans cell histiocytosis, and systemic RDD excluded via negative syphilis serology, negative CD1a, positive S100/CD68 emperipolesis, and absence of nodal/visceral involvement). Managed with clinical observation alone without systemic therapy, achieving spontaneous partial regression of the cheek and chest lesions at 3-month follow-up.

raw_case_text:
A full-term female infant was born at 39 weeks gestation to a 36-year-old mother (O blood type; Rh-positive) via spontaneous vaginal birth. The antenatal visits and ultrasound scans of the mother were unremarkable, and antenatal serology testing for hepatitis B, rubella, syphilis, and HIV were negative. The neonate cried immediately at birth, and her Apgar scores were normal: 8 at 1 min and 9 at 5 min. Cord complete blood count (CBC) showed low hemoglobin (10.8 mg/L), hematocrit (33.6%), white blood cell count (8.6 x 109), and platelet count (229 x 109). Her blood group was B positive and the direct Coombs test was abnormally positive. At 3 h of age, a repeat investigation showed high total serum bilirubin (TSB; 193 mumol/L). Therefore, the neonate was admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit for further investigation and treatment.
At the time of admission, the infant was active and stable; her heart rate was 140 beats/min, her respiratory rate 40 breaths/min, and she was breathing normally in normal saturated room air. The infant's weight on admission was 2,300 g (3rd-5th percentile), length 48 cm (25th percentile), and head circumference 33 cm (10th percentile). Cardiovascular, respiratory, and nervous system examinations were unremarkable. No dysmorphic features were noted. However, her physical examination revealed scleral icterus and abdominal distension with a palpable mass in the left hypochondrium. The septic screen was negative, and liver and renal function tests were unremarkable.
The patient was treated empirically with antibiotics and placed on maintenance intravenous fluid. Packed red blood transfusion and triple phototherapy were initiated, and she received intravenous immunoglobulin (0.5 g/kg).
An abdominal ultrasound on day 1 revealed moderate ascites and a heterogenous hypoechoic lesion anterolateral to the left kidney that measured 5 x 5.5 x 2.5 cm and extended down to the left iliac fossa, displacing the colon laterally but with no vascularity on Doppler. The mass was intraperitoneal rather than retroperitoneal and suspected to be a hematoma. On day 4, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the abdomen showed a well-defined semilunar-shaped structure in the left lumbar region lateral to the descending colon. The left kidney was posterior to the structure and showed no enhancement after intravenous injection of gadolinium except at its hilum. The picture was indicative of an infarcted WS (Figure 1).
A technetium scan at 5 days of life showed an absent/non-visualized, non-functional spleen (Figure 2). Due to the patient's clinical stability, both the medical team and her parents decided to proceed with conservative non-surgical management. The patient was provided supportive care and discharged at 18 days of age with acceptable CBC values. Prophylactic amoxicillin was continued and the child was seen regularly by general pediatrics and pediatric hematology services. A follow-up ultrasound at 3 months of age was consistent with previous ultrasound findings, except that the size of the WS had decreased to 2.7 x 1.2 cm with early calcified foci.
The child gained weight appropriately during the first 2 years of life. She was admitted once to the general pediatric ward with viral bronchiolitis. Lab investigations revealed mild microcytic hypochromic anemia, leukocytosis, and mild thrombocytosis (600-1,000 x 109). Considering her hemogram, the nuclear study was repeated. Static and single-photon emission CT (SPECT-CT) imaging demonstrated two small oval foci of uptake posteriorly in the left hypochondrium, indicative of splenunculi/splenules (Figure 3). A follow-up technetium scan still showed an absent/non-visualized, non-functional spleen (Figure 4). Findings were consistent with asplenia with splenunculi/splenules in the splenic bed.
A 3-year follow-up showed improved blood indices within normal limits. The parents chose to stop her oral penicillin at 3 years of age. The child continued to thrive normally and was subsequently discharged from the pediatric hematology clinic.

subjective.chief_complaint: A full-term female neonate born at 39 weeks' gestation presented at 3 hours of life with ABO-incompatibility hemolytic jaundice, anemia, abdominal distension, and a palpable left hypochondrial/flank mass.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Born at 39 weeks' gestation via spontaneous vaginal delivery (Apgar 8 and 9, birth weight 2,300 g), the neonate was found on cord blood testing to have anemia (hemoglobin 10.8 g/dL) and a positive direct Coombs test (maternal blood group O+, infant B+), followed at 3 hours of life by severe hyperbilirubinemia (TSB 193 umol/L), scleral icterus, abdominal distension, and a left abdominal mass.
subjective.past_medical_history: Born at 39 weeks to a 36-year-old mother (blood type O Rh-positive) with unremarkable prenatal ultrasounds and negative maternal prenatal serologies for syphilis, HIV, hepatitis B, and rubella.
subjective.review_of_systems: Active, normoxic newborn; positive for jaundice and abdominal distension.

objective.physical_examination: Heart rate 140 bpm, respiratory rate 40 breaths/min, weight 2,300 g (3rd-5th percentile), length 48 cm (25th percentile), and head circumference 33 cm (10th percentile). Physical examination revealed scleral icterus, abdominal distension, and a palpable mass in the left hypochondrium/lumbar region, with normal cardiorespiratory and neurological exams.
objective.routine_investigations: Cord blood showed hemoglobin 10.8 g/dL, hematocrit 33.6%, WBC 8.6 x 10^9/L, platelets 229 x 10^9/L, blood group B Rh-positive, and positive direct Coombs test; 3-hour total serum bilirubin was 193 umol/L. Neonatal sepsis screen, liver and renal function tests, and maternal prenatal syphilis, HIV, HBV, and rubella serologies were all negative or normal. Day 1 abdominal ultrasound showed moderate ascites and a 5 x 5.5 x 2.5 cm avascular heterogeneous hypoechoic intraperitoneal mass anterolateral to the left kidney displacing the descending colon.
objective.advanced_workup: Day 4 contrast-enhanced abdominal MRI demonstrated a semilunar non-enhancing infarcted wandering spleen in the left lumbar region anterior to the left kidney (with enhancement limited to the splenic hilum). Day 5 (and 2-year) Technetium-99m nuclear scintigraphy confirmed functional asplenia (non-visualized infarcted spleen, shrinking to 2.7 x 1.2 cm with calcifications by 3 months), while 2-year SPECT-CT identified two small functioning posterior left hypochondrial splenunculi/splenules.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Confirmed neonatal torsion and infarction of a congenital wandering spleen complicated by ABO hemolytic disease of the newborn and functional asplenia with compensatory splenunculi (congenital syphilis, HIV, HBV, and rubella excluded). Managed conservatively without splenectomy using packed RBC transfusion, triple phototherapy, intravenous immunoglobulin (0.5 g/kg), and oral amoxicillin prophylaxis until 3 years of age, with normal growth and hematologic indices at 3-year follow-up.

raw_case_text:
A 58-year-old woman living in rural Saskatchewan, Canada presented with a 2-month history of a pruritic, desquamating, purpuric, exfoliating skin rash affecting the extremities and trunk and sparing the face and mucosal membranes (Figure 1). The eruption began after the introduction of multiple antibiotic regimens for the management of septic arthritis associated with a unilateral hip arthroplasty 6 months prior. The patient initially was seen by Internal Medicine and had a complex medical history including hypothyroidism, alcoholic liver cirrhosis, long-standing seronegative rheumatoid arthritis, vitiligo, gout, peripheral eosinophilia with pulmonary infiltrates (presumed eosinophilic pneumonia), and bilateral knee arthroplasty. Family history was positive for sarcoidosis affecting the patient's sister. Investigations at the time of presentation were notable for microcytic anemia, peripheral eosinophilia, and elevated ALP, AST, GGT, IgE, IgG1, and IgG3 levels. ANA, dsDNA, ANCA panel, and Anti-Jo1 antibody were negative, along with HIV, hepatitis, and syphilis serologies. Computed tomography (CT) of the chest showed nonspecific areas of ground-glass opacity, bilaterally.
Punch biopsies in areas of scaling over the right thigh were performed and showed a mixed dermatitis (Figure 2). Histopathologically, there was an interface dermatitis with numerous civatte and colloid bodies at the dermoepidermal junction. The epidermis was significant for lichen planus-like changes with irregular acanthosis and prominent "saw toothing" and variable compact orthohyperkeratotic scale. The papillary dermis showed perivascular and interstitial lymphohistiocytic inflammation with eosinophils, as well as rare, small, non-necrotizing granulomas. Granulomas were associated with lymphocytes and eosinophils. There was no lymphoid atypia, nor was there any evidence of an acute vasculitis after multiple deeper levels through the tissue block. The deep reticular dermis was unremarkable. Other pertinent negatives included the absence of parasites and other organisms, "flame figures," and polarizable or refractile material. PAS/Alcian blue histochemical stains performed at the time were negative for fungal organisms and dermal mucin (not shown). GMS, ZN, and Fite histochemical stains performed at the time were negative for fungal and acid-fast bacteria respectively (not shown). A differential diagnosis based on the appearance of the skin lesions at the time of the biopsy included a vesiculobullous disorder, so a separate punch biopsy was submitted in Michel's media for direct immunofluorescence (DIF). Cytoid bodies were positive for IgA, IgM, IgG, C3, and fibrinogen (not shown), consistent with an interface dermatitis (not shown).
A highly favored clinical diagnosis was cutaneous manifestation of eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA) given the presence of bilateral pulmonary infiltrates on CT scan and bloodwork with peripheral eosinophilia. EGPA could not be excluded entirely given the granulomas present histologically, despite the lack of other histologic findings typically seen in EGPA. Therefore, the case was sent for external review by five expert dermatopathologists who agreed the case was most compatible with "lichenoid and granulomatous dermatitis" due to the lack of typical triad of vasculitis, granulomata, and eosinophils seen in EGPA. Correlation with ANCA status as well as further investigation of the patient's lung findings was recommended to definitively rule out a cutaneous manifestation of EGPA.
The patient's antibiotic regimen was switched to amoxicillin-clavulanate and skin lesions were managed with topical corticosteroids and topical tacrolimus. The skin lesions eventually improved in line with a downward trending peripheral eosinophilia. Unfortunately, the patient has since been lost to follow-up.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 58-year-old woman from rural Saskatchewan presented with a 2-month history of a pruritic, desquamating, purpuric, exfoliative rash over her trunk and extremities following multiple antibiotic courses for prosthetic hip septic arthritis.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Following multiple systemic antibiotic regimens initiated 6 months earlier for a unilateral prosthetic hip septic arthritis, the patient developed a generalized pruritic, purpuric, scaling eruption across her trunk and limbs (sparing her face and mucosa) that persisted for 2 months.
subjective.past_medical_history: Complex medical history including hypothyroidism, alcoholic liver cirrhosis, long-standing seronegative rheumatoid arthritis, vitiligo, gout, peripheral eosinophilia with pulmonary infiltrates (presumed eosinophilic pneumonia), bilateral total knee arthroplasties, and unilateral hip arthroplasty complicated by septic arthritis 6 months prior. Family history: sister had sarcoidosis.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for pruritic exfoliative truncal/limb rash; negative for facial or mucosal lesions. Recent multiple systemic antibiotic regimens.

objective.physical_examination: Cutaneous examination revealed a generalized pruritic, desquamating, purpuric, and exfoliative dermatitis involving the trunk and upper and lower extremities, with complete sparing of the face and mucous membranes.
objective.routine_investigations: Blood tests showed microcytic anemia, peripheral eosinophilia, elevated ALP, AST, and GGT, and elevated serum IgE, IgG1, and IgG3 levels. ANA, anti-dsDNA, ANCA panel, anti-Jo1 antibody, HIV, viral hepatitis, and syphilis serologies were all negative. Chest CT showed nonspecific bilateral ground-glass opacities.
objective.advanced_workup: Right thigh punch biopsy histopathology and direct immunofluorescence (consensus of 5 dermatopathologists) demonstrated a lichenoid and granulomatous interface dermatitis: irregular acanthosis with 'saw-toothing', compact orthohyperkeratosis, numerous Civatte/colloid bodies at the dermoepidermal junction (positive for IgA, IgM, IgG, C3, and fibrinogen on DIF), and a papillary dermal perivascular/interstitial lymphohistiocytic infiltrate with eosinophils and small non-necrotizing granulomas, without acute necrotizing vasculitis or organisms (negative PAS, Alcian blue, GMS, Ziehl-Neelsen, and Fite stains).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Confirmed drug-induced/reactive lichenoid and granulomatous dermatitis with peripheral eosinophilia and pulmonary ground-glass infiltrates (cutaneous EGPA and secondary syphilis excluded via negative ANCA, absence of necrotizing vasculitis, and negative syphilis serology). Switching her antibiotic regimen to amoxicillin-clavulanate and applying topical corticosteroids and topical tacrolimus resulted in resolution of the cutaneous eruption alongside declining peripheral eosinophilia.

raw_case_text:
A female child, three years old, 16 kg, had complaints of vomiting, weakness, and convulsion-like tremor at the right angle of the mouth a week before the admission. After a week in hospital care, the patient was discharged. A week later, the patient's head tilted to the right while talking, and the patient was less active than before. Therefore, the patient was admitted to the hospital again to be evaluated with brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and brain tissue biopsy.
The patient was diagnosed with tuberculoma based on first brain MRI, brain tissue biopsy and got regimens of anti-tuberculosis therapy. A week after the patient got the anti-tuberculosis therapy, the patient's condition worsened. The patient was consulted to the pediatric neurologist with general weakness, altered consciousness, and hand tremor.
The patient was admitted with fever (39  C), Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) was 7 (E2V2M3); pupils were asymmetric with slow response to the light, tetraparesis (the motoric strength were 1 of 5), increasing physiological reflexes; positive Babinsky with clonus, spastic, and hand tremorShe had high transaminases enzyme without proof of cytomegalovirus (CMV), HSV-1, HSV-2 syphilis, and tuberculosis infection.
First brain MRI (two weeks before admission) (Figure 1), showed hypointense lesion and hyperintense spots in T1W1, which became hyperintense dominance on T2W1 with perifocal edema. The size of the lesion is 7,8 x 8,1 x 7,9 cm in the corpus callosum and frontal lobe bilateral (with right dominance). The lesion adheres to the falx cerebri and bilateral lateral ventricle with compression to the anterior horn of the bilateral lateral ventricle. Another smaller lesion with the same characteristics was found in the left parietal lobe that adheres to the falx cerebri with multiple nodules. These nodules are hyperintense after contrast introduction and located in the left frontal, bilateral parietal, and left temporal lobes. This condition suggests glioblastoma with a differential diagnosis of necrotizing toxoplasma encephalitis.
The brain tissue biopsy showed a gemicytocytic cell adjacent to the edematous loose neutrophil stromal. A few parts of the tissue consisted of extensive necrotic tissue, which forms caseous necrosis with lymphocyte, macrophage, and epithelioid-like cell infiltration. The conclusion was a chronic inflammation in brain tuberculosis. The biopsy specimen was sent for a second opinion. The result showed a necrotic mass and inflammatory cells, suggesting an inflammatory process without malignancy or tuberculosis.
The patient was still treated with anti-tuberculosis, corticosteroid, anti-convulsant, antipyretic, 20% mannitol for high intracranial pressure management.
On the 3rd day of the hospitalization, the GCS was improved (E4V2M3). The second brain MRI was done (Figure 2). The lesions found in the subcortical and juxtacortical of the bilateral fronto-temporo-parietal, right occipital, bilateral parieto-occipital lobes, and bilateral head of the caudate nucleus, in the part of the putamen and the bilateral of globus pallidus without mass effect. This lesion was followed by an early subacute of hemorrhage component in the lesion of bilateral head of caudate nucleus with cortical laminar necrosis at the frontal and bilateral of parietal lobes. Spinal MRI was normal.
Several viral (adenovirus, coronavirus 229E, coronavirus HKU1, coronavirus NL63, coronavirus OC43, SARS-CoV-2, Human Metapneumovirus, Human Rhinovirus/Enterovirus, Influenza A and B, Parainfluenza 1 to 4, Respiratory Syncytial Virus) and bacterial infection (Bordatella parapertussis, Bordatella pertussis, Chlamydia pneumoniae, and Mycoplasma pneumoniae) were excluded by real time-polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) examination. The results of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) examination are clear fluid, 100% mononuclear cells, leukocyte 2 cells/mm3, protein 3 mg/dL, glucose 59 mg/dL, negative Nonne test, positive Pandy test, negative of tuberculosis (Gene Xpert and fast acid bacilli examination) and negative of bacterial culture.
The second MRI showed hemorrhage and necrosis, which were inappropriate with the resolution of tuberculoma; then, the diagnosis ANEC was considered. The anti-tuberculosis therapy was stopped after two weeks. The intravenous (IV) acyclovir was started with consideration of HSV infection as an etiology of ANEC. The patient had 300 mg (dosis perkgBB berapa) of intravenous acyclovir three times a day for 21 days, 375 mg of methylprednisolone IV once a day for five days, and immunoglobulin IV 0,4 gram/kg BW/day for five days.
On the second week of hospitalization, patient's GCS was improved to 11 (E4V2M3), motor strength was increased to 3 of 5. The third brain MRI was done (Figure 3), which showed an extension of the lesion in the subcortical and juxtacortical of the bilateral fronto-temporo-parietal, right occipital, bilateral parieto-occipital lobes, the trunk of the corpus callosum, bilateral head of the caudate nucleus, part of the putamen and bilateral of the globus pallidus. These lesions were followed by the relatively stable early subacute of the hemorrhage component at the lesion, located at the bilateral head of the caudate nucleus, part of the putamen, and bilateral globus pallidus. There was also the addition of cortical laminar necrosis in the frontal and bilateral parietal lobes. On the third week of hospitalization, the clinical condition remained.
Examination of serum showed the negativity of anti-Histoplasma, aspergillus, autoimmune panel for encephalitis, and Ab MOG. The patient showed improvement with GCS 13 (E4V4M5) and slight tetraparesis after five months of discharge.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 3-year-old girl presented with a 3-week biphasic illness beginning with vomiting, weakness, right oral commissure focal motor seizures, and right head tilt, progressing 1 week after starting empiric antituberculosis therapy to high fever, coma, and spastic tetraparesis.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Initially hospitalized for 1 week with vomiting, weakness, and twitching at the right corner of her mouth, the child was readmitted 1 week later with a right head tilt, decreased activity, and a large bifrontal/callosal lesion on MRI initially diagnosed on brain biopsy as cerebral tuberculoma. One week after starting antituberculosis therapy, she deteriorated acutely with high fever (39 C), deep coma (GCS 7), spastic tetraparesis, and hand tremors.
subjective.past_medical_history: 3-year-old female weighing 16 kg.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for vomiting, right facial focal seizures, right head tilt, fever (39 C), stupor/coma, tetraparesis, and hand tremor.

objective.physical_examination: On pediatric neurology consultation, the child was febrile (39 C) and comatose with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 7 (E2V2M3), asymmetric sluggishly reactive pupils, spastic tetraparesis (motor strength 1/5 in all four limbs), hyperreflexia, bilateral positive Babinski signs with ankle clonus, and hand tremors.
objective.routine_investigations: Blood tests showed elevated liver transaminases and negative serologies/PCRs for syphilis, CMV, HSV-1, HSV-2, tuberculosis, Histoplasma, Aspergillus, and a 20-pathogen respiratory viral/bacterial RT-PCR panel (including SARS-CoV-2 and Influenza A/B).
objective.advanced_workup: Initial brain MRI showed a 7.8 x 8.1 x 7.9 cm callosal/bifrontal mass and multiple enhancing frontoparietal/temporal nodules; second-opinion review of the brain biopsy showed necrotizing inflammation with gemistocytic astrocytes and macrophages without malignancy or true tuberculosis. Subsequent serial brain MRIs (days 3 and 14; spinal MRI normal) revealed extensive symmetric hemorrhagic and necrotizing lesions involving the bilateral caudate heads, putamina, globus pallidi, corpus callosum, and fronto-temporo-parieto-occipital subcortical white matter with cortical laminar necrosis. Lumbar puncture yielded clear CSF with 2 mononuclear cells/mm3, protein 3 mg/dL, glucose 59 mg/dL, negative GeneXpert/AFB/bacterial cultures, and negative serum anti-MOG and autoimmune encephalitis panels.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Diagnosed with Acute Necrotizing Encephalopathy of Childhood (ANEC; cerebral tuberculoma, glioblastoma, syphilis, and autoimmune/MOG encephalitis excluded on biopsy review, CSF GeneXpert, and serologies). Antituberculosis drugs were discontinued after 2 weeks, and she was treated with intravenous methylprednisolone (375 mg/day for 5 days), intravenous immunoglobulin (0.4 g/kg/day for 5 days), a 21-day course of IV acyclovir, anticonvulsants, and 20% mannitol, improving to GCS 11 (strength 3/5) by week 2 and GCS 13 (E4V4M5) with only mild residual tetraparesis at 5 months post-discharge.

raw_case_text:
A 48-year-old female presented with progressive pain, redness, and foreign body sensation in the left eye (LE) over the past 6 months. She had a history of peripheral ulcerative keratitis in the right eye (RE) requiring systemic immunosuppression and tectonic lamellar keratoplasty to reconstruct the area of the corneal thinning 15 years ago. Her systemic workup (complete cell blood count, electrolytes, urea, creatinine, liver function test, thyroid function test, C reactive protein (CRP), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), rheumatoid factor, antinuclear antibodies (ANA), antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA), extractable nuclear antigens, anti-citrullinated protein antibody, syphilis, herpetic and hepatitis serologies) was negative 15 years prior. Her systems review at that point revealed a chronically inflamed elbow; therefore, she was started on oral cyclosporine up to 100 mg oral BID and Felodipine 2.5 mg oral daily for presumed seronegative rheumatoid arthritis. This systemic management was successfully tapered off 4 years ago with no recurrence of symptoms in the eye or the elbow joint.
On examination, she had uncorrected Snellen visual acuity of 6/30 on the right and 6/21 on the left. RE revealed an uninflamed tectonic lamellar keratoplasty. The LE was acutely inflamed inferonasally adjacent to an area of peripheral corneal ulceration without perforation. The anterior chamber was deep and quiet bilaterally at this point. She had trace nuclear sclerosis in both eyes.
She was commenced on oral ascorbic acid, topical moxifloxacin QID andprednisolone acetate 1% QID in the LE, and advised to use an eye shield at night. The rheumatology team was consulted again, and she was started on oral prednisone 60 mg daily as well as oral mycophenolate mofetil 1 g BID. On repeat assessment a week later, she had not yet started systemic treatment and had not been using her eye shield. She was found to have a perforation within the area of thinning with a flat anterior chamber (Figure 1).
A bandage contact lens was put on the LE as a temporizing measure before surgical management. She was continued on topical moxifloxacin and prednisolone acetate in the LE. Two days later, a conjunctival recession, amniotic membrane transplant and a temporary tarsorrhaphy was performed under retrobulbar anesthesia. A single piece of folded, multi-layered, fresh frozen amniotic membrane was packed and sutured into the LE corneal defect and held in place using fibrin glue. An overlying large single layer of amniotic membrane with the epithelial side down was sutured with interrupted sutures of 10.0 nylon with tension over the temporal ocular surface in a bandage fashion (Supplementary Video). A medial temporary tarsorrhaphy was carried out using bolsters and 6-0 nylon. Subconjunctival antibiotics of cefazolin and dexamethasone were injected at the end of the procedure. Postoperatively the patient was commenced on moxifloxacin eye drops QID, prednisolone acetate 1% QID and preservative-free lubricants 2-hourly.
The patient had an uneventful post-operative course without further episodes of ulceration, melt or inflammation. The AM patch integrated well into the corneal stroma at the 1-month postoperative visit with Snellen visual acuity of 6/15 and a quiet ocular surface (Figure 2A). Her uncorrected Snellen visual acuity improved to 6/9 at 3-months post op (Figure 2B).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 48-year-old female presented with a 6-month history of progressive pain, redness, and foreign-body sensation in her left eye, complicated 1 week later by inferonasal peripheral corneal perforation.
