objective.physical_examination: A large oval erythematous-violaceous plaque covering more than half of the right pretibial region with slightly elevated, indurated, infiltrative borders and a center scattered with small necrotic crusted ulcers and atrophic scars, accompanied by similar smaller plaques on the left leg and no regional lymphadenopathy.
objective.routine_investigations: CBC, routine biochemistry, urinalysis, bacteriological cultures, and chest radiograph were normal except for hyperglycemia (blood glucose 11.8 mmol/L).
objective.advanced_workup: Skin biopsy histopathology (H&E and Giemsa stains) demonstrated a dense pan-dermal lymphocytic infiltrate with multiple non-necrotizing epithelioid and multinucleated giant-cell granulomas containing intracellular basophilic Leishmania amastigotes.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Histopathology and Giemsa staining of the pretibial skin biopsy confirmed chronic granulomatous Cutaneous Leishmaniasis mimicking necrobiosis lipoidica/granulomatous dermatosis in a patient with type 1 diabetes. Intramuscular meglumine antimoniate (20 mg/kg/day for 15 days) resulted in complete ulcer healing with residual atrophic scarring.

raw_case_text: A 50-year-old Caucasian male, with no relevant past medical records, was referred to SCT with a high-risk acute lymphoblastic B leukemia in first complete remission (CR). Allogeneic SCT was performed with peripheral blood stem cells from an unrelated Portuguese matched 9/10 donor (disparity in locus HLA-A), after myeloablative conditioning regimen (with busulfan, cyclophosphamide, and antilymphocytic serum). Graft versus host disease prophylaxis was performed with tacrolimus and methotrexate. There were no major complications during neutropenic period. Corticotherapy was prescribed for upper digestive graft versus host disease diagnosed 2 months after SCT. In the following months, patient developed mild fluctuating cytopenias, mostly thrombocytopenia (between 60 and 80*109/L). The only significant complaint was intermittent tiredness. Bone marrow evaluation had no signs of relapse disease and patient had complete chimerism. The common causes for thrombocytopenia were excluded:no evidence of graft versus host disease; no signs of viral or bacterial infection; and no signs of relapsed disease/dysplastic changes. The bone marrow smear performed 12 months after transplant revealed an unsuspected diagnosis: a massive bone marrow infiltration with amastigotes:(Figure 1 optical microscopy, Wright Giemsa stain, 100x magnification). Reticuloendothelial cells had exuberant parasitic cytoplasmatic inclusions and a few images of erythrophagocytosis were present (Figure 1). The sample was sent to DNA PCR analysis and Leishmania infantum was identified. Previous bone marrow smears were reviewed and scarce parasites, not previously observed, were found in a smear performed 6 months after SCT. The donor had no history of visceral leishmaniasis. The patient was treated with a total dose of 24 mg/kg of liposomal amphotericin B, with clinical improvement and no signs of leishmania in the bone marrow. Five months later, the patient developed epigastric pain and duodenal biopsy revealed no evidence of graft versus host disease but the presence of inflammatory infiltrate with the presence of amastigotes in the macrophages was evident; a new bone marrow was performed and was positive for leishmania. The patient restarted liposomal amphotericin B and a prolonged maintenance treatment is planned.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 50-year-old Caucasian man presented 12 months after allogeneic stem cell transplantation for B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia with intermittent fatigue and fluctuating thrombocytopenia, followed 5 months later by epigastric pain.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Two months after undergoing a 9/10 HLA-matched unrelated allogeneic peripheral blood stem cell transplant for high-risk B-ALL in first complete remission, the patient received corticosteroids for upper gastrointestinal graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) and subsequently developed persistent mild cytopenias (predominantly thrombocytopenia of 60-80 x 10^9/L) and intermittent tiredness over the ensuing 10 months. Five months after initial antileishmanial treatment, he re-presented with epigastric pain.
subjective.past_medical_history: High-risk B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia in first complete remission status post myeloablative allogeneic SCT (busulfan, cyclophosphamide, antilymphocyte serum conditioning; tacrolimus/methotrexate GVHD prophylaxis) and upper GI GVHD treated with corticosteroids; donor had no history of visceral leishmaniasis.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for intermittent tiredness and subsequent epigastric pain.

objective.routine_investigations: Serial blood counts showed fluctuating mild cytopenias, predominantly thrombocytopenia (60-80 x 10^9/L), with negative viral and bacterial screening.
objective.advanced_workup: Bone marrow aspirate at 12 months post-SCT (Wright-Giemsa stain) showed complete donor chimerism and no leukemia relapse, but revealed massive infiltration of reticuloendothelial cells with cytoplasmic Leishmania amastigotes and erythrophagocytosis (retrospective review of the 6-month post-SCT marrow smear also identified scarce amastigotes). At relapse 5 months later, upper endoscopy with duodenal biopsy and repeat bone marrow aspirate both demonstrated macrophages containing Leishmania amastigotes without GVHD.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Leukemia relapse and active GI/marrow GVHD were excluded; Wright-Giemsa bone marrow microscopy, duodenal mucosal biopsy, and DNA PCR confirmed post-transplant Visceral Leishmaniasis with gastrointestinal involvement caused by Leishmania infantum. An initial course of intravenous liposomal amphotericin B (total dose 24 mg/kg) cleared the bone marrow, and following the duodenal/marrow relapse 5 months later, liposomal amphotericin B was re-initiated with planned long-term secondary maintenance prophylaxis.

raw_case_text: A 37-year-old male from Georgia came to France in October 2012. He had HIV infection since 2006 inconstantly treated with HAART. Other medical conditions were adrenal insufficiency, cirrhosis due to chronic HCV, and treatment-controlled tuberculosis. VL was diagnosed in 2010 and treated in Georgia with meglumine antimoniate and L-AmB (doses and schedules unknown). In November 2012, he presented hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathies, infiltrated cutaneous lesions, anemia, number of CD4 lymphocytes = 133/mm3, viral load < 50 copies/mL, and parasitemia of 6 Leishmania/ml. He received a course of L-AmB followed by maintenance therapy for 5 months (Fig 1B). In May 2013, he had weight loss, hepatosplenomegaly, anemia, number of CD4 lymphocytes = 177/mm3, viral load < 40 copies/mL and parasitemia of 12 Leishmania/ml. L-AmB treatment was intensified, but renal insufficiency and acute thrombocytopenia occurred. In June, the splenomegaly and parasitemia remained unchanged. A course of meglumine antimoniate was administered. Despite pre-existing liver disorders, the treatment was well tolerated except for mild neutropenia. One month later, a marked clinical improvement was observed and parasitemia decreased to 0.2 Leishmania/ml. In July, maintenance treatment with miltefosine (150 mg/day for 3 months) was started. Parasitemia was negative, the number of CD4 lymphocytes increased from 169 to 540/mm3, and viral load was undetectable. Parasitemia remained negative through 18 months.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 37-year-old HIV-positive male from Georgia presented in November 2012 with hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, infiltrated cutaneous lesions, and anemia, followed by a clinical relapse in May 2013 with weight loss, hepatosplenomegaly, and anemia.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Diagnosed with visceral leishmaniasis in Georgia in 2010 and treated with meglumine antimoniate and liposomal amphotericin B (L-AmB), the patient arrived in France in October 2012 and presented in November 2012 with relapsing visceral and cutaneous leishmaniasis. He received an induction course of L-AmB followed by 5 months of maintenance therapy, but relapsed in May 2013 with weight loss, persistent hepatosplenomegaly, anemia, and rising parasitemia; L-AmB intensification caused acute kidney injury and acute thrombocytopenia without clearing parasitemia.
subjective.past_medical_history: HIV-1 infection diagnosed in 2006 (inconsistently treated with HAART); adrenal insufficiency; chronic hepatitis C cirrhosis; treatment-controlled tuberculosis; prior visceral leishmaniasis in Georgia (2010).
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for weight loss, infiltrated skin lesions, and organomegaly.

objective.physical_examination: Hepatosplenomegaly, peripheral lymphadenopathy, and infiltrated cutaneous lesions.
objective.routine_investigations: Labs showed anemia, undetectable HIV viral load (<50 copies/mL in Nov 2012, <40 copies/mL in May 2013), acute renal insufficiency and acute thrombocytopenia during intensified L-AmB in May 2013, and mild neutropenia during subsequent meglumine antimoniate therapy.
objective.advanced_workup: CD4+ T-lymphocyte count was 133 cells/mm3 in November 2012, 177 cells/mm3 in May 2013, and increased from 169 to 540 cells/mm3 during miltefosine maintenance. Quantitative blood PCR demonstrated 6 Leishmania/mL in November 2012 and 12 Leishmania/mL in May/June 2013.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Quantitative blood PCR confirmed L-AmB-refractory relapsing Visceral and Cutaneous Leishmaniasis in an HIV-1 and HCV-cirrhotic patient. Salvage therapy in June 2013 with systemic meglumine antimoniate reduced parasitemia to 0.2 Leishmania/mL within 1 month with only mild neutropenia, and subsequent 3-month maintenance therapy with oral miltefosine (150 mg/day starting July 2013) achieved complete parasite clearance, CD4 recovery to 540/mm3, and 18 months of relapse-free PCR-negative follow-up.

raw_case_text: A 75-year-old male from Algeria had HIV infection since 2001 treated with nevirapine and lamivudine/zidovudine. He had cerebral toxoplasmosis, chronic hepatitis B, gastrointestinal CMV infection, and anal squamous cell carcinoma. In 2013, the patient started treatment with darunavir, ritonavir, raltegravir and emtricitabine. VL had been diagnosed in 2001, and treated with L-AmB 5 mg/Kg/d for 15 days with partial improvement. Maintenance therapy of 3 mg/kg weekly was planned but irregularly administered. Recurrence was reported in March 2011, the infecting specie was identified as L. infantum. The number of CD4 lymphocytes was 33/mm3, and viral load 75000 copies/mL. The patient received 40 mg/kg of L-AmB, followed by 3 mg/kg at 15-day interval. Clinical improvement was obtained but qualitative PCR remained positive. In 2012, L-AmB infusions were administered at 3-week intervals. In 2013, a last course of 50 mg/kg of L-AmB was administered, Despite this complete course of L-AmB, clinical symptoms worsened (weight loss, fatigue), clinical splenomegaly was present (greater diameter 20 cm on the CT scan), and parasitemia remained positive and stable (from 126 Leishmania/ml before treatment to 118 Leishmania/ml after completion of the course 3 weeks later). Meglumine antimoniate was thus administered, initially at low doses (4-10 mg/kg SbV every other day for 7 weeks) because of advanced age. Treatment was well tolerated except for moderate neutropenia. Fatigue resolved and weight increased from 50 to 61 Kg. The spleen was no longer palpable after 2 months of treatment. Number of CD4 lymphocytes increased from 75 to 134/mm3. Parasitemia cleared and remained negative through 13 months of follow-up.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 75-year-old HIV-positive male from Algeria with chronic relapsing visceral leishmaniasis since 2001 presented in 2013 with worsening fatigue, weight loss, and massive splenomegaly refractory to liposomal amphotericin B.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Initially diagnosed with visceral leishmaniasis in 2001 and partially responsive to liposomal amphotericin B (L-AmB 5 mg/kg/day for 15 days) with irregular weekly maintenance (3 mg/kg), the patient relapsed in March 2011 and remained PCR-positive with worsening weight loss, fatigue, and massive splenomegaly in 2013 despite cumulative L-AmB courses of 40 mg/kg (followed by 3 mg/kg every 2-3 weeks) and 50 mg/kg.
subjective.past_medical_history: HIV-1 infection diagnosed in 2001 (treated with nevirapine and lamivudine/zidovudine, switched in 2013 to darunavir, ritonavir, raltegravir, and emtricitabine); cerebral toxoplasmosis; chronic hepatitis B; gastrointestinal CMV infection; anal squamous cell carcinoma.
subjective.review_of_systems: Home ART (from 2013): darunavir, ritonavir, raltegravir, and emtricitabine; positive for fatigue and weight loss (weight 50 kg).

objective.physical_examination: Cachexia/weight loss (50 kg) and massive clinical splenomegaly.
objective.routine_investigations: HIV viral load was 75,000 copies/mL at the March 2011 relapse; moderate neutropenia occurred during meglumine antimoniate therapy.
objective.advanced_workup: CD4+ T-lymphocyte count was 33 cells/mm3 in March 2011 and rose from 75 to 134 cells/mm3 after antimonial therapy. Abdominal CT in 2013 demonstrated a 20-cm enlarged spleen. Species identification confirmed Leishmania infantum, and quantitative blood PCR remained persistently positive before (126 Leishmania/mL) and 3 weeks after (118 Leishmania/mL) the 50 mg/kg L-AmB course in 2013.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Quantitative blood PCR and species typing confirmed L-AmB-refractory relapsing Visceral Leishmaniasis caused by Leishmania infantum in an elderly HIV-coinfected patient. Salvage therapy with low-dose meglumine antimoniate (4-10 mg/kg SbV every other day for 7 weeks) was well tolerated aside from moderate neutropenia, resulting in resolution of fatigue, an 11-kg weight gain (to 61 kg), non-palpable spleen at 2 months, CD4 increase to 134/mm3, and sustained negative Leishmania blood PCR over 13 months of follow-up.

raw_case_text: A 22-month-old girl presented to us with 8-day fever (40 C), and mild cough. On examination, she had hepatosplenomegaly. Past medical history included failure to thrive, but normal neurological development. She was the first child of a non-consanguineous marriage. She had normal brown hair and normal skin. There was no family history of albinism. On physical examination, she was stunted, pale, and had non-tender hepatomegaly of 5-6 cm; the spleen was palpable 4 cm below the left costal margin as confirmed by abdominal ultrasound. The WBC count was 5100/mm3 (ANC 1200/mm3), Hb 9.1 g/dl, and platelets 47.000/mm3. She had mild hypertransaminasemia and hypoalbuminemia. Ferritin was 1134 ng/ml. Soluble IL-2 receptor (sCD25) was 3183 UI/ml. Blood cultures were negative. Serum immunoglobulins and lymphocyte subsets were normal. Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) serology yielded seroreactivity (positive IgM and IgG anti-VCA) with negative IgG anti-EBNA. EBV viral load was 637 copies/ml. Leishmania serology showed both negative immunochromatography and indirect immunofluorescence. Conversely, serum ELISA was slightly positive. Leishmanial antigen in the urine was negative. Bone marrow aspiration revealed hemophagocytosis. The patient worsened clinically, with persistent malaise, progressive splenomegaly, and petechial rash on her chest and legs. Subsequent investigations were WBC 4800/mm3 (ANC 800/mm3), Hb 6.8 g/dl and platelets 27000/mm3, triglycerides 686 mg/dl, ferritin 3849 ng/ml, and sCD25 3596 UI/ml with normal clotting tests as well as perforin expression by flow-cytometry. Hair microscopy was not performed because clinical features of albinism were not present neither in our patient nor in her family. HLH-2004 protocol was started. The following day, Leishmania Polymerase Chain Reaction was done where Leishmanial DNA was detected by nested PCR.) This was confirmed on a bone marrow aspirate as well. Standard therapy with liposomal amphotericin B (3 mg/kg/day IV on days 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 14, and 21) was given. The patient completed HLH-2004 protocol, except for 2 doses of etoposide due to clinical and laboratory improvement without evidence of underlying primary HLH. At 30 month follow up, there is no evidence of relapse. As CD107a degranulation assay was not performed (just normal intracytoplasmic pattern of perforin staining), primary HLH is not absolutely discarded as a differential diagnosis.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 22-month-old girl presented with an 8-day history of high fever up to 40 C and mild cough.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The child presented with 8 days of 40 C fever and mild cough and was found to have hepatosplenomegaly, cytopenias, and bone marrow hemophagocytosis. Her condition worsened in the hospital with persistent malaise, progressive splenomegaly, a petechial rash on the chest and legs, and deepening pancytopenia and hyperferritinemia.
subjective.past_medical_history: History of failure to thrive with normal neurodevelopment; first child of non-consanguineous parents; no personal or family history of albinism.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for high fever, mild cough, malaise, and subsequent petechial rash on the chest and legs.

objective.physical_examination: Stunted growth, pallor, normal brown hair and skin pigmentation, non-tender hepatomegaly (5-6 cm below costal margin), and splenomegaly (4 cm below left costal margin, progressing during admission), later accompanied by a petechial rash over the chest and lower extremities.
objective.routine_investigations: Initial labs showed WBC 5,100/mm3 (ANC 1,200/mm3), Hb 9.1 g/dL, platelets 47,000/mm3, mild hypertransaminasemia, hypoalbuminemia, and ferritin 1,134 ng/mL, worsening to WBC 4,800/mm3 (ANC 800/mm3), Hb 6.8 g/dL, platelets 27,000/mm3, triglycerides 686 mg/dL, and ferritin 3,849 ng/mL with normal coagulation tests. Blood cultures, urinary Leishmania antigen, and Leishmania immunochromatography and IIF serologies were negative, Leishmania serum ELISA was borderline/slightly positive, and EBV serology was positive for anti-VCA IgM and IgG (anti-EBNA IgG negative) with EBV viral load 637 copies/mL. Abdominal ultrasound confirmed hepatosplenomegaly.
objective.advanced_workup: Soluble IL-2 receptor (sCD25) rose from 3,183 UI/mL to 3,596 UI/mL; serum immunoglobulins, lymphocyte subsets, and flow-cytometric intracellular perforin expression were normal. Bone marrow aspiration demonstrated hemophagocytosis, and nested PCR on peripheral blood and bone marrow aspirate detected Leishmania DNA.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Nested PCR on peripheral blood and bone marrow aspirate confirmed Visceral Leishmaniasis-associated secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) co-existing with mild acute EBV viremia (637 copies/mL). Combined treatment with intravenous liposomal amphotericin B (3 mg/kg/day on days 1-5, 14, and 21) and the HLH-2004 protocol (with the final 2 doses of etoposide omitted due to rapid clinical and hematologic recovery) resulted in complete remission with no relapse at 30-month follow-up.

raw_case_text:
A 45-year-old Caucasian male patient was referred to our clinic of endocrinology, because of an incidental finding in a CT scan, suggestive of paraganglioma, performed in the work up for abdominal pain. The abdominal CT scan revealed a 4cm nonspecific retroperitoneal, paraaortic lesion, between celiac trunk and superior mesenteric artery, suggestive of neuroendocrine tumor as the first possibility (Figure 1A). He had a past medical history of smoking, Barret's esophagus, hiatus hernia and gastroesophageal reflux disease treated with omeprazole. He had undergone a sleeve gastrectomy as a surgical weight loss procedure in 2015 and cholecystectomy for cholelithiasis in 2017. After the first visit in our clinic, an initial laboratory investigation was performed for the suspected paraganglioma (references values in parenthesis): glucose 79 mg/dl (74-106); creatinine 0.69 mg/dl (0.70-1.30); alanine aminotransferase 22 IU/L (10-49); ferritin 73 ng/ml (22-322); enolase 19 ng/ml (<16); carcinoembryonic antigen 2.6 ng/ml (<5.0); Ca 19.9: 12 IU/ml (<37); chromogranin A: 3.3 nmol/l (0.4-10.0); hemoglobin 15.4 gr/dl (13.5-17.5); neutrophils 51.7% (40.0-70.0); lymphocytes 33.4% (22.0-44.0), eosinophils 5.3% (RV <8.0). Moreover, total and fractional catecholamines, total metanephrines and excretion of 5-OH-indolacetic in the 24-hour urine analysis were normal. Next, radioisotope imaging was ordered. The whole-body scintigraphy with metaiodobenzylguanidine didn t reveal any clear signs suggesting the existence of catecholamine-producing tumor. The whole-body (99m) Tc-octreotide scintigraphy with SPECT/CT showed a paraaortic abdominal mass, but without evidence of pathological tumor uptake (Figure 2).
After multidisciplinary discussion, it was decided to perform a CT-guided biopsy of the lesion (Figure 1B). Microscopic study of the sample demonstrated no atypia but a tissue with fibrosis, collagenization and presence of spongy-looking structures, suggestive of microorganisms (Figure 3). Unfortunately, no microbiological cultures of the biopsy were done. The patient then was referred to the department of infectious disease for further evaluation. During the focused anamnesis, the patient reported having recently made several business travels to Africa, Central America, South America and the Caribbean. He had no weight loss, fever, diarrhea, or skin lesions and there were no significant findings on physical examination. A Mantoux test was performed which was negative. The following serological studies were carried out: hepatitis A virus; Epstein-Barr virus; Trypanosoma cruzi; cytomegalovirus; Ac HBs; Ag HBs; Ac HBc T; HIV 1 + 2; Toxoplasma gondii; Entamoeba histolytica; Echinococcus granulosus; Taenia solium (IgG); Leishmania spp.; strongyloides and schistosoma. All results were negative and do not showed acute infection, except schistosoma with IgM and IgG positive.
Based on the results obtained in the serological tests, a schistosoma infestation (schistosomiasis) was diagnosed and praziquantel was prescribed. During the follow-up the patient referred remission of the abdominal pain and a CT control one year later showed a shrink in size of the paraaortic lesion.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 45-year-old Caucasian male was referred for evaluation of an incidental 4-cm retroperitoneal para-aortic mass discovered on CT during an abdominal pain workup.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient underwent an abdominal CT for abdominal pain that identified a 4-cm retroperitoneal para-aortic lesion between the celiac trunk and superior mesenteric artery, initially suspected to be a neuroendocrine tumor/paraganglioma.
subjective.past_medical_history: History of smoking, Barrett's esophagus, hiatal hernia, and GERD; sleeve gastrectomy for weight loss in 2015 and cholecystectomy for cholelithiasis in 2017; frequent recent business travel to Africa, Central America, South America, and the Caribbean.
subjective.review_of_systems: Home medication: omeprazole; positive for abdominal pain; negative for weight loss, fever, diarrhea, or skin lesions.

objective.physical_examination: Unremarkable physical examination.
objective.routine_investigations: Labs showed glucose 79 mg/dL, creatinine 0.69 mg/dL, ALT 22 IU/L, ferritin 73 ng/mL, neuron-specific enolase 19 ng/mL (ref <16), CEA 2.6 ng/mL (ref <5.0), CA 19-9 12 IU/mL (ref <37), chromogranin A 3.3 nmol/L (ref 0.4-10.0), Hb 15.4 g/dL, neutrophils 51.7%, lymphocytes 33.4%, eosinophils 5.3% (ref <8.0%), and normal 24-h urinary catecholamines, metanephrines, and 5-HIAA. Mantoux test and serologies for Leishmania spp., Trypanosoma cruzi, Entamoeba histolytica, Echinococcus granulosus, Taenia solium, Strongyloides, Toxoplasma, HAV, HBV, EBV, CMV, and HIV-1/2 were negative, whereas Schistosoma IgM and IgG serologies were positive.
objective.advanced_workup: Abdominal CT showed a 4-cm retroperitoneal para-aortic mass between the celiac trunk and SMA; whole-body 123I-MIBG and 99mTc-octreotide SPECT/CT showed no neuroendocrine tracer avidity. CT-guided core biopsy of the para-aortic mass revealed fibrous, collagenized tissue without atypia containing spongy-appearing structures suggestive of parasitic organisms.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Retroperitoneal paraganglioma/neuroendocrine tumor and other parasitic infections (including Leishmania, Trypanosoma cruzi, and Echinococcus) were excluded by negative functional imaging, biopsy histology, and serologies; positive Schistosoma IgM and IgG serologies alongside the biopsy findings confirmed ectopic retroperitoneal pseudotumoral schistosomiasis acquired during tropical travel. Treatment with oral praziquantel resolved the patient's abdominal pain and produced marked shrinkage of the para-aortic mass on 1-year follow-up CT.

raw_case_text:
A previously disease-free five-year-old boy presented with a three-week history of redness, swelling, and ulceration of the left earlobe. An ulcer had developed at the helix and lobule of the ear a few days after symptom onset. The patient was treated using topical corticosteroids, and the size of the ulcer improved; however, the redness and pain persisted. After three months, lesions started to appear on his right ear, exhibiting the same painful redness and ulceration. Once again, topical steroids were prescribed, but the response was minimal and slow for both ears. As the lesions persisted and no improvement followed the use of oral and topical antibiotics or topical steroids, the patient was seen by a dermatologist and then referred to a pediatric rheumatologist. The patient had no history of fever, skin rash, preceding infection, trauma, or food or drug allergies. He had no respiratory or musculoskeletal symptoms and, upon other systemic reviews, was found to be medically unremarkable. His family and social history were negative for any genetic or autoimmune disease.
The clinical findings at the time of evaluation by the pediatric rheumatologist indicated that the patient was looking well, an alert child with a good body build, afebrile with normal vital signs. Upon local examination of his ear, nose, and throat (ENT), significant redness and erosive wounds were found in both ears, though more on the left side (Figure 1). The ears were tender, and the rest of the ENT examination was normal. Cardiovascular, respiratory, gastrointestinal, musculoskeletal, and central nervous system examinations were clinically normal. Laboratory examinations revealed a white blood cell count of 8.95 x 109/L (normal), an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 32 (slightly elevated), negative C-reactive protein, negative antinuclear antibody, negative leishmania antibody immunoglobulin M, and complement within normal ranges. The antibodies of Type II collagen were not available at our center. A chest computerized tomography (CT) scan was done to rule out respiratory tract involvements, and the results were normal. The patient was screened by the otorhinolaryngology and ophthalmology departments for the involvement of other sites, and these findings were normal. Also, the joint and cardiac evaluations via echocardiogram were negative. Treatment was discussed with the patient s family, and they refused a corticosteroid, so the patient was started on an NSAID (10 mg/kg of ibuprofen every eight hours for six weeks). The patient showed improvement from the fourth week of treatment, with healing of the lesions and disappearance of the redness along with minimal remanence. After six weeks of treatment, he completely recovered (Figure 2), and all inflammatory markers-mainly ESR-normalized.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 5-year-old boy presented with a 3-month history of painful redness, swelling, and erosive ulceration of both ears, beginning on the left ear and spreading to the right ear.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The child initially presented with a 3-week history of painful redness, swelling, and ulceration of the left helix and earlobe that only partially and transiently responded to topical corticosteroids. Three months after onset, identical painful erythematous ulcerative lesions developed on his right ear, failing oral and topical antibiotics and topical corticosteroids and prompting referral to a pediatric rheumatologist.
subjective.past_medical_history: Previously healthy 5-year-old boy with no history of trauma, preceding infection, or allergies; negative family history for genetic or autoimmune diseases.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for bilateral auricular pain, erythema, swelling, and ulceration; negative for fever, rash elsewhere, ocular, nasal, respiratory, or musculoskeletal symptoms.

objective.physical_examination: Well-appearing, alert, afebrile child with normal vital signs; marked tender erythema, swelling, and erosive ulcerations of both pinnae (more pronounced on the left ear); normal nasal, pharyngeal, ophthalmic, cardiovascular, respiratory, abdominal, musculoskeletal, and neurological examinations.
objective.routine_investigations: Labs showed normal WBC count (8.95 x 10^9/L), mildly elevated ESR (32 mm/h), negative CRP, negative ANA, normal complement levels, and negative Leishmania IgM antibody serology. Echocardiogram was normal.
objective.advanced_workup: Chest CT was normal without airway or parenchymal involvement.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Bacterial perichondritis and auricular cutaneous leishmaniasis (negative Leishmania IgM) were excluded, and clinical presentation with sparing of non-cartilaginous systemic organs established pediatric auricular relapsing polychondritis. Because the family declined systemic corticosteroids, treatment with oral ibuprofen (10 mg/kg every 8 hours for 6 weeks) was initiated, producing marked healing by week 4 and complete clinical recovery with normalization of ESR at week 6.

raw_case_text:
In brief, the 29-year old student presented to her general practitioner with recurrent fever up to 40 C in December 2019. Medically, she and her relatives had an uneventful past. After fever persistence for more than two weeks she was admitted to hospital for an extensive work-up. In clinical and ultrasound examinations, abdominal lymph node enlargements and a marked hepatosplenomegaly were noticed. These findings were confirmed in positron emission computer tomography (PET-CT) scanning ( Figures 1A, B ). Her blood counts showed pancytopenia (WBC 1.5 x 109/l, neutrophils 1.0 x 109/l, lymphocytes 0.35 x 109/l, monocytes 0.01 x 109/l, hemoglobin 76 g/l, platelets 78 x 109/l), and additional lab testing revealed hyperferritinemia (3860 g/l), hypertriglyceridemia (4.56 mmol/l), increased serum levels of aspartate aminotransferase (AST 79 U/l), soluble interleukin-2 receptor (sIL-2R, 2710 U/l), and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH 626 U/L). Although fibrinogen was normal (5.1 g/l), a diagnosis of HLH was made based on HLH-2004 criteria [7/8 fulfilled including impaired NK-cell function, see below; ] and an HScore of 239 points [98-99% probability of hemophagocytosis; ], respectively.
After ruling out Leishmania spp., HIV, EBV, and CMV infections by serology and PCR (peripheral blood and bone marrow, BM), biopsies of retroperitoneal lymph nodes were taken. Surprisingly, histopathology did not show lymphoma but demonstrated granulomatous lymphadenitis including acid-fast bacteria, which were further classified as Mycobacterium avium by genotyping (MycoDirect 1.7 LCD array, Chipron, Germany). M. avium was also detected in BM and cultured from bronchoalveolar lavage samples, giving the diagnosis of NTM infection triggering HLH. In BM cytology and histopathology no signs of myelodysplasia were identified.
Treatment with amikacin, azithromycin, ethambutol and rifampicin was initiated promptly, however, the fever and other HLH-signs persisted. Only after intensive immunosuppressive therapy including high-dose dexamethasone, ciclosporin A, intravenous immunoglobulins, and repetitive courses of etoposide (75 mg/m2, twice weekly) the HLH-related symptoms could temporarily be ameliorated. The cause for HLH and NTM was further investigated including CTL and NK-cell function analysis in CD107a-assays. These indicated significant degranulation impairments in both effector cell types ( Figure 2 ). Perforin expression was normal, and genetic variants in UNC13D, STXBP2, RAB27A, and STX11 were excluded in Sanger sequencing. Subsequently, next generation sequencing (NovaSeq 6000 NGS platform) of genes associated with NTM infections [CYBB, GATA2, IFNGR1/R2, IL12B, IL12RB1/RB2, IL23R, IRF8, ISG15, JAK1, RORC, SPPL2A, STAT1, TYK2; ; ] was performed. As result, a novel GATA2 variant (c.177C>G, p.Tyr59Ter) in heterozygous form was identified (DNA from peripheral blood and mucosa cells).
Considering disseminated NTM infection and secondary HLH resulting from primary immunodeficiency due to germline GATA2 deficiency, we aimed for alloHSCT as curative therapy. An HLA-matched unrelated donor (MUD 10/10) was identified, and the patient underwent alloHSCT following reduced-intensity conditioning with fludarabine (150 mg/m2) and treosulfan (30 g/m2) in September 2020. Graft-versus-Host disease (GvHD) prophylaxis consisted of post-transplant cyclophosphamide (100 mg/kg), mycophenolate-mofetil, and ciclosporin. Prior to alloHSCT, the antimycobacterial treatment was switched to azithromycin, clofazimine, and ethambutol. The fever and HLH-signs completely resolved after full hematopoietic engraftment. In the absence of GvHD, ciclosporin was ceased at day +98 post-alloHSCT. Following diagnosis of moderate hepatotoxicity, which appeared drug-related in a liver biopsy, all antibiotics were stopped 6 months after alloHSCT and 1 year after disease onset, respectively. PET-CT scanning at that time demonstrated complete remission of all inflammatory manifestations ( Figures 1C, D ).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 29-year-old female student presented in December 2019 with a >2-week history of recurrent high fevers up to 40 C.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Previously healthy, the patient presented to her general practitioner in December 2019 with recurrent fevers peaking at 40 C that persisted for more than 2 weeks, prompting hospital admission where marked hepatosplenomegaly, abdominal lymphadenopathy, and pancytopenia were identified.
subjective.past_medical_history: Previously healthy 29-year-old student with an unremarkable personal and family medical history.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for persistent high fevers up to 40 C.

objective.physical_examination: Febrile (up to 40 C) with marked hepatosplenomegaly.
objective.routine_investigations: Labs showed pancytopenia (WBC 1.5 x 10^9/L, neutrophils 1.0 x 10^9/L, lymphocytes 0.35 x 10^9/L, monocytes 0.01 x 10^9/L, Hb 76 g/L, platelets 78 x 10^9/L), ferritin 3,860 ug/L, triglycerides 4.56 mmol/L, AST 79 U/L, LDH 626 U/L, and normal fibrinogen (5.1 g/L). Serologies and peripheral blood/bone marrow PCRs for Leishmania spp., HIV, EBV, and CMV were negative. Abdominal ultrasound showed abdominal lymphadenopathy and marked hepatosplenomegaly.
objective.advanced_workup: Soluble IL-2 receptor (sIL-2R) was 2,710 U/L, HScore was 239 (98-99% HLH probability; 7/8 HLH-2004 criteria met), and CD107a assays showed impaired CTL and NK-cell degranulation with normal perforin expression. PET-CT confirmed marked hepatosplenomegaly and hypermetabolic abdominal lymphadenopathy. Retroperitoneal lymph node biopsy revealed granulomatous lymphadenitis with acid-fast bacilli genotyped as Mycobacterium avium (also detected in bone marrow and cultured from BAL fluid), while targeted NGS (NovaSeq 6000) of blood and mucosal DNA identified a novel heterozygous germline nonsense variant in GATA2 (c.177C>G, p.Tyr59Ter).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Lymphoma and viral/parasitic triggers (including Leishmania spp., EBV, CMV, and HIV) were excluded; retroperitoneal lymph node biopsy, bone marrow detection, BAL culture, and targeted NGS confirmed disseminated Mycobacterium avium infection triggering secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) as the first manifestation of germline GATA2 deficiency (c.177C>G, p.Tyr59Ter). Following antimycobacterial therapy (amikacin, azithromycin, ethambutol, and rifampicin, later transitioned to azithromycin, clofazimine, and ethambutol) and HLH immunochemotherapy (high-dose dexamethasone, cyclosporine A, IVIG, and twice-weekly etoposide 75 mg/m2), curative 10/10 matched unrelated donor allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (fludarabine/treosulfan conditioning) in September 2020 achieved complete hematologic and PET-CT remission at 1 year.

raw_case_text:
This article presents a case study of a patient with homozygous variation of PRKCD and clinical manifestation of ALPS, especial elevation of TCRalphabeta + CD4/CD8 double-negative T cells (DNTs) (Figure 1). The age of disease onset and diagnosis was 6 and 10 years old respectively. From 2015, he showed unexplained large-scale splenomegaly and lymphadenopathy, along with recurrent infection. Severe neutropenia and anemia presented in July 2017. The patient experienced pancytopenia and was refractory to first-line treatment of immune thrombocytopenia like steroids (HD-Dex, use 0.6 mg/(kg days) for 4 days every 4 weeks), immunoglobulins (800 mg/kg). The positive phenotype of DNTs were 2.15% of CD3+ and 1.64% for lymphocyte. His immunoglobulin levels were within normal range, elevated for ESR and positive of immunoglobulin G for anti-Epstein Barr viruses, rubella viruses, cytomegalovirus, herpes simplex virus, and antinuclear antibodies. In addition, the analysis of markers for measles virus, parvovirus B19, schistosomiasis, and Leishmania donovani infection was negative. In peripheral blood samples, T lymphocytes (CD3+CD19-) were found to be increased. Moreover, the patient displayed amplified proportions of cytokine IFN-gamma, IL-10, IL-6, however, the serum level of the vitamin B12 is normal. Histological analysis of the bone marrow and spleen did not show signs of hemophagocytosis and Lymphoma.
Based on glucocorticoids, sirolimus (1.5 mg/m2, actual blood concentration range: 4.27-10.3 ng/ml) was added as the other immunosuppressive agent, after which platelet count was restored and spleen recovered to its normal size gradually in 3 months. However, unauthorized withdrawal of sirolimus for half a year, all clinical manifestations relapsed.
The study has been approval by the Medical Ethics Committee of Beijing Children's Hospital (2018-k-97) patient consent. The patient has provided informed consent for publication of the case.
Routine blood results indicated anemia (hemoglobin 7.8-9.0 g/dl) and thrombocytopenia (56-73 x 109/l). Three months after application of sirolimus, platelets (160 x 109/l) and hemoglobin (10.5 g/dl) were raised. The patient displayed persisting T-cell lymphocytosis with a decreased proportion of T-helper lymphocyte (CD3+CD4+), especially Treg (CD3+4+25+Foxp3+T cells). Reduction of DNT and increase of Treg portion was observed after treatment of sirolimus. The percentage of lymphocyte subpopulation, especial DNT and Treg, back to initial condition after withdrawal of sirolimus (Table 1)
We use whole-exome sequencing to screen for suspicious mutations and a homozygous nonsense variation (c.36T>G, p. Y12X) was detected on the PRKCD gene, then we use sanger sequencing for verification on PRKCD gene. After receiving informed consent, we sequenced parents and their daughter who perform both anemia and splenomegaly and lymphadenopathy but not as severe as the boy. The results show that parents are Heterozygote while the boy's sister is homozygous as well. It was verified as a consanguineous marriage of the parents. The variant was not found in dbSNP database or ExAC database (Figure 2).
Medical history, clinical presentation, and results from laboratory tests led to the clinical diagnosis of ALPS-related syndrome, and treatment with sirolimus (1.5 mg/m2, blood concentration 5-15 ng/l) was initiated. Subsequently, the patient's hemoglobin and clinical condition improved gradually. Then, the relapsed clinical manifestations and imbalance DNT/Treg axis may be related to withdrawal of sirolimus for half year.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 10-year-old boy born to consanguineous parents presented with a 4-year history of massive splenomegaly, generalized lymphadenopathy, recurrent infections, and steroid/IVIG-refractory multilineage cytopenias.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Beginning at age 6 (in 2015), the patient developed unexplained massive splenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, and recurrent infections, followed in July 2017 by severe neutropenia, anemia, and thrombocytopenia (pancytopenia) that failed high-dose pulsed dexamethasone (0.6 mg/kg/day x 4 days every 4 weeks) and IVIG (800 mg/kg).
subjective.past_medical_history: Onset of splenomegaly and lymphadenopathy at age 6; born to consanguineous parents; younger sister also had milder anemia, splenomegaly, and lymphadenopathy.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for recurrent infections, splenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, and cytopenia-related symptoms.

objective.physical_examination: Massive splenomegaly and generalized lymphadenopathy.
objective.routine_investigations: Labs showed anemia (Hb 7.8-9.0 g/dL), thrombocytopenia (platelets 56-73 x 10^9/L), severe neutropenia/pancytopenia, elevated ESR, normal serum immunoglobulin and vitamin B12 levels, positive ANA, positive IgG antibodies for EBV, rubella, CMV, and HSV, and negative testing for Leishmania donovani, Schistosoma, measles, and parvovirus B19.
objective.advanced_workup: Bone marrow and splenic histopathology excluded lymphoma and hemophagocytosis. Flow cytometry and cytokine profiling demonstrated persistent T-cell lymphocytosis (CD3+CD19-), elevated TCR-alpha/beta+ CD4-CD8- double-negative T cells (DNTs: 2.15% of CD3+ T cells, 1.64% of total lymphocytes), decreased CD3+CD4+CD25+Foxp3+ regulatory T cells (Tregs), and elevated plasma IFN-gamma, IL-10, and IL-6. Whole-exome sequencing and Sanger validation identified a novel homozygous nonsense mutation in the PRKCD gene (c.36T>G, p.Y12X; parents heterozygous, symptomatic sister also homozygous).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Visceral leishmaniasis (Leishmania donovani), schistosomiasis, HLH, and lymphoma were excluded; elevated TCR-alpha/beta+ double-negative T cells, Treg depletion, elevated IL-10/IL-6/IFN-gamma, and whole-exome/Sanger sequencing confirmed an autoimmune lymphoproliferative syndrome (ALPS)-like disorder caused by homozygous PRKCD deficiency (c.36T>G, p.Y12X). Addition of oral sirolimus (1.5 mg/m2/day, trough target 4.27-15 ng/mL) normalized his platelet count (160 x 10^9/L), increased hemoglobin to 10.5 g/dL, reduced DNT proportions while restoring Tregs, and shrank the spleen to normal size within 3 months (with a relapse after 6 months of unauthorized sirolimus cessation responding to re-initiation).

raw_case_text:
The case was a female patient, 61 years old, with lesions in the right upper limb that began 8 months before her appointment in the medical service of Hospital das Clinicas, Faculdade de Medicina da Universidade de Sao Paulo, Brazil. She was born in Barros Mendes (Bahia, Brazil), but residing in Sao Paulo city (Sao Paulo State, Brazil) for the last 45 years, working as a teacher. She has three healthy cats that regularly visit vets; according to her report, the cats did not scratch her before the onset of cutaneous lesions. One year before the appearance of skin lesions, she traveled to the countryside of Sao Paulo state (Registro town), and although she had contact with the Atlantic forest, skin injury was not observed. Additionally, between travel and appointment at the Hospital das Clinicas, she had no skin injuries or contact with plants and soil. One month after the appearance of the lesion, she was admitted to the Dermatology Service of the Hospital das Clinicas. The lesions were ulcerated, and the borders showed erythema and were infiltrated; the lesions were also covered with yellowish and hematic crusts. Furthermore, some ascendant subcutaneous nodular lesions were detected that suggest lymphangitis in the right upper limb (Figure 1(a)). Mobile and painless lymphadenopathy was detected in the right axillary area. The patient complained of pain in the lesions, and discrete hyaline exudation was verified, and no other local and systemic symptoms were observed. Skin fragments were collected to identify the etiologic agent of the lesions, as the morphology of the lesions suggested lymphocutaneous sporotrichosis, skin tuberculosis, or leishmaniasis. The histopathological study showed chronic granulomatous dermatitis with focal necrosis and neutrophil exudation of neutrophils (Figures 1(b) and 1(c)).
Fite-Faraco and Grocott staining did not evidence the presence of alcohol-acid-resistant bacilli or fungi, respectively. The immunohistochemistry reaction was not positive for BCG. Bacterioscopy and direct fungi research as well as culture of aerobic and anaerobic bacteria were negative. Skin samples cultured in agar-dextrose Sabouraud medium supplemented with chloramphenicol at 25 C allowed the growth of a whitish membranous culture, with a blackened peripheral halo (Figure 2(a)). Microscopically septate hyaline hyphae present in the apex conidiophores and bouquet-like structures were observed, suggesting a fungus belonging to the genus Sporothrix (Figures 2(b) and 2(c)). At 37 C, a white/yellowish colony with a smooth aspect was observed; additionally, yeasts were visualized at this temperature. Techniques of molecular biology were not used to identify species.
Based on these findings, lymphocutaneous sporotrichosis was diagnosed, and potassium iodide was prescribed at 1 g/mL; it was started with three drops per day and gradually increased as the patient tolerated the metallic taste. After one month of treatment, and using 25 drops of potassium iodide per day, the patient reported lack of appetite, nausea, and vomiting. Potassium iodide was replaced by itraconazole, which was administered orally for 12 days at 100 mg/day; as the patient became tolerant, the dose of this antifungal drug was increased to 200 mg/day. The patient reported constant nausea and emetic events after seven days of treatment; however, levels of alanine and aspartate transaminases, alkaline phosphatase, and gamma-glutamyl transferase were normal. Fifty days after the beginning of itraconazole therapy, the patient reported severe gastrointestinal alterations, and the intravenous antiemetic drug metoclopramide was administered to the patient; constant hydration was recommended. Ten days after this event, no improvement of skin lesions was observed. Due to the side effects of both first-line drugs and the resistance of the patient to take oral medicines, such as terbinafine or fluconazole, she was admitted to the Hospital das Clinicas to initiate a treatment with systemic amphotericin B. Additionally, it is important to observe that all these side effects were associated with the therapy with potassium iodide or itraconazole since the patient had no underlying diseases. Electrolytes, renal, and hepatic biochemical tests as well as electrocardiogram were performed, before beginning treatment. Amphotericin B deoxycholate at 50 mg/day (diluted in 500 mL of sodium chloride 0.9% and glucose 5% solution for 6 hours) was given during three days due to the inaccessibility of the liposomal formulation. At the beginning of treatment, episodes of nausea and vomiting were reported, but antiemetic medicines controlled these side effects. Biochemical tests were performed and revealed an increase of serum potassium and creatinine. Correction of electrolyte disturbance was carried out; and to compensate the biochemical alterations, the treatment was suspended for three days. A second set of treatment was performed with liposomal amphotericin B seven days after the infusion with amphotericin B deoxycholate, and it was administered at 150 mg/day (diluted in 500 mL of sodium chloride 0.9% and glucose 5% solution for 6 hours) during 17 days. Clinical improvement of the lesions was observed during treatment (Figures 3(a) and 3(b)). A timeline containing the lesion appearance, diagnosis (Figure 4(a)), and treatment with iodide potassium, itraconazole (Figure 4(b)), or amphotericin B (Figure 4(c)) summarizes the whole treatment performed in this patient. The treatment with liposomal amphotericin B did not change the levels of blood biochemical parameters.
The patient was infused with a total dose of 2600 mg of liposomal amphotericin B and 150 mg of amphotericin B deoxycholate until complete clinical cure, with re-epithelization of the ulcerated lesion and involution of lymphadenopathy. The follow-up has been performed monthly, and relapses were not recorded.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 61-year-old female teacher from Sao Paulo, Brazil, presented with an 8-month history of painful crusted ulcers and ascending subcutaneous nodules along her right upper extremity.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Eight months before evaluation at Hospital das Clinicas in Sao Paulo, the patient developed painful ulcerated lesions with ascending lymphangitic subcutaneous nodules on her right upper limb. Subsequent outpatient courses of oral saturated solution of potassium iodide (1 g/mL, titrated from 3 to 25 drops/day for 1 month) and oral itraconazole (100-200 mg/day for 50 days) failed to heal the lesions and caused severe anorexia, nausea, and vomiting requiring IV metoclopramide and hospitalization.
subjective.past_medical_history: Born in Bahia and resided in Sao Paulo city for 45 years working as a teacher; owned three healthy indoor cats with no history of cat scratches; traveled 1 year prior to onset to Registro (Atlantic forest region in rural Sao Paulo state) without recalled skin trauma.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for right upper-limb lesional pain and severe potassium iodide- and itraconazole-induced nausea, vomiting, and anorexia; negative for baseline systemic symptoms.

objective.physical_examination: Ulcerated lesions with erythematous, infiltrated borders covered by yellowish and hematic crusts and discrete hyaline exudate on the right upper extremity, accompanied by ascending subcutaneous nodules along the lymphatic drainage and mobile, painless right axillary lymphadenopathy.
objective.routine_investigations: Baseline and treatment liver enzymes (ALT, AST, ALP, GGT) and ECG were normal; during a 3-day course of amphotericin B deoxycholate, serum potassium and creatinine transiently increased. Direct microscopy and aerobic/anaerobic bacterial cultures were negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Skin biopsy histopathology showed chronic granulomatous dermatitis with focal necrosis and neutrophilic exudation (negative Fite-Faraco, Grocott, and anti-BCG IHC stains). Sabouraud dextrose agar culture with chloramphenicol at 25 C grew a whitish membranous colony with a blackened peripheral halo and microscopic septate hyaline hyphae with apical bouquet-like conidiophores, converting at 37 C to smooth white-yellowish yeast colonies diagnostic of Sporothrix sp.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Cutaneous leishmaniasis and cutaneous tuberculosis were ruled out by histopathology and thermally dimorphic fungal culture confirming lymphocutaneous sporotrichosis (Sporothrix sp.). Because oral potassium iodide and itraconazole failed and caused intractable emesis and amphotericin B deoxycholate (50 mg/day x 3 days, 150 mg total) caused hyperkalemia and rising creatinine, she was switched to intravenous liposomal amphotericin B (150 mg/day for 17 days, cumulative dose 2,600 mg), achieving complete re-epithelialization of the ulcers and resolution of axillary lymphadenopathy without relapse on monthly follow-up.

raw_case_text:
A 69-year-old male was admitted to the hospital for febrile neutropenia. Twenty-three days before admission he had received the second cycle of RB as second-line treatment for WM. No new medication was started during this period of time. Treatment was initiated due to progressive thrombocytopenia and an increase of the monoclonal component. Prior to RB, he had received 8 R cycles as first-line therapy without major complications.
At the time of admission, physical examination was normal. Complete blood test revealed haemoglobin 93 g/L (120-150 g/L), reticulocytes 22 x109/L (50-100 x109/L), mean corpuscular volume 90 fL (80-100 fL), total white cell count 0.07 x109/L (4-10 x109/L), neutrophils 0.00 x109/L (2-7 x109/L), lymphocytes 0.06 x109/L (1-3 x109/L), platelets 79 x109/L (150-400 x109/L), lactate dehydrogenase 345 IU/L (240-480 IU/L), bilirubin 0.7 mg/dL (0.2-1.2 mg/dL), haptoglobin 80 (30-200mg/dl), total proteins 5.6 g/dL (6-8.3 g/dL) and albumin 2.8 g/dL (3.8-5.1 g/dL). Serum protein electrophoresis and immunofixation showed a monoclonal IgM kappa peak of 6.6 g/L. The immunoglobulin dosage in serum was as follows: IgG 608 mg/dL (700-1600 mg/dL), IgA 113 mg/dL (70-400 mg/dL), IgM 613 mg/dL (40-240 mg/dL). ANA antibodies were negative. A direct antiglobulin test was negative. A blood smear confirmed the cytopenias without other pathological findings. Microbiological cultures revealed a urinary infection due to Escherichia coli with associated bacteriemia.
Broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy and G-CSF were started. Platelets normalized once sepsis parameters were controlled. Despite adequate antibiotic coverage and blood culture negativization, the patient remained feverish for the next 10 days and with a neutrophil count of 0 x 109/L. A body computerized tomography scan ruled out the presence of infection. Serologies for human immunodeficiency virus, hepatitis B virus, hepatitis C virus, Epstein-Barr virus, leishmania, cryptococcus, treponema pallidum, and parvovirus showed no acute infection. The polymerase chain reaction for cytomegalovirus and parvovirus in blood was negative.
Bone marrow biopsy showed the absence of granulocytic lineage with normal erythroid and megakaryocytic lineages ( Figure 1 ). No morphological or immunophenotypic evidence of medullary progression of WM was detected. No evidence of bone marrow dysplasia was observed. A blood immunophenotypic study of T lymphocytes, performed by flow cytometry, was normal ( Figure 2 ). The diagnosis of agranulocytosis was made. Anti-neutrophil antibody test performed by immunofluorescence technique and flow cytometry reading confirmed the presence of antibodies bound to the patient's granulocytes. However, no free anti-neutrophil antibodies were detected in the serum ( Figure 3 ). The genotyped of Immunoglobulin G Fc receptor FcgammaRIIIa 158 polymorphic position, demonstrated the presence of the 158 V/F polymorphism, in heterozygosis.
Given the absence of response to G-CSF, treatment with methylprednisolone (MTP) 1 mg per kilogram of body weight (mg/kg bw) per day and IVIG 1 g/kg bw for two days were started. The absolute neutrophil count 48 and 72 hours later was 0.6 x109/L and 3.1 x109/L, respectively. The patient achieved normalization of blood counts and decreased the monoclonal component after RB, fulfilling the criteria of partial response. Full dose steroid therapy was maintained for a total of 10 days. Subsequently, a slow tapering of the prednisone dose was started until it was stopped 4 months later. The neutrophil count remained normal during the prednisone tapering dose and after it was stopped. At the last follow-up, 24 months after the agranulocytosis event and 20 months after steroid withdrawal, the patient remained in partial response and no additional episodes of neutropenia were observed ( Figure 4 ).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 69-year-old male with Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia was admitted with febrile neutropenia 23 days after receiving his second cycle of second-line rituximab-bendamustine chemoimmunotherapy.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Twenty-three days after completing his second cycle of rituximab-bendamustine (RB) for relapsed/progressive Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia (initiated for progressive thrombocytopenia and rising IgM paraprotein after 8 prior first-line rituximab cycles), the patient presented with febrile agranulocytosis and Escherichia coli bacteremic urinary tract infection. Despite targeted broad-spectrum antibiotics (which cleared his bacteremia and normalized his platelet count) and G-CSF support, his fever and absolute neutrophil count of 0.00 x 10^9/L persisted for 10 days.
subjective.past_medical_history: Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia previously treated with 8 cycles of first-line rituximab monotherapy and 2 cycles of second-line rituximab-bendamustine.
subjective.review_of_systems: No new non-chemotherapy medications prior to admission; positive for persistent fever.

objective.physical_examination: Febrile; physical examination was otherwise unremarkable.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission labs showed Hb 93 g/L (ref 120-150), reticulocytes 22 x 10^9/L (ref 50-100), MCV 90 fL, extreme leukopenia (WBC 0.07 x 10^9/L; ref 4-10) with complete agranulocytosis (ANC 0.00 x 10^9/L; ref 2-7) and severe lymphopenia (0.06 x 10^9/L; ref 1-3), platelets 79 x 10^9/L (ref 150-400), LDH 345 IU/L, bilirubin 0.7 mg/dL, haptoglobin 80 mg/dL, total protein 5.6 g/dL, albumin 2.8 g/dL, monoclonal IgM kappa peak of 6.6 g/L (IgM 613 mg/dL, IgG 608 mg/dL, IgA 113 mg/dL), and negative ANA and direct antiglobulin test. Urine and blood cultures grew Escherichia coli; serologies and blood PCRs for Leishmania, HIV, HBV, HCV, EBV, CMV, parvovirus B19, Cryptococcus, and Treponema pallidum were negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Body CT showed no focal infection. Bone marrow biopsy revealed complete absence of the granulocytic lineage with preserved erythroid and megakaryocytic lineages and no Waldenstrom progression or myelodysplasia. Direct granulocyte immunofluorescence/flow cytometry confirmed cell-bound anti-neutrophil autoantibodies (without free serum antibodies), and FcgammaRIIIa genotyping identified the heterozygous 158 V/F polymorphism.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Infectious causes of marrow suppression (including visceral leishmaniasis, CMV, and parvovirus B19) and medullary Waldenstrom progression were excluded; bone marrow aplasia of the granulocytic lineage and flow-cytometric detection of granulocyte-bound antibodies confirmed rituximab-bendamustine-associated autoimmune agranulocytosis complicated by Escherichia coli urosepsis. Treatment with intravenous methylprednisolone (1 mg/kg/day for 10 days, followed by a 4-month oral prednisone taper) and IVIG (1 g/kg/day for 2 days) restored the ANC to 0.6 x 10^9/L at 48 hours and 3.1 x 10^9/L at 72 hours, with sustained normal neutrophil counts and partial remission of Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia at 24-month follow-up.

raw_case_text:
A 3-year-old boy was referred to our hospital for left ankle swelling and refusal to walk. A few days before, he had sickness, abdominal pain with vomit, rhinitis, and catarrhal cough. Not traumatic events were reported. His family past illnesses history was unremarkable. Physical examination revealed hyperemic pharynx, three small petechiae, respectively on the left buttock, soft palate and chest, a significant swelling of the external peri-malleolar left ankle and of the dorsal region of the left foot, with ecchymotic suffusion and pain on active and passive movements. Ultrasound (US) showed a moderate edema of periarticular soft tissues, without joint effusion or synovial thickening. Blood and urine tests were negative. Nasopharyngeal swabs for SarsCoV2 and group A beta-hemolytic Streptococcus were negative, too. After 24 h of observation, his clinical conditions improved, and he was discharged.
Few days later, he was readmitted to our emergency department for a remarkable painful, warm swelling of the back in the paravertebral lumbar region (Figures 1 and 2). Subcutaneous edema of the right ankle and of both knees was also present. Blood and urine tests were negative.
During hospitalization, he presented fleeting swelling with a deep marked migrating livedo.
He required on-demand oral acetaminophen for abdominal pain for a total of five doses. Corticosteroid therapy was not necessary. In the suspect of an angioedema in HSP, an oral antihistaminic therapy was started with partial benefit, so after 72 h was stopped.
Autoimmunity tests were negative and C1q-ihibitor and tryptase serum levels were normal. Platelets count and coagulation tests were in range, except for a moderate reduction of plasma factor XIII activity (53%, n.v: 70%-140%). Nasopharyngeal swab for an enlarged panel of respiratory virus resulted positive for Rhino/Enterovirus. Viral serology for EBV, CMV, Parvovirus B19, Borrelia, Rickettsiae, Leishmania, and Toxoplasma gondii were negative. Fecal occult blood resulted positive in two samples. Coproculture was negative. Urine tests maintained normochromic, without proteinuria. Abdominal US resulted normal; the US of skin and soft tissues showed a minimal imbibition.
The patient never manifested an evident and typical purpuric rash and progressively recovered. He was discharged with a presumptive diagnosis of HSP. The planned follow-up is still ongoing.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 3-year-old boy presented with acute painful left ankle and dorsal foot swelling with refusal to walk, followed a few days later by a large warm painful lumbar paravertebral swelling, bilateral knee and right ankle edema, abdominal pain, and deep migrating livedo.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Several days after an upper respiratory and gastrointestinal prodrome (malaise, abdominal pain, vomiting, rhinitis, and cough), the child presented with left ankle periarticular swelling and refusal to walk, improved transiently within 24 hours, and was readmitted a few days later with a painful warm paravertebral lumbar mass, subcutaneous edema of the right ankle and both knees, intermittent abdominal pain, and fleeting deep migrating livedo without a classic purpuric rash.
subjective.past_medical_history: Previously healthy 3-year-old boy with no history of trauma and an unremarkable family medical history.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for preceding rhinitis, cough, vomiting, intermittent abdominal pain, joint/periarticular swelling, lumbar back swelling, and migrating livedo.

objective.physical_examination: Initial admission: hyperemic pharynx, three small petechiae (on the left buttock, soft palate, and chest), and painful, ecchymotic peri-malleolar left ankle and dorsal left foot swelling limiting active and passive motion. Readmission: marked warm, tender paravertebral lumbar back swelling, subcutaneous edema of the right ankle and both knees, and fleeting deep migrating livedo without classic palpable purpura.
objective.routine_investigations: Routine blood counts, urinalysis (no hematuria or proteinuria), C1-esterase inhibitor, serum tryptase, autoimmune panel, and standard coagulation tests were normal except for moderately reduced plasma factor XIII activity (53%; ref 70-140%) and two positive fecal occult blood tests. Nasopharyngeal swabs for SARS-CoV-2 and Group A Streptococcus, stool cultures, and serologies for Leishmania, EBV, CMV, parvovirus B19, Borrelia, Rickettsia, and Toxoplasma gondii were negative, while an extended respiratory viral swab was positive for Rhino/Enterovirus. Ankle, abdominal, and soft-tissue ultrasounds showed moderate periarticular and lumbar subcutaneous soft-tissue edema without joint effusion.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Hereditary angioedema, mastocytosis, and infectious vasculitides (including leishmaniasis, rickettsiosis, borreliosis, and Group A Streptococcus) were excluded; the combination of Rhino/Enterovirus trigger, periarticular and lumbar subcutaneous angioedema, migrating livedo, positive fecal occult blood with abdominal pain, and reduced factor XIII activity (53%) established atypical Henoch-Schonlein purpura (IgA vasculitis) sine purpura. The child recovered completely with on-demand oral acetaminophen (5 doses) without requiring corticosteroids.

raw_case_text:
Herein, we present a case of 2-year-old boy with clinical and genetic characteristics of ALPS-FAS and TCRalphabeta + CD4/CD8 double-negative T cell (DNT) elevation. He showed unexplained large-scale splenomegaly and lymphadenopathy, along with multi-lineage autoimmune cytopenia at 2 years of age. The patient had elevated IgG:16.1(5.0-13.0)g/L and IgE:935(<=60)IU/ml [tested before intravenous immune globulin (IVIG)]. The patient was unresponsive to steroids, IVIG, platelet transfusions, and recombinant human platelet growth factors. The elevated proportion (>1.5% of total lymphocytes or >2.5% of CD3 + lymphocytes) of DNTs/CD3 + (6.8%) and chronic (>6 months), non-malignant, non-infectious splenomegaly made us consider the diagnosis of the required criteria of ALPS. However, he was positive for anti-platelet antibodies, anti-Epstein-Barr viruses, rubella viruses, cytomegalovirus, and herpes simplex virus immunoglobulin G. In addition, the analysis of markers for measles virus, parvovirus B19, schistosomiasis, and Leishmania donovani infection was negative. T lymphocytes (CD3 + CD19-) and T helper cells (CD3 + CD4 +) in peripheral blood samples were slightly increased. However, Treg/CD4 + ratio 2.5% (4.5-10%) was significantly decreased. Moreover, the patient displayed amplified proportions of cytokines IFN-gamma:2.48 (0.00-2.10), IL-10:5.59 (1.20-4.55), and IL-6: 2.6 (0.00-2.05) pg/ml, especially IL-10, as a part of the secondary accessory diagnostic criteria for ALPS. Histological analysis of the bone marrow and the spleen did not show signs of hemophagocytosis with obviously splenomegaly. Because of the severe clinical manifestation, we tried the mTOR signal pathway inhibitor before the NGS genetic results, after which the platelet count was restored and the spleen retracted quickly. In addition, the patient's familial history was negative.
We sequenced the ALPS-related genes that may match the primary accessory criteria of ALPS (defective FAS-induced lymphocyte apoptosis somatic or germline pathogenic mutation in FAS, FASL, FADD, or CASP10) and the genes known to cause common variable immunodeficiency. We identified novel spontaneous germline heterozygous missense mutations on the FAS gene (c.857G > A, p.G286E) in exon 9 (Figures 1A-C), causing an amino acid exchange and difference of hydrogen bond formation (Figures 1D-F). Sanger sequencing verification of peripheral blood and nail confirmed the germline mutation. The identified variation, which has been previously observed, is the first disease-causing mutation detected in the intracellular domain of the FAS (neither in the 1,000 Genomes Project, the HapMap Project, Exome Variant Server data sets nor in the dbSNP database or the ExAC-Asian database). No mutations were detected by Sanger sequencing of the FASLG, CASP8, and CASP10 genes.
The patient displayed persisting T-cell lymphocytosis with an increased proportion of DNT, while Treg cells (CD3 + CD4 + CD25 + Foxp3 +) were reduced (compared to health control). After 4 weeks of rapamycin treatment, DNTs/CD3 + and DNTs/lymphocyte were decreased from 6.8 to 4.44% and 4.69 to 3.34%, respectively (Figure 2A). Treg increased to a normal level from 2.5 to 4.12% (Figure 2B).
Medical history, clinical presentation [chronic (>6 months), non-malignant, non-infectious lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly], and laboratory test (elevated DNT >= 2.5% of CD3 + lymphocytes) results led to the required criterion of ALPS. In addition, the autoimmune cytopenias (hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, or neutropenia) and elevated immunoglobulin G levels of this patient also met one of the secondary accessory ALPS diagnostic criteria.
Consequently, the sirolimus treatment (1.5 mg/m2, blood concentration 4.74-11.05 ng/L) was initiated with the probable diagnosis (both required criterion and one secondary accessory criterion) of ALPS. Subsequently, the patient's platelets and hemoglobulin levels improved rapidly (Figures 3A-C). The spleen length reduced from 7.5 to 1.3 cm. When the genetic findings came back, we gave a definitive diagnosis of ALPS-FAS (meet clinical required criteria for ALPS plus germline FAS mutation). Moreover, the DNT ratio continuously decreased during sirolimus application (Figure 3D).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 2-year-old boy presented with chronic unexplained massive splenomegaly, generalized lymphadenopathy, and multilineage autoimmune cytopenias refractory to corticosteroids, IVIG, and platelet transfusions.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Over more than 6 months, the 2-year-old patient exhibited progressive non-infectious, non-malignant splenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, hemolytic anemia, neutropenia, and severe thrombocytopenia that failed to respond to systemic corticosteroids, intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG), platelet transfusions, and recombinant human thrombopoietin.
subjective.past_medical_history: 2-year-old boy with a negative family history for autoimmune or lymphoproliferative disorders.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for chronic splenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, and refractory cytopenias.

objective.physical_examination: Massive splenomegaly (7.5 cm below costal margin) and generalized lymphadenopathy.
objective.routine_investigations: Labs showed multilineage autoimmune cytopenias (anemia, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia with positive anti-platelet antibodies), elevated pre-IVIG serum IgG (16.1 g/L; ref 5.0-13.0) and IgE (935 IU/mL; ref <=60), positive IgG antibodies to EBV, rubella, CMV, and HSV, and negative testing for Leishmania donovani, Schistosoma, measles, and parvovirus B19.
objective.advanced_workup: Bone marrow and splenic histopathology excluded lymphoma and hemophagocytosis. Peripheral blood immunophenotyping and cytokine profiling revealed T-cell lymphocytosis, markedly elevated TCR-alpha/beta+ CD4-CD8- double-negative T cells (DNTs: 6.8% of CD3+ T cells, 4.69% of total lymphocytes), reduced CD3+CD4+CD25+Foxp3+ regulatory T cells (Treg/CD4+ ratio 2.5%; ref 4.5-10%), and elevated plasma IL-10 (5.59 pg/mL; ref 1.20-4.55), IFN-gamma (2.48 pg/mL; ref 0.00-2.10), and IL-6 (2.6 pg/mL; ref 0.00-2.05). Targeted NGS and Sanger sequencing of blood and nail DNA identified a novel de novo germline heterozygous missense mutation in exon 9 of the FAS intracellular death domain (c.857G>A, p.G286E; FASLG, CASP8, and CASP10 wild-type).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Visceral leishmaniasis (Leishmania donovani), schistosomiasis, HLH, and lymphoma were excluded; fulfillment of required and accessory ALPS criteria (chronic >6-month non-malignant/non-infectious splenomegaly and lymphadenopathy, TCR-alpha/beta+ DNT 6.8% of CD3+ cells, autoimmune multilineage cytopenias, elevated IgG and IL-10) and identification of the germline heterozygous FAS exon 9 mutation (c.857G>A, p.G286E) confirmed Autoimmune Lymphoproliferative Syndrome type Ia (ALPS-FAS). Initiation of oral sirolimus (rapamycin 1.5 mg/m2/day, trough 4.74-11.05 ng/mL) rapidly normalized his hemoglobin and platelet counts, reduced splenic length from 7.5 cm to 1.3 cm, lowered DNTs/CD3+ from 6.8% to 4.44%, and restored Tregs from 2.5% to 4.12% within 4 weeks.

raw_case_text:
The patient is an eight-year-old male born to non-consanguineous parents of Arab origin. He has three healthy siblings, and his pregnancy and delivery were normal. In January 2014, at the age of 5 months he presented to the Emergency Department of our hospital with acrofacial ulceronecrotic plaques which appeared initially at the age of 1 month over the cheeks and nose with subsequent development of similar lesions over the hands and feet. The parents reported exacerbations upon exposure to cold temperatures. At his arrival, he was hemodynamically stable and alert with no fever.
Physical examination on admission showed erythematous violaceous indurated plaques with central necrotic ulceration located over the tip of the nose, bilateral cheeks and ear helices. Similar lesions were seen on the knees and extensor surfaces of the arms (Figures 1A-C). There were no cardiopulmonary, gastrointestinal, genitourinary or ophthalmological abnormalities.
The patient was admitted for further investigation and treatment. During his hospitalization he showed signs of poor feeding, weight loss and failure to thrive. A nasogastric tube was inserted that facilitated his feeding, improving his weight. Despite topical wound care and systemic antibiotics including cephalosporins and vancomycin, systemic corticosteroids and antifungals, no improvement was observed, with new lesions appearing on the right hand and right elbow after exposure to cold. In addition, the patient developed unexplained febrile episodes with concurrent deterioration of the ulcers. Extensive laboratory workup was performed, as follows: skin and blood cultures showed no evidence of microbial growth (bacteria, mycobacteria and fungi). Cutaneous leishmaniasis was also excluded by smear and polymerase chain reaction. Blood work showed normal kidney and liver function tests moderate leukocytosis and thrombocytosis, normal hemoglobin level and no marked elevation of C-reactive protein or erythrocyte sedimentation rate. Anti-nuclear antibodies, rheumatoid factor, anti-Ro, anti-La, immunoglobulins, cryoglobulins and cryofibrinogens, C3, C4, C-ANCA and P-ANCA were all within normal limit. A biochemical assay for prolidase deficiency was negative, chest x-ray, abdominal ultrasound, were normal. Serology for human immunodeficiency virus was negative as well.
Two skin biopsies were performed, demonstrating epidermal necrosis, mild parakeratosis, mild focal vacuolar degeneration and apoptosis of basal cell keratinocytes., mononuclear lymphohistiocytic infiltrate surrounding blood vessels, eccrine glands and hair follicles together with fat necrosis and hyalinization suggestive of lipodystrophy. No thickening of the basement membrane was observed (Figures 2A,B).
Given the history of transient sterile pyrexias with pernio-like skin lesions, ulcerations and lipodystrophy, a disorder of type I interferonopathy was suspected. Trio exome sequencing obtained from peripheral blood of the patient and his parents was negative for mutations in genes responsible for different type-1 interferonopathies that were included in our differential diagnosis. Mutations in candidate genes which may explain the phenotype of our patient were not identified as well.

subjective.chief_complaint: An 8-year-old boy of Arab origin initially presented at 5 months of age with cold-exacerbated acrofacial ulceronecrotic plaques over his nose, cheeks, ears, hands, knees, and feet accompanied by recurrent sterile fevers and failure to thrive.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Beginning at 1 month of age, the infant developed cold-aggravated erythematous-violaceous indurated plaques with central necrotic ulceration over his cheeks and nasal tip that spread to his ear helices, hands, elbows, knees, and feet. Admitted at 5 months of age with poor feeding and failure to thrive (requiring nasogastric tube feeding), he experienced recurrent sterile febrile flares with new cold-induced acral ulcers that failed to respond to systemic cephalosporins, vancomycin, antifungals, and systemic corticosteroids.
subjective.past_medical_history: Born after a normal pregnancy and delivery to non-consanguineous Arab parents; three healthy siblings.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for cold-triggered acral/facial skin ulcers, recurrent sterile fevers, poor feeding, weight loss, and failure to thrive; negative for cardiopulmonary, GI, GU, or ocular symptoms.

objective.physical_examination: Alert and hemodynamically stable on admission; erythematous-violaceous indurated plaques with central necrotic ulceration over the nasal tip, bilateral cheeks, ear helices, knees, extensor arms/elbows, hands, and feet, with lipodystrophic changes; normal systemic examination.
objective.routine_investigations: Labs showed moderate leukocytosis and thrombocytosis with normal hemoglobin, normal liver and renal function, no marked CRP or ESR elevation, normal ANA, RF, anti-Ro, anti-La, immunoglobulins, cryoglobulins, cryofibrinogens, C3, C4, c-ANCA, and p-ANCA, negative prolidase deficiency biochemical assay, negative HIV serology, negative skin and blood bacterial/mycobacterial/fungal cultures, and normal chest X-ray and abdominal ultrasound.
objective.advanced_workup: Skin smear and PCR for Cutaneous Leishmaniasis were negative. Two skin biopsies demonstrated epidermal necrosis, mild parakeratosis, basal keratinocyte vacuolar degeneration and apoptosis, perivascular/periadnexal/perifollicular lymphohistiocytic infiltrates, and subcutaneous fat necrosis and hyalinization suggestive of panniculitis/lipodystrophy (without basement membrane thickening). Trio whole-exome sequencing of the patient and parents was negative for known type I interferonopathy genes.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Cutaneous leishmaniasis (negative smear and PCR), bacterial/fungal/mycobacterial infections, prolidase deficiency, cryoglobulinemia, and systemic lupus erythematosus were excluded; based on cold-induced pernio-like acrofacial ulceronecrotic plaques, recurrent sterile pyrexias, and histological interface dermatitis with panniculitis/lipodystrophy, a clinical diagnosis of a genetically uncharacterized type I interferonopathy-like autoinflammatory syndrome was made (with negative trio exome sequencing for known canonical genes).

raw_case_text:
A 45-year-old female patient presented with high-grade continuous fever for 5 days, headache and vomiting for 3 days, disorientation for 1-day, and facial deviation to the left side for 1-day.
On neurological examination, she had neck rigidity with positive Kernig sign. GCS Score was E3M5V4. Right-sided upper motor neuron (UMN) type facial nerve palsy was noted [Figure 3, Right panel]. Motor function, sensory function, deep tendon reflexes, cerebellar function, and autonomic function were all within normal limit. Planter was equivocal in both sides.
MRI scan of brain (plain and contrast) done on 6th day of fever, showed multiple tiny nonenhancing hypo on T1 and hyperintense lesions on T2, T2 fluid attenuation inversion recovery (FLAIR) sequence suggestive of ischemic demyelination in lentiform nucleus, peri- and para-ventricular white matter and centrum semiovale on both sides [Figure 3, Left panel]. So, a diagnosis of dengue meningoencephalitis with right sided UMN type facial palsy was made.
The patient was treated with intravenous (IV) fluid and antipyretics, and at the end of the 2nd week patient became completely afebrile with no neck rigidity but facial palsy persisted partially. Patient was discharged and on follow-up at the end of the 4th week there was complete resolution of facial palsy.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 45-year-old female presented with high-grade continuous fever for 5 days, headache and vomiting for 3 days, and disorientation and leftward facial deviation for 1 day.
