subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient experienced 5 days of continuous high-grade fever, followed by 3 days of headache and vomiting, and 1 day of acute disorientation and left-sided facial deviation.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for continuous high-grade fever, headache, vomiting, disorientation, and facial asymmetry.

objective.physical_examination: GCS E3M5V4, neck rigidity, positive Kernig sign, and right-sided upper motor neuron (UMN) facial nerve palsy; motor, sensory, deep tendon reflex, cerebellar, and autonomic examinations were normal with bilateral equivocal plantar responses.
objective.advanced_workup: Brain MRI (plain and contrast) on day 6 of fever revealed multiple tiny non-enhancing T1-hypointense and T2/FLAIR-hyperintense lesions in the bilateral lentiform nuclei, periventricular/paraventricular white matter, and centrum semiovale suggestive of ischemic demyelination.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Dengue meningoencephalitis complicated by right upper motor neuron facial nerve palsy and subcortical ischemic demyelination on brain MRI. Treated conservatively with intravenous fluids and antipyretics, achieving complete defervescence and resolution of neck rigidity by week 2 and full recovery of facial nerve palsy at 4-week follow-up.

raw_case_text:
Patient 1 was a 10-year-old girl admitted with 2 days of fever, retroorbital headache, vomiting, and myalgia. Her white blood cell (WBC) count on the 3rd day was 2.2 x 103 with 65% neutrophils and platelet count of 117,000. Alanine transaminase (ALT) was 17.8 and aspartate transaminase (AST) was 55.2. Treatment was commenced as dengue fever in febrile phase. By the 4th day, she became sleepy and lethargic and the level of consciousness gradually deteriorated. She was moved to high dependency care for further management. On neurological examination, she had increased tone in all four limbs with cogwheel rigidity. The lowest Glasgow coma scale documented was 10/15. Her vital parameters and serial packed cell volume readings remained stable without signs of fluid leakage.
Lowest WBC count (1.9 x 103) was reported on day 5 of the illness and lowest platelet count was 50,000/mm3 on day 6. Liver enzymes deteriorated (ALT: 357, AST: 478) and serum albumin was 38 g/dL and INR was 1.17 on day 6. Tender liver was palpable 2 cm below the costal margin. Renal functions (sodium: 142 mEq/L, potassium: 4.2 mEq/L, blood urea: 7.6 mmol/L, and serum creatinine: 52 mumol/L) remained normal. Serum calcium remained between 2.08 and 2.69 mmol/L. Primary dengue infection was suggested by the presence of IgM antibodies and absence of IgG antibodies to dengue virus. Dengue NS-1 antigen and the viral load were not performed due to lack of laboratory support. A CT scan revealed hypodense areas in bilateral thalamic and basal ganglia regions (Figure 1). Cerebrospinal fluid examination did not reveal any cells and had normal protein levels (42 mg/dL). Over the next 2 weeks following the acute illness, she showed complete recovery with no residual neurological disability.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 10-year-old girl presented with a 2-day history of fever, retro-orbital headache, vomiting, and myalgia, followed on day 4 by progressive lethargy, somnolence, and four-limb cogwheel rigidity.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient was admitted with 2 days of fever, retro-orbital headache, vomiting, and myalgia, and by day 4 of illness developed somnolence, lethargy, declining consciousness (GCS 10/15), and generalized hypertonia with cogwheel rigidity requiring high-dependency care.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, retro-orbital headache, vomiting, myalgia, somnolence, lethargy, and limb stiffness.

objective.physical_examination: Stable vital parameters without plasma leakage; on day 4, drowsy/lethargic with lowest Glasgow Coma Scale score of 10/15, increased tone in all four limbs with cogwheel rigidity, and a tender liver palpable 2 cm below the costal margin.
objective.routine_investigations: Day 3 CBC: WBC 2.2 x 10^3/mm3 (65% neutrophils), platelets 117,000/mm3, ALT 17.8 U/L, AST 55.2 U/L; serial PCV remained stable. Nadir WBC was 1.9 x 10^3/mm3 on day 5, and nadir platelet count was 50,000/mm3 on day 6 with peak ALT 357 U/L, AST 478 U/L, albumin 38 g/dL, INR 1.17, sodium 142 mEq/L, potassium 4.2 mEq/L, blood urea 7.6 mmol/L, creatinine 52 umol/L, and calcium 2.08-2.69 mmol/L.
objective.advanced_workup: Brain CT revealed symmetric hypodense areas in the bilateral thalamic and basal ganglia regions. CSF examination was acellular with normal protein (42 mg/dL).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Primary dengue encephalitis presenting with acute parkinsonism (cogwheel rigidity) and bilateral thalamic and basal ganglia hypodensities on brain CT, confirmed by positive serum dengue IgM and negative dengue IgG antibodies. Managed supportively in the high-dependency unit, achieving complete neurological recovery without residual disability over the ensuing 2 weeks.

raw_case_text:
Patient 2 was a 3-year-old girl who presented with 3 days of continuous high fever, intermittent abdominal pain, vomiting, and retroorbital headache. There had been one episode of gum bleeding on the first day of illness. She had been apparently a well child without any significant illnesses in the past. WBC count done on day 2, on request of the general practitioner, was 8.15 x 103 with 85% neutrophils and platelet count was 120,000 mm3. She had right hypochondrial tenderness with just palpable liver on day 5. ALT and AST were 16 mEq/L and 69.7 mEq/L, respectively, on day 3 and they increased to 29.7 mEq/L and 122.2 mEq/L on day 5. Initial C-reactive protein was 6 mg/dL and remained normal. She was monitored for vital signs including urine output and packed cell volume (PCV). Baseline PCV was 32 and the highest noted was 35. The lowest platelet count documented was 67,000/mm3 and the lowest WBC count was 2.27 x 103. She did not show signs of fluid leakage. However, there was a second episode of gum bleeding on day 5 with normal clotting profile (INR: 1.1 and APTT: 35). She was positive for IgM and negative for IgG antibodies for dengue virus.
On the 5th day of illness, she developed tremors in her upper limbs. She had cogwheel rigidity, mask like face, and staccato speech. Power was grade four in all four limbs with normal reflexes. CT scan of brain revealed diffuse hypodense areas in bilateral basal ganglia and thalamus with predominant involvement of right side (Figure 2). During the first 48 hours after the onset of neurological symptoms, she showed rapid deterioration and became aphasic with severe paucity of movements. Cerebrospinal fluid examination showed 2 lymphocytes without any polymorphs and normal proteins. She recovered dramatically and showed complete recovery within 3 weeks after onset of illness.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 3-year-old girl presented with a 3-day history of continuous high fever, intermittent abdominal pain, vomiting, retro-orbital headache, and gingival bleeding, followed on day 5 by acute parkinsonism and aphasia.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Previously healthy toddler presented with 3 days of continuous high fever, intermittent abdominal pain, vomiting, retro-orbital headache, and gum bleeding on day 1 (recurring on day 5). On day 5 of illness, she developed upper-limb tremors, cogwheel rigidity, mask-like facies, and staccato speech, progressing over 48 hours to aphasia and severe akinesia/bradykinesia.
subjective.past_medical_history: Previously healthy child with no significant past illnesses.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for continuous high fever, intermittent abdominal pain, vomiting, retro-orbital headache, gum bleeding (days 1 and 5), upper-limb tremors, mask-like facies, staccato speech/aphasia, and paucity of movement.

objective.physical_examination: No signs of plasma leakage; right hypochondrial tenderness with a just-palpable liver on day 5. Neurological exam on day 5 revealed upper-limb tremors, cogwheel rigidity, mask-like facies, staccato speech, grade 4/5 motor power in all four limbs, and normal deep tendon reflexes, progressing over 48 hours to aphasia and severe paucity of movement.
objective.routine_investigations: Day 2 WBC 8.15 x 10^3/mm3 (85% neutrophils; nadir 2.27 x 10^3/mm3) and platelets 120,000/mm3 (nadir 67,000/mm3). Baseline PCV 32% (peak 35%). ALT and AST rose from 16 and 69.7 mEq/L on day 3 to 29.7 and 122.2 mEq/L on day 5. CRP remained normal (6 mg/dL), and day-5 coagulation profile was normal (INR 1.1, aPTT 35 s).
objective.advanced_workup: Brain CT demonstrated diffuse hypodense areas in the bilateral basal ganglia and thalamus (right > left). CSF analysis showed 2 lymphocytes/mm3, 0 polymorphs, and normal protein.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Primary dengue encephalitis presenting with acute parkinsonism (tremor, cogwheel rigidity, hypomimia, bradykinesia, and speech arrest) and bilateral basal ganglia/thalamic lesions on brain CT, confirmed by positive dengue IgM and negative dengue IgG serology. Managed supportively with vital sign, urine output, and PCV monitoring, achieving dramatic and complete neurological recovery within 3 weeks of illness onset.

raw_case_text:
A 28-year-old male patient with a previous history of immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP), diagnosed six years ago but had stopped had treatment approximately five years ago, was hospitalized with clinical and epidemiological diagnosis of arbovirus infection (fever, asthenia, myalgia and arthralgia). On admission, thrombocytopenia (12,000/mm3) and anemia (8.0 g/dL) were observed (Table 1). Oral corticosteroid therapy was started with prednisone 1 mg/kg/day. On the third day of hospitalization, he had headache with vomiting, associated with mental confusion and, subsequently, motor aphasia and right hemiplegia. Considering the sudden worsening of the patient's overall conditions, he was referred to the intensive care unit. Nuclear magnetic resonance imaging of the brain was performed to rule out acute ischemic or hemorrhagic events. The neuroimaging examination showed no alterations. Faced with an acute neurological worsening, the possibility of TTP was considered. Analysis of the peripheral smear showed innumerable schizocytes, confirming the presence of TMA. Plasmapheresis and pulse therapy with methylprednisolone were started due to the hypothesis of TTP.
Serological results were IgM positive for chikungunya and dengue viruses, and initially, the presence of IgG only raised to chikungunya virus (Euroimmun Medizinische Labordiagnostika, Lubeck, Germany). Serological tests for hepatitis virus B and C were negative, as well as for retroviruses (only HIV). Regarding retroviruses, other representatives are not routinely investigated and, in this case, they were not suspected. The patient also had negative results for antinuclear antibody (ANA) (Table 2). During the follow-up, serological results for dengue and chikungunya were confirmed, at this time showing the presence of IgG antibodies to chikungunya as well as to dengue virus. The serological test for zika virus was not performed following guidelines from Brazilian Ministry of Health, which recommend not to test zika virus when serological tests for dengue and chikungunya are positive.
There was a decrease in lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) (Table 1). Plasmapheresis was maintained until platelet counts remained higher than 150,000 for three consecutive days (Figure 1). Complete remission of neurological signs occurred after the first plasmapheresis.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 28-year-old male with a remote history of immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) presented with fever, asthenia, myalgia, and arthralgia, complicated on hospital day 3 by headache, vomiting, confusion, motor aphasia, and right hemiplegia.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Admitted with an acute febrile arboviral syndrome (fever, asthenia, myalgia, arthralgia), severe thrombocytopenia, and anemia, the patient was started on oral prednisone 1 mg/kg/day. On hospital day 3, he acutely developed headache, vomiting, mental confusion, motor aphasia, and complete right-sided hemiplegia requiring ICU transfer.
subjective.past_medical_history: History of immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) diagnosed 6 years prior, off treatment for ~5 years.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, asthenia, myalgia, arthralgia, and day-3 headache, vomiting, confusion, motor aphasia, and right hemiplegia.

objective.physical_examination: On hospital day 3: mental confusion, motor aphasia, and right-sided hemiplegia.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission CBC showed severe thrombocytopenia (platelets 12,000/mm3) and anemia (hemoglobin 8.0 g/dL) with elevated LDH. Peripheral blood smear on day 3 demonstrated innumerable schistocytes confirming thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA). Serologies for HBV, HCV, HIV, and ANA were negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Brain MRI on hospital day 3 showed no acute ischemic or hemorrhagic lesions.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) triggered by concurrent dengue and chikungunya virus coinfection, confirmed by positive dengue and chikungunya IgM and IgG serologies (Euroimmun), innumerable peripheral smear schistocytes, elevated LDH, and normal brain MRI. Treated with daily therapeutic plasma exchange (plasmapheresis) and pulse IV methylprednisolone, achieving complete remission of neurological deficits after the first plasmapheresis session and sustained platelet recovery (>150,000/mm3 for 3 consecutive days).

raw_case_text:
A 34-year-old previously healthy male presented with high grade fever associated with constitutional symptoms of five days' duration. He was complaining of right hypochondrium pain and tea-coloured urine for two days associated with yellowish discolouration of the eyes. He had severe loss of appetite to food and water, but his bowel habits had been normal throughout the illness. On admission, he was afebrile with normal vital signs but was deeply icteric. His abdominal examination revealed a tender, mild hepatomegaly while his cardiovascular, respiratory, and nervous system examination was normal.
His full blood count revealed a white cell count of 3 x 103 muL with a platelet count of 116 x 103 muL. His aspartate aminotransferase (AST) and alanine aminotransferase (ALT) were 5162 U/L and 3964 U/L, respectively. Initial total bilirubin was found to be 61.7 mumol/L with an increased direct fraction. His prothrombin time/international normalized ratio (PT/INR) and serum protein were normal throughout the illness. His dengue IgM antibody done by chromatographic immunoassay was positive on the 6th day of the illness. Hepatitis A IgM antibody done by the ELISA technique was positive on day 6 of the illness, while hepatitis A IgG antibody was negative. Other investigations done during the hospital stay are summarized in Table 1.
During the course of the illness, the patient was closely monitored for features of development of liver failure while continuing with the precritical monitoring of the dengue fever. The patient's hospital stay was uneventful, and he did not develop features of acute liver failure or features of plasma leakage as in DHF. He was discharged on day 10 of the illness. On follow-up, his AST, ALT, and bilirubin have become normal.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 34-year-old male presented with a 5-day history of high-grade fever and constitutional symptoms, and a 2-day history of right hypochondrial pain, tea-colored urine, scleral icterus, and severe anorexia.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Previously healthy man developed 5 days of high-grade fever with constitutional symptoms, followed 2 days prior to admission by right upper quadrant abdominal pain, dark tea-colored urine, yellowing of the eyes, and profound loss of appetite for food and water.
subjective.past_medical_history: Previously healthy.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for 5-day high-grade fever, constitutional symptoms, right hypochondrial pain, tea-colored urine, scleral icterus, and severe anorexia. Normal bowel habits.

objective.physical_examination: Afebrile on admission with normal vital signs, deep scleral and cutaneous icterus, and tender mild hepatomegaly; cardiovascular, respiratory, and neurological examinations were normal, with no clinical signs of hepatic encephalopathy or plasma leakage.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission FBC showed leukopenia (WBC 3 x 10^3/uL) and mild thrombocytopenia (platelets 116 x 10^3/uL). Liver panel revealed marked transaminitis with AST 5,162 U/L and ALT 3,964 U/L, total bilirubin 61.7 umol/L (predominantly direct hyperbilirubinemia), and normal prothrombin time/INR and serum protein throughout hospitalization. Hepatitis A IgM ELISA was positive on day 6 of illness (with negative hepatitis A IgG).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Concurrent acute dengue fever and acute viral hepatitis A coinfection presenting with severe transaminitis (AST >5,000 U/L, ALT >3,900 U/L) without acute liver failure or plasma leakage, confirmed on day 6 of illness by positive dengue IgM chromatographic immunoassay and positive hepatitis A IgM ELISA. Managed supportively with close hepatic and dengue pre-critical monitoring, discharged uneventfully on day 10 of illness, and achieved complete normalization of AST, ALT, and bilirubin on outpatient follow-up.

raw_case_text:
A 26-year-old male with a history of subtotal colectomy and ileostomy for an inflammatory pelvic mass was referred to our unit for further assessment. He had no other medical comorbidities and had good exercise tolerance. Assessment with contrast enhanced computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging showed resolution of the inflammatory mass, and a decision was made to restore the bowel continuity. Six months following the initial surgery, he underwent excision of the rectal stump (as it was found to be fibrotic) followed by an ileal pouch-anal anastomosis.
On the second postoperative day, he developed respiratory distress, tachycardia, and fever. Inflammatory markers were elevated with a white blood cell count (WBC) of 22 x 109/l. Arterial blood gas showed a type 1 respiratory failure. A computed tomography (CT) pulmonary angiogram was performed suspecting a pulmonary embolism which was negative. However, there was bilateral basal consolidation. He improved with supportive care with resolution of fever within 24 hours.
Thereafter, his recovery was uneventful till day 5 with a functioning ileostomy and the abdominal drain was removed on day 4. On day 6, he had continuous bleeding from the drain site. On day 7, he again developed respiratory distress with a drop in saturation to 88% on air. There was drain-site oozing. He had no fever, and the haemodynamic parameters including urine output were normal. His full blood count revealed severe thrombocytopenia and haemoconcentration (WBC: 4.4, haemoglobin: 24.2 g/dl, haematocrit: 67.8, and platelet: 9), and C-reactive protein was 290 mg/dl (Figures 1 and 2). His liver enzymes were mildly elevated and renal functions were normal. His abdomen was nontender, and ileostomy was functioning normally. Ultrasound scan showed bilateral moderate-to-massive pleural effusion and moderate ascites. A right intercostal tube was inserted, and he was transferred to the ICU for intensive monitoring. The dengue IgM and IgG were positive. He was managed for dengue haemorrhagic fever and bilateral lower zone pneumonia with intravenous antibiotics, targeted fluid therapy, supportive care, and monitoring. Platelet transfusion was given as he had persistent drain-site oozing. He improved with supportive care. The drain site oozing seized after 48 hours, and the intercostal tube was removed on day 11. Thereafter, his recovery was uneventful and was discharged (Figure 3). Informed written consent was obtained from the patient prior to collection of data for publication.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 26-year-old male recovering from rectal stump excision and ileal pouch-anal anastomosis developed postoperative day-2 fever and respiratory distress, followed on days 6-7 by continuous surgical drain-site bleeding, hypoxia, and severe hemoconcentration.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Six months after subtotal colectomy and ileostomy for an inflammatory pelvic mass, the patient underwent restorative rectal stump excision and ileal pouch-anal anastomosis. After a transient febrile respiratory episode on postoperative day 2 ( bilateral basal consolidation, negative CTPA), he developed continuous oozing from his abdominal drain site on day 6 and acute hypoxemic respiratory distress (SpO2 88% on room air) on day 7.
subjective.past_medical_history: History of subtotal colectomy and ileostomy 6 months prior for an inflammatory pelvic mass; no other medical comorbidities.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for postoperative day-2 fever and dyspnea, followed on days 6-7 by surgical drain-site bleeding and recurrent acute respiratory distress.

objective.physical_examination: Postoperative day 2: febrile, tachycardic, and tachypneic. Postoperative day 7: afebrile, SpO2 88% on room air, persistent blood oozing from the abdominal drain site, stable hemodynamics and urine output, nontender abdomen, and normally functioning ileostomy.
objective.routine_investigations: Postoperative day 2: WBC 22 x 10^9/L and type 1 respiratory failure on ABG. Postoperative day 7: severe thrombocytopenia (platelets 9 x 10^9/L), profound hemoconcentration (hemoglobin 24.2 g/dL, hematocrit 67.8%), WBC 4.4 x 10^9/L, CRP 290 mg/dL, mildly elevated liver enzymes, and normal renal function. Bedside ultrasound on day 7 revealed bilateral moderate-to-massive pleural effusions and moderate ascites.
objective.advanced_workup: Postoperative day 2 CT pulmonary angiogram (CTPA) excluded pulmonary embolism and showed bilateral basal lung consolidation.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Postoperative dengue hemorrhagic fever with severe plasma leakage (hematocrit 67.8%, massive pleural effusions, ascites), severe thrombocytopenia (9 x 10^9/L) with surgical drain-site hemorrhage, and bilateral lower-zone pneumonia, confirmed by positive dengue IgM and IgG serology on postoperative day 7. Managed in the ICU with right intercostal chest tube drainage (removed day 11), platelet transfusions, targeted fluid therapy, and IV antibiotics, with cessation of drain oozing within 48 hours and an uneventful recovery.

raw_case_text:
A 16-year-old female patient was admitted during the summer with a 4-day history of diffuse myalgia, retro-orbital headache, abdominal pain, fever, and chills. On admission, the patient looked pale and icteric, with tachycardia (123/min), palpable liver 1 cm below the right costal border, and the spleen was not palpable. The patient's blood pressure was normal. Arterial oxygen saturation in room air was 99%. The patient had Sbeta+-thalassemia (genotype S/thal beta), and the average laboratory data from outpatient follow-up was serum hemoglobin concentration (Hb) 11.7 g/dL, mean corpuscular volume 62 fL, leucocyte count of 6.7 x 109/L, and platelet count of 123 x 109/L. The patient did not use hydroxyurea.
The initial laboratory test results are presented in Table 1. Metabolic acidosis was detected (pH 7.29; pCO2 28 mmHg; HCO3 13.8 mmol/L). Serology for viral hepatitis (A, B, and C) was non-reactive. Abdominal ultrasound revealed hepatosplenomegaly, moderate ascites, and bilateral pleural effusion without detection of gallstones or dilatation of the intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts. Based on the local epidemiological, clinical, and laboratory data for a SCD patient along with serological confirmation of dengue (IgM reagent - risk group D according to the criteria of the Brazilian Ministry of Health), the diagnosis of SCIC associated with dengue (dengue hemorrhagic fever) was considered. The patient was treated with vigorous hydration, analgesia, transfusion of packed red blood cells to achieve a target hemoglobin S (HbS) concentration < 30% (exchange transfusion), and intravenous antibiotic therapy (ceftriaxone 2 g/day).
Twelve hours after admission, the clinical condition worsened with the onset of respiratory distress, drowsiness, and intensification of abdominal pain with rapidly increasing hepatosplenomegaly (spleen and liver palpable at the level of the iliac crests). Laboratory parameters deteriorated with intensifying anemia, elevated LDH, and kidney and liver dysfunction (Table 1). Further management included maintenance of packed red blood cell transfusion (achieved HbS 19.8%) and supportive measures such as hemodialysis and mechanical ventilation in the intensive care unit. There was worsening organ failure, and the patient died eight days later.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 16-year-old female with sickle beta+-thalassemia (HbS/beta+-thalassemia) presented with a 4-day history of diffuse myalgia, retro-orbital headache, abdominal pain, fever, and chills.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented during the summer with 4 days of diffuse myalgia, retro-orbital headache, abdominal pain, fever, and chills. Twelve hours after admission, she deteriorated rapidly with acute respiratory distress, drowsiness, severe abdominal pain, and massive hepatosplenomegaly reaching the iliac crests.
subjective.past_medical_history: Sickle beta+-thalassemia (genotype S/beta+ thalassemia; baseline outpatient Hb 11.7 g/dL, MCV 62 fL, WBC 6.7 x 10^9/L, platelets 123 x 10^9/L); not taking hydroxyurea.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for diffuse myalgia, retro-orbital headache, abdominal pain, fever, chills, and inpatient respiratory distress and drowsiness.

objective.physical_examination: On admission: pale, icteric, tachycardic (123/min), normal blood pressure, room-air SpO2 99%, liver palpable 1 cm below the right costal margin, and non-palpable spleen. At 12 hours post-admission: respiratory distress, drowsiness, and massive hepatosplenomegaly with both liver and spleen palpable down to the iliac crests.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission ABG showed metabolic acidosis (pH 7.29, pCO2 28 mmHg, HCO3- 13.8 mmol/L); serial labs showed severe worsening anemia, thrombocytopenia, elevated LDH, and acute hepatic and renal dysfunction; hepatitis A, B, and C serologies were non-reactive. Abdominal ultrasound revealed hepatosplenomegaly, moderate ascites, and bilateral pleural effusions without gallstones or biliary dilatation.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Fatal dengue hemorrhagic fever (Brazilian Ministry of Health risk group D) triggering acute sickle cell intrahepatic cholestasis (SCIC), splenic/hepatic sequestration, and multiorgan failure in a patient with HbS/beta+-thalassemia, confirmed by reactive dengue IgM serology. Managed in the ICU with vigorous hydration, analgesia, IV ceftriaxone (2 g/day), exchange red blood cell transfusions (reducing HbS to 19.8%), mechanical ventilation, and hemodialysis, but she died of progressive multiorgan failure on hospital day 8.

raw_case_text:
A 6-year-old male patient (weight: 19 kg, SD: -0.70; height 113 cm, SD: -0.56; BMI: 14.9 SD: -0.41) with no significant medical history, coming from the first level of care with clinical manifestation of 5-day evolution, consistent nonquantified fever, asthenia, adynamia, myalgia, arthralgia, emetic episodes, abdominal pain, and headache. The patient was hospitalized with a probable dengue diagnosis with warning signs. He shows a torpid clinical course, with epistaxis, progressive thrombopenia, dengue hepatitis, oligoanuria, 20% right pleural effusion, fever persistence, and hepatosplenomegaly. The patient was taken to the pediatric ICU due to his proven severe dengue diagnosis. In follow-up tests, positive IgM serology for dengue, hematological affection was documented due to bicytopenia (anemia and thrombopenia) without evidence of external or hidden bleeding (Figure 1) requiring platelet transfusion on two occasions; it was decided to transfuse because the patient had already overcome the dengue critical phase, and this decrease was progressive until high-bleeding risk values from vital organ are associated with severe hemodynamic affection, secondary to Evans syndrome and not to a hematological manifestation of dengue.
Given the atypical course of the disease, an interdisciplinary approach was used on the part of the pediatric subspecialties of infectious diseases, hemato-oncology, and rheumatology. Studies were prolonged including autoimmunity profile, bone marrow aspiration, and biopsy (findings: nonnecrotizing epithelioid granuloma), polycultures (negative blood cultures 1 and 2, negative urine culture, and negative myeloid culture), negative infectious profile (IgM and IgG serologies for negative Toxoplasma gondii; negative cytomegalovirus; negative Epstein-Barr; negative hepatitis A, B, and C studies; nonreactive HIV ELISA; and nonreactive VDRL), and biomarkers (positive Coombs test). The patient was considered to have Evans syndrome, and treatment with immunoglobulin was suggested, 2 g/kg/total dose, with a partial response and subsequently a steroid cycle with prednisolone, a dose of 1 mg/kg/day initially with programmed titration until suspended. Outpatient follow-up was carried out for 6 months after discharge, and the patient was discharged due to pediatric hemato-oncology and rheumatology. Clinical improvement was documented with supervision of the described condition without relapse on cytopenia and nonadministration of the oral steroid.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 6-year-old boy presented with a 5-day history of fever, asthenia, adynamia, myalgia, arthralgia, vomiting, abdominal pain, and headache.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Previously healthy boy presented from primary care with 5 days of fever, constitutional symptoms, vomiting, abdominal pain, and headache. During hospitalization, he experienced a torpid course with epistaxis, persistent fever, oligoanuria, hepatosplenomegaly, right pleural effusion, and persistent post-critical-phase bicytopenia (hemolytic anemia and severe thrombocytopenia).
subjective.past_medical_history: No significant past medical history (weight 19 kg, height 113 cm, BMI 14.9 kg/m2).
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, asthenia, adynamia, myalgia, arthralgia, vomiting, abdominal pain, headache, and inpatient epistaxis and oligoanuria.

objective.physical_examination: Persistent fever, epistaxis, hepatosplenomegaly, 20% right pleural effusion, and oligoanuria.
objective.routine_investigations: Bicytopenia (autoimmune hemolytic anemia and severe thrombocytopenia), positive direct Coombs test, dengue hepatitis, and 20% right pleural effusion. Blood (x2), urine, and bone marrow cultures were sterile, and serologies for Toxoplasma gondii, CMV, EBV, hepatitis A/B/C, HIV ELISA, and VDRL were negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy demonstrated non-necrotizing epithelioid granulomas without malignancy.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Severe dengue fever complicated by secondary Evans syndrome (Coombs-positive autoimmune hemolytic anemia and immune thrombocytopenia) and bone marrow non-necrotizing granulomas, confirmed by positive dengue IgM serology, positive direct Coombs test, and multidisciplinary hemato-oncology/rheumatology evaluation. Managed in the PICU with two platelet transfusions, intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG 2 g/kg total dose), and an oral prednisolone taper (starting at 1 mg/kg/day), achieving complete hematological remission off steroids at 6-month follow-up.

raw_case_text:
A 10-year-old male presented with a 12-day history of high-grade fever and chills. He also had headaches, retro-orbital pain and occasional episodes of vomiting. He developed an acute onset of right upper and lower limb weakness five days later, followed by weakness of the left upper limb and a decreased level of consciousness. Haematological investigations revealed a platelet count of 80 000/microl with anti-dengue positive IgM and negative IgG status. Dual antigen for malaria and serology markers for Japanese encephalitis and herpes simplex virus (HSV-1) were negative.
Brain MRI revealed multiple patchy hyperintense areas on T2-weighted and FLAIR images in the left temporoparietal lobe and bilateral cerebellar hemispheres, involving the cortex and subcortical white matter, the body of the corpus callosum and the lower medulla (Figures 3a-e). The lesions showed no diffusion restriction and no enhancement on post-contrast T1FS images (Figure 3f). MRI screening of the spine revealed T2 hyperintense signal in the inferior part of the medulla, at the cervicomedullary junction and spinal cord up to the C3 vertebral level as well as in the terminal dorsal cord and conus medullaris from the T11 to the L1 vertebral level (Figure 4a-c).
A diagnosis of acute disseminated encephalomyelitis (ADEM) secondary to dengue infection was made based on the clinical history, laboratory findings and typical MRI findings.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 10-year-old boy presented with a 12-day history of high-grade fever, chills, headache, retro-orbital pain, and occasional vomiting, complicated 5 days later by asymmetric quadriparesis and decreased consciousness.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient experienced 12 days of high-grade fever, chills, headache, retro-orbital pain, and occasional emesis, followed 5 days later by acute right hemiparesis progressing to left upper-limb weakness and obtundation.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for high-grade fever, chills, headache, retro-orbital pain, vomiting, right upper/lower limb and left upper-limb weakness, and decreased consciousness.

objective.physical_examination: Decreased level of consciousness with weakness of the right upper limb, right lower limb, and left upper limb.
objective.routine_investigations: Platelet count 80,000/uL; malaria dual antigen test and serological markers for Japanese encephalitis and herpes simplex virus (HSV-1) were negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Brain MRI revealed multiple patchy non-enhancing T2/FLAIR hyperintense lesions without diffusion restriction involving the left temporoparietal cortex/subcortical white matter, bilateral cerebellar hemispheres, body of the corpus callosum, and lower medulla. Whole-spine MRI demonstrated longitudinally extensive T2 hyperintensity in the inferior medulla, cervicomedullary junction, cervical cord up to C3, and terminal thoracic cord/conus medullaris from T11 to L1.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Post-dengue acute disseminated encephalomyelitis (ADEM) with brain, brainstem, cervical (to C3), and thoracolumbar (T11-L1) spinal cord involvement, confirmed by positive anti-dengue IgM (negative IgG) serology and characteristic multifocal brain and spinal cord MRI findings.

raw_case_text:
A 37-year-old male presented with on-and-off fever (102 degrees F) for four days and generalized weakness in both upper and lower limbs. All necessary investigations were performed. On evaluation, the patient was diagnosed with dengue fever with thrombocytopenia. On examination, the patient was conscious and coherent with the following vital signs: blood pressure of 180/100 mmHg, pulse rate of 54 bpm, and saturation of peripheral oxygen (Spo2) of 95%. Neurological examination revealed sensory loss below the T4 level with absent deep tendon reflexes. The patient had a Glasgow coma score (GCS) of 15 without any signs of meningeal irritation. The pupillary size and reaction were normal. Serological tests for malaria and typhoid infection were negative. He had a hematocrit of 46%, and thrombocytopenia (1.01 lakhs/cumm) with an increased total leukocyte count (19,400 cells/cumm) and a normal coagulation profile (prothrombin time (PT) 14.1 sec, international normalized ratio (INR) 1.2). The rest of the laboratory results were unremarkable.
The patient was started on intravenous antibiotics (doxycycline 100mg), analgesics, and other supportive medications. His weakness gradually progressed with the inability to walk or stand. The patient was referred for a spine MRI, which showed long-segment spinal epidural hemorrhage in the cervical and dorsal spine (up to D8 level) causing mild to moderate lateral compression and anterior displacement of the cord at these levels (Figures 1, 2). An MRI of the brain was also performed which revealed mild diffuse subarachnoid hemorrhage with subtle dependent hemorrhage in the bilateral occipital horns of the lateral ventricles which correlated with CT (Figure 3). After the radiology report, a neurosurgeon was consulted regarding the MRI findings and explained the grave risk and poor prognosis in relation to the radiological findings. Since the epidural hemorrhage was a long-segment (cervicodorsal spine epidural hematoma from C2 to D7 level) and not focal, surgical treatment was not possible and conservative management was advised. The patient was intubated due to unresponsiveness on day 10 of the dengue fever diagnosis. On the same day, the patient's family members decided to have the patient discharged against medical advice. Subsequently, the patient died of the disease.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 37-year-old male presented with a 4-day history of intermittent fever (102 F) and progressive generalized weakness in both upper and lower limbs.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed 4 days of intermittent fever (102 F) and four-limb weakness that progressively worsened during hospitalization to complete inability to stand or walk, culminating in unresponsiveness requiring endotracheal intubation on day 10 of illness.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for intermittent fever (102 F), progressive four-limb weakness, inability to stand or walk, and sensory loss below the upper chest.

objective.physical_examination: On admission: conscious and coherent (GCS 15/15), blood pressure 180/100 mmHg, bradycardia with pulse 54 bpm, SpO2 95%, normal pupillary size and reaction, no meningeal irritation signs, sensory loss below the T4 dermatome level, and globally absent deep tendon reflexes; progressed to inability to stand/walk and unresponsiveness on day 10.
objective.routine_investigations: Hematocrit 46%, thrombocytopenia with platelet count 1.01 lakhs/cumm, leukocytosis with TLC 19,400 cells/cumm, normal coagulation profile (PT 14.1 s, INR 1.2), and negative malaria and typhoid serologies.
objective.advanced_workup: Cervicodorsal spine MRI revealed a long-segment spinal epidural hemorrhage extending from C2 to D7/D8 causing mild-to-moderate lateral compression and anterior displacement of the spinal cord. Brain MRI and head CT demonstrated mild diffuse subarachnoid hemorrhage with subtle dependent intraventricular hemorrhage in the bilateral occipital horns.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Severe dengue fever with thrombocytopenia complicated by spontaneous long-segment cervicodorsal spinal epidural hematoma (C2-D8) with compressive myelopathy and spontaneous cranial subarachnoid and intraventricular hemorrhage, confirmed by dengue diagnostic workup and brain/spine MRI. Deemed non-operable due to the extensive longitudinal span of the epidural hemorrhage and managed conservatively with IV doxycycline (100 mg), analgesics, and endotracheal intubation on day 10; the family took discharge against medical advice on day 10 and the patient subsequently died.

raw_case_text:
A 53-year-old morbidly obese female with a history of hypertension presented to the emergency department (ED), with a sudden onset of loss of consciousness, left-sided weakness, and altered sensorium for two days, which was associated with high-grade fever and vomiting. At admission, she was unconscious (Glasgow coma scale, or GCS, score = 5); had tachypnea (respiratory rate, or RR, 30-35 minute-1), tachycardia (heart rate, or HR, 114 bpm), and blood pressure (BP) 153/90 mmHg; was maintaining oxygen saturation of 94% to 94% (on room air) on spontaneous respiration; and was passing urine output around 40-50 mL/hour. Given airway protection, tracheal intubation was performed immediately. Post intubation, the GCS was 6. Noncontrast computerized tomography (NCCT) of the brain revealed right basal ganglia bleeding with intraventricular hemorrhage (Figure 1).
Then she was transferred to ICU, where cerebral protection strategy (head-up position, neck in a neutral position, osmotic diuretics, mean arterial pressure (MAP) 85-90 mm Hg, normoxia, normocarbia, euglycemia, normothermia, and maintenance of sodium (Na+) levels between 145 and 155 mEq/L) and further supportive care was initiated. Laboratory evaluation at admission is summarized in Table 1. Electrocardiography (ECG) showed sinus tachycardia. Chest X-ray (CXR) was normal.   
After a few days of ICU admission, she started spiking high-grade temperature (core temperature as high as 106-107  F), which was associated with rhabdomyolysis (serum creatine kinase (CK-total) = 10,000 IU/L), stage III acute kidney injury (AKI, requiring five sessions of renal replacement therapy), and coagulopathy (requiring blood component therapy). On workup, cultures turned out to be sterile. Other possibilities of hyperthermia (such as drug toxicity) were ruled out. NCCT head was repeated, which did not reveal any hematoma expansion. Workup for COVID-19 was also negative. On account of a history of fever with chill and myalgia around a week before ED admission, a tropical workup was sent for malaria, typhoid, leptospirosis, dengue, chikungunya, and scrub typhus, in which serology (IgM antibodies) for dengue turned out to be positive. Gradually, the temperature trends, renal functions, and coagulopathy recovered. In intercurrent issues, she had septic shock (secondary to ventilator-associated pneumonia and grade IV pressure injury in the sacral region) and neuromuscular weakness, resulting in prolonged weaning. Eventually, the patient was discharged after six months of ICU stay in tracheostomized condition, with a GCS score of 9, accepting Ryle's tube feeding and passing adequate urine output.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 53-year-old morbidly obese, hypertensive female presented unconscious with a 2-day history of sudden loss of consciousness, left-sided weakness, high-grade fever, and vomiting, preceded 1 week earlier by fever with chills and myalgia.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: One week after experiencing fever with chills and myalgia, the patient developed high-grade fever, vomiting, acute left-sided weakness, and coma for 2 days prior to ED presentation. During her ICU stay for a right basal ganglia intracerebral hemorrhage, she developed extreme hyperpyrexia (106-107 F), severe rhabdomyolysis, stage III acute kidney injury requiring dialysis, and coagulopathy.
subjective.past_medical_history: Morbid obesity and hypertension; febrile prodrome with chills and myalgia 1 week prior to admission.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for prodromal fever, chills, and myalgia, followed by high-grade fever (spiking to 106-107 F in ICU), vomiting, left-sided hemiparesis, and coma.

objective.physical_examination: On admission: unconscious with GCS 5/15 (6/15 post-intubation), tachypneic (RR 30-35/min), tachycardic (HR 114 bpm), blood pressure 153/90 mmHg, room-air SpO2 94%, left-sided weakness, and urine output 40-50 mL/h. In the ICU: extreme core hyperthermia (106-107 F), later complicated by a grade IV sacral pressure injury and ICU neuromuscular weakness.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission ECG showed sinus tachycardia and CXR was normal. In the ICU, she developed severe rhabdomyolysis (serum total CK 10,000 IU/L), stage III AKI, and coagulopathy; blood/body fluid cultures, COVID-19 testing, and tropical fever tests for malaria, typhoid, leptospirosis, chikungunya, and scrub typhus were all negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Admission non-contrast head CT revealed a right basal ganglia intracerebral hemorrhage with intraventricular extension (repeat head CT showed no hematoma expansion).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Acute dengue fever complicated by right basal ganglia intracerebral and intraventricular hemorrhage, extreme central/infectious hyperpyrexia (106-107 F), rhabdomyolysis (CK 10,000 IU/L), coagulopathy, and stage III acute kidney injury, confirmed by positive dengue IgM serology and head CT. Managed in the ICU with neuroprotective mechanical ventilation, osmotic diuretics, 5 sessions of renal replacement therapy, blood component transfusions, and treatment for secondary ventilator-associated pneumonia and sacral pressure ulcer; discharged after 6 months tracheostomized with GCS 9, normal renal function, and nasogastric feeding.

raw_case_text:
An 18-years-old male presented with fever for 12 days: the fever was sudden in onset, high-grade, of continuous pattern and associated with rigors. The patient was initially managed as a presumed case of dengue fever based on serology: positive Ig M antibody and negative Ig G antibody. Eight days later, the patient developed left-sided chest pain that used to get aggravated on lying flat and somewhat relieved on leaning forward. There was no history of burning micturition, diarrhoea, productive cough or headache. Past medical record mentioned PDA. There was also history of contact with an active tuberculosis patient, his grandfather, in the past. The patient had a blood pressure of 140/80 mm Hg at presentation, regular pulse at 140 bpm, temperature of 101 degree Fahrenheit, respiratory rate of 20/minute and an oxygen saturation of 90% at room air.
General physical examination showed notable pallor. There were no puncture marks suggestive of possible intravenous drug abuse. There was no jugular venous distension or engorged neck veins. On examination of the precordium, apex beat was not shifted. There was a machinery murmur, at left 2nd intercostal space; however, there was no pericardial rub. On auscultation of the back of chest, there was normal vesicular breathing with decreased air entry at left basal area. The systemic examination was unremarkable other than that.
The initial ECG showed sinus tachycardia with concave ST-elevation and PR depression in leads I, II, aVL, V2. There was reciprocal ST depression and PR elevation in lead aVR. Laboratory investigations on day one showed a haemoglobin of 12.1 g/dl with a raised white cell count of 17 X 10^9/L. The ESR was also raised at 60 mm/hour. The blood cultures showed growth of methicillin-resistant staphylococcus aureus. The serological tests showed dengue Ig M positivity; however, the tuberculosis ICT was negative. Chest X ray posterior-anterior view (Fig.1) showed increased cardiothoracic ratio, with somewhat prominent pulmonary artery marking on the left side. There were irregular-shaped opacities in the lung fields bilaterally. The two-dimensional echocardiography showed circumferential pericardial effusion and a small-sized PDA. The left ventricular function was normal. Nevertheless, the definitive cause of the pericardial effusion was not known.
Approximately 12 hours after the admission, the patient developed acute shortness of breath associated with chest pain and apprehension on the night of the first day of admission. Blood pressure was 90/60 with heart rate of 150/minute. We suspected impending cardiac tamponade and cardiac surgeon was consulted. Pericardial window was planned together with PDA ligation. It was speculated to be infective endocarditis in association with patent ductus arteriosus. The CT chest (Fig.2) showed presence of infiltrates in the lung fields. Infective endocarditis in association with PDA was considered a possibility due to the presence of one major criterion and three minor criteria: the Duke's criteria.
The blood cultures showed growth (major criterion) and there was fever >38 degree C, a predisposing cardiac lesion and vascular phenomena (septic emboli in lung fields). After consultation with cardiac surgery the initial plan was to do a left thoracotomy for PDA ligation and pericardial window to drain what was presumed to be purulent pericarditis. Upon drainage of the clotted blood in the pericardium, a perforation was discovered in the main pulmonary artery. The bleeding was controlled with finger pressure.
This resulted in a difficult situation where CPB was required during a left thoracotomy. Initially, the left femoral vessels were exposed, however the femoral artery was found to be too small to accept an adequate sized femoral cannula. Hence, the perforation was tightly packed with gauze and the pericardium oversewn to re-create partial tamponade of the perforation. The patient was flipped to supine position from the right decubitus position. CPB was initiated via median sternotomy with aorto-atrial cannulation. At 26 degree C, and under brief intermittent periods of circulatory arrest lasting less than three minutes the PDA was overseen from inside the pulmonary artery. Perforation was debrided and repaired with fresh autologous pericardium. It was inferred that infective endocarditis had led to perforation of the main pulmonary artery, resulting in haemopericardium. Intravenous antibiotics were continued for 14 days in the cardiothoracic surgical intensive care unit and the patient was discharged afterwards on oral linezolid for four additional weeks. At follow-up the patient is doing well off antibiotics with normal cardiac function.

subjective.chief_complaint: An 18-year-old male presented with sudden-onset continuous high-grade fever with rigors for 12 days and positional left-sided chest pain for 4 days.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed continuous high-grade fever with rigors 12 days prior to admission and was initially managed as presumed dengue fever. Eight days into his illness (4 days prior to presentation), he developed left-sided chest pain exacerbated by lying flat and relieved by leaning forward. Twelve hours after admission, he developed acute dyspnea, chest pain, apprehension, and hypotension.
subjective.past_medical_history: Known patent ductus arteriosus (PDA); past household contact with active tuberculosis (grandfather).
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for continuous high-grade fever, rigors, positional left-sided chest pain, and subsequent acute dyspnea and apprehension. Negative for dysuria, diarrhea, productive cough, or headache.

objective.physical_examination: On presentation: blood pressure 140/80 mmHg, regular pulse 140 bpm, temperature 101 F, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 90% on room air, notable pallor, no IV drug injection marks, no JVD, non-shifted apex beat, continuous machinery murmur at the left 2nd intercostal space without pericardial rub, and decreased air entry at the left lung base. Twelve hours post-admission: blood pressure dropped to 90/60 mmHg with heart rate 150 bpm (impending cardiac tamponade).
objective.routine_investigations: ECG showed sinus tachycardia with concave ST-elevation and PR depression in leads I, II, aVL, and V2, and reciprocal ST depression/PR elevation in aVR. Day 1 labs: hemoglobin 12.1 g/dL, leukocytosis (WBC 17 x 10^9/L), ESR 60 mm/h, negative tuberculosis ICT, and blood cultures growing methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA). Chest X-ray showed cardiomegaly, prominent left pulmonary artery markings, and bilateral irregular lung opacities. 2D echocardiography showed circumferential pericardial effusion, a small PDA, and normal LV function.
objective.advanced_workup: Chest CT demonstrated bilateral pulmonary infiltrates consistent with septic pulmonary emboli. Intraoperative exploration via left thoracotomy and subsequent median sternotomy on cardiopulmonary bypass revealed hemopericardium (clotted blood) and a perforation in the main pulmonary artery.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: MRSA infective endocarditis complicating patent ductus arteriosus (fulfilling Duke's criteria) with septic pulmonary emboli, main pulmonary artery perforation, and hemopericardium, alongside positive dengue IgM (negative IgG) serology. Managed with emergency median sternotomy under cardiopulmonary bypass and brief hypothermic circulatory arrest (26 C) for internal PDA closure and autologous pericardial patch repair of the pulmonary artery perforation, plus 14 days of inpatient IV antibiotics followed by 4 weeks of oral linezolid, achieving full recovery and normal cardiac function at follow-up.

raw_case_text: A 75-year-old female had a history of fall at home after which she became unconscious and was brought to our hospital emergency. After resuscitation, a CT scan was taken which showed a right temporal lobe hematoma [Figure 9]. She underwent craniotomy and evacuation of hematoma after which she regained consciousness. She had an uneventful postoperative period until the 2nd week. Postoperative CT scan showed no fresh bleeding [Figure 10]. She was set to be discharged when she developed mild fever and altered sensorium. She was transferred to Intensive care unit and evaluated. Investigations revealed she had thrombocytopenia (63,000/mm3) which prompted us to evaluate her for dengue. She was positive for NS1 antigen and IgM antibody. Her INR was 1.3 and APTT was 40 s. She was administered platelet concentrates without a notable rise in her thrombocytopenia. After 4 days, her consciousness further deteriorated and chest X-rays revealed she had severe chest infection [Figure 11a and b]. She was ventilated as she further developed respiratory failure sequelae to ARDS. Throughout her illness, her platelet counts never recovered to normal levels despite several platelet transfusions. Finally, she succumbed to her disease after a prolonged period of ventilation.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 75-year-old female recovering in the hospital 2 weeks after craniotomy for a traumatic right temporal lobe hematoma developed acute mild fever and altered sensorium just prior to planned discharge.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Initially admitted unconscious after a fall at home with a right temporal lobe hematoma that was successfully evacuated via craniotomy (with full recovery of consciousness and a clean postoperative CT), the patient developed mild fever and altered sensorium in the 2nd postoperative week, followed 4 days later by worsening obtundation, severe pneumonia, and ARDS.
subjective.past_medical_history: Recent fall at home with traumatic right temporal lobe intracerebral hematoma status post craniotomy evacuation 2 weeks prior.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for prior fall/unconsciousness and subsequent 2nd-week postoperative fever, altered sensorium, and respiratory failure.

objective.physical_examination: Initially unconscious after fall, regaining consciousness post-craniotomy; in the 2nd postoperative week, developed mild fever, progressive deterioration in consciousness, and respiratory failure.
objective.routine_investigations: Second-week ICU workup revealed persistent thrombocytopenia (platelet count 63,000/mm3, refractory to repeated platelet concentrate transfusions), INR 1.3, and aPTT 40 s. Chest X-rays 4 days later showed severe bilateral pneumonia and ARDS.
objective.advanced_workup: Initial admission head CT showed a right temporal lobe hematoma; postoperative head CT prior to dengue onset showed complete evacuation without fresh bleeding.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Hospital/postoperatively acquired dengue fever with refractory thrombocytopenia (63,000/mm3), encephalopathy, severe pneumonia, and fatal ARDS following craniotomy for traumatic intracerebral hemorrhage, confirmed by positive dengue NS1 antigen and dengue IgM antibody testing. Managed in the ICU with multiple platelet concentrate transfusions and prolonged mechanical ventilation, but she succumbed to her illness.

raw_case_text: A 17-year-old male recipient of matched-sibling donor transplant for myelodysplastic syndrome, on immunosuppressive agent, presented with fever and body ache on day +317. Donor chimerism at day +180 was >90%. At presentation, CBC showed Hb = 16.5 g/dL, hematocrit (HCT) = 48%, platelet = 90 x 109/L. Physical examination revealed harsh vesicular breathing. Dengue NS1 antigen was detected. Blood cultures were negative. He was managed conservatively for 1 week as inpatient with intravenous hydration, analgesics, and antipyretics. Platelet count dropped to 24 x 109/L followed by recovery without need for transfusion.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 17-year-old male hematopoietic stem cell transplant recipient presented on day +317 post-transplant with fever and body ache.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient, who underwent matched-sibling donor transplantation for myelodysplastic syndrome and remained on immunosuppressive therapy, presented on post-transplant day +317 with acute fever and generalized body aches.
subjective.past_medical_history: Myelodysplastic syndrome status post matched-sibling donor stem cell transplant (day +317; donor chimerism >90% at day +180).
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever and body ache. Home medication: immunosuppressive agent.

objective.physical_examination: Harsh vesicular breathing on chest auscultation.
objective.routine_investigations: At presentation: hemoglobin 16.5 g/dL, hematocrit 48%, platelet count 90 x 10^9/L (subsequently dropping to a nadir of 24 x 10^9/L). Blood cultures were negative.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Dengue fever in a post-allogeneic stem cell transplant recipient, confirmed by positive dengue NS1 antigen and negative blood cultures. Managed conservatively as an inpatient for 1 week with intravenous hydration, analgesics, and antipyretics, achieving full platelet count recovery from a nadir of 24 x 10^9/L without platelet transfusion.

raw_case_text: A 16-year-old boy, with severe aplastic anemia, presented in transplant emergency with high-grade fever associated with shivering, pain in right hypochondrium and loose watery stools for 2 days, on day +88 posttransplant. Pan cultures and other infective workup were negative while Dengue NS1 antigen was detected. His platelet count declined rapidly with rising hematocrit level. He was managed aggressively with supportive care, intravenous hydration, and platelet transfusions during critical phase. He also had slightly deranged renal function and liver enzymes were elevated two times upper normal limit. However, the coagulation profile was normal. Mild pleural effusion and moderate ascites were also observed on ultrasound. He stayed in the hospital for 15 days for management of dengue fever.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 16-year-old male stem cell transplant recipient presented on day +88 post-transplant with high-grade fever, shivering, right hypochondrial pain, and loose watery stools for 2 days.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: On day +88 following stem cell transplantation for severe aplastic anemia, the patient presented to the transplant emergency department with a 2-day history of high-grade fever with shivering, right upper quadrant pain, and watery diarrhea.
subjective.past_medical_history: Severe aplastic anemia status post stem cell transplantation (day +88).
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for high-grade fever, shivering, right hypochondrial pain, and loose watery stools.

objective.routine_investigations: Rapidly declining platelet count with rising hematocrit (hemoconcentration), mildly deranged renal function, liver enzymes elevated to 2x upper limit of normal, and normal coagulation profile. Pan-cultures and other infectious workup were negative. Abdominal/chest ultrasound demonstrated mild pleural effusion and moderate ascites.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Severe dengue fever with plasma leakage (pleural effusion, ascites, hemoconcentration) in a post-transplant severe aplastic anemia patient, confirmed by positive dengue NS1 antigen and negative pan-cultures. Managed aggressively over a 15-day hospitalization with supportive care, intravenous hydration, and platelet transfusions during the critical phase, resulting in recovery.

raw_case_text:
A 7-year-old girl, from the district of Hooghly district in West Bengal, with no significant past history presented to us with fever for 15 days, difficulty in walking for last 4 days, and impairment of vision for 1 day. The fever was high grade (102.4 F on initial presentation) and intermittent in nature without chills, rigor, or rash. It used to subside on taking antipyretics. The fever was associated with headache and few episodes of projectile vomiting. Four days before presentation, the patient started having difficulty in walking with a tendency to fall to any one side and over the course of 4 days, she was not able to walk. Visual impairment was suddenly onset, with the child having difficulty in reading books and was associated with diplopia. The child had no history of spectacle use for refractive errors. There was neither any history of seizures, loss of consciousness, altered sensorium, trauma, low back pain, or any weakness nor of tinnitus, vertigo, or ear discharge. There was also no history of eye pain or redness. Bladder and bowel habit was normal. There was no history of similar disease in the family or of any developmental delay or regression. All immunizations were up-to-date, with no recent history of vaccination.
On further evaluation, child was febrile, irritable, and sick looking. There was no other abnormal finding on general survey, no apparent rash or neurocutaneous marker noted. No eschar was noted after thorough examination of entire body surface, including flexural areas, external genitalia, and scalp. Pulse was 120/min, with no special character. Blood pressure was 117/80, which is just above the 95th percentile for age, sex, and height. Respiratory rate was 24/min.
 Neurological examination: Higher functions were normal with no impairment in memory, speech, or language. Patient was well oriented to time, place, and person. There was no muscle weakness or hyper/hypotonia. Tendon reflexes were normal as were the superficial reflexes. There was no impairment in smell or taste. Visual acuity testing could not be done initially as the child was not cooperative. On reexamination after stabilization, visual acuity testing was 6/6 in both unaided eyes. Cranial nerve VI was affected, with latent squint of right eye manifested on asking the child to look toward the right. We suspected that the apparent impairment of vision and abducens nerve involvement were due to raised intracranial tension. All other cranial nerves were within normal limit. Sensory system examination revealed no impairment in fine touch, pain, temperature, position, and vibration sense. Romberg test was within normal limit. Cerebellar examination revealed unsteady gait with inability to walk in a straight line and tendency to fall to one side along with past pointing on finger nose test and dysdiadochokinesia. Neck rigidity was present, but Kernig's and Brudzinski's signs were negative. Fundoscopic examination did not reveal any signs of papilledema. There was no organomegaly on abdominal examination. Cardiovascular and respiratory systems were within normal limit.
 Investigations: There was moderate anemia with Hb:7.2 g/dl with microcytosis and hypochromia, probably due to nutritional iron deficiency. Leukocytosis was present (TLC- 15010/cmm), with neutrophilic predominance (N62 L32 M4 E2 B0). Malarial parasite was negative on peripheral blood smear; malarial parasite dual antigen testing was negative. Liver function and kidney function tests and electrolytes were also normal for age and sex.
Tests for dengue and typhoid, Japanese encephalitis, Herpes simplex, and human immunodeficiency virus were performed as per routine investigations for fever, all of which were negative. Blood culture revealed no growth. Urinalysis was normal and urine culture revealed no growth. Blood for Scrub typhus was IgM-Positive.
Cerebrospinal fluid- Cell type and count- 102 cells/cmm, 92% being mononuclear, 8% being polymorphs. Glucose -59 mg/dL. Cerebrospinal fluid protein was elevated to 119 mg/dL.
Cerebrospinal fluid Gram' stain showed no white blood cells, no microorganisms, and no growth after 48 hours incubation. Cerebrospinal fluid serology revealed Scrub typhus IgM/immunoglobulin G Positive. Magnetic resonance imaging brain showed no abnormality.
The patient was initially given intravenous fluid and antibiotic injection, Ceftriaxone as per standard recommendations on an empirical basis, after blood samples were drawn and lumbar puncture was done. We also started management of raised intracranial tension with head end elevation, control of fever with antipyretics, and hypertonic saline infusion at 0.5 mL/kg/h. This was continued for 24 hours till there was resolution of irritability, hypertension, improvement of vision, and subsidence of squint. On receiving the Scrub typhus reports, we started oral doxycycline at 5 mg/kg/d which led to dramatic improvement in 48 hours, with steadying of gait. Doxycycline was continued for a total of 7 days, following which the general condition improved and child became afebrile. She now had a visual acuity of 6/6, no sensorimotor or cognitive deficit and no problem with balance and coordination. We then discharged the child after a stay of 8 days after documenting the favorable neurological outcome.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 7-year-old girl from West Bengal presented with a 15-day history of intermittent high-grade fever, headache, and projectile vomiting, 4 days of progressive gait ataxia, and 1 day of acute diplopia and near-vision impairment.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Previously healthy child developed 15 days of intermittent high-grade fever (102.4 F) with headache and projectile vomiting, followed 4 days prior to presentation by truncal/gait instability progressing to complete inability to walk, and 1 day prior by sudden-onset difficulty reading and binocular diplopia.
subjective.past_medical_history: No significant past medical or family history; normal development; up-to-date immunizations.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for intermittent high-grade fever (102.4 F), headache, projectile vomiting, gait ataxia with tendency to fall, blurred near vision, and diplopia. Negative for chills, rigors, rash, seizures, loss of consciousness, trauma, back pain, limb weakness, tinnitus, vertigo, ear discharge, ocular pain/redness, or bowel/bladder dysfunction.

objective.physical_examination: Febrile (102.4 F), irritable, sick-appearing; pulse 120/min, blood pressure 117/80 mmHg (>95th percentile), respiratory rate 24/min, and no rash, eschar, or organomegaly. Neurological exam showed intact cognition/orientation, normal motor tone/power/reflexes/sensation, unaided visual acuity 6/6 OU (after stabilization), right cranial nerve VI (abducens) palsy with esotropia on rightward gaze, neck rigidity (negative Kernig/Brudzinski signs), normal fundoscopy without papilledema, and cerebellar signs including ataxic gait, past-pointing on finger-to-nose testing, and dysdiadochokinesia.
objective.routine_investigations: Moderate microcytic hypochromic anemia (Hb 7.2 g/dL), neutrophilic leukocytosis (TLC 15,010/cumm; N62 L32 M4 E2), normal liver/kidney function and electrolytes, normal urinalysis, sterile blood and urine cultures, negative malaria peripheral smear and dual antigen test, negative typhoid, Japanese encephalitis, HSV, and HIV tests, and positive serum scrub typhus IgM.
objective.advanced_workup: CSF analysis revealed mononuclear pleocytosis (102 cells/cumm; 92% mononuclear, 8% polymorphs), elevated protein (119 mg/dL), glucose 59 mg/dL, negative Gram stain and 48-hour bacterial culture, and positive CSF scrub typhus IgM and IgG. Brain MRI was normal.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Scrub typhus meningoencephalitis with acute cerebellitis and raised intracranial pressure (false-localizing right abducens nerve palsy), confirmed by positive serum scrub typhus IgM and positive CSF scrub typhus IgM and IgG. Dengue fever was ruled out by negative dengue testing. Treated with 24 hours of hypertonic saline infusion (0.5 mL/kg/h) and head elevation for intracranial hypertension, empiric IV ceftriaxone, and a 7-day course of oral doxycycline (5 mg/kg/day), achieving dramatic neurological recovery within 48 hours and discharge on hospital day 8 with 6/6 vision and normal gait.

raw_case_text:
A 24-year-old previously healthy male soldier experienced an upper respiratory tract infection (URI) 2 weeks prior to his presentation. One week after the infection subsided, he had dysphagia, truncal and limb ataxia, and symmetrical proximal muscles weakness. On the third day of his neurological illness, total ophthalmoplegia, cerebellar dysarthria, and generalized hyporeflexia were evidenced at a primary hospital, and then, he was immediately transferred to our hospital. He had never been exposed to food or substances containing neurological toxins. On admission to our center, the weakness of limbs and respiratory muscles progressed rapidly to flaccid quadriparesis, which was dominant in the upper limbs, and respiratory muscle paralysis so that mechanical ventilation was indicated. All deep tendon reflexes were absent. Nevertheless, his consciousness, pinprick sensation, and proprioception were absolutely intact. MFS and GBS overlap syndrome was a provisional diagnosis at initial evaluation. The GBS disability score at that time was 5. Medical Research Council sum score was 44; the muscle strength was symmetrical as follows: both shoulders abduction 3; elbow flexion 3; wrist extension 4; hip flexion 4; knee flexion 4, and ankle dorsiflexion 4.
The results of routine blood chemistry tests, anti-HIV, anti-HBV, anti-HCV, as well as a panel of serology tests of autoimmune disorders were unremarkable. The cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis revealed clear CSF, normal pressure, and no blood cells. The CSF/serum glucose ratio was 83/110 mg/dL. CSF protein was 74.9 mg/dL. CSF culture and polymerase chain reaction for possible organisms, such as bacteria, mycobacterium tuberculosis, herpes viruses, Japanese B virus, and Dengue viruses, yielded negative results. The electroneuromyographic (ENMG) study showed symmetrical sensorimotor axonal polyneuropathy, which was dominant in both upper limbs. Left facial axonal neuropathy was detected as well (Fig. 1). A panel of AGAbs, including anti-GM1, -GM2, -GM3, -GD1a, -GD1b, -GT1b, and -GQ1b, was negative. Based on the clinical presentation and ENMG results, MFS/AMSAN-GBS overlap syndrome was the final diagnosis, and intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) therapy was immediately initiated. The neurological symptoms dramatically resolved 4 days after the treatment. GBS disability score became 2 eventually.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 24-year-old male soldier presented with a 3-day history of dysphagia, truncal and limb ataxia, symmetrical proximal muscle weakness, total ophthalmoplegia, and cerebellar dysarthria 1 week after an upper respiratory tract infection.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: One week after resolution of an upper respiratory tract infection (2 weeks prior to presentation), the previously healthy soldier developed dysphagia, truncal and limb ataxia, and symmetrical proximal muscle weakness, followed on day 3 of neurological symptoms by complete external ophthalmoplegia, cerebellar dysarthria, and generalized hyporeflexia, rapidly progressing on admission to upper-limb-predominant flaccid quadriparesis, areflexia, and respiratory muscle paralysis.
subjective.past_medical_history: Previously healthy soldier; upper respiratory tract infection 2 weeks prior; no neurotoxin exposure.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for antecedent URI, dysphagia, diplopia/ophthalmoplegia, dysarthria, truncal/limb ataxia, rapidly progressive four-limb weakness, and respiratory distress.

objective.physical_examination: Intact consciousness, pinprick sensation, and proprioception; total bilateral ophthalmoplegia, cerebellar dysarthria, left facial nerve weakness, symmetrical upper-limb-predominant flaccid quadriparesis (MRC sum score 44: bilateral shoulder abduction 3/5, elbow flexion 3/5, wrist extension 4/5, hip flexion 4/5, knee flexion 4/5, ankle dorsiflexion 4/5; GBS disability score 5), global absence of deep tendon reflexes, truncal/limb ataxia, and respiratory muscle paralysis requiring mechanical ventilation.
objective.routine_investigations: Routine blood chemistry, anti-HIV, anti-HBV, anti-HCV, autoimmune serology panel, and serum antiganglioside antibody panel (anti-GM1, -GM2, -GM3, -GD1a, -GD1b, -GT1b, -GQ1b) were all negative/normal. Electroneuromyography (ENMG) demonstrated symmetrical upper-limb-predominant sensorimotor axonal polyneuropathy and left facial axonal neuropathy.
objective.advanced_workup: CSF analysis revealed albuminocytologic dissociation with clear acellular fluid (0 cells), normal opening pressure, CSF protein 74.9 mg/dL, CSF/serum glucose 83/110 mg/dL, and negative CSF bacterial culture and PCR for M. tuberculosis, herpesviruses, Japanese encephalitis B virus, and dengue viruses.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Miller Fisher syndrome and acute motor-sensory axonal neuropathy Guillain-Barre syndrome (MFS/AMSAN-GBS) overlap syndrome, confirmed by clinical triad (ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, areflexia) plus axonal sensorimotor quadriparesis on ENMG and CSF albuminocytologic dissociation. Dengue virus was ruled out by negative CSF dengue PCR. Treated with mechanical ventilation and immediate intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) therapy, achieving dramatic neurological improvement within 4 days and recovery to a GBS disability score of 2.

raw_case_text:
A five-year-old male non-Caucasian patient presented with fever, myalgia, headache, and conjunctivitis for 5 days. His past medical history was unremarkable, with normal psychomotor development, no family history neurological diseases and no consanguinity. The patient was born and lived in Ceara, northeast Brazil, and family reported no recent travels.
After 1 week he developed tonic-clonic seizures. Neurological examination was normal at this point. Complete blood count, liver functions and acute reactants were normal. Serologies for HSV-1, HSV-2, CMV, EBV, VZV, HIV, and toxoplasmosis were negative. Brain MRI was normal. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed 15 cells, protein 16.6 mg/dL and glucose 68 mg/dL. He was started on acyclovir and ceftriaxone.
Two weeks after seizure onset, he presented with dystonia (Video 1) and oromandibular dyskinesia. On physical examination the patient was awake, his speech output was decreased, pupils were normal. Cranial nerves examination was unremarkable. Muscle strength was symmetric and deep tendon reflexes were normoactive and symmetric. One week later he developed focal motor seizures followed by decreased level of consciousness, dysautonomia, and central apnea. EEG showed extreme delta brush and valproate and phenytoin were started. He also received methylprednisolone followed by intravenous immunoglobulin with seizure resolution and improvement of level of consciousness, dysautonomia and orofacial dyskinesias within 2 weeks.
Anti-NMDAR antibodies were detected in serum (titer 1:25600) and CSF (titer 1:1024) after 3 weeks of symptom onset using tissue and cell-based assays as previously reported. CHIK serology was positive for both IgM and IgG, suggesting a recent infection. Dengue and Zika serologies were negative. CSF PCR for herpes viruses and arboviruses (CHIK, Dengue and Zika) were negative. Whole body CT and testis ultrasound were normal. Because of partial improvement (persistence of orofacial dyskinesias and impaired speech), the patient received rituximab and cyclophosphamide with good response. After 8 months he is seizure-free and has returned to school with only mild restlessness and inattention. Figure 1 describes the timeline of clinical features, investigation and treatment of the case report.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 5-year-old boy from Ceara, Brazil presented with a 5-day history of fever, myalgia, headache, and conjunctivitis, followed 1 week later by tonic-clonic seizures and 2 weeks later by dystonia, oromandibular dyskinesia, reduced speech, dysautonomia, and central apnea.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Previously healthy boy developed 5 days of fever, myalgia, headache, and conjunctivitis, followed 1 week later by generalized tonic-clonic seizures. Two weeks after seizure onset, he developed dystonia, oromandibular dyskinesia, and decreased speech output, progressing 1 week later to focal motor seizures, obtundation, dysautonomia, and central apnea.
subjective.past_medical_history: Unremarkable past medical and family history; normal psychomotor development; non-consanguineous parents; resident of Ceara, Brazil with no recent travel.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for prodromal fever, myalgia, headache, and conjunctivitis, followed by generalized and focal seizures, dystonia, orofacial dyskinesias, decreased speech, decreased consciousness, dysautonomia, and central apnea.

objective.physical_examination: Initial neurological exam at first seizure was normal. Two weeks later: awake with decreased speech output, dystonia, and oromandibular dyskinesia, with normal pupils, cranial nerves, symmetric muscle strength, and normoactive reflexes. One week later: focal motor seizures, decreased consciousness, autonomic instability, and central apnea.
objective.routine_investigations: CBC, liver function tests, and acute-phase reactants were normal; serologies for HSV-1/2, CMV, EBV, VZV, HIV, toxoplasmosis, and Zika were negative; testicular ultrasound was normal. EEG demonstrated an 'extreme delta brush' pattern. Chikungunya virus IgM and IgG serologies were positive, and cell/tissue-based assays at week 3 detected high-titer anti-NMDAR antibodies in serum (1:25,600) and CSF (1:1,024).
objective.advanced_workup: Brain MRI and whole-body CT were normal. Initial CSF analysis showed 15 cells/mm3, protein 16.6 mg/dL, glucose 68 mg/dL, negative PCR for herpesviruses, chikungunya, dengue, and Zika viruses, and positive CSF anti-NMDAR antibodies (titer 1:1,024).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Post-infectious anti-N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor (anti-NMDAR) autoimmune encephalitis triggered by acute chikungunya virus infection, confirmed by positive serum (1:25,600) and CSF (1:1,024) anti-NMDAR antibodies, extreme delta brush on EEG, and positive CHIKV IgM/IgG serology. Dengue and Zika viruses were ruled out by negative serum serology and CSF RT-PCR. Treated initially with acyclovir, ceftriaxone, valproate, phenytoin, IV methylprednisolone, and IVIG, followed by second-line immunotherapy with rituximab and cyclophosphamide, achieving complete seizure freedom and return to school at 8-month follow-up.

raw_case_text:
A two-and-a-half years old child was born at term, out of non-consanguineous marriage to a primigravidae, by normal delivery. The child was apparently asymptomatic till 18 days of life, when he developed fever following BCG vaccination, and was treated with intravenous antibiotics to which he responded.
