Hematoxylin and Eosin stain and methenamine silver stain revealed fungal organisms with thin separate hyphae and regular branching, morphologically consistent with Aspergillus species. As revealed in the previous labs and imaging results, the patient had no evidence of disseminated Aspergillosis. The patient's postoperative course was uneventful, and he was discharged on Voriconazole 200 mg PO bid for a period of 1 year after which he completely improved.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 45-year-old immunocompetent white male presented for a 1-year outpatient follow-up of a presumed pulmonary embolism and was found to have an ascending thoracic aortic pseudoaneurysm with upper and lower extremity blood pressure and pulse asymmetry.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: One year prior to presentation, the patient was misdiagnosed at an outside hospital with a pulmonary embolism and started on oral anticoagulation. At his 1-year follow-up visit, repeat chest CT angiography showed no pulmonary embolism but revealed a 2.4 x 1.5 cm ascending aortic pseudoaneurysm surrounded by a large mediastinal and intrapericardial hematoma.
subjective.past_medical_history: Hospitalized 3 years prior for uncomplicated community-acquired Klebsiella pneumonia (resolved after 5 days); misdiagnosed with pulmonary embolism 1 year prior (on oral anticoagulation); 14 pack-year ex-smoker; employed at a water desalination plant; no history of diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidemia, trauma, or prior surgery.
subjective.review_of_systems: Negative for chest pain, dyspnea, fever, weight loss, night sweats, arthralgias, skin rash, or neurological symptoms.

objective.physical_examination: BMI 24.2 kg/m2; poor oral hygiene with dental caries. Cardiovascular exam revealed marked blood pressure asymmetry between the upper extremities (120/83 mmHg in the left arm vs. 107/46 mmHg in the right arm) and diminished right radial and right femoral pulses compared to the left.
objective.routine_investigations: Labs showed mildly elevated CRP of 13 mg/L, normal procalcitonin (0.1 ng/mL), normal ESR (10 mm/h), and normal CBC, cardiac enzymes, BNP, renal and liver function, and coagulation profile. Autoimmune panel (ANA, ANCA, anti-dsDNA, C3, C4), HIV and syphilis serologies, and bacterial and fungal blood and urine cultures were all negative. ECG showed normal sinus rhythm; chest X-ray showed cardiomegaly and a blunted right cardiophrenic angle; TTE and TEE showed LVEF 55%, moderate tricuspid regurgitation, and no valvular vegetations.
objective.advanced_workup: Brain CT angiography was normal. Chest CT angiography demonstrated a 2.4 x 1.5 cm focal pseudoaneurysm (1.1 cm neck) arising from the right anterior wall of the ascending thoracic aorta 2.5 cm above the aortic valve, accompanied by a large anterior mediastinal and intrapericardial hematoma, pericardial thickening, and mild hemorrhagic pericardial effusion. Intraoperative exploration confirmed an adherent thickened pericardium and a contained cheesy hematoma over the right ventricle and ascending aorta; H&E and Gomori methenamine silver staining of the excised pseudoaneurysm wall/pericardial biopsy revealed regular branching thin septate fungal hyphae morphologically consistent with Aspergillus species.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Primary isolated Aspergillus mycotic pseudoaneurysm of the ascending thoracic aorta with contained intrapericardial hematoma in an immunocompetent host (initially misdiagnosed 1 year earlier as pulmonary embolism), definitively confirmed by intraoperative biopsy H&E and methenamine silver histopathology demonstrating regular branching thin septate Aspergillus hyphae. Treated with surgical ascending aortic debridement, bovine pericardial patch repair, and pericardial debridement followed by a 1-year course of oral voriconazole (200 mg twice daily), achieving complete clinical recovery.

raw_case_text:
A child of age below 6 years old was diagnosed for pre-B acute lymphoblastic leukemia, rearranged TEL/AML = t (12; 21), SNC1; hence, chemotherapy started according to the international collaborative treatment protocol AIEOP2017. At day 52 after the start of chemotherapy, fever occurred (38.6 C) (also accompanied by a 20-day catarrhal cough), and it was managed with Piperacillin-Tazobactam therapy. Diagnostic insights also revealed positivity only for Rhinovirus in the superficial respiratory secretions. At day 63, because of good general conditions, the patient was discharged; however, at day 66, the child was accompanied to the emergency department for fever recurrence. Bone marrow aplasia with very severe leukopenia (0.3 x 103/muL), thrombocytopenia (7 x 103/muL), and anemia (hemoglobin: 7.0 g/dL) were diagnosed, requiring hospitalization in pediatric onco-hematology. Positivity for Aspergillus and pan-fungal antigens (i.e., galatomannan and beta-D-glucan, respectively) was detected (Table 1); mycete culture in nasopharyngeal aspirate and peripheral blood were negative. Cytomegalovirus (CMV) presence was also shown. Additionally, in a clinical setting characterized by the persistence of medullary aplasia, a computed tomography (CT) scan showed the presence of a worsening interstitial pneumonia. Therapy consisted of antibiotics (Piperacillin-Tazobactam), antivirals (Foscavir), and antifungals (Amphotericin B); transfusions of both platelets and concentrated red blood cells were also performed, together with granulocyte colony-stimulating factor administration. Specifically, as regards antifungal therapy, Amphotericin B dosage was adjusted over time (Table 1): from 3 mg/kg/day (days 69-76) to 5 mg/kg/day (days 77-82). At day 83, the child was transferred to the pediatric intensive care unit; positivity for aspergillary and pan-fungal antigens together with the presence of CMV-DNA persisted. The dosage of Amphotericin B therapy was increased to 6.25 mg/kg/day. At day 90, responsiveness to antibiotic/antiviral/antifungal treatments led to a significant improvement of the clinical picture; however, 3 days later, following a sudden cough, the child presented a very abundant bleeding from the oral cavity initially supposed to be of gastric origin. The hemorrhage required resuscitation with ventilation, tracheal intubation, and external cardiac massage for the onset of extreme bradycardia followed by asystole. Despite the resuscitation maneuvers, the infusion of fluids, adrenaline, and bicarbonate, the child died (Table 1).
At autopsy, blood presence was observed in the lumen of the upper tracts of the alimentary canal (i.e., the oral cavity, pharynx, esophagus, stomach, and duodenum) in the absence of wall injury (Figures 1A-C).
Considering the laryngotracheal tract, three ulcerative lesions with destruction of the cartilage components were observed; necrotic pseudomembranous features were partly also recognized (Figures 2A-D). Specifically, the ulcers were located at the anterior aspect of the cricoid cartilage (circular appearance, 1 cm in diameter); at the left antero-lateral aspect of the first tracheal ring (circular appearance, 1 cm in diameter); at the right antero-lateral side of the trachea along the first tracheal rings (oriented according to the tracheal axis, 1 x 4.5 cm) (Figures 2A-C). Death occurred as a consequence of right inferior thyroid artery lesion due to full-thickness ulcerative perforation of the tracheal wall. An artery protruded at the cranial end of the right anterolateral tracheal ulcer (Figure 2C, insert).
Macroscopic examination of the lungs showed patchy black/red areas of hemorrhagic invasion of airspaces (Figure 3A).
The laryngo-tracheal lesions and the lungs were sampled, fixed in 10% buffered formalin, and processed for histopathological analyses. Specifically, all tissues underwent hematoxylin and eosin staining (Figures 2D, 3B,C, respectively) and the presence of hyphae was detected by Grocott-Gomori's methenamine silver (GMS) staining (Figures 2E, 3D, respectively). In parallel, immunoperoxidase staining was performed on a Dako EnVision Autostainer according to manufacturer recommendations; antibody for E-13 CMV (monoclonal mouse anti-human, aurogene, code number: 11-003) was used to detect presence of eventual positive cellular elements. Regarding the lung tissue, focal areas of necrosis, likely associated to Aspergillus infection (as confirmed by hyphae presence) and interstitial pneumonia evidence, consistent with CMV etiopathogenesis, were observed; hemorrhagic invasion of airspaces was also found (Figures 3B-E).

subjective.chief_complaint: A child under 6 years of age with TEL/AML1-rearranged pre-B acute lymphoblastic leukemia presented with febrile neutropenia, bone marrow aplasia, and a 20-day catarrhal cough during chemotherapy, culminating on day 93 in sudden massive fatal oral hemorrhage after coughing.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Treated on the AIEOP 2017 protocol for CNS-negative (SNC1) t(12;21) TEL/AML1 pre-B ALL, the child developed fever (38.6 C) and a 20-day catarrhal cough on day 52 (with rhinovirus in upper airway secretions), transiently improved on piperacillin-tazobactam, and was readmitted on day 66 with recurrent fever, profound bone marrow aplasia, CMV viremia, positive serum galactomannan and beta-D-glucan, and worsening interstitial pneumonia. Transferred to the PICU on day 83 and treated with escalated amphotericin B (up to 6.25 mg/kg/day), foscarnet, and piperacillin-tazobactam, the child clinically improved by day 90, but on day 93 suffered a sudden paroxysm of cough followed by torrential fatal arterial hemorrhage from the oral cavity.
subjective.past_medical_history: Pre-B acute lymphoblastic leukemia with t(12;21) TEL/AML1 rearrangement (SNC1) undergoing induction/consolidation chemotherapy per AIEOP 2017 protocol.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for persistent catarrhal cough, recurrent neutropenic fever, dyspnea, and terminal massive hemoptysis/oral hemorrhage.

objective.physical_examination: Febrile (38.6 C) on day 52 and day 66; on day 93, suffered sudden massive bright-red oral hemorrhage following a cough, rapidly progressing to severe bradycardia and fatal asystole despite endotracheal intubation and cardiopulmonary resuscitation.
objective.routine_investigations: Day 52 nasopharyngeal swab was positive for rhinovirus. Day 66 CBC showed profound trilineage bone marrow aplasia: WBC 0.3 x 10^3/uL, hemoglobin 7.0 g/dL, and platelets 7 x 10^3/uL. Peripheral blood and nasopharyngeal fungal cultures were negative, while blood CMV-DNA was persistently positive.
objective.advanced_workup: Serial serum Aspergillus galactomannan and panfungal 1,3-beta-D-glucan assays were persistently positive from day 66 through day 83, and chest CT showed worsening interstitial pneumonia. Postmortem autopsy revealed three deep necrotizing pseudomembranous laryngotracheal ulcers destroying the underlying cricoid and upper tracheal cartilage (a 1-cm anterior cricoid ulcer, a 1-cm left anterolateral first-ring ulcer, and a 1 x 4.5 cm longitudinal right anterolateral tracheal ulcer) with full-thickness tracheal perforation and direct erosion/protrusion of the right inferior thyroid artery causing exsanguination into the airway and upper GI tract. Grocott-Gomori methenamine silver (GMS) staining and anti-CMV E-13 immunohistochemistry of the laryngotracheal ulcers and hemorrhagic/necrotic lungs confirmed invasive Aspergillus hyphae in the trachea and lung necrosis alongside CMV interstitial pneumonitis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Fatal ulcerative pseudomembranous Aspergillus tracheobronchitis and invasive pulmonary aspergillosis coexisting with cytomegalovirus (CMV) interstitial pneumonitis during prolonged chemotherapy-induced bone marrow aplasia in a child with pre-B ALL, complicated on day 93 by full-thickness tracheal ulceration and fatal erosion of the right inferior thyroid artery, confirmed premortem by positive serum galactomannan, beta-D-glucan, and CMV-DNA and proven at autopsy by GMS fungal staining and CMV immunohistochemistry. Despite G-CSF, blood product support, foscarnet, piperacillin-tazobactam, and dose-escalated amphotericin B (3 to 6.25 mg/kg/day), the child died of catastrophic tracheo-arterial fistula hemorrhage on day 93.

raw_case_text:
A 54-year-old female patient, active smoker (35 pack-years), with a history of pulmonary tuberculosis in adolescence, was admitted to the Department of Lung Diseases and Tuberculosis due to productive cough, weakness, low exercise tolerance, weight loss (about 7 kg). Symptoms exacerbated during last 6 months. She was treated empirically with oral antibiotics in standard doses (amoxicillin, amoxicillin-clavulanate, levofloxacin, and cefuroxime) without clinical improvement. Three and a half years earlier, the patient underwent radiochemotherapy for locally advanced non-small-cell lung cancer of the right upper lobe (adenocarcinoma, the clinical stage of the tumor was T3N2Mo CS IIIA /T:tumor, N:lymph node, M:metastasis/, Figure 1a). Platinum-based chemotherapy with etoposide (three cycles) was combined with radical radiotherapy of the right lung tumor area, hilum, and mediastinal lymph nodes (66 Gy in 33 fractions). This treatment was well-tolerated and no early complications were observed. Since then, the patient has been under strict oncological control. Follow-up CT images of the chest and abdomen were taken regularly every 6 months. A cavitary lesion developed at the site of the tumor of the right lung 2 years after the end of lung cancer treatment (Figure 1b).
Chest CT scans showed an irregular cavity in the upper part of the right lung with thick walls and accompanying mass of the posterior wall, surrounded by solid consolidation, dilated surrounding bronchus, and emphysema (Figure 1c). Imaging diagnostics was extended to PET-CT, which revealed the unclear nature of the hypermetabolic masses in the right lung, more likely inflammation (Figure 1d).
Physical examination revealed numerous wheezing and rales during lung auscultation. During bronchoscopy, purulent bronchitis was confirmed (Figures 2a,b). Laboratory tests showed increased concentration of C-reactive protein (CRP) (90 mg/dl, normal range <5 mg/dl). Lung function tests revealed a moderate impairment on pulmonary transfer coefficient for carbon monoxide (TLCO; 41% predicted value). No obstruction or restriction was observed.
Microbiological tests (smears, aerobic and anaerobic cultures) of the sputum and bronchial wash were negative for bacteria and fungi. Ziehl-Neelsen staining, cartridge-based nucleic acid amplification test (CBNAAT), and culture of sputum and bronchial wash did not show evidence of Mycobacterial infection. Aspergillus fumigatus precipitins were positive in serum. The test was performed using the qualitative Ouchterlony double immunodiffusion method in an agarose gel. The test was developed with its own research methodology and performed in the Department of Biological Health Hazards and Parasitology, Institute of Rural Health, Lublin, Poland. The result was assessed on the basis of the formed precipitation lines, validated with a negative control serum test. Ceftriaxone (2.0 g per day) and levofloxacin (500 mg twice a day) were administered empirically intravenously with a moderate clinical effect. Control bronchoscopy revealed a partial reduction of purulent mucus.
Due to the suspicion of lung cancer recurrence, a transthoracic, CT-guided fine-needle aspiration of the peripheral margin of the right lung cavity was performed. Only macrophages and inflammatory cells such as lymphocytes and neutrophils were observed in aspirated cytological samples. No microbiological tests were performed because of the small amount of the collected sample. Also, forceps biopsy of bronchial tissue collected from the second right bronchus during the bronchoscopy was negative for neoplastic cells. Moreover, no other clinical or radiographic signs of malignancy were observed.
The low value of transfer factor of the lung for carbon monoxide (TLCO) disqualified the patient from surgical resection of the right lung (pneumonectomy).
The patient met diagnostic criteria for CPA and antifungal treatment with itraconazole was initiated (200 mg orally twice a day). The therapy was well-tolerated. Two months later, sputum culture was positive for A. fumigatus. A sabouraud dextrose agar (SDA) medium with chloramphenicol and gentamicin was used as a selective medium for the isolation of fungi. The species was determined on the basis of both macro- (colony morphology in SDA) and microscopic morphology (conidiophores, vesicles, metules, phialides, and conidia). Drug susceptibility was determined by the microdilution method (Thermo Scientific). The minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) for itraconazole was 0.12 mug/ml. Every 8 weeks, the patient was re-evaluated clinically by physical examination and radiologically on the basis of chest CT (Figures 3a-d) and x-rays (Figures 4a-d). Follow-up bronchoscopy and microbiological tests of bronchial wash were also performed. Four months after initiation of itraconazole treatment, sputum culture was positive for itraconazole sensitive A. flavus (MIC = 0.25 mug/ml). Taking into account the well-graded clinical response, radiological improvement, and good tolerability, therapy was continued for up to 6 months.
Six months later, the patient was re-admitted to the Department of Lung Diseases and Tuberculosis with symptoms of increasing weakness, productive cough, night sweats, chest pain on the right side, and weight loss (3 kg). Chest imaging confirmed CPA progression (Figures 5a, 6a). Microbiological tests for fungi and bacteria were negative. A bronchial biopsy ruled out cancer recurrence. Once again antifungal treatment with itraconazole (200 mg orally twice a day) was initiated. After 3 months, antifungal medication was switched to orally administered voriconazole (200 mg twice daily) due to radiographic progression (Figures 5b, 6b). The tolerance of the therapy was poor. Four weeks after starting the voriconazole treatment, the patient reported pain in the chest and right upper abdominal quadrant, further weight loss (a total of 7 kg), and temporary visual disturbances. On bronchoscopy, massive purulent bronchitis and concentric stenosis of the right upper lobe were detected. In the cytological examination of the bronchial wash, fungal hyphae were detected for the first time during the entire diagnostic process (Figure 2c). Chest CT images showed further progression. The cavity in the upper right lobe was larger, with a level of thickened, heterogeneous fluid and air in the upper part (Figures 5c, 6c). Physical examination and CT images of the abdominal cavity confirmed the hepatomegaly. The laboratory test revealed elevated transaminases (>5x upper limit of normal), high CRP (90 mg/dl), and anemia (red blood cells-3.4 x 106/mul, hemoglobin-10.2g/dl).
The antifungal treatment was modified again. Itraconazole (200 mg orally twice a day) bridging therapy was used in anticipation of the unavailability of liposomal amphotericin B as part of emergency access to therapy.
After 1 month of itraconazole treatment, clinical and radiological improvement was achieved. The patient confirmed her well-being, an increase in appetite and body weight (2 kg), and good tolerance of the antifungal therapy. Control imaging showed partial regression (Figures 5d, 6d). It was decided to continue treatment with itraconazole for at least 12 months under close clinical and radiological monitoring. The antifungal treatment is still ongoing. Follow-up visits are scheduled. A timeline with all relevant data from this clinical case is available in Figure 7.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 54-year-old female active smoker with a history of adolescent pulmonary tuberculosis and chemoradiotherapy-treated stage IIIA right upper lobe lung adenocarcinoma presented with a 6-month exacerbation of productive cough, weakness, low exercise tolerance, and a 7-kg weight loss.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Three and a half years after completing definitive chemoradiotherapy (3 cycles of platinum/etoposide plus 66 Gy in 33 fractions) for stage IIIA right upper lobe lung adenocarcinoma—which had evolved into a post-radiation right upper lobe cavity 2 years post-treatment—the patient presented with 6 months of worsening productive cough, weakness, reduced exercise tolerance, and a 7-kg weight loss refractory to outpatient oral amoxicillin, amoxicillin-clavulanate, levofloxacin, and cefuroxime.
subjective.past_medical_history: Adolescent pulmonary tuberculosis; stage IIIA (T3N2M0) right upper lobe lung adenocarcinoma treated 3.5 years prior with radical chemoradiotherapy (66 Gy + platinum/etoposide); active 35 pack-year smoker.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for chronic productive cough, weakness, poor exercise tolerance, 7-kg weight loss, and during a 6-month relapse night sweats and right chest pain; later experienced voriconazole-induced transient visual disturbances and right upper quadrant abdominal pain.

objective.physical_examination: Lung auscultation revealed numerous wheezes and rales. During a subsequent voriconazole-induced hepatotoxicity episode, physical exam revealed hepatomegaly.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission CRP was elevated at 90 mg/dL (normal <5 mg/dL). Pulmonary function testing showed moderately impaired diffusing capacity (TLCO 41% predicted) without airflow obstruction or restriction, precluding right pneumonectomy. Initial sputum and bronchial wash bacterial, fungal, and mycobacterial (Ziehl-Neelsen, CBNAAT, culture) tests were negative, while serum Ouchterlony double immunodiffusion was positive for Aspergillus fumigatus precipitins. During subsequent voriconazole therapy, labs showed transaminases >5x ULN, CRP 90 mg/dL, RBC 3.4 x 10^6/uL, and hemoglobin 10.2 g/dL.
objective.advanced_workup: Chest CT and PET-CT demonstrated a thick-walled irregular right upper lobe cavity containing a posterior wall mass, surrounding consolidation, traction bronchiectasis, and emphysema. CT-guided transthoracic FNA and repeated bronchoscopic forceps biopsies confirmed purulent bronchitis and chronic inflammation without lung cancer recurrence. Sabouraud dextrose agar sputum cultures grew itraconazole-susceptible Aspergillus fumigatus (MIC 0.12 ug/mL) at 2 months and Aspergillus flavus (MIC 0.25 ug/mL) at 4 months; during a later relapse on voriconazole, bronchoscopy showed concentric right upper lobe stenosis and bronchial wash cytology directly visualized fungal hyphae.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Chronic cavitary pulmonary aspergillosis (CPA) caused by Aspergillus fumigatus and Aspergillus flavus arising in a post-chemoradiotherapy right upper lobe cavity in a patient with prior lung adenocarcinoma and adolescent TB, confirmed by chest CT, positive serum A. fumigatus precipitins, sputum cultures growing A. fumigatus and A. flavus, and bronchial wash cytology showing fungal hyphae (with cancer recurrence and active TB excluded). Treated initially with 6 months of oral itraconazole (200 mg twice daily); when CPA relapsed 6 months later and a switch to oral voriconazole (200 mg twice daily) provoked acute hepatotoxicity (hepatomegaly, transaminases >5x ULN) and visual disturbances at 4 weeks, re-initiation of long-term oral itraconazole (200 mg twice daily for >=12 months) achieved clinical weight gain and radiographic regression.

raw_case_text:
A 69-year-old male with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) presented with a chief complaint of nausea and gait disorder. The patient's eldest daughter also had SLE. He had no smoking history, no drinking, no travel history, no outdoor activities, and no sexual activity.
The patient's present medical history was as follows. The patient became aware of dyspnea and edema of the lower extremities during exercise; thus, he consulted a family doctor. The examination revealed hypertension, proteinuria, and hematuria. A chest X-ray revealed bilateral pleural effusion. Because of an increase in antinuclear antibodies (Anti-ds-DNA antibody 218.5) and a decline in complement (C3 51 and C4 12.3), a connective tissue disease was suspected, and the patient was referred to our Department of Rheumatic Collagen Disease. After 2 months, he was hospitalized for examination and diagnosed with SLE because of (i) renal lesions, (ii) leukopenia, (iii) positive anti-ds-DNA antibody, and (iv) positive antinuclear antibody. Based on the renal biopsy results 2 months later, he was diagnosed with lupus nephritis Class IV. Accordingly, steroid pulse therapy (methylprednisolone, 1000 mg) and tacrolimus (2 mg/day) were initiated intravenously. As SLE and lupus nephritis improved, the patient received prednisolone (25 mg/day) + tacrolimus (2 mg/day) + azathioprine (100 mg/day) orally and was discharged after 6 months. He returned for follow-up as an outpatient.
After 1 year, the patient visited a family doctor for nausea and dizziness. A brain computed tomography (CT) revealed a multilocular cystic lesion with edema. Thus, he was referred to our department for neurosurgery.
On day 1 of admission, the initial brain CT in the axial plane shows the low-density area in the right parietal lobe [Figure 1a]. Moreover, we suspected a cerebral abscess because a multilocular cystic lesion, which was imaged in a ring shape, was observed on the enhanced T1-weighted magnetic resonance imaging axial image [Figure 1b]. On day 10 of admission, the cranial brain abscess was excreted by burr hole surgery used by stereotactic techniques, and intravenous meropenem (MEPM; 1 g TID) + vancomycin (0.5 g BID) was started postoperatively. Of note, Gram-positive bacilli, suspected to be actinomycetes, were detected in the puncture fluid collected intraoperatively. Since the culture specimen was positive for Kinyoun staining, Gram-positive bacilli were found to belong to the Nocardia genus [Figures 1c and d]. On day 15 of admission, vancomycin was discontinued because it was later determined as N. thailandica based on the 16S rRNA sequence and matrix-assisted laser desorption ionization time-of-flight mass spectrometry [MALDI-TOFMS; Figures 2a and b]. The change to an ST combination was considered, but the patient had an allergic function. Hence, intravenous MEPM (1 g TID) was continued. On day 20 of admission, a blood test revealed improved inflammatory response, but renal function had deteriorated, resulting in decreased MEPM (1 g BID).
The patient remained hospitalized for 30 days without further deterioration of renal function; however, consciousness disorder appeared because of deteriorating central nervous system lupus. Consequently, oral administration became difficult; thus, we switched to ceftriaxone (CTRX; 2 g BID) intravenously. A brain CT revealed that the brain abscess had decreased gradually. The treatment of the abscess and SLE was progressing smoothly. However, on day 77 of admission, the patient developed a catheter-associated urinary tract infection and catheter-associated bloodstream infection due to Corynebacterium striatum and extended spectrum beta-lactamase Escherichia coli. Gradually, the patient's condition worsened and he died 86 days after admission. After death, a pathological autopsy was performed with the approval of the patient's family. We established the formation of microabscesses in the lungs, mitral valve, liver, and kidneys; however, no Gram-positive bacilli suspected of being Nocardia were detected in the brain or other organs. Since filamentous fungi, suspected of Aspergillus, and yeast-like fungi, suspected of Candida, were detected in the abscesses and blood vessels, the cause of death was established as aspergillosis and disseminated candidiasis due to bacterial replacement caused by the prolonged administration of antibiotics [Figure 3].

subjective.chief_complaint: A 69-year-old male on triple immunosuppression for systemic lupus erythematosus and class IV lupus nephritis presented with nausea, dizziness, and a gait disorder.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Diagnosed 1 year earlier with SLE and biopsy-proven class IV lupus nephritis (initially presenting with exertional dyspnea, leg edema, hypertension, proteinuria, hematuria, and bilateral pleural effusions) and maintained on oral prednisolone (25 mg/day), tacrolimus (2 mg/day), and azathioprine (100 mg/day), the patient presented to his family physician with nausea, dizziness, and gait disturbance and was found on brain CT to have a right parietal cystic mass with edema.
subjective.past_medical_history: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and class IV lupus nephritis diagnosed 1 year prior, treated with pulse IV methylprednisolone (1,000 mg) followed by maintenance oral prednisolone (25 mg/day), tacrolimus (2 mg/day), and azathioprine (100 mg/day); drug allergy to trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. Family history of SLE in his eldest daughter; lifetime non-smoker and non-drinker.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for nausea, dizziness, gait disturbance, and subsequent depressed consciousness from CNS lupus and late sepsis.

objective.physical_examination: Presented with gait disorder; subsequently developed impaired consciousness around hospital day 30 attributed to CNS lupus, followed by septic deterioration on day 77 and death on day 86.
objective.routine_investigations: Initial SLE diagnosis labs 1 year prior showed leukopenia, positive ANA, elevated anti-dsDNA (218.5), low C3 (51) and C4 (12.3), proteinuria, and hematuria. On hospital day 77 of the current admission, catheter-associated urine and blood cultures grew Corynebacterium striatum and ESBL-producing Escherichia coli.
objective.advanced_workup: Admission head CT and contrast-enhanced T1-weighted brain MRI demonstrated a multilocular ring-enhancing cystic abscess in the right parietal lobe with surrounding vasogenic edema (which gradually shrank on follow-up CT after drainage and carbapenem/ceftriaxone therapy). Stereotactic burr-hole aspiration on hospital day 10 yielded Gram-positive, Kinyoun-acid-fast branching bacilli identified by 16S rRNA gene sequencing and MALDI-TOF MS as Nocardia thailandica. Following death on hospital day 86, postmortem autopsy revealed complete eradication of Nocardia from the brain and systemic organs, but demonstrated disseminated microabscesses and vascular invasion by both filamentous Aspergillus-like hyphae and Candida-like yeasts in the lungs, mitral valve, liver, and kidneys.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Right parietal Nocardia thailandica cerebral abscess in an immunosuppressed patient with SLE and class IV lupus nephritis (confirmed by stereotactic aspiration, Kinyoun stain, 16S rRNA sequencing, and MALDI-TOF MS), complicated after prolonged broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotic therapy (meropenem 1 g tid/bid followed by ceftriaxone 2 g bid due to TMP-SMX allergy) and catheter-related ESBL E. coli/Corynebacterium striatum sepsis by fatal superinfection with disseminated aspergillosis and candidiasis involving the lungs, mitral valve, liver, and kidneys (proven at autopsy).

raw_case_text:
A 28-year-old woman was admitted to the Second Xiangya Hospital of Central South University, Hunan, China because of recurrent cough for 6 years and wheezing for 7 months, which aggravated for half a month in May 2021. The patient started to cough sputum early in September 2014, and pulmonary tuberculosis was considered the reason at the local hospital and therefore anti-tuberculosis was given. The symptoms improved significantly until 2015; the patient complained of cough with fever during the anti-tuberculosis therapy and visited our hospital for the first time. Laboratory tests showed an elevated level of leukocyte count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein level, and serum total IgE (2,500 IU/ml, normal range: <130 IU/ml). The chest CT revealed multiple cavitary lesions in both upper lungs and the dorsal segment of the left lower lung and bronchiectasis of bilateral lobes (Figure 1A). A combined infection of aspergillosis and Staphylococcus aureus was confirmed by positive culture of both sputum and bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF). Anti-infection with teicoplanin and itraconazole was prescribed, and her symptoms were relieved on therapy. The patient remained stable until 2019; she began coughing intermittently and the symptoms gradually worsened when accompanied with dyspnea and wheezing. She visited our hospital for the second time in December 2020. Blood tests showed a moderately elevated level of eosinophil count (0.97 x 109/L, normal range: 0.02-0.52 x 109/L) and a markedly increased serum total IgE level (>2,500 IU/ml). Total levels of aspergillosis-specific IgE, IgM, and IgG were above normal. A pulmonary function test revealed decreased FVC (2.41 L; expected value: 2.92 L), decreased FEV1 (1.54 L, expected value: 2.53 L), and decreased FEV1/FVC (63.68%, expected value: 84.52%), indicating moderate obstructive pulmonary ventilation dysfunction and positive bronchodilation test (FEV1 increased by 16.8%). The chest CT revealed bilateral multiple bronchiectases, pulmonary bulla, and atelectasis in the right middle lung lobe (Figure 1B). Based on these data, a diagnosis of allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA) was made. Oral voriconazole 200 mg two times daily and methylprednisolone 16 mg per day plus inhaler were prescribed but were demonstrated to be insufficient without the improvement of symptoms. Since February 2021, she was given omalizumab 600 mg three times every month; she was readmitted due to the aggravation of cough and wheezing. The patient denied any history of food or drug allergies. Her family history was negative for any inherited genetic diseases.
On physical examination, her body weight was 58 kg on admission. She exhibited facial flushing, a full moony face, buffalo back, and mossy skin changes on the scalp. Moist rales could be heard on bilateral lung fields. Her laboratory findings on admission revealed moderate C-reactive protein level (33.6 mg/l, reference range: 0-6 mg/l) and a normal level of leukocyte count and erythrocyte sedimentation. Serum IgE was above normal (770 IU/ml, reference range: <130 IU/ml); serum -beta-D-glucan test, galactomannan test, anti-nuclear antibody, anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, vasculitis antibodies, antiphospholipid antibodies, antibodies to extractable nuclear antigens, and rheumatoid factor were negative. Pulmonary CT suggested diffuse multiple ground glass shadows and scattered striae in both lungs and more cystic lesions than previously observed (Figure 1C). Bronchoscopy showed viscous jelly-like secretions in the tracheal lumen. The next-generation sequence (NGS) of BALF indicated Pneumocystis jirovecii (sequence reads 34909), Human Herpes Virus Type 5 (also named CMV, sequence reads 1843), and Human Herpes Virus Type 4 (also named EBV, sequence reads 7). With classic diffuse ground-glass lesions appearing in the chest CT images and high sequence reads of CMV and P. jirovecii in BALF detected by mNGS, we identified that the patient had CMV and P. jirovecii coinfection. The sequence reads of EBV, which is ubiquitous in most of the population, were too few to be identified as pathogenic. SMZ-TMP and ganciclovir were given and symptoms were gradually relieved (Figure 2).
Given that the young patient was predisposed to multiple pathogens, including some opportunistic strains, we carefully reviewed the patient's medical history. Surprisingly, she had multiple skin rashes and pruritus all over the body since childhood. A minor traumatic fracture of the right calf occurred at the age of 12. She underwent cutaneous abscesses requiring incision and drainage at 13 years of age. The patient also had a previous diagnosis of pelvic abscess, tubal occlusion, and primary infertility. The patient had recurrent infections of different strains including opportunistic pathogens in multiple organs, skin rashes, and markedly elevated IgE levels. HIES were suspected, and she scored 45 points on the National Institutes of Health clinical HIES scoring system. Further whole-exome sequencing (WES) was performed to screen potential mutations, indicating a heterozygous missense mutation in exon 15 of STAT3 (c.1294G>T, g.62382G>T, p.Val432Leu, NM_139276.2). Consequently, the final diagnosis was made as AD-HIES. Her parents and younger sister are wild-type genotypes. In addition to the standard anti-infection therapy, we prescribed omalizumab 300 mg every 2 weeks and Seretide inhalation. Oral corticosteroids gradually reduced and stopped. During 6 months of follow-up, the patient did not experience recurrent infection. After an initial fluctuation of the level, serum IgE remained stable recently. The patient's symptoms and lung function improved on therapy (Figure 3). The chest CT scan demonstrated improved infiltrates (Figure 1D).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 28-year-old woman with a 6-year history of recurrent cavitary pulmonary aspergillosis and allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis presented with a 2-week acute exacerbation of cough and wheezing.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Having experienced chronic productive cough since September 2014 (initially treated empirically for TB), the patient was diagnosed at our hospital in 2015 with bilateral cavitary pulmonary aspergillosis and Staphylococcus aureus co-infection (treated with itraconazole and teicoplanin) and in December 2020 with allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA; treated with voriconazole 200 mg bid, methylprednisolone 16 mg/day, and omalizumab 600 mg 3x/month starting February 2021). In May 2021, she was readmitted with a half-month aggravation of cough and wheezing.
subjective.past_medical_history: Generalized pruritic skin rashes since childhood; minimal-trauma right calf fracture at age 12; cutaneous abscesses requiring incision and drainage at age 13; pelvic abscess, fallopian tube occlusion, and primary infertility; bilateral cavitary pulmonary aspergillosis + S. aureus pneumonia (2015); allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (2020). Unremarkable family history (parents and younger sister wild-type for STAT3).
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for chronic recurrent productive cough, wheezing, dyspnea, and childhood pruritic dermatitis.

objective.physical_examination: Weight 58 kg; cushingoid features from chronic steroid use (facial flushing, moon facies, dorsocervical fat pad/buffalo hump), mossy hyperkeratotic skin changes on the scalp, and bilateral pulmonary moist rales on auscultation.
objective.routine_investigations: In 2015, sputum and BALF cultures grew Aspergillus and Staphylococcus aureus with serum total IgE 2,500 IU/mL. In December 2020, labs showed eosinophilia (0.97 x 10^9/L), total IgE >2,500 IU/mL, elevated Aspergillus-specific IgE, IgM, and IgG, and reversible moderate obstructive ventilatory dysfunction on spirometry (FVC 2.41 L, FEV1 1.54 L, FEV1/FVC 63.68%, +16.8% bronchodilator response). On May 2021 admission, labs showed CRP 33.6 mg/L, normal WBC and ESR, total IgE 770 IU/mL (reference <130), and negative ANA, ENA, ANCA, antiphospholipid antibodies, and rheumatoid factor; NIH clinical HIES score was 45 points.
objective.advanced_workup: May 2021 serum 1,3-beta-D-glucan and galactomannan assays were negative. Chest CT in May 2021 showed new diffuse bilateral ground-glass opacities, linear striae, and increased cystic/bronchiectatic lesions compared to 2015 and 2020 scans. Bronchoscopy revealed viscous jelly-like tracheal secretions, and bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) mNGS detected high sequence reads of Pneumocystis jirovecii (34,909 reads) and cytomegalovirus (HHV-5, 1,843 reads; plus 7 background EBV reads). Whole-exome sequencing (WES) identified a de novo heterozygous missense mutation in exon 15 of STAT3 (NM_139276.2: c.1294G>T, p.Val432Leu).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Autosomal dominant hyper-IgE syndrome (AD-HIES, Job's syndrome; NIH score 45, confirmed by heterozygous STAT3 exon 15 c.1294G>T [p.Val432Leu] mutation) underlying a 6-year history of cavitary pulmonary aspergillosis and allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA), complicated in May 2021 by opportunistic Pneumocystis jirovecii and cytomegalovirus (CMV) pneumonia co-infection (confirmed by BALF mNGS and diffuse ground-glass opacities on chest CT). Treated with oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and intravenous ganciclovir for PJP/CMV co-infection, followed by maintenance subcutaneous omalizumab (300 mg every 2 weeks) and inhaled salmeterol/fluticasone (Seretide), allowing complete discontinuation of oral corticosteroids and achieving 6 months of infection-free clinical, spirometric, and radiographic improvement.

raw_case_text:
Forty-seven-year-old, male, ex-smoker (30 pack-year), diagnosed with AS HLA B27 + at the age of 30. He had, for several years, symptoms of cervical morning stiffness and axial pain of inflammatory rhythm, conditioning frequent use of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory medication, bilateral sacroiliitis grade IV, lumbar spine ankylosis and syndesmophytes as well as a restrictive ventilatory pattern. He had been medicated with Infliximab for almost 2 years, after negative screening for latent TB (4.5 years prior to first contact with the Pulmonary Department), was no longer under biological therapy and had abandoned ambulatory follow-up in Rheumatology 3 years ago.
He was admitted at the Pulmonary Department of a District Hospital with a 3-month evolution worsening dyspnea, productive cough with mucopurulent sputum, evening sweating and fever, anorexia, and unquantified weight loss. On initial physical examination, there was low body mass index (BMI <18.5 kg/m2), muscle wasting, pronounced thoracic kyphosis, decreased chest wall expansion, and crepitant rales over the upper thirds of both hemithorax. Laboratory study revealed elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (120 mm/h) and C-reactive protein (CRP 23 mg/dL), anemia (hemoglobin (Hb) 10.3 g/dL), and hypoalbuminemia (albumin 3.1 g/dL). Chest x-ray (Figure 1A) showed hypotransparency of the upper thirds of both pulmonary hemifields with retractile findings and lung volume loss as well as a cavity in the right upper lobe (RUL). Chest CT confirmed RUL consolidation with cavitation; left upper lobe (LUL) peripheral consolidation with air bronchogram; important upper lobe (UL) volume loss and multiple cylindric bronchiectasis (Figure 1 B and C). Sputum molecular tests detected Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex (MTC) and first-line anti-bacillary therapy was initiated. Since fever and cough persisted, a flexible bronchoscopy was performed, and a methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) was isolated on bronchial biopsies. The patient was treated according to drug-susceptibility test, with improvement. On the seventh month of anti-bacillary therapy, he developed persistent dry cough. A new chest CT was performed, which revealed retractile AFBD, with significant lung volume loss and bronchiectasis as well as a bulky RUL-cavitated lesion with mediastinal contact. 
Flexible bronchoscopy with bronchial wash and biopsies was repeated, with no microbiological isolation or characteristic histopathological findings. The diagnoses of progressive AFBD secondary to AS aggravated by TB sequelae were assumed. The patient was referred for physical and pulmonary rehabilitation, re-evaluation by a rheumatologist (after patients' consent and willingness) and evaluation by a thoracic surgeon. However, 9 months later (16 months after first admission), the patient worsened, and was admitted again at the Pulmonology Department, presenting a 1-month evolution worsening of productive cough, increased purulent sputum, hemoptysis, and weight loss. On physical examination, he had worsening muscle wasting, low oxygen saturation on pulse oximetry and bilateral crepitant rales. Blood tests revealed microcytic hypochromic anemia (Hb 9.2 g/dL), leukocytosis 18.100 with neutrophilia 93% and elevated CRP 18.7 mg/dL. He had worsened chest x-ray findings with a significant wider cavitation in the RUL and bilateral reticular infiltrates at the right lower lobe and LUL (Figure 2A). Empirical antibiotic therapy was initiated. Revaluation by chest CT revealed size increase of RUL cavitation, condensation with air bronchogram particularly at the ULs, mass-like lesion inside LUL cavitation, diffuse multifocal ground-glass opacities, sub-pleural micronodules, and tree-in-bud (Figure 2 B and C). Sputum microbiology was inconclusive. A new flexible bronchoscopy was performed and Aspergillus fumigatus (AF) was isolated in the bronchial wash with an elevated bronchial wash Galactomannan antigen test and elevated serum AF IgG levels. He initiated voriconazole for the treatment of CCPA. During hospitalization, he presented fast worsening of respiratory failure and severe acute hemoptysis with a sudden 3 g/dL drop of Hb and the evidence of a new chest x-ray finding of an air-fluid level at the RUL cavity (Figure 2D). Poor performance status conditioned by low BMI, sarcopenia and extent of pulmonary and extra-pulmonary disease determined unfitness for surgical intervention and other major invasive procedures. The patient worsened fast and died despite optimized medical treatment before arterial embolization could be attempted.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 47-year-old cachectic male ex-smoker with HLA-B27-positive ankylosing spondylitis and post-tuberculous apical fibrobullous lung disease presented with a 1-month worsening of productive purulent cough, hemoptysis, and weight loss.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Sixteen months earlier, the patient had presented with 3 months of dyspnea, mucopurulent cough, evening fevers/sweats, and weight loss, and was treated for cavitary right upper lobe Mycobacterium tuberculosis and endobronchial MRSA infection, leaving progressive ankylosing-spondylitis-associated apical fibrobullous disease (AFBD) with a large right upper lobe cavity at 7 months. Nine months after completing anti-TB therapy (16 months after first admission), he was readmitted with a 1-month exacerbation of purulent cough, hemoptysis, and weight loss, rapidly complicated in-hospital by acute massive hemoptysis and respiratory failure.
subjective.past_medical_history: HLA-B27-positive ankylosing spondylitis diagnosed at age 30 (grade IV bilateral sacroiliitis, lumbar ankylosis/syndesmophytes, restrictive ventilatory defect; treated with infliximab for ~2 years until 3 years prior to first pulmonary admission); cavitary right upper lobe pulmonary tuberculosis and MRSA bronchitis treated 16 months prior; 30 pack-year ex-smoker.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for chronic axial stiffness/pain, progressive purulent cough, hemoptysis (culminating in acute massive hemoptysis), dyspnea, and severe weight loss.

objective.physical_examination: Severe cachexia (BMI <18.5 kg/m2) with worsening muscle wasting, pronounced thoracic kyphosis, reduced chest wall expansion, hypoxemia on pulse oximetry, and bilateral upper-zone crepitant rales.
objective.routine_investigations: At initial TB admission (16 months prior): ESR 120 mm/h, CRP 23 mg/dL, hemoglobin 10.3 g/dL, albumin 3.1 g/dL, positive sputum Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex molecular assay, and bronchial biopsy isolating MRSA. On readmission at 16 months: microcytic hypochromic anemia with hemoglobin 9.2 g/dL (dropping acutely by 3 g/dL during in-hospital massive hemoptysis), leukocytosis (WBC 18,100/uL with 93% neutrophils), and elevated CRP (18.7 mg/dL). Serum Aspergillus fumigatus-specific IgG was elevated.
objective.advanced_workup: Readmission chest X-ray and chest CT demonstrated enlargement of the right upper lobe cavity (subsequently developing an acute air-fluid level during massive hemoptysis), a new intracavitary mass-like lesion (fungus ball) inside a left upper lobe cavity, upper lobe consolidations with air bronchograms, traction bronchiectasis, diffuse ground-glass opacities, subpleural micronodules, and tree-in-bud opacities. Repeat flexible bronchoscopy with bronchial wash isolated Aspergillus fumigatus and yielded an elevated bronchial wash galactomannan antigen.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Fatal chronic cavitary pulmonary aspergillosis (CCPA) caused by Aspergillus fumigatus complicating HLA-B27-positive ankylosing spondylitis apical fibrobullous disease and post-tuberculous bilateral upper lobe cavitation, confirmed by bilateral cavitary progression with a left upper lobe intracavitary fungus ball on chest CT, bronchial wash culture growing A. fumigatus, positive bronchial wash galactomannan, and elevated serum A. fumigatus IgG. Deemed unfit for thoracic surgery due to severe cachexia and poor cardiopulmonary reserve, he was started on voriconazole and optimized medical care, but suffered sudden massive intracavitary hemoptysis (3 g/dL hemoglobin drop with a new right upper lobe air-fluid level) and died of acute respiratory failure before bronchial artery embolization could be performed.

raw_case_text:
A 56 years-old diabetic patient was admitted in February 2021 in ICU for a severe COVID-19 which required immediate mechanical ventilation. The patient received 10 days dexamethasone associated with two doses of tocilizumab according to the local standard of care protocol. One week after ICU admission, COVID-associated pulmonary aspergillosis was diagnosed based on the growth of Aspergillus flavus in broncho-alveolar fluid (BAL) culture, positive galactomannan both in BAL (index: 5.9) and in serum (index: 1.9) and new pulmonary infiltrates (Figure 1A). Voriconazole was started. A month later, abnormal neurological examination after sedation interruption led to the discovery of two brain abscesses associated with ethmoidal sinusitis (Figure 1B). ENT surgery was performed revealing bilateral extensive necrosis of sinonasal mucosa, maxillary and ethmoidal bone. Pathological tissues were respectively removed and drilled until reaching healthy hemorrhagic tissue. A transethmoidal roof procedure allowed for the drainage of the most anterior abscess. Rhizopus & Mucor PCR was positive in blood as well as in most of per-operative sinus and cerebral samples (Figure 1C). Pathology showed aseptate, broad-angled hyphae in the skull bones. Liposomal amphotericin B (L-AmB) was added and voriconazole was switched for isavuconazole when the diagnosis of cerebral mucormycosis was confirmed. Unfortunately, additional debridement was not feasible due to the vicinity of cerebral vessels and brain parenchyma. After ten days of dual antifungal therapy, the patient's condition worsened as the size of the non-drained abscess increased. Of note, the neutrophils level varied between 4.5 and 12 G/L.
At this step we analyzed by flow cytometry circulating T cells. The total T cell count was normal (1624/mm3) but the CD4/CD8 ratio was below 1 (CD4 = 557/mm3). Major lymphocyte subsets were further characterized by their expression of activation/differentiation markers and immune checkpoint molecules. The CD8+ T cell count was increased (CD8 = 938/mm3), and 60% of CD8+ T cells co-expressed CD38 and HLA-DR, that are late activation markers. CD4+ T cell expressed also high levels of HLA-DR (33%). Furthermore both CD8+ and CD4+ T cells expressed high levels of programmed cell death-1 (PD-1, 56% and 70%), an immune checkpoint molecule that has been associated with T-cell exhaustion. We also measured Aspergillosis and SARS-CoV-2 specific memory T cells using IFN-gamma ELISpot assay. We detected SARS-CoV-2 but no Aspergillus specific T cells in peripheral blood.
Because of the poor prognosis and high percentage of PD-1-expressing circulating CD4 and CD8 T-cells, immunoadjuvant therapy with IFN-gamma and nivolumab was started. The patient received 100 mg of interferon-gamma SC 3 times a week during a month and 2 IV injections of nivolumab 240 mg (3 mg/kg) four weeks apart. After two weeks of this treatment, the percentage of circulating CD4+ and CD8+ T cells expressing PD-1 substantially decreased, percentage that remained steadily low afterward (Figure 1D). After 3 weeks of immunoadjuvant therapy, an increase in CD4 T cells activation (as shown by the rise of CD4 T cells percentage expressing HLA DR) and CD8 T cells proliferative capacity (as indicated by the 4-fold increase of Ki67 expression) were observed (Figure 1D). Still, no Aspergillus specific T cells could be detected using IFN-gamma ELISpot assay. Under combined immunoadjuvant and dual antifungal therapy, the cerebral abscesses decreased in size and serum galactomannan and Mucorales PCR turned negative (Figures 1B, C).
Unfortunately, after one month the patient developed septic shock following ventilation acquired pneumonia with oliguric renal failure and hepatic cytolysis. L-AmB and IFN gamma were stopped and the patient remained under isavuconazole only. Despite several antibiotics and a good monitoring of isavuconazole residual concentration (between 3.1 and 4.2 mg/L) the patient's condition deteriorated. The size and number of cerebral abscesses increased and the Mucorales PCR was found positive in the CSF. After multidisciplinary concertation, palliative care was started, and the patient died 17 weeks after his initial hospitalization.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 56-year-old diabetic patient mechanically ventilated for severe COVID-19 developed COVID-19-associated pulmonary aspergillosis 1 week after ICU admission, followed 1 month later by abnormal awakening neurological examination from sinonasal and cerebral mucormycosis.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Admitted to the ICU in February 2021 for mechanically ventilated severe COVID-19 pneumonia and treated with 10 days of dexamethasone and two doses of tocilizumab, the patient developed pulmonary Aspergillus flavus infection on ICU day 7 (treated with voriconazole). One month after ICU admission, failure to awaken properly upon sedation interruption led to the discovery of ethmoidal sinusitis and two bifrontal brain abscesses caused by invasive rhino-orbito-cerebral mucormycosis.
subjective.past_medical_history: Diabetes mellitus; severe COVID-19 pneumonia treated with dexamethasone (10 days) and tocilizumab (2 doses).
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for severe hypoxemic respiratory failure and subsequent persistent coma/abnormal neurological exam upon sedation weaning.

objective.physical_examination: Mechanically ventilated; abnormal neurological examination after sedation interruption at 1 month. Intraoperative ENT endoscopy revealed extensive bilateral necrosis of the sinonasal mucosa and maxillary and ethmoidal bones.
objective.routine_investigations: Neutrophil counts remained preserved between 4.5 and 12 G/L. Immune profiling at 1 month showed normal total T-cell count (1,624/mm3) with an inverted CD4/CD8 ratio <1 (CD4+ 557/mm3, CD8+ 938/mm3), marked T-cell activation (60% CD38+HLA-DR+ CD8+ T cells, 33% HLA-DR+ CD4+ T cells), and profound PD-1 exhaustion marker expression (56% of CD8+ and 70% of CD4+ T cells; reversing after nivolumab/IFN-gamma with a 4-fold rise in CD8+ Ki-67 proliferation), while IFN-gamma ELISpot detected SARS-CoV-2-specific T cells but zero Aspergillus-specific memory T cells.
objective.advanced_workup: At week 1, chest CT showed new pulmonary infiltrates, BAL culture grew Aspergillus flavus, and galactomannan was positive in both BAL (index 5.9) and serum (index 1.9). At 1 month, cranial MRI demonstrated ethmoidal sinusitis and two frontal brain abscesses. Skull-base bone histopathology from endoscopic transethmoidal debridement and anterior brain abscess drainage revealed broad, wide-angle aseptate hyphae, and Rhizopus/Mucor PCR was positive in peripheral blood, intraoperative sinus and cerebral samples, and later terminal CSF.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: COVID-19-associated pulmonary aspergillosis (Aspergillus flavus; confirmed by BAL culture and positive BAL [5.9] and serum [1.9] galactomannan) followed by fatal rhino-ethmoido-cerebral mucormycosis (confirmed by skull bone pathology showing broad aseptate hyphae and positive blood, sinus, brain, and CSF Rhizopus/Mucor PCR) in a diabetic patient treated with dexamethasone and tocilizumab. Treated with endoscopic sinonasal and transethmoidal anterior brain abscess drainage, switch from voriconazole to dual liposomal amphotericin B plus TDM-guided isavuconazole (troughs 3.1-4.2 mg/L), and salvage immunoadjuvant therapy with subcutaneous interferon-gamma (100 ug 3x/week for 1 month) plus IV nivolumab (240 mg q4w x 2 doses), which reversed T-cell PD-1 exhaustion, cleared serum galactomannan and blood Mucorales PCR, and shrank the brain abscesses; however, subsequent ventilator-associated pneumonia with septic shock, oliguric AKI, and hepatic cytolysis forced discontinuation of L-AmB and IFN-gamma, leading to CNS mucormycosis relapse and death at week 17.

raw_case_text:
A 23-year-old female initially presented with a 2-month history of severe frontal sinus headaches and upward gaze diplopia. She had no other significant medical issues and denied nasal symptoms. An outside magnetic resonance imaging scan of her brain was obtained that showed a left ethmoid mass measuring 2.4 x 2.3 x 2.5 cm extending into the left frontal sinus. A computed tomography sinus was then done in the office that revealed an expansile mass destroying the left lamina papyracea and fiberoptic laryngoscopy demonstrated a mass in the posterior nasopharynx adjacent to the left orbit and posterior to the left middle turbinate (Figure 1).
She was taken emergently to the operating room for functional endoscopic sinus surgery (ESS) under COVID restrictions and the frontal ethmoid mucocele was completely decompressed. A culture of the left frontal sinus was taken and did not show any fungal organisms. The patient then performed daily nasal saline irrigations and presented to postoperative appointments with mild orbital pain that decreased in intensity with each subsequent visit. Monthly nasal endoscopies consistently revealed an open, wide area at the site of the decompressed mucocele for three consecutive months. Three weeks later, she called the surgeon (N.L.S.) one Saturday night complaining of sudden onset, sharp pain that felt like she had a "knife in her left eye." She was treated conservatively over the weekend with nasal irrigations and a nasal corticosteroid spray. A video endoscopy in the office revealed a sharp object penetrating the left orbital tissue (Figure 2). Attempted removal under video endoscopy failed and was painful as the spicule was impacted into the periorbital tissue that was now unprotected because the bony lamina papyracea had been resorbed by pressure from the mucocele. The object was finally irrigated under general anesthesia in the operating room. Spicule fragments were cultured and sent to pathology. Both reports were consistent with Aspergillus fumigatus. The patient's "knife-like" pain was relieved after the procedure, but orbital pressure persisted until the fungal infection was brought under control.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 23-year-old female presented with a 2-month history of severe frontal sinus headaches and upward gaze diplopia, followed postoperatively by sudden-onset sharp knife-like left eye pain.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient initially developed severe frontal sinus headaches and upward gaze diplopia over 2 months without nasal symptoms. After emergent functional endoscopic sinus surgery (ESS) to decompress a left fronto-ethmoid mucocele, she performed daily nasal saline irrigations and experienced mild orbital pain that progressively improved over 3 consecutive monthly follow-up visits. Three weeks after her third monthly visit, she experienced sudden-onset sharp pain described as feeling like a knife in her left eye, which did not resolve with weekend conservative therapy using nasal saline irrigations and nasal corticosteroid spray.
subjective.past_medical_history: No significant prior medical issues; underwent functional endoscopic sinus surgery (ESS) for left fronto-ethmoid mucocele decompression.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for severe frontal sinus headache, upward gaze diplopia, and subsequent acute sharp left orbital pain; negative for nasal symptoms.

objective.physical_examination: Initial office fiberoptic laryngoscopy demonstrated a mass in the posterior nasopharynx adjacent to the left orbit and posterior to the left middle turbinate. Postoperative monthly nasal endoscopies for 3 months showed a wide, open decompressed mucocele cavity. Subsequent office video endoscopy during acute pain revealed a sharp spicule penetrating the unprotected left periorbital tissue where the bony lamina papyracea had been resorbed; attempted in-office removal was painful and unsuccessful.
objective.advanced_workup: Initial outside brain MRI showed a left ethmoid mass measuring 2.4 x 2.3 x 2.5 cm extending into the left frontal sinus. Office sinus CT revealed an expansile mass destroying the left lamina papyracea. Initial intraoperative left frontal sinus culture at ESS showed no fungal organisms. Following operating room irrigation and removal of the penetrating orbital spicule under general anesthesia, pathology and fungal culture of the spicule fragments were both positive for Aspergillus fumigatus.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Left fronto-ethmoid mucocele complicated by secondary orbital/sinonasal Aspergillus fumigatus infection with a fungal spicule penetrating the periorbital tissue through a resorbed lamina papyracea, confirmed by histopathology and fungal culture of extracted spicule fragments. Treated initially with emergent functional endoscopic sinus surgery, daily saline irrigations, and nasal corticosteroid spray, followed by operating room irrigation and spicule removal under general anesthesia and targeted antifungal therapy. Knife-like pain resolved immediately after surgical removal, and residual orbital pressure resolved once the Aspergillus fumigatus infection was controlled.

raw_case_text:
During our study, no cases of malignancy nor gastrointestinal perforation were observed. Only minor effects were observed on blood cell counts over time ( Figures 2A-C ). Alterations of blood lipid profile, resulting in the initiation of statin therapy, were not observed in any subject. Moreover, no elevation of liver enzymes was seen, and no cases of herpes zoster were found. Nevertheless, two patients were affected by serious side effects (Aspergillus fumigatus infection and Enterococcus faecalis bacteremia, respectively). The first patient was a previously healthy 69-year-old man with GCA verified by TAB in 2020. One year later, before the initiation of baricitinib, he performed a chest CT which showed three pulmonary nodules. The nodules prompted a PET-CT, showing uptake of radioactive glucose considered a possible sign of malignancy. In February 2022 (1 month after the start of baricitinib), the size of the nodules had increased and begun to cavitate. Cultures from broncho-alveolar lavage at bronchoscopy showed A. fumigatus. Baricitinib was continued, and isavuconazonium was initiated, in parallel to rapidly decreasing doses of prednisolone, which led to improvement in pulmonary CT. The second patient was a 78-year-old lady with diabetes and hypertension. She had been prescribed tofacitinib for 20 months without prior episodes of infection when she was admitted to the hospital with 1 day's duration of fevers and abdominal pain. CRP was increased (120 mg/ml) and abdominal CT showed dilated bile ducts. Enterococcus faecalis grew in blood cultures. The infection was successfully treated with piperacillin/tazobactam followed by amoxicillin/clavulanic acid. Tofacitinib was reintroduced to the patient as soon as she had ended the antibiotics.
Aside from the 15 patients described above, three individuals were excluded from the case series as they did not prevail on JAKi for 6 months or had poor adherence to therapy.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 69-year-old man on baricitinib and prednisolone for giant cell arteritis presented with enlarging, cavitating pulmonary nodules on follow-up imaging, and a 78-year-old woman on tofacitinib presented with a 1-day history of fever and abdominal pain.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: In a cohort of giant cell arteritis (GCA) patients treated with JAK inhibitors, two patients developed serious infections. The first patient, a 69-year-old man with temporal artery biopsy-verified GCA diagnosed in 2020, had three pulmonary nodules noted on chest CT 1 year later (prior to starting baricitinib) that showed FDG uptake on PET-CT suspicious for malignancy; in February 2022, 1 month after starting baricitinib, the pulmonary nodules enlarged and began to cavitate. The second patient, a 78-year-old woman treated with tofacitinib for 20 months without prior infections, presented to the hospital with 1 day of fevers and abdominal pain.
subjective.past_medical_history: Patient 1: Previously healthy 69-year-old man with temporal artery biopsy-verified giant cell arteritis (2020) treated with baricitinib and prednisolone. Patient 2: 78-year-old woman with diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and giant cell arteritis treated with tofacitinib for 20 months.
subjective.review_of_systems: Patient 2 reported fever and abdominal pain for 1 day; no cases of malignancy, gastrointestinal perforation, or herpes zoster were observed in the cohort.

objective.routine_investigations: In the overall study cohort, only minor effects on blood cell counts and no liver enzyme elevations or lipid alterations requiring statins were observed. In Patient 2, CRP was elevated at 120 mg/mL and blood cultures grew Enterococcus faecalis.
objective.advanced_workup: In Patient 1, baseline pre-baricitinib chest CT showed three pulmonary nodules with FDG uptake on PET-CT; repeat chest CT 1 month after starting baricitinib (February 2022) showed nodule enlargement and cavitation, and bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) culture obtained via bronchoscopy grew Aspergillus fumigatus. In Patient 2, abdominal CT demonstrated dilated bile ducts.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Patient 1 was diagnosed with pulmonary Aspergillus fumigatus infection (confirmed by bronchoalveolar lavage culture) complicating baricitinib and corticosteroid therapy for giant cell arteritis; baricitinib was continued while isavuconazonium was initiated alongside rapid prednisolone tapering, resulting in chest CT improvement. Patient 2 was diagnosed with Enterococcus faecalis bacteremia and biliary tract infection (confirmed by blood culture and abdominal CT), which resolved with piperacillin/tazobactam followed by amoxicillin/clavulanic acid, allowing safe reintroduction of tofacitinib.

raw_case_text:
A 30-year-old female farmer and nonsmoker with chief complaints of hemoptysis from time to time for 3 years with increased amount and frequency for the last 30 days was admitted to Manmohan Cardiothoracic Vascular and Transplant Center, Kathmandu, Nepal. At the time of admission, she complained of cough with associated hemoptysis and chest pain.
She was in her usual state of health 3 years back when she developed coughing up blood with a frequency of 1-2 episodes a month. With these symptoms, 7 months later, she visited a nearby medical center where she was diagnosed and treated for pneumonia. The symptoms persisted with occasional episodes of coughing up blood for which no medical intervention was sought. Around a year back from now, she noticed the presence of whitish pieces mixed with blood for 2 episodes while coughing up, which was associated with a sour/bitter taste in her mouth. With the persistence of her symptoms of coughing up blood, a few months later she visited a tuberculosis center near her village where a CT scan demonstrated lesion on her lungs, and she was diagnosed of having a hydatid cyst in her lungs. From there, she was referred to our center for further management.
She denied a history of fever, shortness of breath, night sweats, significant weight loss, contact with TB, history of travel, family history of malignancy, the use of immunosuppressive drugs, and similar illnesses in family members. There was no history of pre-existing pulmonary diseases, extrapulmonary symptoms, and known previous medical problems in the patient. Tracing her history, her home was near a jungle, and including hers, nearly all homes had domesticated dogs. She gave a history of prolonged exposure to domesticated dogs. She was a nonsmoker, nonalcoholic, and consumed a mixed diet.
In our center, her vital signs showed normality with a blood pressure of 118/70 mm Hg, a pulse rate of 80 beats/minute, a respiratory rate of 18 breaths/minute, an oxygen saturation of 97% in room air, and an axial body temperature of 98 degrees Fahrenheit. Routine laboratory examination showed no abnormality with hemoglobin of 12 g/dl and there was no eosinophilia on peripheral blood examination. Total and differential leukocyte counts were within normal limits. Serum electrolytes, liver function tests, renal function tests, and other systemic examinations were unremarkable. Sputum smears were negative for acid-fast bacilli. She was nonreactive for Hepatitis B and HIV antigens. Physical findings were confined to the chest with decreased breath sound on the right hemithorax. The laboratory parameters of our patient at the time of admission are tabulated in Table 1.
Her chest CT upon presentation showed well-defined nonenhancing cystic lesion in the anterior basal segment of the right lower lobe adjacent to a major fissure. Multiple air foci were seen within it. There was a segmental bronchus seen within the cyst with the possibility of communication with the cyst. It was causing segmental collapse with the upward pull of the right hemidiaphragm. No obvious pleural or chest wall communication was seen (Figures 1 (d) and (e)). There was no associated liver lesion on abdominal ultrasonography.
The surgery was performed via the right posterolateral thoracotomy from the 5th intercostal space. Intraoperatively, the cyst was approximately of size 7.5 * 5.5 cm in the superior segment of the right lower lobe. Four bronchial communications were identified. A cystectomy was done, and at least 4 cystobronchiole communications were noted which were individually closed with nonabsorbable sutures, and then capitonnage was also performed. The excised cyst was sent for histopathological examination. What was exceptional was the presence of a laminated membrane of the ectocyst along with fungal elements (Aspergillus) in the form of septate hyphae with acute angle branching in hematoxylin and eosin stain (H&E) (Figures 1 (a) and (b)). To further confirm this finding, Periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) staining was done which also showed acute angle branching with thin septa (Figure 1 (c)). This led us to the final diagnosis of coinfection by Echinococcus and Aspergillus. She has been on oral albendazole since the first postoperative day at a dose of 10-15 mg/kg/day in divided doses. Her stay after surgery was uneventful and she was discharged on 3 postoperative days. She had been on routine follow-up.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 30-year-old female farmer presented with a 3-year history of intermittent hemoptysis that increased in frequency and volume over the past 30 days, accompanied by cough and chest pain.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed episodic hemoptysis (1-2 times/month) 3 years prior to admission and was initially treated for pneumonia 7 months into her illness without resolution. About 1 year prior to admission, she expectorated whitish fragments mixed with blood on two occasions, associated with a sour/bitter taste. A few months later, a chest CT at a local tuberculosis center revealed a lung lesion diagnosed as a pulmonary hydatid cyst, and she was referred to our center after experiencing worsening hemoptysis over the preceding 30 days along with cough and chest pain.
subjective.past_medical_history: No prior medical conditions, pre-existing pulmonary disease, or immunosuppressive therapy. Nonsmoker and nonalcoholic; lived near a jungle in Nepal with prolonged exposure to domesticated dogs.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for cough, hemoptysis, expectoration of whitish cyst fragments, sour/bitter taste, and chest pain; negative for fever, dyspnea, night sweats, weight loss, or extrapulmonary symptoms.

objective.physical_examination: Vital signs were normal: blood pressure 118/70 mmHg, pulse 80 bpm, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, SpO2 97% on room air, and axillary temperature 98 F. Chest auscultation revealed decreased breath sounds over the right hemithorax; other systemic examinations were normal.
objective.routine_investigations: Routine blood tests were normal: hemoglobin 12 g/dL, normal total and differential leukocyte counts without peripheral eosinophilia, and normal serum electrolytes, liver function, and renal function tests. Sputum AFB smears, Hepatitis B antigen, and HIV tests were negative. Abdominal ultrasonography showed no liver lesions.
objective.advanced_workup: Chest CT demonstrated a well-defined, nonenhancing cystic lesion (approx. 7.5 x 5.5 cm intraoperatively) in the right lower lobe adjacent to the major fissure containing multiple internal air foci, communicating with a segmental bronchus, and causing segmental collapse with upward elevation of the right hemidiaphragm. Following right posterolateral thoracotomy, cystectomy, closure of 4 cystobronchial communications, and capitonnage, histopathological examination of the excised cyst (H&E and PAS staining) demonstrated the laminated ectocyst membrane of Echinococcus infiltrated by thin septate fungal hyphae with acute-angle branching characteristic of Aspergillus.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Right lower lobe pulmonary hydatid cyst (Echinococcus) coinfected with Aspergillus saprophytic colonization/infection, definitively confirmed by histopathology (H&E and PAS stains) of the resected cyst wall showing laminated hydatid ectocyst membrane alongside acute-angle branching septate Aspergillus hyphae. Treated with surgical cystectomy, suture closure of four bronchial fistulae, and capitonnage via right posterolateral thoracotomy, followed by oral albendazole (10-15 mg/kg/day in divided doses) initiated on postoperative day 1. The postoperative course was uneventful, and she was discharged on postoperative day 3 in good condition.

raw_case_text:
A 28-year-old Saudi male from the Southern province underwent uncomplicated conventional retinal detachment surgery, at the King Khaled Eye Specialist Hospital in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, in the form of cryopexy, subretinal fluid drainage and scleral buckle (grooved segmental # 505 sponge and circumferential # 240 band with # 270 sleeve) for a macula on retinal detachment in the left eye.
The patient had undergone renal transplant for chronic renal failure three years earlier. In addition, he had hypertension and normocytic normochromic anemia secondary to his renal condition and was otherwise stable on hemodialysis twice weekly.
Four years after the retinal detachment surgery, he presented with a six-month history of conjunctival injection and discharge from the left eye.
On examination, visual acuity in his left eye was 20/200 and intraocular pressure (IOP) was 14mmHg. The conjunctiva was severely hyperemic and an exposed buckle could be seen inferonasally (Fig. 1) with white discharge around it. The cornea was clear and the anterior chamber was deep and quiet. Dilated fundus examination showed a flat retina.
The infected scleral buckle was removed under local anesthesia; it was intact with visible discoloration (Fig. 2). Sub-conjunctival irrigation with 50 mg solution of Vancomycin, and sub-conjunctival injection of 25mg of Vancomycin were given. Microbiological studies revealed infection with methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) and silver staining of moderate Aspergillus flavus hyphae (Fig. 3).
The patient was treated postoperatively for 1 month with topical Vancomycin 50mg/ml, Bacitracin ointment and Predforet drops. Visual acuity improved gradually to 20/60 and the conjunctival appearance returned back to normal with flat retina on fundus examination. The patient was followed up for 2 years before being discharged from the hospital.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 28-year-old Saudi male presented with a 6-month history of conjunctival redness, white ocular discharge, and decreased vision in the left eye 4 years after scleral buckling surgery.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Four years after undergoing uncomplicated left eye retinal detachment repair (cryopexy, subretinal fluid drainage, and placement of a grooved segmental #505 silicone sponge and circumferential #240 band with #270 sleeve), the patient presented with 6 months of persistent left conjunctival injection and mucopurulent discharge.
subjective.past_medical_history: Left eye macula-on rhegmatogenous retinal detachment repaired 4 years prior; chronic renal failure status post renal transplantation 7 years prior (subsequently returned to twice-weekly maintenance hemodialysis); hypertension; normocytic normochromic anemia.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for left eye redness, white discharge, and blurred vision.

objective.physical_examination: Left eye visual acuity was 20/200 and intraocular pressure was 14 mmHg. Slit-lamp examination showed severe conjunctival hyperemia and an inferonasally extruded, discolored scleral buckle surrounded by white purulent discharge; the cornea was clear, the anterior chamber was deep and quiet, and dilated fundus exam showed a flat, attached retina.
objective.advanced_workup: Following surgical removal of the intact, discolored scleral buckle under local anesthesia, microbiological cultures and Gomori methenamine silver staining of the explanted buckle elements demonstrated co-infection with methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) and moderate Aspergillus flavus septate hyphae.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Extruded scleral buckle infection co-infected with methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) and Aspergillus flavus in a hemodialysis/post-renal-transplant patient, confirmed by microbiological culture and silver staining of the explanted scleral buckle. Treated with surgical removal of the scleral buckle, intraoperative subconjunctival vancomycin irrigation (50 mg) and injection (25 mg), and a 1-month postoperative course of topical vancomycin (50 mg/mL), bacitracin ointment, and prednisolone acetate drops, resulting in resolution of conjunctival inflammation, maintenance of a flat retina, and visual acuity improvement from 20/200 to 20/60 over 2 years of follow-up.

raw_case_text:
A 66-year-old male, smoker, with diffuse atheromatosis, presented with intracranial hypertension, gradually increasing in gravity. A left occipital tumor was biopsied, leading to the discovery of a cerebral grade III-IV glioma (WHO 2007 classification) near the left ventricular atrium, not operable because of its critical location close to functional areas. Radiotherapy was decided to deliver 60 Gy in the tumor volume associated with corticotherapy. The treatment was well tolerated. Temozolomide chemotherapy was secondarily planned.
