objective.physical_examination: At 20 months: severe cognitive impairment (MMSE 15/30, MoCA 9/30), dysarthria, bilateral limb cogwheel rigidity and hypermyotonia, diffuse deep tendon hyperreflexia, impaired finger-to-nose and heel-knee-shin tests secondary to intention/postural tremor, and unsteady tandem gait.
objective.routine_investigations: Autoimmune screening, tumor markers, paraneoplastic antibody panel (Amphiphysin, CV2, Ma2/Ta, Ri, Yo, Hu, titin, SOX1, recoverin, Zic4, GAD65, Tr/DNER), and serum/CSF infectious testing for HIV, Cryptococcus, syphilis, tuberculosis, bacteria, fungi, and viruses were all negative.
objective.advanced_workup: CSF 14-3-3 protein and skin/CSF real-time quaking-induced conversion (RT-QuIC) assays were negative; EEG at 22 months showed diffuse slow waves. Brain MRI (DWI and T2/FLAIR) demonstrated restricted diffusion ('cortical ribboning') in the bilateral frontal and parietal cortices as well as hyperintensities in the bilateral caudate, putamen, pulvinar, and dorsomedial thalami; 18F-FDG PET showed bilateral cortical and right basal ganglia hypometabolism. Direct sequencing of the PRNP gene from peripheral blood leukocytes identified a rare pathogenic heterozygous G114V missense mutation coupled with a 1-octapeptide repeat deletion (1-OPRD) (also detected in his asymptomatic 61-year-old mother and 10-year-old elder son).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis of genetic Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (gCJD) with a prolonged clinical course caused by a germline PRNP G114V mutation and 1-octapeptide repeat deletion (1-OPRD), confirmed by PRNP gene sequencing and classic cortical, striatal, and pulvinar DWI hyperintensities and FDG-PET hypometabolism after excluding autoimmune/paraneoplastic encephalitis and Cryptococcus, HIV, syphilitic, and tuberculous meningoencephalitis. An empirical course of pulsed IVIG yielded no improvement; the patient progressed to aphasia, gait disorder, and urinary/fecal incontinence by 30 months (MRC Prion Disease Rating Scale score 2/20 at 4 years) while remaining alive with preserved swallowing 4 years after symptom onset.

raw_case_text:
A fifty-year-old female patient presented to us 45 days after an uneventful manual small incision cataract surgery. The patient was from a farming background and otherwise she did not have any health issues and she was not a diabetic. She gave history of mild pain, redness, and blurred vision in the operated eye (left eye) for five days. On examination, visual acuity in the right eye was 6/6 and in the left eye hand movements were perceived close to face. On slit lamp examination, left eye had corneal epithelial edema and fluffy white cotton ball-like exudates in the anterior chamber and the intraocular lens was surrounded by the same exudates in the capsular bag (Figure 1). Intraocular pressure was normal. Ultrasound of the eye showed fine vitreous opacities of low reflectivity with flat retina (Figure 2).
Because of delayed onset and the type of exudates in the anterior chamber, fungal endophthalmitis was a strong suspicion. Pars plana vitrectomy with anterior chamber wash was done and intravitreal vancomycin, ceftazidime, and voriconazole were given. Direct microscopic examination of vitreous and anterior chamber fluid showed Gram-positive thin long beaded branching filaments and acid fast thin long filaments in modified acid fast staining (Kinyoun stain) (Figure 3). On blood agar dry, raised, chalky white colonies were seen after 2 days of incubation (Figure 4). The colonies were further identified as Nocardia asteroids based on colony morphology and biochemical reactions. The isolate was susceptible to amikacin, gentamicin, ciprofloxacin, ofloxacin, gatifloxacin, moxifloxacin, and co-trimoxazole.
Depending on the sensitivity report, intravitreal amikacin (200 mug/0.1 mL) was given. The dose of intravitreal amikacin was halved because it was a vitrectomised eye. Topical gatifloxacin and gentamicin eye drops were continued. Systemically, tablet co-trimoxazole was started and given for 6 weeks. Two weeks later, vision had improved to counting fingers at one meter. Anterior segment was quiet, mildly hazy vitreous and the macula was pale and cloudy looking with multiple intraretinal hemorrhages (Figure 5). Amikacin induced macular infarction was suspected. Fluorescein angiography showed multiple capillary nonperfusion areas (Figure 6). The OCT showed increased macular thickness (central foveal thickness 342 mum), hyperreflectivity of inner retinal layers corresponding to areas of retinal edema (Figure 7).
To treat this ischemia and inflammation induced macular edema, intravitreal steroids could not be used in the backdrop of endophthalmitis. Intravitreal Bevacizumab was used for its anti-inflammatory properties. The vision improved to counting fingers at 2 meters and the macular edema subsided (Figure 8). On OCT, the macular thickness had decreased but the differentiation of different retinal layers was not evident and foveal centre showed hyper dense and adherent RPE and retinal layers (Figure 9). After follow-up of more than three months now, the condition of the eye is stable.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 50-year-old female farmer presented 45 days after uneventful left cataract surgery with a 5-day history of mild left eye pain, redness, and blurred vision.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Forty-five days after undergoing an uneventful manual small-incision cataract surgery in the left eye, the patient developed mild ocular pain, redness, and decreased vision over 5 days.
subjective.past_medical_history: Uneventful left manual small-incision cataract surgery 45 days prior; farming background; non-diabetic with no other systemic comorbidities.

objective.physical_examination: Visual acuity was 6/6 in the right eye and hand movements close to the face in the left eye; intraocular pressure was normal. Slit-lamp examination of the left eye revealed corneal epithelial edema and fluffy white cotton-ball-like exudates in the anterior chamber and surrounding the intraocular lens within the capsular bag.
objective.routine_investigations: B-scan ocular ultrasound of the left eye showed fine low-reflectivity vitreous opacities with an attached flat retina.
objective.advanced_workup: Pars plana vitrectomy and anterior chamber washout were performed. Antibiotic susceptibility testing of the intraocular isolate showed susceptibility to amikacin, gentamicin, ciprofloxacin, ofloxacin, gatifloxacin, moxifloxacin, and co-trimoxazole. Two weeks after intravitreal amikacin, funduscopy showed a pale, cloudy macula with multiple intraretinal hemorrhages; fluorescein angiography demonstrated multiple areas of capillary nonperfusion; and macular OCT showed retinal edema with central foveal thickness of 342 um and inner retinal hyperreflectivity.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Delayed-onset postoperative endophthalmitis caused by Nocardia asteroides complicated by amikacin-induced macular infarction was confirmed: direct microscopy of vitreous and anterior chamber fluid demonstrated Gram-positive thin beaded branching filaments that were partially acid-fast on modified Kinyoun stain, and blood agar culture grew dry, raised, chalky-white colonies after 2 days identified as Nocardia asteroides. Following initial intravitreal vancomycin, ceftazidime, and voriconazole, she received half-dose intravitreal amikacin (200 ug/0.1 mL in a vitrectomized eye), topical gatifloxacin and gentamicin drops, and oral co-trimoxazole for 6 weeks. Amikacin-induced macular ischemia/edema was subsequently treated with intravitreal bevacizumab, resolving the macular edema and stabilizing visual acuity at counting fingers at 2 meters at >3-month follow-up.

raw_case_text: A 64 year old male with well-controlled diabetes mellitus and fibrocystic sarcoidosis on steroids presented to the department of Pulmonology, Manipal Hospitals, Bengaluru, India, in October 2013 with a one week history of discharging ulcer and skin rash, and one day history of seizures with altered sensorium. His medications included oxygen at 1l/min, insulin, aspirin, 15 mg prednisolone, pantoprazole and calcium. Clinical examination showed a 2x2.5 cm ulcer with clean base and serous discharge over the left thigh. Multiple 2 x 3 cm reddish non-pruritic papules were present over both lower limbs and abdomen (Fig. 1). Repeat computed tomography of the chest did not show any new consolidation or cavitation (Fig. 2), but confirmed stage IV sarcoidosis. CT-head showed multiple space occupying lesions (Fig. 3A); magnetic resonance imaging of the head revealed multiple enhancing intracranial ring lesions (Fig. 3B). Cerebrospinal fluid examination showed 400 polymorphs/mul, elevated protein (105 mg/dl) and depressed sugar values (45 mg/dl, corresponding blood glucose 145 mg/dl) with normal adenosine deaminase levels (3 U/l, normal <8 U/l). Biopsy from nodules showed necrosis with lympho-mononuclear dermal infiltration and Grocott's stain revealed filamentous branching structures. Discharge from the ulcer showed long thin filamentous forms suggesting Nocardia that was confirmed on modified acid-fast staining (Fig. 4A); cultures were confirmed to be Nocardia asteroides (Fig. 4B). The patient was treated with phenytoin, ceftriaxone, amikacin and oral trimethoprim-sulphamethaxazole. Insulin and oxygen were continued and prednisolone tapered. Neurological abnormalities normalized by one week. At 12 months follow up, the patient was well.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 64-year-old male with stage IV fibrocystic sarcoidosis on chronic prednisolone presented with a 1-week history of a discharging left thigh ulcer and skin rash, and a 1-day history of seizures and altered sensorium.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented in October 2013 with a 1-week history of a serous-discharging ulcer on the left thigh and a non-pruritic papular rash on the lower limbs and abdomen, followed 1 day prior to admission by new-onset seizures and altered mental status.
subjective.past_medical_history: Fibrocystic sarcoidosis (stage IV) on long-term oral prednisolone (15 mg/day) and home oxygen (1 L/min), and well-controlled diabetes mellitus on insulin.
subjective.review_of_systems: Home medications included oxygen (1 L/min), insulin, aspirin, prednisolone (15 mg/day), pantoprazole, and calcium.

objective.physical_examination: Altered sensorium. Cutaneous exam revealed a 2 x 2.5 cm ulcer with a clean base and serous discharge over the left thigh, along with multiple 2 x 3 cm reddish, non-pruritic papules over both lower limbs and the abdomen.
objective.routine_investigations: Blood glucose was 145 mg/dL.
objective.advanced_workup: Repeat chest CT confirmed stage IV fibrocystic sarcoidosis without new consolidation or cavitation. Head CT showed multiple space-occupying lesions, and brain MRI revealed multiple contrast-enhancing intracranial ring lesions. CSF analysis showed polymorphonuclear pleocytosis (400 polymorphs/uL), elevated protein (105 mg/dL), hypoglycorrhachia (glucose 45 mg/dL vs. blood glucose 145 mg/dL), and normal adenosine deaminase (3 U/L, reference <8 U/L). Skin nodule biopsy demonstrated necrosis with lymphomononuclear dermal infiltration and filamentous branching organisms on Grocott methenamine silver stain.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Disseminated (cutaneous and central nervous system) nocardiosis caused by Nocardia asteroides in a steroid-treated sarcoidosis patient was confirmed: smear of the left thigh ulcer discharge showed long, thin filamentous organisms positive on modified acid-fast stain, Grocott stain of skin nodule biopsy showed branching filaments, and cultures isolated Nocardia asteroides. Treatment with phenytoin, ceftriaxone, amikacin, and oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole alongside steroid tapering normalized his neurological status within 1 week, and he remained well at 12-month follow-up.

raw_case_text:
A 35-year-old-male patient presented with sudden loss of vision associated with periorbital swelling in both eyes (OU). He had systemic complaints of fever and pedal edema. The patient was already undergoing treatment for membranoproliferative glomerulnephritis, and for the previous seven months was taking oral prednisone (pg. mg/day) and Angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor. Ocular examination revealed visual acuity of light perception (LP) with inaccurate ray projection in OU.
Slit lamp biomicroscopic examination revealed 2+ cells in anterior chamber and pigments over the anterior lens surface in OU. Fundus examination revealed hazy media along with retinal detachment in the inferotemporal area in OU. Sub-retinal exudates, intraretinal hemorrhages along with dilated veins and narrowed arteries were visible. Intraocular pressure (IOP) was 16 mmHg in OU. The patient had blood pressure of 160/100 mmHg and bradycardia. Hence, the initial diagnosis was hypertension related exudative retinal detachment, although both atypical central serous chorioretinopathy and Vogt-Koyanagi Harada syndrome were also considered in differential diagnosis. After receiving a nephrologist's opinion, the patient was stabilized with an injection of hydrocortisone 200 mg OD, frusemide 40 mg OD, cefixime 200 mg BD along with amlodipine 5 mg OD as a hypertensive drug.
After two days, the patient developed generalized hypotony, a staggering gait, truncal ataxia, and buccal and proximal weakness with decreased plantar reflexes. After neurology consultation, a pontomedullary lesion or cytomegalovirus meningitis was considered as an initial cause. A cerebrospinal fluid tap was performed to rule out meningitis; the results were normal. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain [Figure 1a and b] showed multiple cystic-enhancing lesions over both cerebral hemispheres, suggestive of tuberculomas or neurocysticercosis.
The patient was started on anti-tubercular treatment (ATT) along with oral steroids. Four days after starting ATT, the patient had a generalized tonic-clonic seizure. A contrast MRI showed disseminated parenchymal lesions. At the beginning of anti-epileptic treatment, patient showed signs of improvement over the next two weeks; however after this period the patient started worsening. The patient had restricted abduction, sluggishly reacting pupils, 3+ cells in the anterior chamber OU with IOP of 66 and 52 mmHg in the right and left eyes, respectively. Fundus examination revealed increased exudates, increased height of retinal detachment and vitreous cells OU. A diagnosis of disseminated toxoplasma or malignancy was considered. Analysis of an aqueous tap via polymerase chain reaction (PCR) was negative for malignant cells, tuberculosis, cytomegalovirus (CMV), herpes simplex virus (HSV), varicella zoster virus (VZV), and toxoplasma.
An Ahmed glaucoma valve was implanted in the left eye subsequent to failure of IOP control with maximum medical therapy. Postoperatively, the left eye was stony hard with severe conjunctival chemosis and a shallow anterior chamber [Figure 2].
Due to suspicion of metastatic endophthalmitis, five weeks after initial presentation, a vitreous biopsy was performed through pars plana vitrectomy. Intravitreal vancomycin (1 mg/0.1 ml), ceftazidime (2.5 mg/0.1 ml), and voriconazole (1 mg/0.1 ml) were instilled at the end of the procedure and the patient was started on fortified cefazolin 5% and tobramycin 1.4% every hour and Natamycin 5% (every six hours) for presumptive fungal endophthalmitis. All tissue sample smears and cultures that were tested for bacterial and fungal organisms were negative.
Subsequently, the patient had no LP along with severe conjunctival chemosis, exposure keratopathy, and conjunctival abscesses. Cerebrospinal fluid was negative for CMV and Cryptococcus sp. Blood tests were negative for HIV and TORCH (Toxoplasma gondii, other viruses [HIV, measles, and so on), rubella [German measles]), CMV, and herpes simplex. Blood culture showed no evidence of bacterial and fungal organism growth. A bone marrow biopsy was performed to rule out blood cell malignancy but results were normal.
Due to the progressive worsening of patients' systemic status and severe cachexia, a repeat MRI of the brain was done, and revealed a large right parieto-occipital mass lesion [Figure 1c and d]. The orbital region showed bilateral globe deformities, intraocular hemorrhages, and extraocular soft-tissue inflammation [Figure 1e and f].
A multiloculated intracerebral abscess was drained, and a brain biopsy was performed, revealing the presence of the Nocardia organism along with granulomatous reactions [Figure 3a-d]. The patient was administered intravenous imipenem for two weeks, amikacin for four weeks, and later, oral cotrimoxazole and trimethoprim. However, the patient had no LP in both eyes despite anti-nocardial treatment, probably because of delayed diagnosis and severity of involvement. Although the patient improved systemically over next two weeks, he subsequently developed phthisis of both eyes.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 35-year-old male on chronic prednisone for membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis presented with sudden bilateral vision loss, bilateral periorbital swelling, fever, and pedal edema.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with sudden bilateral visual loss down to light perception, periorbital swelling, fever, and pedal edema. Two days after admission, he developed generalized hypotonia, staggering gait, truncal ataxia, and buccal and proximal limb weakness, followed 4 days after starting empirical anti-tubercular therapy by a generalized tonic-clonic seizure, refractory bilateral secondary glaucoma, conjunctival abscesses, and progressive cachexia.
subjective.past_medical_history: Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis treated for the preceding 7 months with oral prednisone and an ACE inhibitor.
subjective.review_of_systems: Home medications: oral prednisone and an ACE inhibitor.

objective.physical_examination: Admission BP 160/100 mmHg with bradycardia and pedal edema. Ocular exam showed bilateral visual acuity of light perception with inaccurate projection, IOP 16 mmHg OU (later rising to 66 mmHg OD and 52 mmHg OS), 2+ anterior chamber cells (progressing to 3+ cells, restricted abduction, sluggish pupils, severe chemosis, exposure keratopathy, and conjunctival abscesses), lens pigment, hazy media, bilateral inferotemporal exudative retinal detachments, subretinal exudates, intraretinal hemorrhages, dilated veins, and narrowed arteries. Neurological exam on day 2 showed generalized hypotonia, staggering gait, truncal ataxia, buccal and proximal muscle weakness, and decreased plantar reflexes.
objective.routine_investigations: HIV, TORCH panel (Toxoplasma, rubella, CMV, HSV), and blood cultures were all negative.
objective.advanced_workup: CSF analysis was normal and negative for CMV and Cryptococcus sp.; bone marrow biopsy was normal. Initial brain MRI showed multiple bilateral cerebral cystic-enhancing lesions; repeat brain and orbital MRI at 5+ weeks revealed a large right parieto-occipital multiloculated abscess plus bilateral globe deformities, intraocular hemorrhages, and extraocular soft-tissue inflammation. Aqueous tap PCR (negative for malignancy, TB, CMV, HSV, VZV, Toxoplasma) and week-5 pars plana vitrectomy biopsy smears and bacterial/fungal cultures were negative. Craniotomy with drainage and biopsy of the multiloculated right parieto-occipital brain abscess was performed.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Disseminated cerebral and bilateral ocular (metastatic endophthalmitis) nocardiosis in a corticosteroid-treated glomerulonephritis patient was confirmed via brain abscess drainage and biopsy demonstrating filamentous Nocardia organisms within granulomatous inflammation. Prior empirical therapies (hydrocortisone, furosemide, cefixime, amlodipine, anti-tubercular therapy, antiepileptics, left Ahmed glaucoma valve implantation, and intravitreal vancomycin/ceftazidime/voriconazole plus topical cefazolin/tobramycin/natamycin) had failed to halt progression. Targeted therapy with IV imipenem for 2 weeks, IV amikacin for 4 weeks, and subsequent oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole led to systemic and neurological recovery over 2 weeks, though both eyes progressed to phthisis bulbi with no light perception.

raw_case_text:
A 63-year-old white woman diagnosed with diabetes mellitus underwent right lung transplant for bronchiolitis obliterans syndrome (BOS) three years after an original left single lung transplant for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. Induction immunotherapy prior to re-transplantation consisted of antithymocyte globulin (ATG) and methylprednisolone. She had also received a course of ATG for management of BOS in her initial left lung transplant. Current maintenance immunosuppression included mycophenolate mofetil, tacrolimus, and prednisone, in addition to post-transplant antimicrobial prophylaxis with TMP-SMZ, valganciclovir, and itraconazole. She had multiple episodes of Epstein-Barr viremia within the first six months after transplant. She also experienced multiple infectious complications, including pseudomonas pneumonia, enterococcal tracheobronchitis, and most recently invasive right lower lobe pulmonary aspergillosis treated with isavuconazonium sulfate two and a half years after her redo lung transplant.
She presented to the emergency department three years after her redo lung transplant experiencing fluctuating, insidious-onset right lower abdominal pain. Her symptoms had been present for ten days and were associated with nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. Four weeks earlier, she had been prescribed oral antibiotics for a lower urinary tract infection. Upon presentation, the patient was afebrile with sinus tachycardia (heart rate: 114 beats per minute) and otherwise normal vital signs. Her chest and abdominal examinations were unremarkable. Her laboratory data were significant for mild neutrophilic leukocytosis of 14.6 x 106/microL, stable microcytic hypochromic anemia of 10.4 g/dl, and stable hyponatremia of 131 mmol/L. Urinalysis showed hazy urine with few squamous cells, >50 WBC, 3-10 RBCs, 30 mg/dl protein, moderate leukocyte esterase, and 11-25 hyaline casts/LPF.
An abdominal ultrasound revealed a 3.3 x 2.8 x 3.1 cm complex, solid-appearing mass within the mid-pole of the right kidney with peripheral vascularity. This mass was not seen on an abdominal computed tomogram (CT) performed four weeks earlier. A CT with contrast confirmed the 4.5 x 3.3 cm heterogeneous, enhancing soft tissue right renal mass with patent renal vein and no retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy (Figure 1). These imaging findings raised suspicion for renal cell carcinoma (RCC) and prompted magnetic resonance imaging of the abdomen. This showed a T1/T2 hypointense, diffusion-restricting, right mid-renal mass very suspicious for RCC. The patient subsequently underwent a staging positron emission tomography-CT that showed an intensely fluorodeoxyglucose-avid right renal mass (standard uptake value = 14.3) (Figure 2).
The patient was then evaluated by urology and oncology and underwent a hand-assisted right nephrectomy for a presumptive pre-operative diagnosis of RCC. Histopathology revealed a blue-green necrotic renal mass measuring 5.5 x 5 x 4 cm, located in the superior lateral pole, and compressing the superior calyx without pelvicalyceal involvement. There was no evidence of malignancy, but multiple filamentous bacteria consistent with the Nocardia species were identified. Methenamine silver stain showed filamentous bacteria-like structures staining positive on gram stain which were weakly positive on the Fite staining method, supporting a diagnosis of Nocardia renal abscess (Figure 3). CTs of the head and chest revealed no lesions suspicious for nocardiosis. Because the suspicion of RCC was extremely high based on imaging, the entire renal specimen was sent for pathological analysis as a fixed specimen but not for culture. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) for Nocardia species on this nephrectomy specimen revealed N. paucivorans. She was subsequently started on dual therapy with imipenem and double strength TMP-SMZ. Imipenem was continued for 8 weeks, and TMP-SMZ was to be continued for 9 to 12 months thereafter.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 63-year-old white female bilateral sequential lung transplant recipient presented 3 years after her redo right lung transplant with a 10-day history of insidious, fluctuating right lower quadrant abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Ten days prior to presentation, the patient developed fluctuating right lower abdominal pain accompanied by nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. Four weeks earlier, she had been treated with oral antibiotics for a lower urinary tract infection and had a normal abdominal CT at that time.
subjective.past_medical_history: Diabetes mellitus; initial left single-lung transplant for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis complicated by bronchiolitis obliterans syndrome (treated with ATG), followed 3 years later (3 years prior to current presentation) by a redo right single-lung transplant with ATG and methylprednisolone induction, maintained on mycophenolate mofetil, tacrolimus, and prednisone alongside prophylactic TMP-SMZ, valganciclovir, and itraconazole. Post-transplant history included recurrent EBV viremia, Pseudomonas pneumonia, enterococcal tracheobronchitis, and invasive right lower lobe pulmonary aspergillosis treated with isavuconazonium sulfate 6 months prior.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea; afebrile. Home medications included mycophenolate mofetil, tacrolimus, prednisone, prophylactic TMP-SMZ, valganciclovir, and itraconazole.

objective.physical_examination: Afebrile with sinus tachycardia (heart rate 114 bpm) and otherwise normal vital signs; chest and abdominal examinations were unremarkable.
objective.routine_investigations: Labs showed mild neutrophilic leukocytosis (WBC 14.6 x 10^3/uL), stable microcytic hypochromic anemia (Hb 10.4 g/dL), and stable hyponatremia (131 mmol/L). Urinalysis showed hazy urine with few squamous cells, >50 WBC/HPF, 3-10 RBCs/HPF, 30 mg/dL protein, moderate leukocyte esterase, and 11-25 hyaline casts/LPF. Abdominal ultrasound revealed a new 3.3 x 2.8 x 3.1 cm complex solid-appearing mass in the mid-pole of the right kidney with peripheral vascularity.
objective.advanced_workup: Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT confirmed a 4.5 x 3.3 cm heterogeneous enhancing right renal soft-tissue mass with a patent renal vein and no retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy. Abdominal MRI showed a T1/T2-hypointense, diffusion-restricting right mid-renal mass, and staging 18F-FDG PET-CT demonstrated intense FDG avidity (SUV 14.3) suspicious for renal cell carcinoma. Head and chest CT scans showed no lesions suspicious for nocardiosis. Hand-assisted right radical nephrectomy was performed; gross and histopathological examination revealed a 5.5 x 5 x 4 cm blue-green necrotic abscess in the superior lateral pole without malignancy, containing Gram-positive, methenamine silver-positive, weakly Fite-positive filamentous branching bacteria.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Primary isolated right renal nocardiosis abscess caused by Nocardia paucivorans (masquerading radiologically as FDG-avid renal cell carcinoma despite TMP-SMZ prophylaxis) in a redo lung transplant recipient was confirmed via histopathology (Gram, methenamine silver, and Fite stains) and Nocardia species-specific PCR on the fixed nephrectomy specimen identifying Nocardia paucivorans. Following hand-assisted right nephrectomy, she was treated with intravenous imipenem for 8 weeks combined with oral double-strength trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMZ) planned for 9-12 months.

raw_case_text:
The index case was a 53-year old woman with acute renal failure, who had elevated serum creatinine of 380.7mumol/L (reference 44.2-132.6mumol/L), positive ANCA against myeoperoxidase and biopsy-confirmed type III crescentic glomerulonephritis. Besides four sessions of plasmapheresis, she was treated for ANCA-associated renal vasculitis with daily intravenous mythelprednisolone of 320mg for three consecutive days and 40mg thereafter. Free of pulmonary infection (PI) (Figure 1), the patient was discharged one month later with a daily oral dose of 40mg mythelprednisolone.
Readmission occurred seven days post hoc due to fever (38.6 C) and hemoptysis. CT scan on admission (Day 1) found PI with cavitation. Laboratory tests showed WBC count 20.3x109/L with 96.9% neutrophils, T-lymphocyte count 102/uL (690-1760/uL), hemoglobin 110g/L (130-150g/L), platelet 170x109/L (100-300x109/L), C-reaction protein 185.2mg/L (<10mg/L), calcitonin 1.6ng/mL (<0.05ng/mL), (1,3)-beta glucan D detection test (G-test) 67.8pg/mL (<10pg/mL), serum creatinine 300.0umol/L, normal coagulation function including D-dimer and negative ANCA. Aerobic sputum but not blood cultures produced aeruginosa. She was immediately given intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics with dose and form respectively determined by creatinine clearance and CT findings (Figure 1): meropenem and voriconazole (Day 1 to 8), piperacillin sodium/tazobactam sodium and voriconazole with double-dose (Day 9 to 14), cefoperazone/sulbactam and micafungi (Day 15 to 19). The use of steroid was continued but reduced to half-dose two days after admission. Meanwhile, recurrent hypernatremia emerged (150-170mmol/L) which was only remedial to blood purification. There was sudden aphasia and right hemiparesis, prompting the collection of blood and sputum from deep trachea for specific microbial tests by our pharmacological center, which is a reliable and sophisticated research institution. In short notice thereafter, brain abscess was detected by MRI (Figure 2). The patient's condition further worsened and her vitals were no longer sustainable (Day 20). After that, growth of Nocardia asteroids from the said sputum was found on the Loewenstein-Jensen media and subsequently confirmed by the 16S rDNA sequence analysis.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 53-year-old woman with MPO-ANCA-associated crescentic glomerulonephritis on high-dose methylprednisolone presented 7 days after hospital discharge with acute fever (38.6 C) and hemoptysis.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: One month after starting intensive immunosuppression (four sessions of plasmapheresis, IV methylprednisolone 320 mg/day for 3 days then 40 mg/day) for biopsy-proven type III crescentic glomerulonephritis and 7 days after being discharged on oral methylprednisolone 40 mg/day, the patient was readmitted with fever (38.6 C) and hemoptysis. During hospitalization, she developed refractory hypernatremia (150-170 mmol/L) and acute-onset aphasia and right hemiparesis.
subjective.past_medical_history: MPO-ANCA-positive type III crescentic glomerulonephritis with acute renal failure (baseline creatinine 380.7 umol/L, reference 44.2-132.6 umol/L) diagnosed 5 weeks prior and treated with plasmapheresis and high-dose methylprednisolone.
subjective.review_of_systems: Home medication: oral methylprednisolone 40 mg daily.

objective.physical_examination: Febrile at 38.6 C on admission; subsequently developed sudden-onset aphasia and right hemiparesis prior to hemodynamic collapse on hospital day 20.
objective.routine_investigations: Readmission labs (day 1) showed leukocytosis with WBC 20.3 x 10^9/L (96.9% neutrophils), hemoglobin 110 g/L (reference: 130-150 g/L), platelets 170 x 10^9/L (reference: 100-300 x 10^9/L), CRP 185.2 mg/L (reference: <10 mg/L), procalcitonin 1.6 ng/mL (reference: <0.05 ng/mL), serum creatinine 300.0 umol/L, normal coagulation/D-dimer, and negative ANCA; serum (1,3)-beta-D-glucan (G-test) was elevated at 67.8 pg/mL (reference: <10 pg/mL). Aerobic sputum culture initially grew Pseudomonas aeruginosa; blood cultures were negative.
objective.advanced_workup: T-lymphocyte count was severely depressed at 102/uL (reference: 690-1,760/uL). Day-1 chest CT demonstrated cavitary pulmonary infection. Following acute onset of aphasia and right hemiparesis, brain MRI revealed a cerebral abscess.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Disseminated (cavitary pulmonary and cerebral abscess) nocardiosis caused by Nocardia asteroides (with concomitant Pseudomonas aeruginosa respiratory infection) in a steroid-treated ANCA-vasculitis patient was confirmed post-mortem when deep tracheal sputum cultured on Lowenstein-Jensen media grew Nocardia asteroides, verified by 16S rDNA sequencing. During hospitalization, she had received sequential empirical regimens adjusted for renal function—meropenem plus voriconazole (days 1-8), piperacillin-tazobactam plus double-dose voriconazole (days 9-14), and cefoperazone-sulbactam plus micafungin (days 15-19)—alongside 50% steroid dose reduction and continuous blood purification for severe hypernatremia, but died on hospital day 20 before Nocardia culture confirmation.

raw_case_text:
A 40-year-old male presented to the outpatient clinic of the tertiary care hospital with complaints of cough, expectoration, hemoptysis, and fever off and on particularly in the evenings. He had been treated for pulmonary tuberculosis previously in the year 2009 and subsequently in the year 2012 following its remission. He was on oral and inhalational steroids for several years for wheeze-like symptoms. He had sought consultation and had been admitted in other hospitals several times for similar complaints. The patient did not have any other comorbid conditions. He was a welder by occupation and so exposure to fumes and fine metallic dust particles was noted as a significant factor in the clinical history. Physical examination of the respiratory system revealed bilateral coarse crepitations. Examination of other systems did not reveal any contributory findings. Chest radiograph and routine blood workup were undertaken. Chest X-ray revealed bilateral midzone and lower zone consolidation (Figure 1). With a diagnosis of bilateral bronchiectasis, he was admitted to the hospital for further evaluation and to investigate the status of pulmonary tuberculosis in the light of hemoptysis.
The patient was initially started on intravenous piperacillin/tazobactam for empiric treatment of community-acquired secondary pulmonary infection. Despite the antibiotic, the patient had sustained decrease in oxygen saturation leading to deterioration in pulmonary function over the next few days. With impending respiratory failure, he was shifted to the Intensive Care Unit (ICU). The antibiotic was escalated to meropenem due to his deteriorating clinical condition. Blood and urine cultures were sterile, and 20% acid-fast staining of sputum and respiratory secretion was also negative. Sputum was sent for bacterial culture. The culture plates initially had scanty growth of normal flora, but on Gram stain there were few branching Gram-positive bacilli observed which was suggestive of Nocardia (Figure 2). In view of this, modified acid-fast staining with 1% acid was performed on the smear, and it revealed plenty of weakly acid-fast branching slender and filamentous bacilli characteristic of Nocardia (Figure 3). The culture media on further incubation of 72 hours yielded dry chalky white colonies (Figure 4). Gram's stain and acid-fast stain of these colonies confirmed them as Nocardia. For species identification, 16S rRNA gene sequencing was undertaken. BLAST search of the sequence was done using the taxonomy browser of the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI). The 662 bp of the sequence revealed a 100% match with Nocardia cyriacigeorgica. The sequence has been submitted to GenBank with accession number MK641487.
 Nocardia cyriacigeorgica belongs to Nocardia asteroides complex (vi). This species was first described in 2001, and strains of N. cyriacigeorgica have since been recovered as the etiologic agent of human infection in Western Europe, Greece, Turkey, Japan, Thailand, and Canada. Most cases of infection have occurred in the context of HIV-related or iatrogenic immune suppression. Pulmonary nocardiosis caused by Nocardia cyriacigeorgica in patients with Mycobacterium avium complex lung disease has been described before. It has also been identified as the causative agent of an anterior mediastinal abscess in a patient with preexisting lung disease and the aetiological agent of native valve endocarditis in a patient with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).
In addition to sulfonamide susceptibility, they are generally susceptible to broad-spectrum cephalosporins, amikacin, imipenem, and linezolid but resistant to penicillin, clarithromycin, and ciprofloxacin. It has been reported in the literature that serious life-threatening infections caused by Nocardia cyriacigeorgica are controlled well with dual therapy. In view of the species identification, the patient was started on injection imipenem and oral trimethoprim sulphamethoxazole. The patient began to improve clinically with this therapy. Oxygen saturation levels improved, fever declined, and the patient was shifted out of the Intensive Care Unit. Subsequently, with sustained improvement, he was discharged from the hospital in good health with the advice to continue oral cotrimoxazole for six months. The patient continues to remain relapse free.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 40-year-old male welder presented with intermittent evening fever, productive cough, and hemoptysis.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented to the tertiary outpatient clinic with recurrent cough, expectoration, hemoptysis, and intermittent evening fevers that had required multiple prior hospitalizations. After admission and empirical IV piperacillin/tazobactam, his oxygen saturation progressively declined, requiring ICU transfer for impending respiratory failure.
subjective.past_medical_history: History of pulmonary tuberculosis treated in 2009 and retreated in 2012; chronic wheezing treated for several years with oral and inhaled corticosteroids; welder by occupation with chronic exposure to welding fumes and fine metallic dust particles; no other comorbidities.
subjective.review_of_systems: Home medications included long-term oral and inhalational corticosteroids.

objective.physical_examination: Respiratory examination revealed bilateral coarse crepitations; examination of other organ systems was unremarkable.
objective.routine_investigations: Chest radiograph demonstrated bilateral mid-zone and lower-zone consolidation with bronchiectasis. Blood and urine cultures were sterile, and standard 20% acid-fast staining of sputum and respiratory secretions was negative for Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
objective.advanced_workup: Sputum Gram stain revealed branching Gram-positive bacilli, modified acid-fast stain (1% acid) showed abundant weakly acid-fast slender branching filamentous bacilli, and 72-hour culture grew dry, chalky-white colonies.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Pulmonary nocardiosis caused by Nocardia cyriacigeorgica superimposed on post-tubercular bilateral bronchiectasis in a chronic steroid user was confirmed via modified acid-fast staining, sputum culture, and 16S rRNA gene sequencing (662 bp showing 100% identity to Nocardia cyriacigeorgica; GenBank MK641487). Following clinical deterioration on empirical piperacillin/tazobactam and escalation to meropenem in the ICU, initiation of targeted dual therapy with intravenous imipenem and oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole resolved his fever and hypoxemia, allowing ICU transfer and discharge on a 6-month course of oral cotrimoxazole without relapse.

raw_case_text:
In October 2016, a 40-year-old woman was admitted to another hospital for a diagnosis of BC. One month prior to admission, a routinary mammography had shown the presence of a mass of 15 mm in diameter confirmed by a subsequent MRI scan. She was treated with right quadrantectomy and axillary dissection, and the histopathology provided a diagnosis of grade III invasive poorly differentiated ductal carcinoma. Immunohistochemistry was positive for estrogen and progesterone receptors (75%), with a high Ki67 proliferation index (30%) and mild expression of HER-2 (+1). However, fluorescent in situ hybridization for the HER2 gene was negative (staging pT1N2M0). In November, she started adjuvant chemotherapy regimen with doxorubicin 60 mg/m2/day and cyclophosphamide 600 mg/m2/day for 4 cycles, followed by maintenance with paclitaxel 80 mg/m2 since April 2017 and endocrine therapy with tamoxifen. Peripheral blood cell count at the start of chemotherapy showed leukopenia (white blood cells count 1.0 x 109/L), not further investigated, with mild anemia (hemoglobin 11.6 g/dl) and normal platelets count (168 x 109/L). In June 2017, during breast adjuvant radiotherapy, the patient was persistently pancytopenic (hemoglobin 9.6 g/dl, white blood cells 0.9 x 109/L, and platelets 101 x 109/L). Bone marrow was cellular (+3) and showed 82% of CD34/CD117/CD13+ and CD33/CD7/CD11b/CD14/cMPO blasts of small-medium size, round nucleus, and basophilic cytoplasm with rare granules, consistent with a diagnosis of AML. Cytogenetic analysis showed a normal karyotype (46, XX), and the gene mutation status was wild type for FLT3/ITD and TKD, AML1/ETO, Cbf/MYH11, NPM1, PML-RARalpha, BCR-ABL1, and MLL. The patient was treated with ICE induction chemotherapy, consisting of a combination of idarubicin 10 mg/m2 days 1, 3, and 5, cytarabine 100 mg/m2 days 1-7, and etoposide 100 mg/m2 days 1-5, but proved refractory. In September 2017, the patient was referred to our centre and underwent a salvage chemotherapy with the G-CLAC schedule: clofarabine 30 mg/m2 days 1-5, cytarabine 2000 mg/m2 days 1-5, and granulocyte colony stimulating factor (G-CSF) until hemopoietic recovery. On day +13 from chemotherapy, the patient was pancytopenic (hemoglobin 8.5 g/dl, white blood cells 0.750 x 109/L, neutrophils 0.2 x 109/L, and platelets 20 x 109/L) and presented a septic shock, associated with acute abdominal pain with positive Murphy sign and positive blood cultures for Escherichia coli, Staphylococcus haemolyticus, and Candida glabrata. She received antibiotic and antifungal treatment (meropenem, tigecycline, and caspofungin) and supportive care with fluids and inotropic agents. An abdominal ultrasound and an MRI allowed to make a diagnosis of acute cholecistytis and in October 2017 (on day +30 from chemotherapy), after a full hematologic recovery, she underwent a laparoscopic cholecystectomy. The microbiologic examination of pericholecistic liquid revealed a multidrug-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa. In the same period, she became a KPC-Klebsiella pneumoniae rectal carrier. On day +35, the bone marrow aspiration showed a complete remission (CR). For this reason, in November 2017, on day +56 from chemotherapy, she underwent an allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) from the haploidentical brother after a preparative regimen with TBF (thiotepa 5 mg/kg days -7, -6; fludarabine 50 mg/m2 days -5, -4, -3; busulfan 3.2 mg/kg days -5, -4, -3). No major toxicity was observed during the aplastic phase, and the engraftment was obtained on day +17 for PMN and on day +25 for platelets. On day +20, the bone marrow aspirate confirmed a CR with complete donor chimerism, and on day +30, the patient was discharged.
Two months after discharge, she was readmitted to the hospital due to an acute left chest pain, fever, and neutropenia (hemoglobin 8.9 g/dl, white blood cells 0.62 x 109/L, neutrophils 0.34 x 109/L, and platelets 21 x 109/L); chest computed tomographic scan showed a basal bilateral pneumonia associated with diffuse pulmonary nodules and bronchial obliteration. A microbiological examination of bronchoalveolar lavage proved the presence of a Nocardia spp. Despite targeted antibiotic therapy with high-dose sulfametoxazole-trimethoprim in association with broad-spectrum and specific antibiotics in different timing (amikacin, ceftadizime-avibactam, levoxacin, ceftolozane-tazobactam, tigecycline, imipenem, and linezolid), pulmonary nocardial lesions persisted (and progressed toward) with the formation of a pulmonary organized abscess (Figure 1). Due to the persistence of fever and worsening of clinical conditions, the patient was submitted to a lower pulmonary lobectomy by left lateral thoracotomy; histological examination confirmed the presence of a Nocardia spp. She had a good postoperative course with disappearance of fever and complete resolution of the pneumonia.
Currently, the patient is alive in continuous CR for AML and BC, with a follow-up from diagnosis of 29 months and 37 months, respectively. She is in good general conditions with an excellent quality of life.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 40-year-old female haploidentical hematopoietic stem cell transplant recipient for therapy-related acute myeloid leukemia presented 2 months post-transplant with acute left chest pain and fever.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Two months after undergoing a haploidentical allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplant (HSCT) in complete remission from therapy-related acute myeloid leukemia (AML), the patient was readmitted with acute left-sided chest pain, fever, and severe pancytopenia.
subjective.past_medical_history: Grade III ER/PR-positive, HER2-negative invasive ductal breast carcinoma (pT1N2M0) diagnosed in October 2016 and treated with right quadrantectomy/axillary dissection, 4 cycles of doxorubicin/cyclophosphamide, paclitaxel, tamoxifen, and radiotherapy; therapy-related AML diagnosed in June 2017 (refractory to ICE induction, achieved complete remission after salvage G-CLAC chemotherapy complicated by polymicrobial septic shock, acute cholecystitis requiring laparoscopic cholecystectomy, and KPC-Klebsiella pneumoniae rectal colonization), followed in November 2017 by haploidentical allogeneic HSCT conditioned with thiotepa, fludarabine, and busulfan (TBF).

objective.physical_examination: Febrile with acute left-sided chest pain.
objective.routine_investigations: Readmission CBC showed severe pancytopenia: hemoglobin 8.9 g/dL, WBC 0.62 x 10^9/L, absolute neutrophils 0.34 x 10^9/L, and platelets 21 x 10^9/L.
objective.advanced_workup: Chest CT demonstrated bilateral basal pneumonia with diffuse pulmonary nodules and bronchial obliteration, which subsequently progressed despite medical therapy into an organized left lower lobe pulmonary abscess. Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) and subsequent left lower pulmonary lobectomy via left lateral thoracotomy were performed.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Refractory pulmonary nocardiosis with organized lung abscess formation caused by Nocardia spp. in a haploidentical allogeneic HSCT recipient was confirmed via bronchoalveolar lavage microbiology and histopathological examination of the resected left lower pulmonary lobe. Because the organized lung abscess and fever progressed despite high-dose trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and multiple sequential combination regimens (amikacin, ceftazidime-avibactam, levofloxacin, ceftolozane-tazobactam, tigecycline, imipenem, and linezolid), she underwent left lower lobectomy via left lateral thoracotomy, resulting in rapid defervescence, complete resolution of pneumonia, and continuous complete remission of both AML (29 months) and breast cancer (37 months).

raw_case_text:
A 93-year-old Caucasian woman was referred to the Internal Medicine Consultation due to cervical adenopathies with 3 months duration. With respect to past medical history, 4 years earlier she had been diagnosed with cutaneous sarcomatoid carcinoma of the face and submitted to surgical excision. The patient denied having fever, asthenia, fatigue, weight loss or night sweats; furthermore, there were no respiratory symptoms. She denied having a previous history of tuberculosis (TB) and recent contact with people with known or suspected TB. There was no epidemiological context or contact with animals. On physical examination, an enlarged, mobile and painful right cervical lymph node was evident; the remainder of the examination was unremarkable.
Cervico-thoraco-abdominal-pelvic computed tomography (CT) showed a right cervical mass (Fig. 1) with multiple adenopathies and some fibrotic lesions in the upper right lobe; there were no other adenopathies nor evidence of neoplastic disease. Fine needle aspiration (FNA) biopsy of the cervical node was performed and yielded a noncaseous granulomatous process. There was no evidence of Reed-Sternberg cells or neoplastic cells; Ziehl-Neelsen staining was negative, as well as polymerase chain reaction (PCR) assessment for Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MT) and culture. The patient was kept under close surveillance. In the meantime, an IgG lambda monoclonal gammopathy was diagnosed; renal function and calcium metabolism were normal, there was no anaemia or elevated urinary free light chains and beta-2 microglobulin was normal. Peripheral blood immunophenotyping demonstrated a polyclonal B cell population. In addition, serology tests for syphilis, human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), hepatitis B virus and hepatitis C virus were negative, and QuantiFERON testing was positive. Two months later, the adenopathies had grown and there was cutaneous fistulization with suppurative lymphadenitis (Figs. 2A and 2B).
Microbiologic examination of a suppuration swab was positive for Staphylococcus aureus and the patient was treated with cefuroxime, displaying only slight improvement. An excisional biopsy was programmed and histological examination revealed granulomas with caseous necrosis and suppuration.
PCR assessment of the samples was negative for MT, Nocardia, Mycobacterium avium complex, Toxoplasma gondii, Aspergillus fumigatus, Bartonella spp., Treponema pallidum and Leishmania infantum. Considering the presence of persistent cervical lymphadenopathy with caseous granulomas, a positive QuantiFERON test, and the exclusion of other potential causes, the hypothesis of cervical tuberculous lymphadenitis was strongly suspected, even without a positive PCR test for MT. The patient started presumptive treatment with isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol. Afterwards, diagnostic confirmation was obtained by isolation of MT in one of the lymph node cultures. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing did not demonstrate resistances. The patient presented a favourable clinical outcome with gradual reduction in the size of the adenopathies and there were no side effects attributable to the antituberculous drugs.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 93-year-old Caucasian woman presented with a 3-month history of a painful, enlarging right cervical lymphadenopathy.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient was referred to the Internal Medicine clinic for a 3-month history of right cervical lymphadenopathy without constitutional or respiratory symptoms. Over 2 months of outpatient surveillance, the cervical nodes enlarged further and fistulized to the skin with purulent drainage that showed minimal response to oral cefuroxime after a swab grew Staphylococcus aureus.
subjective.past_medical_history: Cutaneous sarcomatoid carcinoma of the face excised 4 years prior; newly identified asymptomatic IgG-lambda monoclonal gammopathy; no prior tuberculosis, TB contacts, or animal exposures.
subjective.review_of_systems: Negative for fever, asthenia, fatigue, weight loss, night sweats, or respiratory symptoms.

objective.physical_examination: Initial exam revealed an enlarged, mobile, tender right cervical lymph node with an otherwise unremarkable systemic exam; 2 months later, the mass had enlarged with cutaneous fistulization and suppurative drainage.
objective.routine_investigations: Renal function, calcium metabolism, hemoglobin, urinary free light chains, and beta-2 microglobulin were normal; serum protein electrophoresis showed an IgG-lambda monoclonal gammopathy with polyclonal B-cell peripheral immunophenotyping. Syphilis, HIV, HBV, and HCV serologies were negative, while QuantiFERON-TB Gold testing was positive. Swab of the cutaneous fistula initially grew Staphylococcus aureus.
objective.advanced_workup: Cervico-thoraco-abdomino-pelvic CT showed a right cervical necrotic mass with multiple adjacent adenopathies and right upper lobe fibrotic scarring without distant neoplasia. Initial fine-needle aspiration (FNA) biopsy showed noncaseating granulomas negative for Reed-Sternberg/malignant cells, Ziehl-Neelsen stain, M. tuberculosis PCR, and culture. Subsequent excisional lymph node biopsy revealed granulomas with caseous necrosis and suppuration; multiplex PCR on biopsy tissue was negative for M. tuberculosis, Nocardia, Mycobacterium avium complex, Toxoplasma gondii, Aspergillus fumigatus, Bartonella spp., Treponema pallidum, and Leishmania infantum.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Cervical tuberculous lymphadenitis (scrofula) caused by pan-susceptible Mycobacterium tuberculosis (with Nocardia and other granulomatous pathogens excluded by PCR) was confirmed when excisional lymph node biopsy culture isolated Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Four-drug antituberculous therapy with isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol led to progressive regression of the cervical adenopathies without drug-related adverse events.

raw_case_text:
A 9-month-old boy was admitted to our unit due to dry cough and wheezing for 2 weeks, and tachypnea for 5 days. He is the second child of nonconsanguineous parents with an uneventful birth history. Medical history revealed three prior episodes of lower respiratory tract infections necessitating hospitalization and one instance of methylprednisolone treatment before referral to our hospital.
Physical examination revealed that the Z-score of weight for age and weight for height was 0.60; respiratory rate, 66 bpm; heart rate, 156 bpm, and temperature, 36.6 C. A depression of the suprasternal and supraclavicular fossa with coarse breath sounds without rale were noted in both lungs. The liver and spleen were non-palpable below the costal margin. Laboratory data showed a high white blood cell count, 30.61 x 109 cells/L, with 41.1% neutrophils; hemoglobin, 130 g/L; hypersensitive C-reactive protein, <1 mg/L; erythrocyte sedimentation rate, 8.0 mm/h, and serum lactate dehydrogenase, 323 U/L (normal range, 135.0-215.0 U/L). Additionally, low levels of immunoglobulin A, 0.04 g/L (normal range, 0.10-0.56 g/L) and immunoglobulin G, 0.15 g/L (normal range, 3.60-9.20 g/L), and normal levels of immunoglobulin M, 0.48 g/L (normal range 0.40-1.28 g/L), were found. T cell subsets:CD19+, CD20+, CD4+, CD4+, and CD4+/CD8+-were in their normal ranges. Screening tests for HIV, syphilis, hepatitis C, mycobacteria, nocardia, Epstein-Barr virus, and fungal pathogens were negative or within normal range. Antinuclear, anti-double-stranded DNA, anti-smooth muscle actin, anti-ribonucleoprotein, and anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies were negative, respectively.
Computed tomography (CT) scan of the chest showed ground-glass density images in both lungs (Figure 1). On the 7th day of hospitalization, bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage and lung biopsy was performed under general anesthesia. The bronchoalveolar lavage fluid appeared milky (Figure 2A), while hematoxylin-eosin staining showed extensive macrophage infiltration in the alveolar and bronchial cavities without evidence of fibrosis and hexamine-silver staining for bronchoalveolar lavage fluid revealed the presence of P. jirovecii (Figure 2B). Moreover, large amount of periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) stain-positive and diastase-Periodic acid-Schiff (D-PAS) stain-positive substance was found in the alveolar and bronchial cavities (Figures 3A,B), consistent with pathological characteristics of PAP and non-specific interstitial pneumonia.
Whole exome sequencing was conducted by Huada Inspection Center (Shenzhen, China) to detect gene mutation related to immunodeficiency, alveolar surface-active substance or inherited disorder associated with PAP. A c.511dupA hemizygous mutation in the EX5E region of the CD40 ligand (CD40LG, OMIM 300386) gene, present on Xq26.3 and coding for CD40L protein, was noted. Bioinformatic analysis suggested a frameshift mutation inducing the early termination of the amino acid-encoded protein (p.I171N). Genetic analysis of the patient's parents indicated maternal inheritance of the mutation.
Following the confirmation of P. jirovecii infection, imipenem, sulperazone, and erythromycin were administered intravenously, and sulfamethoxazole was given orally. Meanwhile, sodium bicarbonate tablets were given to alkalize urine and methylprednisolone and human immunoglobulin was used for anti-inflammatory and immune support therapy. Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage was repeated 10 days later, and significant clearing of the lavage fluid was observed. The patient displayed gradual improvement and was eventually discharged on the 48th day of hospitalization.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 9-month-old boy presented with a 2-week history of dry cough and wheezing and a 5-day history of tachypnea.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The infant was admitted with 2 weeks of dry cough and wheezing that progressed to tachypnea over the 5 days prior to hospitalization.
subjective.past_medical_history: Second child of nonconsanguineous parents with an uneventful birth history; history of three prior hospitalizations for lower respiratory tract infections and one prior course of methylprednisolone.

objective.physical_examination: Weight-for-age and weight-for-height Z-scores were 0.60; respiratory rate 66 breaths/min, heart rate 156 bpm, and temperature 36.6 C. Suprasternal and supraclavicular retractions were present with bilateral coarse breath sounds without rales; liver and spleen were not palpable.
objective.routine_investigations: Labs showed marked leukocytosis (WBC 30.61 x 10^9/L, 41.1% neutrophils), hemoglobin 130 g/L, hs-CRP <1 mg/L, ESR 8.0 mm/h, and elevated LDH 323 U/L (reference: 135.0-215.0 U/L). Screening tests for HIV, syphilis, HCV, mycobacteria, Nocardia, EBV, fungal pathogens, ANA, anti-dsDNA, anti-SMA, anti-RNP, and ANCA were all negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Immunological workup revealed selective IgA and IgG deficiency with IgA 0.04 g/L (reference: 0.10-0.56 g/L), IgG 0.15 g/L (reference: 3.60-9.20 g/L), normal IgM 0.48 g/L (reference: 0.40-1.28 g/L), and normal lymphocyte subsets (CD19+, CD20+, CD4+, CD4+/CD8+). Chest CT demonstrated diffuse bilateral ground-glass opacities. Day-7 bronchoscopy with BAL and transbronchial lung biopsy yielded milky BALF with extensive alveolar macrophage infiltration, abundant PAS- and D-PAS-positive intra-alveolar lipoproteinaceous material consistent with pulmonary alveolar proteinosis (PAP), and Pneumocystis jirovecii cysts on Gomori hexamine-silver staining. Whole-exome and Sanger sequencing identified a maternally inherited hemizygous frameshift mutation in the CD40LG gene (Xq26.3, EX5E region, c.511dupA, p.I171N) causing X-linked hyper-IgM syndrome.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: X-linked hyper-IgM syndrome (hemizygous CD40LG c.511dupA mutation) presenting with Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia and secondary pulmonary alveolar proteinosis (PAP) (with Nocardia and mycobacterial infections excluded) was confirmed via BAL hexamine-silver staining, lung biopsy PAS/D-PAS histopathology, and whole-exome sequencing. Treatment with oral sulfamethoxazole (with sodium bicarbonate urinary alkalinization), IV imipenem, cefoperazone-sulbactam, erythromycin, methylprednisolone, intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG), and repeat therapeutic bronchoalveolar lavage on day 17 led to clinical recovery and discharge on hospital day 48.

raw_case_text:
A previously healthy 20-year-old female patient presented at the emergency department with 4 days history of concurrent severe right-sided pleuritic chest pain and moderate ipsilateral clavicular pain, shortness of breath on exertion, as well as combined right upper limb weakness and bilateral fingertip numbness. No other symptoms were reported. She accounted no recent travel or family history, including neurofibromatosis.
On admission, the ECG and troponins were found to be within normal limits. However, the ensuing chest X-ray (CXR) showed a large oval mass-like density in the posterior segment of the right upper lobe [Figure 1].
The complementary CT scan of the chest with contrast showed a low density 7.2 x 10.5 x 8.3 cm mass in the posterior segment of the right upper lobe with no nodular enhancement, potentially originating at the right T5-T6 neural foramen. A 16 mm thick right pleural effusion was also described [Figure 2]. Although nonspecific, the findings suggested the presence of a peripheral nerve sheath tumor such as neurofibroma or schwannoma.
The ensuing MRI with gadolinium demonstrated a large (at least 7.2 x 9.2 x 8.5 cm) T1 isointense and a mild T2 hyperintense (heterogenic) mass relative to the muscle and within the right upper/mid posterior hemithorax. A focal contrast-enhancing protrusion of the right posterior medial aspect of the mass extending into the right T5-6 neural foramen suggested that the mass emanated from the neural foramen [Figure 3]. Of note, the bronchoalveolar lavage cultures were found negative for pulmonary pathogens, including acid-fast bacilli, chlamydia, Mycobacterium marinum, Mycobacterium avium, Nocardia, Legionella, yeast, fungus, or viruses.
In view of the patient's age, concurrent symptomatology, Karnofsky Performance Scale (KPS) of 70 (mainly due to presenting symptoms), size of the lesion, and topoanatomical constraints, we decided to remove the tumor using a right- sided posterolateral thoracotomy followed by a perilesional dissection; the mass was successfully freed from the corresponding posterior rib and transverse process. We then proceeded to follow the pedicle into the right T5-T6 foramen, ultimately achieving "en bloc" tumor resection including the proximal nerve root. No spinal fluid leak or persistent bleeding was noted; the surgical site was closed accordingly and without complications.
The microscopic examination of the collected samples demonstrated a well-circumscribed encapsulated tumor composed of interlacing fascicles of bland spindled cells with alternating areas of hyper- and hypocellularity, thick hyalinized vessels, and occasional areas of nuclear palisading (Verocay bodies). Areas of lipidized/xanthoma cells were also noted. Non-neoplastic nerve structures were found adjacent to the neoplasm. No significant atypia or mitotic activity was seen. Finally, the immunohistochemical staining proved positive for S-100 protein, SOX-10 while negative for p63, PAX-8, neurofilament, and desmin. The findings confirmed the diagnosis of schwannoma [Table 1].
The patient was transferred to the intensive care unit postoperatively; her evolution at the hospital proved uncomplicated with follow-up serial CXRs remaining unremarkable [Figure 4a]. The patient was discharged 7 days following surgery. A CT scan of the chest 1 month postsurgery showed normal findings [Figure 4b and c]. In view of her good prognosis, adjuvant chemotherapy or radiotherapy was deemed not necessary at this stage. The patient has remained asymptomatic since her discharge from hospital; her KPS is of 100 currently (6 months postsurgery). As expected, she remains on follow-up. Due to the low risk of recurrence after schwannoma resection, repeated CT scan will be scheduled after 12 months postsurgery.

subjective.chief_complaint: A previously healthy 20-year-old female presented with a 4-day history of severe right-sided pleuritic chest pain, ipsilateral clavicular pain, exertional dyspnea, right upper limb weakness, and bilateral fingertip numbness.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Over the 4 days prior to emergency department presentation, the patient developed acute severe right-sided pleuritic chest pain, moderate right clavicular pain, shortness of breath on exertion, right upper-extremity weakness, and bilateral fingertip paresthesias.
subjective.past_medical_history: Previously healthy female with no history of recent travel and no family history of neurofibromatosis.
subjective.review_of_systems: Negative for other constitutional or systemic symptoms.

objective.physical_examination: Karnofsky Performance Scale (KPS) score was 70 due to pain and right upper-limb weakness.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission ECG and serum troponin levels were normal. Chest X-ray revealed a large oval mass-like density in the posterior segment of the right upper lobe.
objective.advanced_workup: Contrast-enhanced chest CT demonstrated a 7.2 x 10.5 x 8.3 cm low-density mass in the posterior right upper lobe without nodular enhancement, extending toward the right T5-T6 neural foramen, accompanied by a 16-mm right pleural effusion. Gadolinium-enhanced thoracic MRI confirmed a 7.2 x 9.2 x 8.5 cm T1-isointense, heterogeneously T2-hyperintense posterior hemithorax mass protruding into the right T5-T6 neural foramen. Bronchoalveolar lavage cultures were negative for AFB, Chlamydia, Mycobacterium marinum, Mycobacterium avium, Nocardia, Legionella, fungi, and viruses. Right posterolateral thoracotomy with en bloc tumor resection (including the proximal T5-T6 nerve root) was performed; histopathology showed an encapsulated spindle-cell neoplasm with Antoni A/B areas, Verocay bodies, hyalinized vessels, and xanthomatous cells strongly positive for S-100 and SOX-10 and negative for p63, PAX-8, neurofilament, and desmin.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Giant benign posterior mediastinal/intrathoracic schwannoma arising from the right T5-T6 spinal nerve root (with pulmonary infections including Nocardia and mycobacteria excluded on BAL) was confirmed via surgical histopathology and S-100/SOX-10 immunohistochemistry. Following uncomplicated en bloc resection via right posterolateral thoracotomy, she was discharged on postoperative day 7, had normal 1-month follow-up chest CT findings without need for adjuvant therapy, and remained asymptomatic with a Karnofsky Performance Scale score of 100 at 6-month follow-up.

raw_case_text:
Her previous medical history revealed that she was diagnosed with RA at the age of 58 years old and was receiving orally 20 mg of leflunomide per day. She had been treated with methotrexate and hydroxychloroquine in the past, under which she had experienced many relapses that required oral corticosteroids. It was only when her antirheumatic therapy was switched to leflunomide that she had a long-term remission. The last time she had received oral corticosteroids was 3 years ago for a period of 6 months.
Initial laboratory studies were normal, apart from a slightly elevated C-reactive protein (CRP) (CRP: 4.7 mg/dl, normal range: <0.5 mg/dl) with a normal white blood cell count (WBC: 6,9 x 103/mul) and no history of fever.
In the next 48 h a single fever wave of 39 C was documented, followed by subfebrile body temperatures, and a slight deterioration of her speech and orientation. A brain MRI demonstrated a left parietal, rim-enhancing collection of fluid with diffusion restriction and dimensions of 48 mm x 25 mm x 19 mm that resembled a BA [Figure 2a-d]. Blood cultures were obtained and a CT scan of the thorax, abdomen and pelvis as well as a transesophageal echocardiogram were performed, to rule out a possible primary location. The initial antibiotic regimen included ceftriaxone, metronidazole, and vancomycin. Due to the suspected BA, dexamethasone was discontinued and a prophylactic therapy with levetiracetam 1000 mgIVq 12H was initiated, given the high risk of seizure. In the next 48 h her hemiparesis improved, as well as her laboratory infection parameters. However, her aphasia deteriorated further and she additionally developed dyscalculia. This deterioration of the neurological status was attributed to the space-occupying effect of the BA during the stage of the early capsule formation, as well as the expansion of the surrounding edema, due to the discontinuation of dexamethasone. Neurosurgery consultation led to patient's immediate surgical treatment. A left craniotomy was performed and an intraparechymal abscess was detected and evacuated. Cultures for common microbes as well as Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Nocardia were obtained intraoperatively from both the liquid and the solid part of the BA. The patient was extubated successfully and at her postoperative clinical evaluation she had a significant improvement of her neurological status. The intraoperatively obtained cultures came up negative, probably because of the early start of empirical antibiotic therapy. Histopathology revealed an aggregation of lymphocytes, macrophages, and neutrophils in a loose extracellular matrix, consistent with an abscess. No malignant cells were present.
Seven days postoperatively only a slight paresis of patient's right upper extremity remained. The patient was discharged 6 weeks after her surgery and she continued receiving an oral antibiotic therapy (amoxicillin/clavulanic acid in combination with levofloxacin) for another 4 weeks. At her follow-up examination (1 month postoperative) she did not have any focal neurological deficits and she was able to resume her daily activities. The postoperative brain MRI demonstrated only the usual postoperative changes of the brain without any sign of fluid collection or gadolinium enhancement [Figure 2e].
Despite this incident, leflunomide was resumed after the termination of the antibiotic therapy, since her RA was refractory to the other antirheumatic therapies.

subjective.chief_complaint: A female patient with rheumatoid arthritis on leflunomide presented with hemiparesis, speech impairment, and disorientation, developing a 39 C fever spike within 48 hours of admission.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented afebrile with neurological deficits (hemiparesis and speech/orientation changes). Within 48 hours of admission, she experienced a single fever spike of 39 C followed by subfebrile temperatures and worsening speech and orientation. Following discontinuation of dexamethasone and initiation of empirical ceftriaxone, metronidazole, vancomycin, and levetiracetam, her hemiparesis transiently improved but her aphasia worsened and she developed dyscalculia.
subjective.past_medical_history: Rheumatoid arthritis diagnosed at age 58, currently in long-term remission on oral leflunomide 20 mg/day; previously treated with methotrexate, hydroxychloroquine, and multiple courses of oral corticosteroids (last steroid course was 3 years prior for 6 months).
subjective.review_of_systems: Home medication: oral leflunomide 20 mg/day.

objective.physical_examination: Initial right hemiparesis with subsequent fever spike to 39 C, progressive aphasia, disorientation, and dyscalculia.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission labs were normal except for mildly elevated CRP (4.7 mg/dL, reference: <0.5 mg/dL) with a normal WBC count (6.9 x 10^3/uL). Blood cultures and transesophageal echocardiogram were negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Brain MRI demonstrated a 48 x 25 x 19 mm left parietal rim-enhancing fluid collection with central diffusion restriction and perilesional edema consistent with a brain abscess. Chest, abdominal, and pelvic CT scans showed no primary infectious focus. Left parietal craniotomy and abscess evacuation were performed; intraoperative liquid and solid abscess cultures for common bacteria, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, and Nocardia were negative (following empirical antibiotics), while histopathology confirmed a benign suppurative abscess (lymphocytes, macrophages, and neutrophils in a loose matrix without malignancy).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Culture-negative left parietal bacterial brain abscess in a rheumatoid arthritis patient on leflunomide (with Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Nocardia, and malignancy excluded on intraoperative cultures and histopathology). Following left craniotomy and abscess evacuation, empirical IV ceftriaxone, metronidazole, and vancomycin (plus levetiracetam 1,000 mg IV q12h), and 6 weeks of inpatient care, she was discharged on a 4-week course of oral amoxicillin/clavulanic acid plus levofloxacin. At 1-month postoperative follow-up, she had no focal neurological deficits, complete abscess resolution on brain MRI, and safely resumed leflunomide.

raw_case_text:
A 51-year-old woman was admitted with 3 weeks of cough, initially dry then productive of a small amount of clear sputum, and 6 days of subjective fevers, chills and dyspnea on exertion. On the day prior to admission, she experienced worsening malaise, fatigue and dyspnea. Her past medical history included HIV infection diagnosed 2 years earlier, with a CD4 cell count of 220 cells/ul measured 2 months prior to admission, cervical dysplasia with cone biopsy 8 months earlier and chronic anemia. She reported no recent travel history or sick exposures. Her ART regimen was lamivudine/zidovudine plus lopinavir/ritonavir, with TMP/SMX 800/160 mg 3 times weekly for PCP prophylaxis.
On physical examination, the patient was in no acute distress. She was febrile at 102  F, pulse was 84 beats/minute, and respirations were 22 breaths/minute. Blood pressure was 86/50 mm Hg and oxygen saturation was 99% on room air. Lungs were clear, with bilateral breath sounds. There was no palpable lymphadenopathy. Laboratory values were significant for a lactate dehydrogenase level of 217 U/L (100-190), albumin 2.0 g/dl, hemoglobin 10.7g/dl, and white blood cell count 7.9 cells/ul, with differential: 71.1% neutrophils, 15.9% lymphocytes, 12.1% monocytes, 0.4% eosinophils and 0.8% basophils.
Computed Tomography (CT) of the chest revealed subcarinal, prevascular and right hilar lymphadenopathy. Multiple masses and nodules were scattered throughout both lungs, the largest cavitating and abutting the major fissure in the left upper lobe measuring 4.2 x 4.2 cm, with another large mass at the right cardiophrenic angle measuring 2.2 x 4.6 cm. There were also bilateral pleural effusions with associated compressive atelectasis of the lower lobes and fibrotic changes in the left apical region, (Fig. 1).
The patient was admitted with the diagnosis of pneumonia of uncertain etiology, placed on airborne isolation for tuberculosis, and was started on ceftriaxone 1g Intravenous (IV) daily, azithromycin 500 mg IV daily and TMP/SMX 2 double strength tablets orally every 8 hours. Sputum Gram stain and bacterial culture, 3 Acid-Fast Bacilli sputum smears and purified protein derivative testing were negative. The patient continued to have intermittent fevers 101-102  F for the next 4 days, then became afebrile and started feeling overall better. She experienced nausea and vomiting as a side effect of TMP/SMX.
Five days after admission, the patient underwent fiberoptic bronchoscopy under moderate sedation. There were no abnormalities in the airways, and Bronchoalveolar Lavage (BAL) of the lingula as well as 5 Transbronchial Biopsies (TBBx) of the left upper lobe were performed. All cultures and smears were negative. Cytology was negative for malignancy and PCP. The TBBx of the left upper lobe showed benign bronchial tissue and a fragment of lung parenchyma with interstitial fibrosis. TMP/SMX was discontinued in view of negative results for PCP while azithromycin and ceftriaxone were continued. Three days later, fever and malaise restarted, and because of suspicion for nocardiosis, TMP/SMX was restarted. CT of the head showed maxillary, frontal and ethmoid sinus disease, without other pathology. That day, 2 transthoracic core needle biopsies were performed in the left upper lung cavitating pleural-based mass. Pathology revealed lung parenchyma and bronchial tissue with acute inflammation and fibrosis, and granulomas with coagulation necrosis with organisms within morphologically consistent with Pneumocystis jiroveci noted on Gomori methenamine silver (GMS) stain by direct microscopy, and negative Acid-Fast Bacilli stain, (Fig. 2).
Azithromycin and ceftriaxone were stopped. The patient was restarted on oral TMP/SMX and again became afebrile; malaise and fatigue improved. Due to persistent nausea and vomiting, therapy was switched to IV formulation. She continued to improve and felt back to baseline and was discharged 1 week later on oral clindamycin and primaquine. CT of the chest 3 months later revealed nearly complete resolution of the previous findings, with a significantly improved cavitating left upper lobe nodule, multiple peripheral bilateral sub-cm non calcified pulmonary nodules, and resolution of bilateral pleural effusions and mediastinal lymphadenopathy (Fig. 1).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 51-year-old woman with HIV infection presented with a 3-week history of cough and a 6-day history of subjective fevers, chills, and exertional dyspnea.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Three weeks prior to admission, the patient developed a dry cough that became productive of scant clear sputum, followed 6 days prior to admission by subjective fevers, chills, and exertional dyspnea, and 1 day prior to admission by worsening malaise, fatigue, and dyspnea.
subjective.past_medical_history: HIV infection diagnosed 2 years earlier (CD4 count 220 cells/uL 2 months prior to admission) maintained on lamivudine/zidovudine, lopinavir/ritonavir, and prophylactic TMP/SMX (800/160 mg three times weekly); cervical dysplasia status post cone biopsy 8 months prior; chronic anemia; no recent travel or sick contacts.
subjective.review_of_systems: Home medications: lamivudine/zidovudine, lopinavir/ritonavir, and TMP/SMX 800/160 mg thrice weekly. Experienced severe nausea and vomiting with oral TMP/SMX during hospitalization.

objective.physical_examination: In no acute distress; temperature 102 F, pulse 84 beats/min, respiratory rate 22 breaths/min, BP 86/50 mmHg, and SpO2 99% on room air. Lungs were clear to auscultation bilaterally and no lymphadenopathy was palpable.
objective.routine_investigations: Labs showed elevated LDH 217 U/L (reference: 100-190), hypoalbuminemia 2.0 g/dL, anemia (Hb 10.7 g/dL), and WBC 7.9 x 10^3/uL (71.1% neutrophils, 15.9% lymphocytes, 12.1% monocytes, 0.4% eosinophils, 0.8% basophils). Sputum Gram stain, bacterial culture, three sputum AFB smears, and tuberculin PPD skin test were negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Chest CT demonstrated subcarinal, prevascular, and right hilar lymphadenopathy, multiple bilateral pulmonary masses and nodules (largest 4.2 x 4.2 cm cavitating mass abutting the left major fissure in the left upper lobe and a 2.2 x 4.6 cm right cardiophrenic angle mass), bilateral pleural effusions with lower-lobe compressive atelectasis, and left apical fibrosis. Head CT showed maxillary, frontal, and ethmoid sinusitis without intracranial pathology. Day-5 fiberoptic bronchoscopy with lingular BAL and five left upper lobe transbronchial biopsies were negative on smears, cultures, and cytology. Subsequent CT-guided transthoracic core needle biopsy of the cavitating left upper lobe pleural-based mass revealed necrotizing granulomas with coagulation necrosis containing Pneumocystis jirovecii organisms on Gomori methenamine silver (GMS) stain with negative AFB staining.
