Plan and clinical course: Initially started on dexamethasone (6 mg) and apixaban for suspected COVID-19 and pulmonary embolism; following HIV-1 diagnosis and BAL PCR confirmation of P. jirovecii, therapy was switched to intravenous trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (400 mg q8h), oral prednisone (40 mg twice daily), and antiretroviral therapy (emtricitabine/tenofovir plus dolutegravir) alongside continued apixaban. After 1 additional week of inpatient treatment, he improved and was discharged on home oxygen, oral TMP-SMX (800/160 mg), prednisone taper, apixaban, and dolutegravir plus emtricitabine/tenofovir.

raw_case_text: The patient was admitted to the Department of Acquired Immune Deficiency for the first time on November 18, 2020 and was hospitalized for 3 months. Upon admission to the ward, the patient was febrile, with clinical manifestations of pneumonia - cough and shortness of breath, cachexia and candidal plaques in the oral cavity. The laboratory tests revealed severe anemia (hemoglobin values of 54 g/l) and elevated leucocytes upon admission (11,2 G/l). There were no pathological changes in the patient's biochemical profile. The patient's immune status revealed extremely severe immune deficiency as follows: Cluster of differentiation 4 (CD4) + T-cell count of 12 cells/microl; CD8 + T-cell count of 347 cells/microl. Her viral load (VL) was 10 1000 c/microl. The patient's x-ray showed bilateral pneumonia, and microbiological analysis showed Pneumocystis jirovecii and Candida albicans from sputum, as well as Candida albicans from throat secretions and faeces. Accordingly, the patient was treated with trimethoprim-cotrimoxazole, fluconazole, and antiretroviral therapy (ART) was initiated with emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide/darunavir/cobicistat. The patient was discharged from the department at the end of February, after the pneumonia had cleared, with negative microbiological tests, and controlled immune status as follows: CD4 count at 144 cells/microl; CD8 count at 1278 cells/microl. Her VL was 313 c/microl. At the end of March, she was hospitalized again because of high fever, chills, vomitting and severe lethargy. Laboratory tests showed severe anemia again - hemoglobin values of 45 g/l and thrombocytopenia - 109 G / l, with high c reactive protein (CRP) - 208 g/l, low albumin - 20.3 g/l and elevated gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT) - 244 IU/l. Lung radiography showed no pathological findings. Computed tomography of the abdomen showed expressed hepatosplenomegaly. Of the microbiological tests performed, only Candida albicans was isolated from the faeces. During the hospitalization, the patient received empirical antibiotic combination - Ceftriaxone + Vancomycin, Fluconazole, multiple blood transfusions and infusion of human albumin. During the hospitalization, the patient had a temporary improvement of her condition, but a gradual progression of splenomegaly was observed. On April 20, due to acute pain in the left hypochondrium, the patient was transferred to a surgical clinic, where splenectomy was performed, with evidence of multiple splenic infarctions. Histological examination of the spleen showed histiocytic infiltration and the diagnosis of Erdheim Chester's disease was observed. After discharge from the surgical clinic, the patient was referred to the hematology department to clarify the diagnosis. During the hospitalization of the patient in the hematology ward in May, Gaucher's disease was observed, for which samples for genetic testing were sent to Germany. Meanwhile, during spontaneous bending, the patient suffered severe back pain and was immobilized from the waist down, experiencing severe back and limb pain. A magnetic resonance imaging /MRI/ revealed tumor formation and fracture of the ninth vertebra (Figures 1 and 2), similar tumor formations of the sixth thoracic and first lumbar vertebrae. In May, the patient's immune status and viral load were as follows: CD4 + T - cell count of 164 cells/microl; CD8 + T - cell count of 1634 cells/microl; and viral load (VL) was undetectable <2  c/microl. The patient was referred to a neurosurgical clinic, where a biopsy of the relevant formations in the vertebrae was performed and the fracture was filled with bone cement. The histological analysis result of the material from the vertebrae showed an infiltration of macrophages/histiocytes with abundant, mostly small vacuolated or foamy rather than fibrillary cytoplasm. Immunohistochemical study revealed CD 68 ( + ) positive abundant cell composition, S100 granular and diffuse marking; PAH8 - negative marking. Simultaneously, we received the data from the enzyme tests for Niemann's - Pick and Gaucher diseases from Germany, which were negative. Under the corticosteroid treatment, the fever subsided, but the anemic syndrome and swelling of the lower extremities persisted. A tumor formation of the skull was also observed. It was located on the right temporal bone with dimensions of about 2 cm and was painless. Following another consultation with a hematologist and after obtaining consent for performing high-risk chemotherapy, she was transferred to the haematological clinic. The patient underwent two courses of chemotherapy with Ciclophosphamid, Prednisone, Vincristin. However, she died five days after the second chemotherapy treatment.

subjective.chief_complaint: A female patient with newly diagnosed advanced HIV/AIDS initially presented in November 2020 with fever, cough, shortness of breath, cachexia, and oral thrush, and 1 month after recovering from Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia re-presented with high fever, chills, vomiting, severe lethargy, progressive hepatosplenomegaly, and pathological T9 vertebral fracture.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: First admitted on November 18, 2020, for a 3-month hospitalization with febrile bilateral Pneumocystis jirovecii and Candida albicans pneumonia, severe anemia (Hb 54 g/L), and profound HIV-induced immunodeficiency (CD4 12 cells/μL, viral load 1,010,000 copies/μL), she was successfully treated with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, fluconazole, and Biktarvy-like ART (emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide/darunavir/cobicistat) and discharged in late February 2021 with cleared pneumonia and improved immunity (CD4 144 cells/μL, VL 313 copies/μL). At the end of March 2021, she was readmitted with high fever, chills, vomiting, severe lethargy, severe anemia (Hb 45 g/L), thrombocytopenia, and progressive massive splenomegaly culminating on April 20 in acute left upper quadrant pain from splenic infarction requiring splenectomy, followed in May 2021 by acute paraplegia from a T9 vertebral pathological fracture and a 2 cm right temporal skull tumor.
subjective.past_medical_history: Advanced HIV/AIDS diagnosed in November 2020; resolved Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia and oral/fecal/respiratory candidiasis (November 2020 – February 2021).
subjective.review_of_systems: Initial November 2020 admission positive for fever, cough, shortness of breath, cachexia, and oral thrush; March–May 2021 readmissions positive for high fever, chills, vomiting, lethargy, acute left hypochondriac pain, severe back and lower limb pain with paraplegia, lower extremity edema, and a painless 2 cm right temporal skull mass.

objective.physical_examination: November 2020 admission: Febrile, cachectic, dyspneic, with oral candidal plaques. March–May 2021 readmissions: Febrile, lethargic, massive progressive hepatosplenomegaly with acute left upper quadrant tenderness, acute paraplegia/immobilization below the waist, bilateral lower extremity edema, and a painless 2 cm right temporal skull mass.
objective.routine_investigations: November 2020 admission labs: Hemoglobin 54 g/L, WBC 11.2 G/L, normal biochemistry, plasma HIV viral load 1,010,000 copies/μL (falling to 313 copies/μL in February 2021 and <2 copies/μL in May 2021); chest X-ray showed bilateral pneumonia; sputum positive for Pneumocystis jirovecii and Candida albicans (throat and feces positive for C. albicans). March 2021 readmission labs: Hemoglobin 45 g/L, platelets 109 G/L, CRP 208 mg/L, serum albumin 20.3 g/L, GGT 244 IU/L; normal chest X-ray; fecal culture positive for C. albicans; negative enzymatic testing for Gaucher and Niemann-Pick diseases.
objective.advanced_workup: Serial lymphocyte subsets: CD4+ count 12 cells/μL and CD8+ 347 cells/μL in November 2020, rising on ART to CD4+ 144 cells/μL (CD8+ 1,278 cells/μL) in February 2021 and CD4+ 164 cells/μL (CD8+ 1,634 cells/μL) in May 2021. Abdominal CT and splenectomy histopathology (April 2021): Marked hepatosplenomegaly with multiple splenic infarctions; splenic histopathology demonstrated diffuse lipid-laden histiocytic infiltration diagnostic of Erdheim-Chester disease. Spine MRI and T9 vertebral biopsy/immunohistochemistry (May 2021): Tumor formations in T6, T9 (with pathological fracture), and L1 vertebrae plus a 2 cm right temporal skull lesion; vertebral biopsy showed sheets of foamy/vacuolated macrophages/histiocytes strongly positive for CD68 (+) and S100 (granular/diffuse) and negative for PAX8.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Newly diagnosed advanced HIV/AIDS (initial CD4 12 cells/μL) complicated initially by Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (confirmed on sputum microbiology) and mucocutaneous candidiasis, and subsequently (following ART-induced immune recovery to CD4 164 cells/μL) by aggressive multisystem non-Langerhans cell histiocytosis / Erdheim-Chester disease involving the spleen, liver, T6/T9/L1 vertebrae, and right temporal skull (confirmed by splenectomy and vertebral biopsy histopathology and CD68+/S100+ immunohistochemistry, with Gaucher and Niemann-Pick diseases enzymatically excluded). Plan and clinical course: Initial PJP and candidiasis were cured with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, fluconazole, and darunavir/cobicistat/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide. Subsequent Erdheim-Chester disease was managed with splenectomy, T9 vertebroplasty, corticosteroids, and two cycles of cyclophosphamide, prednisone, and vincristine chemotherapy; however, the patient died 5 days after the second chemotherapy cycle.

raw_case_text:
As a child the patient had suffered from repeated bouts of otitis media, and already as a 6-year-old had suffered from pneumonia confirmed by X-ray imaging. His history included the classic AD-HIES characteristic of retention of primary teeth and typical facies including a wide nose. He had also suffered from fungal nail infections but never fungal infections in any of his mucous linings. He did not suffer from asthma.
In terms of presenting symptoms, the patient had experienced mild productive clear coloured sputum in the mornings for a few years. He had, however, no dyspnoea, weight loss or fever. Pulmonary function tests showed normal dynamic volumes, static volumes and diffusion capacity. A bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) was performed and the culture was positive for Streptococcus pneumoniae, sensitive for penicillin. Cultures also grew Achromobacter sp. And polymerase chain reaction (PCR) was positive for Pneumocystis jirovecii, which was treated with Sulfatrim. However, BAL was negative for Aspergillus sp. and other fungal moulds. PCR and microscopy for Aspergillus sp. were negative as well. Biochemically the titre for Aspergillus IgG antibody was 0.0 arbitrary unit/mL and therefore negative. Immunological studies showed normal IgG and IgM, but elevated IgA = 6.22 g/L and reduced IgG2 = 1.53 g/L. The Galactomannan antigen test was negative. Furthermore, the BAL showed negative microscopy for Mycobacterium sp. The BAL culture for Mycobacterium sp. was negative as well. The interferon gamma release assay (IGRA) test was also negative. The value of total serum IgE was slightly elevated at 158 international units (IU)/mL (reference < 115 IU/mL).
The patient was treated with phenoxymethylpenicillin for 10 days because of the BAL findings of S. pneumoniae and Achromobacter sp. Because of the high suspicion of pulmonary Aspergillosis, empiric Voriconazole treatment was prescribed for 11 months (Figure 2). No tissue biopsy was obtained before initiating treatment. The level of plasma-Voriconazole was monitored throughout the treatment period and found to be within therapeutic levels. A control CT/positron emission tomography (PET) (Figure 3) 2 months later showed increased fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) uptake at the level of the cavity; 8 months later a high-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) scan (Figure 4) showed further progression of cavitating lesion in the right upper lobe and new infiltrates caudally. A new BAL was performed where Pseudomonas aeruginosa was cultured. The second BAL fluid was negative for Aspergillus sp., Mycobacterium sp. and Pneumocystis sp. Blood test was again negative for Galactomannan antigen. The patient was given 2 weeks of intravenous (IV) Tazobactam and Ciprofloxacin to eradicate the P. aeruginosa. A PET/CT scan was done 3 months later. The pulmonary cavity was unchanged with no PET activity in the perceived fungal ball. However, new pulmonary infiltrates were visible in the right upper lobe. After this, a superdimension-bronchoscopy with brush biopsies was performed. It came out with normal cells. A CT-guided transthoracic coarse needle biopsy showed chronic inflammation with no evidence of malignancy or any fungal infection.
Finally, as the clinic and all examinations performed did not point towards fungal infection as only signs of chronic inflammation were present and because the radiological findings progressed despite Voriconazole treatment, a new strategy was agreed upon. The patient would now be treated for non-infectious inflammation. The patient was started on prednisolone 25 mg/day (2.5 mg/kg). A control CT thorax (Figure 5) after 1 month of this treatment regimen showed some regression of the infiltrate. A further follow-up CT thorax (Figure 6) 12 months later showed further regression of the infiltrate. The Prednisolone treatment was subsequently stopped (Figure 7). The patient has been followed in the infectious disease clinic ever since, and his condition has been stable. He now runs 5 km a few times a week without any issues. He continues to be treated prophylactically with Sulfatrim and Itraconazole. A follow-up CT thorax in 2021 showed no progression of infiltrate. During the 4 years of follow-up the cavity with a fungal ball looking appearance in the right lung had only regressed from 21 mm in 2017 to 19 mm in 2021. A follow-up IGRA test in 2022 was negative for Mycobacterium tuberculosis with a positive control (mitogen-nil = 10.00 kIU/L and nil = 0.10 kIU/L).
Apr 2017 BAL: positive cultures for Pneumococcus sp., Achromobacter sp., Pneumocystis sp.; negative for Aspergillus sp. Cytology showed inflammation with macrocytosis and granulocytosis. No tumour cells were seen.
Apr 2017 BAL: negative microscopy for Mycobacterium sp., negative cultures for Mycobacterium sp.
Feb 2018 BAL: negative cultures. Negative for Aspergillus sp. Cytology unchanged from April 2017.
Apr 2018: superdimension-bronchoscopy with brush biopsies: normal cells.
May 2018: CT-guided transthoracic coarse needle biopsy: chronic inflammation, no malignant cells. No fungal cells.
Mar 2017: HRCT: multiple cavitating lesions in the right upper lobe.
May 2017: PET/CT: multiple cavitating processes in the right upper lobe with high FDG uptake. New infiltrative changes posteriorly and caudally to the known cavity, possible progression of known lesion.
Dec 2017: HRCT: discrete regression of cavitary lesion in right upper lobe. Regression of scattered areas of ground glass opacity.
May 2018: CT: multiple cavitating as well as solid and semisolid changes in the right upper lobe with increased FDG uptake.
May 2019: HRCT: regression of known right-side infiltrate.
May 2020 (HRCT) and May 2021 (CT): unchanged status.
June 2021: lymphocyte-population investigation (Th17-assay): Reduced amount of Th17-helper cells (<0.1% of all T-helper cells).

subjective.chief_complaint: An adult male with autosomal dominant hyper-IgE syndrome (AD-HIES) presented with a multi-year history of mild morning cough productive of clear sputum and multiple right upper lobe cavitary lung lesions.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Having suffered recurrent childhood otitis media, pneumonia at age 6, onychomycosis, retained primary teeth, and characteristic coarse facies with a broad nasal bridge typical of autosomal dominant hyper-IgE syndrome (AD-HIES), the patient presented with a several-year history of mild morning expectoration of clear sputum without dyspnea, fever, or weight loss, and was found on HRCT (March 2017) to have multiple cavitary lesions containing a mycetoma-like intracavitary mass in the right upper lobe.
subjective.past_medical_history: Autosomal dominant hyper-IgE syndrome (AD-HIES) with retained primary dentition, characteristic wide nasal bridge facies, recurrent childhood otitis media, childhood pneumonia at age 6, and fungal onychomycosis; no history of asthma or mucocutaneous candidiasis.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for mild morning productive cough with clear sputum; negative for dyspnea, fever, or weight loss.

objective.physical_examination: Characteristic AD-HIES facial features including a broad nasal bridge and history of retained primary teeth; fungal nail infections.
objective.routine_investigations: Pulmonary function tests: Normal dynamic and static lung volumes and normal diffusing capacity. Immunological and biochemical workup: Slightly elevated total serum IgE at 158 IU/mL (reference <115 IU/mL), normal total IgG and IgM, elevated IgA at 6.22 g/L, reduced IgG2 subclass at 1.53 g/L, negative serum Aspergillus IgG (0.0 AU/mL), negative serum galactomannan (2017 and 2018), and negative interferon-gamma release assays (IGRA, 2017 and 2022).
objective.advanced_workup: Lymphocyte subpopulation Th17 assay (June 2021): Severely reduced Th17 helper T-cell fraction (<0.1% of total T-helper cells). Serial HRCT and 18F-FDG PET/CT scans (2017–2021): March/May 2017 HRCT and PET/CT showed multiple FDG-avid right upper lobe cavitary lesions (~21 mm cavity containing a fungal-ball-like intracavitary density) that progressed with new caudal solid/semisolid infiltrates through May 2018 despite 11 months of therapeutic voriconazole, then regressed significantly after 1 and 12 months of oral prednisolone (May 2019–2021). Serial bronchoscopies with BAL (April 2017, February 2018, April 2018 superDimension brush biopsy) and CT-guided transthoracic core needle biopsy (May 2018): April 2017 BAL was positive for Pneumocystis jirovecii by PCR and grew penicillin-sensitive Streptococcus pneumoniae and Achromobacter sp. (negative for Aspergillus and Mycobacterium spp.); February 2018 BAL grew Pseudomonas aeruginosa (negative for Pneumocystis, Aspergillus, and Mycobacterium); April 2018 navigational brush biopsy and May 2018 CT-guided core needle biopsy showed chronic non-infectious inflammation without fungal elements or malignancy.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Autosomal dominant hyper-IgE syndrome (AD-HIES with <0.1% Th17 cells) complicated by a chronic right upper lobe pulmonary cavity colonized initially by Pneumocystis jirovecii (confirmed on April 2017 BAL PCR), Streptococcus pneumoniae, and Achromobacter sp. (and later Pseudomonas aeruginosa), alongside a persistent sterile inflammatory pseudomycetoma / organizing cavitary infiltrate that mimicked pulmonary aspergilloma (with Aspergillus and mycobacteria repeatedly ruled out by BAL, galactomannan, IgG, and CT-guided core biopsy). Plan and clinical course: Initial April 2017 P. jirovecii, S. pneumoniae, and Achromobacter infections were eradicated with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (Sulfatrim) and a 10-day course of phenoxymethylpenicillin (and February 2018 P. aeruginosa with 2 weeks of IV piperacillin-tazobactam and ciprofloxacin). After 11 months of empiric therapeutic voriconazole failed to halt right upper lobe infiltrative progression and core biopsy confirmed sterile chronic inflammation, a 12-month course of oral prednisolone (25 mg/day) induced marked radiographic regression; he remains clinically well (running 5 km several times weekly) on long-term Sulfatrim and itraconazole prophylaxis.

raw_case_text: A 62-year-old male took dexamethasone tablets (2.25 mg three times per day) and ornidazole tablets (0.5g two times per day) orally after tooth extraction. Ten days later, he developed fever (body temperature of 39 C) accompanied by chills, headache, bloating, tinnitus, and hearing loss. Treatment at the local hospital was not effective, and he was transferred to our hospital three days later. On admission, the patient's body temperature was 38.6 C, blood pressure was 134/74 mmHg, respiration was 16 beats/min, heart rate was 75 beats/min, and he was conscious. Relevant examinations were as follows: white blood cell count of 4.40x109/L, neutrophil percentage of 89.8%, lymphocyte count of 0.17x109/L, CD4+ lymphocyte count of 32/mm3, C-reactive protein level of 14.38 mg/L, creatinine level of 37.05 umol/L, pH of 7.399, procalcitonin level of 0.123 ng/mL, and 1,3-beta-d-glucan level of 253.73 pg/mL. Cranial magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed multiple lesions in the brain. Enhanced MRI of the head showed multiple abnormal enhancement shadows in the brain: hematogenous disseminated lesions were possible. Chest computed tomography (CT) showed multiple ground-glass opacities in the anterior segment and lower lobe of the left lung. The patient's cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) had a white blood cell count of 1352x106/L, neutrophil percentage of 92%, glucose level of 0.59 mmol/L, and protein level of 1.48 g/L. Next-generation sequencing (NGS) of the patient's CSF reported 37,235 sequences from N. farcinica and 8 sequences from human cytomegalovirus. Blood NGS reported 61 sequences from Nocardia farcinica, 543 sequences from human cytomegalovirus, and 8 sequences from P. jirovecii. The patient's condition gradually deteriorated, and he developed confusion and respiratory failure, requiring an invasive ventilator to assist breathing. After a week of treatment with meropenem, compound sulfamethoxazole (SMZ), linezolid, and ganciclovir, the patient's symptoms improved slightly and he could breathe independently (Figure 1). On the 18th day, the patient's sputum culture was positive for A. fumigatus and lung CT showed new lesions. N. farcinica and P. jirovecii were not found in the sputum culture and we did not perform NGS again. The doctor administered voriconazole by intravenous drip (400 mg every 12 hours on the first day then 200 mg every 12 hours) to fight infection. The patient showed minimal response for about a week, with occasional hemoptysis, and the voriconazole trough concentration was 0.8 mg/L. We added oral omeprazole to the patient's regimen. On the 31st day, the patient's voriconazole trough concentration was 1.1 mg/L, and the blood no longer appeared in the sputum. CT showed that the lesions were absorbed better than before. The patient still had occasional headaches. On the 35th day, head MRI still revealed multiple infection lesions, similar to previous scans (Figure 2). We replaced meropenem with imipenem. On the 70th day, head MRI revealed a significantly reduced number of lesions. On the 78th day, the patient was transferred to a local hospital for continued treatment, and the treatment plan was changed to SMZ combined with linezolid, amoxicillin, and clavulanate potassium. The patient fully recovered after six months of treatment.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 62-year-old male presented with a 13-day history of high fever (up to 39 °C), chills, headache, abdominal bloating, tinnitus, and hearing loss that began 10 days after taking oral dexamethasone and ornidazole for a tooth extraction.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Following a dental extraction, the patient took oral dexamethasone (2.25 mg TID) and ornidazole (0.5 g BID). Ten days later, he developed high fever (39 °C), chills, headache, bloating, tinnitus, and hearing loss. After 3 days of ineffective treatment at a local hospital, he was transferred to our institution, where he subsequently developed confusion and acute respiratory failure requiring invasive mechanical ventilation.
subjective.past_medical_history: Recent tooth extraction treated for 10 days with oral dexamethasone (2.25 mg three times daily) and ornidazole (0.5 g twice daily).
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for high fever (39 °C), chills, headache, tinnitus, hearing loss, abdominal bloating, and subsequent confusion, respiratory failure, and hemoptysis.

objective.physical_examination: Admission vital signs: Body temperature 38.6 °C, blood pressure 134/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, heart rate 75 beats/min, and initially conscious before deteriorating into confusion and acute respiratory failure requiring endotracheal intubation.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission blood tests: WBC 4.40 x 10^9/L (89.8% neutrophils), severe lymphopenia with absolute lymphocyte count 0.17 x 10^9/L, C-reactive protein (CRP) 14.38 mg/L, serum creatinine 37.05 μmol/L, arterial pH 7.399, and procalcitonin 0.123 ng/mL. Lumbar puncture / cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis: Neutrophilic pleocytosis with WBC 1,352 x 10^6/L (92% neutrophils), hypoglycorrhachia with CSF glucose 0.59 mmol/L, and elevated CSF protein 1.48 g/L. Day 18 sputum culture: Positive for Aspergillus fumigatus.
objective.advanced_workup: Admission immunological and fungal biomarkers: Profound CD4+ T-cell depletion with CD4+ count of 32/mm3; elevated serum 1,3-beta-D-glucan at 253.73 pg/mL. Admission neuroimaging and chest CT: Cranial contrast-enhanced MRI demonstrated multiple ring/nodular enhancing parenchymal brain abscesses consistent with hematogenous dissemination; chest CT showed multiple ground-glass opacities in the left upper lobe anterior segment and left lower lobe (with new pulmonary lesions appearing on day 18). Paired CSF and peripheral blood metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS): CSF mNGS detected Nocardia farcinica (37,235 sequence reads) and human cytomegalovirus (8 reads); peripheral blood mNGS detected Nocardia farcinica (61 reads), human cytomegalovirus (543 reads), and Pneumocystis jirovecii (8 reads).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Disseminated Nocardia farcinica infection (purulent meningitis/multiple brain abscesses and bloodstream infection confirmed by 37,235 CSF mNGS reads and 61 blood mNGS reads) co-infected with Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia and cytomegalovirus (confirmed by blood mNGS [8 P. jirovecii and 543 CMV reads], serum 1,3-beta-D-glucan 253.73 pg/mL, and left lung ground-glass opacities) and secondary hospital-day-18 invasive pulmonary Aspergillus fumigatus infection, precipitated by post-dental dexamethasone therapy and severe CD4+ lymphopenia (32/mm3). Plan and clinical course: Managed with invasive mechanical ventilation, intravenous meropenem (later switched to imipenem on day 35), compound sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX), linezolid, and ganciclovir, allowing ventilator weaning within 1 week. When day 18 sputum culture grew A. fumigatus with new lung lesions and hemoptysis, intravenous voriconazole (400 mg q12h loading, 200 mg q12h maintenance) was added, and oral omeprazole was co-administered via CYP2C19 inhibition to boost subtherapeutic voriconazole troughs from 0.8 mg/L to 1.1 mg/L by day 31, resolving hemoptysis and lung lesions. Brain MRI lesions regressed by day 70; he was transferred on day 78 on oral TMP-SMX, linezolid, and amoxicillin-clavulanate and achieved complete recovery after 6 months of treatment.

raw_case_text:
The patient in question is a 30-year-old Caucasian gentleman who was being followed up regularly by one of the local nephrology firms following a live-donor kidney transplant a few years back. The patient complained of a few weeks' history of dyspnoea and tachycardia on minimal exertion. He denied having other symptoms, but mild pitting lower limb oedema was noted on examination. The gentleman also complained of multiple patches of skin eruptions which had been slowly developing over the past 6 months.
His past medical and surgical history included chronic kidney disease secondary to meningococcal septicaemia at eight years of age. This progressed to end-stage chronic kidney disease at the age of twenty-one. He was first started on peritoneal dialysis and later converted to haemodialysis. At age twenty-eight, the patient received a live kidney transplant from his brother. Four months later, the transplanted kidney was biopsied after a rise in serum creatinine was noted. Histology showed mild tubulitis, suggesting early cell-mediated rejection, which led to the doses of his immunosuppressive medications to be increased.
At the time of presentation, the patient was on tacrolimus 3 mg twice daily, mycophenolate 720 mg twice daily, prednisolone 5 mg daily, omeprazole 20 mg daily, folic acid 5 mg daily, and bumetanide 0.5 mg daily. He had no known drug allergies. Family and social history were unremarkable.
Initial examination revealed a regular pulse rate of 95 beats per minute which increased to 120 beats per minute on walking, a blood pressure of 120/80 mmHg, and a SpO2 of 98% which remained stable on exertion. The patient was afebrile at the time of examination. Bilateral mild pitting oedema up to the ankles was present.
Initial investigations included laboratory tests which showed a normal neutrophil count of 8.30 (4.30-11.40 x 109/L) with a lymphopenia of 0.74 (2.10-3.60 x 109/L). Normocytic anaemia was present with a haemoglobin level of 11.0 g/dL (14.1-17.2 g/dL) and a haematocrit of 34.1% (40.4-50.4%). Platelet count was normal at 186 (146 - 302 x 109/L). Creatinine was 120 mumol/L (59-104 mumol/L), which remained relatively stable since the renal transplant occurred, with a urea of 13.2 mmol/L (1.7-8.3 mmol/L) and an eGFR of 64 mL/min/1.73m2. C-reactive protein and erythrocyte sedimentation rate were slightly elevated at 14.4 mg/L (0-5 mg/L) and 14 mm 1st hr (8-12 mm 1st hr), respectively. Natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) level was also slightly elevated at 147 pg/mL (5-125 pg/mL). Liver function tests were normal. The serum albumin had decreased slightly when compared to previous results at 34 g/L (32-52 g/L), previously 48 g/L, however, still in the normal range. The serum tacrolimus level was 8.8 ng/mL which was in range. Serological tests for toxoplasma and leishmania and the autoimmune screen were all negative. A virology screen was carried out which included polymerase chain reaction (PCR) tests for herpes simplex, varicella zoster, cytomegalovirus, Epstein-Barr virus, BK virus, COVID-19, and other viral respiratory pathogens, all of which turned out negative. The lactate dehydrogenase level was normal but beta-D glucan was detected at >523 pg/mL (positive > 80 pg/mL). Urinalysis and urine microscopy, culture, and sensitivity were all normal. An electrocardiogram showed a normal sinus rhythm at 90 bpm, and an echocardiogram excluded any cardiac pathology. Chest X-ray was unremarkable.
A few days after the nephrology team started their investigations, the patient presented to our eye emergency department complaining of sudden onset painless and rapidly progressive bilateral blurring of vision. Right eye visual acuity (VA) was 6/36, which improved to 6/36+1 with pinhole while the left eye VA was 6/60 and did not improve with pinhole. Pupils were both reactive with no RAPD. Ishihara colour testing was not possible as the patient could not read the test plate. Examination of the anterior segment was unremarkable. The intraocular pressures were 15 mmHg bilaterally. On dilated fundoscopy, the discs were unremarkable except for mild nasal blurring of the disc margins. Both maculae were surrounded by small patches of retinal pallor, cotton wool spots, and intraretinal haemorrhages were observed across the posterior pole and mid-periphery in both eyes (Figure 1). Optical coherence tomography (OCT) revealed bilateral hyperreflective patches at the level of the inner nuclear layer suggestive of paracentral acute middle maculopathy (Figure 2). Fluorescein angiography revealed an enlarged foveal avascular zone as well as early patchy hyperfluorescence (Figures 3 and 4). In view of a lack of history of trauma and the typical findings of perivascular patchy pallor, haemorrhages, and cotton wool spots, a diagnosis of PLR was made.
After discussion with the caring nephrology firm, it was agreed to wait for the CT-pulmonary angiogram (CTPA) before attempting a trial of steroids.
The CTPA excluded pulmonary embolism as the cause for dyspnoea and sinus tachycardia but showed faint diffuse ground glass changes which were more predominant in the perihilar areas. This was suggestive of pneumocystis pneumonia. PCR performed on bronchoalveolar lavage samples detected Pneumocystis jirovecii which confirmed the diagnosis of PCP. Tests for mycobacteria and galactomannan antigen were negative, and cytological analysis of the samples was unremarkable.
Given these findings, the tacrolimus dose was decreased in order to reduce the serum levels to 5-6 ng/mL, while mycophenolate was stopped temporarily. The PCP was treated with trimethoprim-sulfamethaxozole at 960 mg three times daily for a total of 21 days and then reduced to 480 mg daily indefinitely. A trial of pulsed methyl prednisolone was attempted to treat the PLR. This consisted of three doses of 250 mg IV methyl prednisolone over three days with omeprazole cover. This was followed by a course of oral prednisolone which was tapered down gradually. The patient was then left on a maintenance dose of 5 mg daily.
After commencing therapy, the dyspnoea and tachycardia resolved with PCP resolution also being confirmed on repeat CT Thorax. Patient was restarted on mycophenolate but on a lower dose of 360 mg twice daily, and the tacrolimus dose adjusted to maintain levels of around 5 ng/mL. His renal function and creatinine clearance remained stable all throughout. The patient was also seen by the dermatology team in view of the rash and was diagnosed with trichodysplasia spinulosa after histopathological analysis of a skin biopsy specimen revealed keratohyaline granules and a glass chromatic pattern. Even though viral immunostaining was negative, the patient responded well to empirical valganciclovir treatment, and the rash ultimately resolved.
Unfortunately, the ischaemia brought about by the PLR progressed as the patient continued losing his visual acuity. Four weeks postpresentation, the patient's VA was down to counting fingers eccentrically in both eyes. There was an increase in intraretinal haemorrhages and macular oedema on repeat fundoscopy (Figures 5-7). At that point, he was offered intravitreal bevacizumab injections but was not keen to commence such treatment. After a week, the patient accepted to undergo a trial of intravitreal bevacizumab in both eyes. The patient later developed bilateral neovascularisation at the disc (NVD) as well as a mild vitreous haemorrhage in the left eye. Bilateral pan-retinal photocoagulation was performed.
On examination, 4 weeks later, the condition was still worsening with florid NVDs present, and an epiretinal membrane had formed bilaterally. Further photocoagulation fill-in was performed.
Despite all our efforts, the VA had decreased to hand movements bilaterally at 4 months postpresentation. On fundoscopy of the right eye, one could observe a thickened posterior hyaloid and an extensive preretinal bleed which was obstructing the posterior pole view associated with a florid fibrovascular NVD (Figure 8) while in the left eye, there was a preretinal haemorrhage inferiorly as well as similar NVD plexus. A vitreoretinal opinion was obtained but due to the poor prognosis and high risk of surgery, it was agreed to proceed with further intravitreal bevacizumab injections and then consider surgery if there was no improvement.
The patient continued deteriorating with the visual field becoming more constricted and the VA decreasing to light perception in both eyes. At this point, it was agreed that surgery would not provide any benefit in view of the poor prognosis.
The patient is still being followed up in the outpatient clinic as he is at a high risk of neovascular glaucoma due to the extensive ischaemia affecting both retinas.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 30-year-old Caucasian male living-related kidney transplant recipient presented with a several-week history of exertional dyspnea, exertional tachycardia, and a 6-month papular skin eruption, followed a few days later by sudden-onset painless bilateral visual blurring.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Having received a living-related kidney transplant from his brother at age 28 (with maintenance tacrolimus 3 mg BID, mycophenolate 720 mg BID, and prednisolone 5 mg daily intensified 4 months post-transplant for mild tubulitis/early cellular rejection), the patient presented to nephrology clinic with a few weeks of dyspnea and tachycardia on minimal exertion and a 6-month slowly progressive skin eruption. A few days into his outpatient workup, he presented emergently to ophthalmology with acute painless, rapidly progressive bilateral vision loss.
subjective.past_medical_history: End-stage chronic kidney disease secondary to childhood meningococcal septicemia at age 8 (treated with peritoneal dialysis and hemodialysis at age 21, followed by living-donor kidney transplant from his brother at age 28); mild allograft tubulitis 4 months post-transplant requiring augmented immunosuppression.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for exertional dyspnea, exertional tachycardia, mild ankle swelling, a 6-month slowly progressive skin eruption, and acute painless bilateral visual loss. No known drug allergies. Home medications were tacrolimus 3 mg BID, mycophenolate 720 mg BID, prednisolone 5 mg daily, omeprazole 20 mg daily, folic acid 5 mg daily, and bumetanide 0.5 mg daily.

objective.physical_examination: General and cardiopulmonary exam: Afebrile, blood pressure 120/80 mmHg, resting regular pulse 95 beats/min rising to 120 beats/min on walking, SpO2 98% at rest and on exertion, and mild bilateral ankle pitting edema. Ophthalmic exam: Visual acuity 6/36+1 OD and 6/60 OS (progressing over 4 months to light perception OU), reactive pupils without RAPD, normal anterior segments and IOP (15 mmHg OU); dilated fundoscopy revealed bilateral peripapillary/macular patches of retinal whitening (Purtscher flecken), cotton-wool spots, and intraretinal hemorrhages across the posterior pole and mid-periphery (later complicated by bilateral florid neovascularization of the disc [NVD], preretinal/vitreous hemorrhage, and epiretinal membranes).
objective.routine_investigations: Admission laboratory tests: Normal neutrophils (8.30 x 10^9/L) with lymphopenia (0.74 x 10^9/L, reference: 2.10–3.60 x 10^9/L), normocytic anemia (Hb 11.0 g/dL, Hct 34.1%), normal platelets (186 x 10^9/L), stable baseline allograft function (creatinine 120 μmol/L, urea 13.2 mmol/L, eGFR 64 mL/min/1.73m2), mildly elevated CRP (14.4 mg/L) and ESR (14 mm/1st hr), slightly elevated NT-proBNP (147 pg/mL), normal LFTs and LDH, serum albumin 34 g/L, and therapeutic tacrolimus level (8.8 ng/mL). Negative infectious and autoimmune screening: Negative Toxoplasma/Leishmania serologies, negative autoimmune screen, negative viral PCR panel (HSV, VZV, CMV, EBV, BK virus, SARS-CoV-2, respiratory viruses), and normal urinalysis/culture. Cardiopulmonary baseline: Normal ECG (sinus rhythm 90 bpm), normal echocardiogram, and unremarkable chest X-ray.
objective.advanced_workup: Fungal biomarker: Markedly elevated serum 1,3-beta-D-glucan at >523 pg/mL (positive >80 pg/mL). Ophthalmic imaging (OCT and fluorescein angiography): Bilateral inner nuclear layer hyperreflective bands (paracentral acute middle maculopathy [PAMM]), enlarged foveal avascular zone, and early patchy hyperfluorescence/capillary nonperfusion diagnostic of Purtscher-like retinopathy (PLR). CT pulmonary angiogram (CTPA) and bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL): Excluded pulmonary embolism and demonstrated faint diffuse perihilar-predominant ground-glass opacities; BAL PCR tested positive for Pneumocystis jirovecii (negative for mycobacteria, galactomannan, and malignant cytology). Skin biopsy histopathology: Expanded inner root sheath cells with enlarged eosinophilic keratohyaline granules and a glassy chromatin pattern diagnostic of trichodysplasia spinulosa.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Concurrent Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP; confirmed by positive BAL PCR, serum beta-D-glucan >523 pg/mL, and perihilar ground-glass opacities on CTPA), biopsy-proven cutaneous trichodysplasia spinulosa, and severe bilateral Purtscher-like retinopathy (PLR) in a living-donor renal transplant recipient on tacrolimus, mycophenolate, and prednisolone. Plan and clinical course: Mycophenolate was temporarily held (later resumed at 360 mg BID) and tacrolimus target troughs were reduced to 5–6 ng/mL. PCP was cured with oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (960 mg TID for 21 days, followed by lifelong 480 mg daily prophylaxis) with complete CT resolution, and cutaneous trichodysplasia spinulosa resolved with empirical oral valganciclovir. Despite a 3-day IV methylprednisolone pulse (250 mg/day) followed by an oral prednisolone taper, bilateral intravitreal bevacizumab injections, and panretinal photocoagulation, retinal ischemia from Purtscher-like retinopathy progressed to bilateral florid disc neovascularization, preretinal hemorrhage, and light-perception vision.

raw_case_text:
A 67-year-old woman, with a history of arterial hypertension, diabetes mellitus type II, thyroidectomy, osteoporosis, hyperlipidemia and rheumatoid arthritis being treated with methotrexate and corticosteroids, presented to our Pulmonology Department in August 2019 with progressive dyspnea at rest and fatigue over the last two days. 
Clinical examination revealed an afebrile patient with crackles on auscultation at all lung fields. Blood pressure was 100/80 mmHg, heart rate was 120 beats per minute, oxygen saturation was 79% on room air and body temperature 36.5  C on admission. Electrocardiography showed sinus tachycardia. Arterial blood gas analysis revealed pO2 40mmHg, pCO2 35mmHg, pH 7.48 and HCO3  29.2 mmol/L on room air. Chest X-ray showed patchy diffuse infiltrates in both lungs mostly in the left lower lobe (Figure 1A).
Complete blood count was normal. The blood biochemistry parameters and thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) were normal, with the exception of an elevated serum lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) 311 U/L (normal <225 U/L), serum glycose 263 mg/dl (normal 60-100 mg/dL) and C-reactive protein (CRP) 122.3 mg/L (normal <6 mg/L). Urinalysis was normal. 
The reversed transcription polymerase chain reaction (RTau-PCR) test for Influenza A and B in nasopharyngeal and oropharyngeal samples were performed and were negative. Urinary antigen tests for Legionella pneumophila and Streptococcus pneumoniae, serological testing for Mycoplasma pneumonia and blood cultures were negative. 
The patient received oxygen therapy with Venturi mask delivering 60% oxygen and intravenous antibiotic therapy with ceftriaxone, azithromycin and trimethoprim-sulfomethoxazole empirically. After the first two days of hospitalization the patient presented with respiratory deterioration and diffuse lung infiltrates (Figure 1B), was intubated and admitted to intensive care unit.
Computed tomography (CT) of the chest was performed. Chest CT revealed diffuse ground glass opacities in all lung fields (Figure 1C, 1D) and bilateral pleural effusion (Figure 1E, 1F). The patient underwent echocardiography with normal ejection fraction and valve function. Bronchoscopy was performed and bronchial washings and bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) were obtained from lingula and right middle lobe. Cytological and microbiological examination of bronchial washings and BAL was negative. Direct immunofluorescence and PCR for Pneumocystis jirovecii in BAL were negative and administration of trimethoprim-sulfomethoxazole was discontinued. Respiratory virus panel test in BA for detection of human respiratory viruses by use of multiplex RT-PCR was performed and revealed HCoV-HKU1. 
The patient after five days of intubation presented with improvement, was extubated and received oxygen therapy with Venturi mask. The patient had gradually completely recovered without any specific therapy. She denied recent travel or contact with a person that had recently returned from a travel abroad.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 67-year-old woman on methotrexate and corticosteroids for rheumatoid arthritis presented in August 2019 with a 2-day history of progressive resting dyspnea and fatigue.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient, who was receiving methotrexate and corticosteroids for rheumatoid arthritis, presented to the pulmonology department with rapidly progressive shortness of breath at rest and fatigue over the preceding 48 hours. She denied recent travel or sick contacts.
subjective.past_medical_history: Rheumatoid arthritis treated with methotrexate and corticosteroids; arterial hypertension; type 2 diabetes mellitus; status post thyroidectomy; osteoporosis; hyperlipidemia.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for resting dyspnea and fatigue for 2 days; negative for fever. Home medications included methotrexate and corticosteroids.

objective.physical_examination: Admission vital signs: Afebrile (36.5 °C), blood pressure 100/80 mmHg, heart rate 120 beats/min, and room-air SpO2 79%. Chest auscultation: Diffuse crackles across all lung fields bilaterally.
objective.routine_investigations: Room-air arterial blood gas: Severe hypoxemia with pO2 40 mmHg, pCO2 35 mmHg, pH 7.48, and HCO3- 29.2 mmol/L. Laboratory tests: Normal CBC, electrolytes, renal/liver function, TSH, and urinalysis; elevated serum LDH at 311 U/L (normal <225 U/L), blood glucose 263 mg/dL (normal: 60–100 mg/dL), and C-reactive protein (CRP) 122.3 mg/L (normal <6 mg/L). Negative baseline microbiology: Negative nasopharyngeal/oropharyngeal influenza A/B RT-PCR, negative urinary Legionella pneumophila and Streptococcus pneumoniae antigens, negative Mycoplasma pneumoniae serology, and negative blood cultures. ECG and echocardiography: Sinus tachycardia with normal left ventricular ejection fraction and valve function. Serial chest X-rays: Patchy bilateral infiltrates (predominantly left lower lobe) progressing to diffuse bilateral infiltrates on day 2.
objective.advanced_workup: Chest CT scan (hospital day 2): Diffuse ground-glass opacities across all lung fields and bilateral pleural effusions. Bronchoscopy with bronchial washings and bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) from the lingula and right middle lobe: Negative bacterial/fungal cultures and cytology; negative BAL direct immunofluorescence and PCR for Pneumocystis jirovecii; multiplex respiratory virus RT-PCR panel on BAL fluid tested positive for human coronavirus HKU1 (HCoV-HKU1).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Severe human coronavirus HKU1 (HCoV-HKU1) pneumonia causing diffuse ground-glass opacities and acute hypoxemic respiratory failure in an immunocompromised patient with rheumatoid arthritis on methotrexate and corticosteroids, definitively diagnosed by BAL multiplex RT-PCR after excluding Pneumocystis jirovecii by BAL direct immunofluorescence and PCR. Plan and clinical course: Initially managed with 60% Venturi mask oxygen and empiric IV ceftriaxone, azithromycin, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, then intubated on hospital day 2 for progressive respiratory failure. Following negative BAL P. jirovecii DFA/PCR and positive HCoV-HKU1 detection, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole was discontinued; she improved with supportive ICU care, was extubated after 5 days to a Venturi mask, and achieved full recovery.

raw_case_text:
A 19-year-old male with relapsed Philadelphia chromosome-like B cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia who received a haploidentical stem cell transplant developed fever on post-transplant day +16. Blood culture was positive for Bacillus cereus, which was treated with vancomycin and cefepime.
On day +17, he developed a headache and became somnolent. Computed tomography (CT) scan of the head showed a small left frontal intraparenchymal hemorrhage. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain revealed multiple ring-enhancing lesions consistent with possible septic emboli, shown in Figure 1A. Magnetic resonance angiography did not show evidence of intracranial aneurysm. Transthoracic echocardiogram showed no evidence of intracardiac shunt, valve disease, or vegetation. The patient was broadened to vancomycin and meropenem for treatment of presumed disseminated B. cereus. Due to persistent fever despite bloodstream clearance of B. cereus, MRI with ring-enhancing lesions, and the patient's known immunoglobulin G (IgG) seropositivity for T. gondii, trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole (TMP/SMX) was started empirically from days +22 to +25. This was discontinued given the negative T. gondii PCR testing from blood, cerebrospinal fluid, and bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) specimens. Diagnostic workup was negative for Aspergillus, Pneumocystis jirovecii, Cryptococcus, and viral infection.
Given the ongoing fever, development of vomiting, and diarrhea, an endoscopy was performed on day +49. Methylprednisolone was given from day +49 to +52 for empiric management of gastrointestinal graft-vs.-host disease (GVHD), but pathology showed rare apoptotic bodies in the duodenum and colon and did not support a diagnosis of GVHD.
On day +51, the patient developed rapid-onset respiratory failure and progressive somnolence. CT scan of the chest showed diffuse ground glass opacities. He was transferred to the pediatric intensive care unit (PICU), where he developed MODS with severe hypoxemic respiratory failure and septic shock requiring mechanical ventilation and significant vasoactive support. He was treated empirically with gentamicin, meropenem, TMP/SMX, amphotericin, cidofovir, albendazole, and ivermectin, with plan to start pyrimethamine/sulfadiazine when available. PCR testing of repeat BAL fluid identified T. gondii. A splenic lesion was also identified on ultrasound and biopsied, with PCR testing positive for T. gondii. All other bacterial, viral, and fungal studies were negative. TMP/SMX was dose-adjusted for the treatment of disseminated toxoplasmosis.
In addition to antimicrobials, the patient was concurrently treated with plasma exchange and intravenous immunoglobulin for thrombocytopenia-associated multiple organ failure from day +55 to +57. Despite therapy, he developed hyperferritinemia (peak level, 49,000 ng/mL) with concurrent hepatobiliary dysfunction and coagulopathy. The results of his clinical cytokine panel from day +54 are shown in Table 1. He was also treated with anakinra based on a reanalysis of a phase III randomized trial showing a mortality benefit of interleukin-1 receptor antagonist treatment in adult severe sepsis. A timeline of his immune dysregulation and associated therapeutics is shown in Figure 2A.
Given the patient's declining respiratory status and persistent MODS despite maximal support, his family elected to discontinue life-sustaining therapy on day +58. Autopsy findings were notable for evidence of disseminated toxoplasmosis, as shown in Figure 1B. Numerous inflammatory foci and T. gondii bradyzoites were seen in the myocardium and diaphragm. Neuropathologic evaluation revealed numerous hemorrhagic subcortical infarcts containing granulomatous inflammation and T. gondii bradyzoite cysts.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 19-year-old male with relapsed Philadelphia chromosome-like B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia developed persistent fever on day +16, headache and somnolence on day +17, vomiting and diarrhea on day +49, and fulminant hypoxemic respiratory failure on day +51 following haploidentical hematopoietic stem cell transplantation.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Known to be Toxoplasma gondii IgG-seropositive pre-transplant, the patient underwent a haploidentical stem cell transplant for relapsed Ph-like B-ALL and developed Bacillus cereus bacteremia on day +16 (treated with vancomycin/cefepime, then vancomycin/meropenem) followed on day +17 by headache, somnolence, a small left frontal hemorrhage on head CT, and multiple ring-enhancing brain lesions on MRI. Empiric TMP/SMX was given briefly from days +22 to +25 and stopped when initial blood, CSF, and BAL T. gondii PCRs returned negative. On day +49, persistent fever, vomiting, and diarrhea prompted upper/lower endoscopy and empiric methylprednisolone (days +49 to +52) for suspected GI GVHD. On day +51, he developed rapid-onset severe hypoxemic respiratory failure, progressive somnolence, septic shock, and multiple organ dysfunction syndrome (MODS).
subjective.past_medical_history: Relapsed Philadelphia chromosome-like B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (Ph-like B-ALL) status post haploidentical stem cell transplantation; pre-transplant Toxoplasma gondii IgG seropositive; post-transplant day +16 Bacillus cereus bacteremia.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for persistent fever, headache, somnolence, vomiting, diarrhea, and acute respiratory failure.

objective.physical_examination: Somnolent with headache on day +17; rapid progression on day +51 to severe hypoxemic respiratory failure, septic shock, and multiorgan dysfunction requiring PICU mechanical ventilation and high-dose vasoactive support.
objective.routine_investigations: Microbiology and hyperinflammatory markers: Day +16 blood culture positive for Bacillus cereus (subsequently cleared); initial blood, CSF, and BAL negative for Aspergillus, Pneumocystis jirovecii, Cryptococcus, viruses, and initial T. gondii PCR; day +55–57 profound hyperferritinemia (peak 49,000 ng/mL), hepatobiliary dysfunction, coagulopathy, thrombocytopenia, and markedly elevated inflammatory cytokines (day +54 cytokine panel). Transthoracic echocardiogram (day +17): Normal without intracardiac shunt or vegetations.
objective.advanced_workup: Neuroimaging (day +17): Head CT showed a small left frontal intraparenchymal hemorrhage; brain MRI revealed multiple ring-enhancing lesions (MRA negative for mycotic aneurysm). Day +49 GI endoscopy and biopsies: Rare duodenal and colonic apoptotic bodies, negative for GVHD. Day +51 chest CT, splenic ultrasound/biopsy, and repeat BAL PCR: Chest CT showed diffuse bilateral ground-glass opacities; repeat BAL fluid PCR and ultrasound-guided splenic lesion biopsy PCR both tested positive for Toxoplasma gondii. Post-mortem autopsy (day +58): Confirmed disseminated toxoplasmosis with numerous T. gondii bradyzoites and inflammatory foci in the myocardium and diaphragm, and multiple hemorrhagic subcortical cerebral infarcts containing granulomatous inflammation and T. gondii bradyzoite cysts.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Fatal Reactivated disseminated toxoplasmosis (involving the brain, lungs, heart, diaphragm, and spleen) complicated by hyperferritinemic multiple organ dysfunction syndrome (MODS; peak ferritin 49,000 ng/mL) following haploidentical stem cell transplantation in a T. gondii IgG-seropositive patient with Ph-like B-ALL, definitively confirmed by positive repeat BAL and splenic biopsy T. gondii PCRs and post-mortem autopsy (after false-negative day +22 blood/CSF/BAL T. gondii PCRs and negative Pneumocystis jirovecii workup). Plan and clinical course: Treated in the PICU on day +51 with mechanical ventilation, vasoactive support, high-dose therapeutic TMP/SMX (plus empiric meropenem, gentamicin, amphotericin, cidofovir, albendazole, and ivermectin), plasma exchange, IVIG (days +55 to +57), and anakinra (IL-1 receptor antagonist). Due to refractory MODS and progressive respiratory decline, life-sustaining support was withdrawn on day +58.

raw_case_text:
A 20-year-old male with immune-mediated aplastic anemia refractory to prior immune suppression therapy received an unrelated donor peripheral stem cell transplant. Toxoplasma serologies were not obtained during his pre-transplant evaluation as per institutional practice. His initial transplant course was uncomplicated, and he was discharged home on post-transplant day +21. On day +52, he was readmitted for fever and diarrhea. Due to fever and hypoxemia, a CT scan of the chest was obtained on day +55 and showed bilateral centrilobular nodules with right-sided predominance, as shown in Figure 1C. His infectious workup included multiple BALs, blood, and urine cultures and evaluation for Pneumocystis jirovecii and viral etiologies, which were all negative. He was maintained on broad-spectrum antibiotics and antifungal medications given the persistent fever despite negative cultures. Due to progressive hypoxemic respiratory failure, he was transferred to the PICU on day +61, where he required intubation and mechanical ventilation. Given the refractory hypoxemic respiratory failure, he was cannulated to venous-venous extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) within 24 h of PICU transfer. His ECMO course was complicated by shock, hyperferritinemia, and acute kidney injury requiring renal replacement therapy.
Multimodal therapy for his immune dysregulation included pulse dose methylprednisolone (2 g/day) followed by a prolonged methylprednisolone course, plasma exchange, tocilizumab for IL-6 blockade, and etanercept for tumor necrosis factor alpha blockade, which was later transitioned to infliximab. A timeline of the immunomodulatory therapies is shown in Figure 2B. With improvement in his hyperinflammatory state, he was decannulated from ECMO on day +73.
On day +90, he had recurrence of fever without other changes in exam in the setting of a methylprednisolone taper; after a multidisciplinary discussion, tocilizumab, infliximab, and pulse dose methylprednisolone were administered for the management of immune dysregulation. The results of his clinical cytokine panel from day +64 to +92 are shown in Table 1. Despite these interventions, he had worsening hyperferritinemia by day +94 (peak level, 202,000 ng/mL), so anakinra was administered and plasma exchange was repeated. Despite immunomodulation, he continued to have refractory MODS with severe hypoxemic respiratory failure and catecholamine-refractory shock. At the request of his family, resuscitative efforts were discontinued on day +95. On the day of his death, T. gondii tachyzoites were noted on his peripheral blood smear (shown in Figure 1D), which were subsequently confirmed to be T. gondii by PCR and immunostaining. Postmortem analyses of the BAL specimens from day +60 and +65 were also positive for T. gondii by PCR. Postmortem T. gondii serologic testing was performed on a pre-transplant blood specimen and was positive for IgG.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 20-year-old male with refractory immune-mediated aplastic anemia presented on day +52 after unrelated-donor peripheral blood stem cell transplantation with fever, diarrhea, and progressive hypoxemic respiratory failure.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Following an uncomplicated initial course after an unrelated-donor peripheral blood stem cell transplant for refractory aplastic anemia (discharged on day +21 without pre-transplant Toxoplasma serologic screening), the patient was readmitted on day +52 with fever and diarrhea, rapidly developing hypoxemia by day +55 and refractory hypoxemic respiratory failure requiring PICU intubation and veno-venous extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VV-ECMO) cannulation on day +61.
subjective.past_medical_history: Refractory immune-mediated aplastic anemia status post unrelated-donor peripheral blood stem cell transplantation.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, diarrhea, and severe progressive dyspnea/hypoxemia.

objective.physical_examination: Febrile and hypoxemic on day +55, progressing to catecholamine-refractory shock and severe hypoxemic respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation and VV-ECMO on day +61 (decannulated day +73, with recurrent febrile shock and MODS on days +90 to +95).
objective.routine_investigations: Routine microbiological and hyperinflammatory workup: Multiple blood, urine, and BAL cultures and evaluations for Pneumocystis jirovecii and viruses were negative; severe hyperferritinemia peaking at 202,000 ng/mL on day +94 with marked hypercytokinemia (days +64 to +92) and acute kidney injury requiring renal replacement therapy. Day +95 peripheral blood smear (on day of death): Directly visualized circulating extracellular/intracellular Toxoplasma gondii tachyzoites.
objective.advanced_workup: Day +55 chest CT: Bilateral centrilobular pulmonary nodules with right-sided predominance. Post-mortem molecular and serological confirmation: Peripheral blood smear tachyzoites were confirmed as Toxoplasma gondii by PCR and immunostaining; retrospective PCR analysis of stored BAL specimens from days +60 and +65 tested positive for T. gondii; retrospective testing of stored pre-transplant serum was positive for T. gondii IgG.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Fatal reactivated disseminated toxoplasmosis and Toxoplasma pneumonia masquerading as idiopathic post-transplant hyperinflammatory immune dysregulation / secondary HLH (peak ferritin 202,000 ng/mL) requiring VV-ECMO after unrelated-donor stem cell transplantation for aplastic anemia, definitively diagnosed on day +95 by T. gondii tachyzoites on peripheral blood smear (confirmed by PCR/immunostaining) and retrospective positive T. gondii PCR on day +60/+65 BAL fluid (with Pneumocystis jirovecii excluded). Plan and clinical course: Managed on VV-ECMO (days +61 to +73) and CRRT with broad-spectrum antibacterials/antifungals and intensive anti-cytokine immunomodulation (pulse methylprednisolone 2 g/day, plasma exchange, tocilizumab, etanercept, infliximab, and anakinra), which transiently allowed ECMO decannulation on day +73 before a fatal relapse of refractory shock and MODS on days +90 to +95.

raw_case_text: A 67-year-old woman with RA visited the emergency room with a one-week history of fever and dyspnea on exertion. The patient's vitals on physical exam were as follows: blood pressure, 145/98 mmHg; heart rate, 109 beats/min; respiratory rate, 18 cycles/min; body temperature, 37.4 C; and oxygen saturation, 90%. Blood tests showed leukocytosis (9,580 cells/muL) and elevated C-reactive protein (28.1 mg/L) levels. Liver and renal function tests were normal, except for elevated lactate dehydrogenase (296 IU/L). Blood gas analysis on room air showed hypoxemia (pO2 51.7 Torr) and respiratory alkalosis (pH 7.495, pCO2 29.6 Torr, and HCO3 22.6). Electrocardiogram showed normal axis, sinus tachycardia, and a small Q wave in lead III without ST segment change. Radiography (Figure 1(a)) and CT (Figure 1(b)) of her chest revealed pulmonary infiltrates with GGO in the left lower lung. The patient was immunocompromised as she was receiving methotrexate (8 mg/week) and tacrolimus (1 mg/day) for the treatment of RA. We, therefore, suspected that the patient had a lower respiratory tract infection, such as bacterial or pneumocystis pneumonia. However, since the patient had tachycardia, unexpectedly severe hypoxemia given the degree of chest infiltration, and slightly elevated D-dimer levels (8.1 mg/L), a contrast-enhanced CT was performed to rule out PE. The patient was subsequently diagnosed with left deep vein thrombosis (DVT) and PE (Figure 2(a)). She was successfully treated with continuous heparin infusion and warfarin therapy. A systemic search for the cause of her thrombophilia showed no abnormalities other than mild obesity and RA. Dual-energy CT of the lesion showed a pulmonary blood flow defect in the left lung at a site consistent with the pulmonary infiltrates (Figure 2(b)). Thus, pneumonia due to her immunosuppression was not the cause of the pulmonary infiltrates. The diagnosis of pulmonary infarction was confirmed by the presence of a "Hampton's hump"-like consolidation 3 days later.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 67-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis treated with methotrexate and tacrolimus presented to the emergency department with a 1-week history of fever and exertional dyspnea.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient, who was receiving weekly methotrexate (8 mg/week) and daily tacrolimus (1 mg/day) for rheumatoid arthritis, presented to the emergency room after 1 week of fever and shortness of breath on exertion.
subjective.past_medical_history: Rheumatoid arthritis treated with methotrexate (8 mg/week) and tacrolimus (1 mg/day); mild obesity.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for 1 week of fever and exertional dyspnea. Home medications were methotrexate 8 mg/week and tacrolimus 1 mg/day.

objective.physical_examination: Admission vital signs: Blood pressure 145/98 mmHg, heart rate 109 beats/min, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, body temperature 37.4 °C, and SpO2 90% on room air.
objective.routine_investigations: Room-air arterial blood gas: Disproportionate hypoxemia (pO2 51.7 Torr) and respiratory alkalosis (pH 7.495, pCO2 29.6 Torr, HCO3- 22.6 mmol/L). Blood tests: Leukocytosis (WBC 9,580 cells/μL), elevated C-reactive protein (CRP 28.1 mg/L), elevated LDH (296 IU/L), normal hepatic and renal function, elevated D-dimer (8.1 mg/L), and negative systemic thrombophilia screen. Electrocardiogram: Normal axis, sinus tachycardia, and a small Q wave in lead III without ST-segment changes. Chest radiograph: Left lower lung field infiltrates.
objective.advanced_workup: Non-contrast, contrast-enhanced, and dual-energy chest/lower-extremity CT scans: Initial chest CT showed pulmonary infiltrates with ground-glass opacity (GGO) in the left lower lobe initially suspicious for bacterial or Pneumocystis pneumonia; contrast-enhanced CT and dual-energy perfusion CT confirmed left lower-extremity deep vein thrombosis (DVT), acute pulmonary embolism (PE), and a matching left lung perfusion defect at the site of the GGO infiltrate, which evolved 3 days later into a classic wedge-shaped 'Hampton's hump' pulmonary infarction.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Acute pulmonary embolism and left lower lobe pulmonary infarction (confirmed by contrast-enhanced CT, dual-energy CT perfusion defect, and subsequent Hampton's hump consolidation) secondary to left deep vein thrombosis, initially mimicking opportunistic Pneumocystis or bacterial pneumonia in a rheumatoid arthritis patient on methotrexate and tacrolimus. Plan and clinical course: Successfully treated with continuous intravenous unfractionated heparin infusion followed by oral warfarin anticoagulation.

raw_case_text:
The patient was a 35-year-old African American female with a history of asthma and polysubstance abuse who presented to the emergency department (ED) with severe shortness of breath. She reported that the shortness of breath was progressive over several months and associated with weight loss. She denied a history of HIV infection. The patient's only known home medication was albuterol as needed for asthma. She also reported a history of smoking 10 cigarettes a day and drinking alcohol a couple of times a week.
On physical examination, she was cachectic, ill-appearing and tachypneic with the use of accessory muscles for respiration. Her blood pressure was 88/55 mm Hg, temperature was 37.4 C, pulse rate was 146 beats per minute and regular, oxygen saturation of 70% on room air, and body mass index of 18.9. Lung auscultation revealed bilateral rhonchi. Heart auscultation revealed normal S1 and S2 without significant murmurs or rubs. She was placed on a non-rebreather mask with FiO2 of 100% without improvement of respiratory status and was switched to non-invasive mechanical ventilation. Her status continued to decline, and she underwent endotracheal intubation within an hour of arriving at the ED for hypoxic respiratory failure. SARS-CoV-2 testing done upon arrival in the ED was negative. She tested positive for HIV, and further evaluation revealed an initial viral load of 343,636 copies per milliliter and an absolute CD4 count of 5 cells/muL.
On day 1, a chest radiograph (Figure 1(a)) revealed extensive right lung opacities, most prominent in the right middle lobe. The cardiac silhouette was slightly enlarged. A chest CT scan with intravenous contrast (Figure 2) revealed severe cavitary and partially necrotic opacities in the right upper lobe. There was also a small right pleural effusion and a moderate pericardial effusion. An echocardiogram (Figure 3) revealed a large pericardial effusion, as large as 4.16 cm, with no signs of tamponade.
Initially, she was placed on vancomycin, cefepime, azithromycin, anidulafungin, trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole (TMP/SXM) and methylprednisolone. She also required norepinephrine and vasopressin for the first 5 days for hypotension, most likely due to septic shock. On day 5, she underwent bronchoscopy for BAL after tuberculosis was ruled out with three negative sputum acid-fast bacillus smears and a negative polymerase chain reaction (PCR) test. Chest radiography on day 8 (Figure 1(b)) revealed an increase in the right-sided infiltrates and new patchy infiltrates at the left lung base.
On day 13, PCR of the BAL was positive for CMV with CMV DNA of 197,000 IU/mL. Fungal culture of the BAL fluid did grow Candida albicans, which was determined to be a colonization. All other tests performed on the BAL (summarized in Table 1) were negative. Additionally, tests for Cryptococcus antigen, Histoplasma antigen, Legionella antigen, A. Galactomannan antigen and (1,3)-beta-D-glucan were negative. She was started on IV ganciclovir 250 mg twice a day for CMV pneumonia and antiretroviral therapy for HIV. Anidulafungin, methylprednisolone and all other antibiotics were discontinued except for TMP/SXM, which was continued for Pneumocystis jiroveci pneumonia (PJP) prophylaxis. She was extubated on day 13 and switched to high-flow nasal cannula. 
On day 17, a follow-up echocardiogram showed that she still had a large circumferential pericardial effusion that had not changed significantly in size since the day of admission. Pericardiocentesis was performed, draining 500 mL of straw-colored fluid. Pericardial fluid analysis was positive for CMV DNA using PCR and negative for adenosine deaminase. All other tests performed on the pericardial fluid (summarized in Table 1) were negative.
A chest radiograph on day 22 (Figure 1(c)) showed reduced infiltrates in the right lung field, with a moderate overlying pleural effusion. Her HIV viral load had decreased to 5,522 RNA copies per milliliter. She was breathing comfortably on room air. She was discharged on oral valganciclovir 900 mg twice a day until her CD4 count improved to over 100 cells/muL, TMP/SXM for PJP prophylaxis and Biktarvy as antiretroviral therapy.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 35-year-old African American female with asthma and polysubstance abuse presented to the emergency department with several months of progressively worsening shortness of breath and weight loss.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented to the emergency department in severe respiratory distress after several months of progressively worsening dyspnea and unintentional weight loss, requiring endotracheal intubation within 1 hour of arrival after failing 100% FiO2 non-rebreather mask and noninvasive ventilation.
subjective.past_medical_history: Asthma; polysubstance abuse; active tobacco smoker (10 cigarettes/day) and alcohol use twice weekly; previously undiagnosed advanced HIV/AIDS discovered in the emergency department.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for progressive shortness of breath over several months and weight loss. Only home medication was inhaled albuterol as needed.

objective.physical_examination: Emergency department vital signs and anthropometrics: Blood pressure 88/55 mmHg, temperature 37.4 °C, regular tachycardia at 146 beats/min, room-air SpO2 70%, and cachexia with BMI 18.9 kg/m2. Physical exam: Ill-appearing, tachypneic with accessory respiratory muscle use; bilateral rhonchi on lung auscultation; normal S1/S2 without murmurs or rubs.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission virological and microbiological screening: Positive HIV test with initial plasma HIV viral load of 343,636 copies/mL (decreasing to 5,522 copies/mL by day 22); negative SARS-CoV-2 test; three negative sputum AFB smears and negative MTB PCR; negative Cryptococcus, Histoplasma, and Legionella antigens. Serial chest radiographs: Day 1 CXR showed extensive right lung opacities (most prominent in the right middle lobe) and cardiomegaly; day 8 CXR showed progression of right-sided infiltrates and new patchy left basilar infiltrates; day 22 CXR showed marked clearance of right lung infiltrates with a residual moderate right pleural effusion. Echocardiograms (days 1 and 17): Large circumferential pericardial effusion measuring up to 4.16 cm without cardiac tamponade.
objective.advanced_workup: Immunological and fungal biomarkers: Profound CD4+ T-cell depletion with absolute CD4 count of 5 cells/μL; negative serum Aspergillus galactomannan and negative (1,3)-beta-D-glucan. Contrast-enhanced chest CT (day 1): Severe cavitary and partially necrotic opacities in the right upper lobe, small right pleural effusion, and moderate-to-large pericardial effusion. Day 5 bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL; results returned day 13): Positive quantitative CMV PCR with BAL CMV DNA load of 197,000 IU/mL and Candida albicans colonization on fungal culture; negative for Pneumocystis jirovecii, bacteria, mycobacteria, and endemic fungi. Day 17 therapeutic pericardiocentesis (draining 500 mL straw-colored fluid): Pericardial fluid PCR tested positive for cytomegalovirus (CMV) DNA and negative for adenosine deaminase (ADA) and other pathogens.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Newly diagnosed advanced HIV/AIDS (CD4 count 5 cells/μL, viral load 343,636 copies/mL) presenting with necrotizing cavitary right upper lobe cytomegalovirus (CMV) pneumonia and large CMV pericardial effusion (confirmed by BAL CMV DNA of 197,000 IU/mL and positive pericardial fluid CMV PCR, with Pneumocystis jirovecii and tuberculosis excluded by negative BAL studies, AFB smears/PCR, and negative serum beta-D-glucan). Plan and clinical course: Intubated in the ED and supported for the first 5 days with norepinephrine and vasopressin alongside empiric vancomycin, cefepime, azithromycin, anidulafungin, therapeutic TMP/SMX, and methylprednisolone. On day 13, upon BAL confirmation of CMV pneumonia and exclusion of PJP, she was extubated to HFNC, switched to intravenous ganciclovir (250 mg twice daily), prophylactic-dose TMP/SMX, and antiretroviral therapy (bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide [Biktarvy]), and underwent pericardiocentesis (500 mL) on day 17. She was discharged on room air on day 22 on oral valganciclovir (900 mg twice daily until CD4 >100 cells/μL), prophylactic TMP/SMX, and Biktarvy.

raw_case_text: A 64-years-old female patient was admitted to the emergency department because of fever, dyspnea, and productive cough. The patient had a history of sarcoidosis diagnosed after cosmetic eyebrow tattooing and was receiving daily prednisolone (15-20mg) since the diagnosis and weakly methotrexate (10-15mg) 4 months ago. At the time of admission, the patient was febrile (37.8 C axillary) and had decreased oxygen saturation (89%). The rest of the physical examination was unremarkable except for a bilateral crackle on chest auscultation. By possible diagnosis of pneumonia, the patient received meropenem and ciprofloxacin. The laboratory results revealed a white blood cell count of 4400 (94% of neutrophil), platelet count of 163000, erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 57, creatinine level of 1.3, lactate dehydrogenase level of 800. According to the laboratory results and previous history of receiving prednisolone, a therapeutic dose of cotrimoxazole was added to the antimicrobial regimen to cover pneumocystis jirovecii infection. The primary chest x-ray imaging revealed bilateral infiltration, especially in the upper lobes and hilar lymphadenopathy. The lung high resolution computed tomography (HRCT) showed a bilateral diffuse nodular pattern (figure 1). After 72 hours of antimicrobial treatment, the fever was still present and the patient candidate for fiberoptic bronchoscopy. There was not any endobronchial lesion. Also, there was not any malignant cell or inclusion body reported. The gram staining of the bronchial fluid, polymerase chain reaction (PCR) for tuberculosis, and PCP was also unremarkable. However, the PCR for cytomegalovirus (CMV) was positive. While the PCR for PCP was negative, the cotrimoxazole was discontinued. The quantitative PCR for CMV form blood sample was taken and the result came back as 3.6*103. With the impression of CMV pneumonia, a daily dose of 5mg of ganciclovir was prescribed. After 3 weeks of receiving 5mg/kg of ganciclovir twice daily (600mg daily), clinical symptoms, and dyspnea improved, likewise the radiological findings (figure 2).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 64-year-old female with sarcoidosis treated with daily prednisolone and weekly methotrexate presented to the emergency department with fever, dyspnea, and productive cough.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient, who had been diagnosed with sarcoidosis following cosmetic eyebrow tattooing and was maintained on daily oral prednisolone (15–20 mg) plus weekly methotrexate (10–15 mg started 4 months prior), presented to the emergency department with acute fever, shortness of breath, and a productive cough.
subjective.past_medical_history: Sarcoidosis diagnosed after cosmetic eyebrow tattooing, treated with daily prednisolone (15–20 mg) and weekly methotrexate (10–15 mg for the past 4 months).
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, dyspnea, and productive cough. Home medications were prednisolone (15–20 mg daily) and methotrexate (10–15 mg weekly).

objective.physical_examination: Admission vital signs: Axillary temperature 37.8 °C and decreased peripheral oxygen saturation (SpO2 89%). Chest auscultation: Bilateral crackles; remainder of physical examination unremarkable.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission laboratory tests: WBC 4,400/μL (94% neutrophils), platelets 163,000/μL, ESR 57 mm/h, serum creatinine 1.3 mg/dL, and markedly elevated lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) at 800 U/L. Peripheral blood quantitative CMV PCR: Positive at 3.6 x 10^3 copies/mL. Admission chest radiograph: Bilateral pulmonary infiltrates (predominantly in the upper lobes) and hilar lymphadenopathy.
objective.advanced_workup: High-resolution chest CT (HRCT): Bilateral diffuse micronodular/nodular pattern. Fiberoptic bronchoscopy and bronchial fluid analysis (after 72 hours of persistent fever): No endobronchial lesions, malignant cells, or viral inclusion bodies; negative Gram stain, negative Mycobacterium tuberculosis PCR, and negative Pneumocystis jirovecii (PCP) PCR; bronchial fluid PCR tested positive for cytomegalovirus (CMV).
